papers.title: Lower Bounds Above $\sqrt{3}$ for Online Makespan Minimization on Four Identical Machines
papers.abstract:
For deterministic online makespan minimization, $m = 4$ identical machines is the smallest case whose optimal competitive ratio is open: it is known only to lie between $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205$ and $26/15 \approx 1.73333$. We prove a lower bound of $14383/8304 \approx 1.73206$ using a single branching layer, and refine the construction with a second, mirrored branching layer to obtain $14350/8283 \approx 1.73246$, closing about a third of the gap.
  Our constructions are the first branching adversaries for $m = 4$ machines, and the first explicit lower bounds for online makespan minimization in which the adversary presents jobs in non-monotone order of size.
papers.intro:
Makespan minimization on parallel, identical machines is one of the foundational problems in scheduling theory and competitive analysis [26]: jobs arrive one by one, and each job must be assigned immediately to one of mm machines so as to keep the maximum machine load within a factor cc of the offline optimum. Graham [26] established the optimal deterministic competitive ratio 32\tfrac{3}{2} for m=2m=2 machines in 1966, and Faigle, Kern, and Turán [21] established 53\tfrac{5}{3} for m=3m=3 in 1989. On m=4m=4 machines, by contrast, the best known upper bound of 2615\tfrac{26}{15} has stood since 1994 [17] and the lower bound of 3\sqrt{3} since 2001 [35, 36]. Like every previous lower bound for m=4m=4 machines (and every explicit layered construction for general mm), the 3\sqrt{3} bound uses a linear adversary: the job sequence is fixed in advance, and the online algorithm’s choices affect only when the sequence stops. In this paper, we introduce branching adversaries for m=4m=4 machines that choose the sizes of future jobs depending on where the online algorithm placed earlier ones, obtaining the first lower bounds strictly above 3\sqrt{3}.

Graham [26] showed that his List Scheduling (Greedy) strategy is (2−1m)(2-\tfrac{1}{m})-competitive. Galambos and Woeginger [24] beat this bound for every m≥4m\geq 4 by preventing schedules from becoming flat, though their improvement vanishes as mm grows. Bartal, Fiat, Karloff, and Vohra [11] gave the first algorithm whose competitive ratio stays bounded away from 22 for all mm, achieving 2−170≈1.9862-\tfrac{1}{70}\approx 1.986 by keeping a constant fraction of the machines lightly loaded. Subsequent improvements to 1.9451.945 by Karger, Phillips, and Torng [28] and to 1.9231.923 by Albers [1] culminated in the 1.92011.9201-competitive algorithm of Fleischer and Wahl [22], which remains the best known deterministic upper bound for large mm.

papers.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Population-Level Universality and Environmental Structuring of 450/850 $\mu$m Polarization Signatures
papers.abstract: We observed 69 molecular cloud regions at 450 and 850 $\mu$m with the POL-2 polarimeter on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope and matched the maps to a common $12.6''$ beam. Polarization fractions are typically lower at 450 $\mu$m. The median of 30 measured ratios is $P_{450}/P_{850} = 0.69 \pm 0.02_{\rm sys} \pm 0.03_{\rm stat}$. Across 35 regions with reliable spectral indices of total ($\alpha$) and polarized ($\gamma$) intensity, the medians over sources are $\langle\alpha\rangle = 3.33$ and $\langle\gamma\rangle = 2.85$-$3.04$. The median $\gamma - \alpha$ is $-0.57$ to $-0.45$, with $\gamma < \alpha$ in 24-27 regions. These ranges span the two extreme placements of $3\sigma$ limits for polarized intensity below the noise floor. The position angles at the two wavelengths agree within $10^\circ$ in 10 of 13 regional medians, disfavoring a geometric origin that would rotate the angles. The medians of $\gamma-\alpha$ in 9 low-mass, 19 high-mass and 7 Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) regions are not ordered low-mass $<$ high-mass $<$ CMZ (Jonckheere-Terpstra $p = 0.43$-$0.70$). A difference among classes is not robustly detected. The Kruskal-Wallis $p = 0.056$-$0.078$ becomes $p = 0.026$-$0.041$ when the Rosette Molecular Cloud alone is excluded, although the high-mass class has the lowest median in every treatment. The classes follow a distance sequence (the beam spans 0.008-0.51 pc), coupling environment and physical scale. Within clouds, the 450 $\mu$m polarization fraction decreases with Herschel column density in all 7 fields with sufficient dynamic range. Coefficients from pooled pixels mix trends within clouds, differences between clouds, and the influence of OMC 1. They therefore do not define a single law for individual pixels. The wavelength dependence across sources provides a benchmark for grain alignment. We cannot order it by environment and do not propose a unique mechanism.

papers.title: On the Convergence of First-Order Methods in Signaling Games
papers.abstract: We study first-order learning dynamics in Bayesian signaling games, a minimal extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information. In these games, a Sender observes a private type and chooses a signal, after which a Receiver forms a posterior belief and selects an action. This Bayesian belief update makes the induced learning field fundamentally different from the affine game-gradient fields of normal-form games. Empirically, we find a sharp dichotomy: standard online learning algorithms reliably converge to strict Perfect Bayesian Equilibria (PE), but not to non-strict ones. We show that this behavior cannot be explained by the global geometric conditions commonly used to prove last-iterate convergence, such as monotonicity or the Minty variational inequality. Indeed, these conditions can fail even in binary signaling games. Instead, we identify the relevant local geometry. Our main result characterizes variational stability in finite signaling games: a PE is variationally stable if and only if it is strict. This yields local last-iterate convergence guarantees for online mirror descent and regularized dual averaging near every strict PE. We then study global average-iterate convergence and identify a class of signaling games in which coarse-trigger regret-minimizing dynamics converge to the unique PE. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments comparing projected gradient ascent, mirror-based methods, optimistic variants, and PPO across canonical signaling-game families. The results position signaling games as a compact testbed for understanding how Bayesian belief formation reshapes the convergence geometry of multi-agent learning.

papers.intro:
A central objective in learning in games is to understand when online learning algorithms converge to equilibrium. In normal-form games, many of the strongest convergence guarantees are obtained by imposing geometric conditions on the game-gradient field, such as monotonicity [Facchinei and Pang, 2003], the Minty variational inequality [Mertikopoulos et al., 2018], and variational stability [Mertikopoulos and Zhou, 2019]. These conditions connect local payoff improvements to global or local convergence guarantees for first-order learning dynamics, including online mirror descent [Zhou et al., 2017], regularized dual averaging [Mertikopoulos and Zhou, 2019], extragradient methods [Mokhtari et al., 2020], and optimistic variants [Daskalakis et al., 2018]. A key reason why this theory is tractable in finite normal-form games is that expected payoffs are multilinear in mixed strategies, so the induced game-gradient field is affine on the mixed extension of the game. Much less is known about whether this geometric perspective extends to extensive-form games with asymmetric information, where beliefs and strategies interact through Bayesian updating.

We study this question in finite Bayesian signaling games, the canonical extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information [Spence, 1978, Crawford and Sobel, 1982, Sobel, 2020]. A Sender observes a private type and chooses a signal; a Receiver observes the signal, forms a posterior belief over types, and then chooses an action. Signaling games are a minimal setting in which first-order learning must interact with endogenous belief formation. The analogue of the game-gradient field is the payoff-difference field, which records the directions of local payoff improvement across signals and actions. Unlike in normal-form games, this field depends on the Receiver’s posterior belief, which is determined by Bayes’ rule from the Sender’s strategy. Consequently, the payoff-difference field is not multilinear, is generally not affine, and is only canonically defined on the region where every signal is reached with positive probability. We call this region the Bayes-defined region.11 1 Outside this set, the Receiver’s beliefs are not pinned down by Bayes’ rule; which beliefs should be considered rational is a central issue in the signaling-games literature [Cho and Kreps, 1987, Sobel, 2020].

In our experiments, standard online learning algorithms converge reliably to strict perfect Bayesian equilibria (PE\mathrm{PE}), but fail to converge to non-strict ones (Section 5). Strict PE\mathrm{PE} are pure-strategy equilibria in which each Sender type chooses a unique signal and the Receiver has a unique best response at every signal. They include important separating and pooling equilibria, such as the Riley outcome in Spence’s job-market signaling model [Spence, 1978, Riley, 1979]. However, this observed convergence cannot be explained by the global geometric conditions that are standard tools for analyzing first-order learning in normal-form games, as these do not extend directly to signaling games. Indeed, Theorem 1 shows that even with two types, two signals, and two actions, there are signaling games and strict PE\mathrm{PE} for which neither monotonicity nor the Minty variational inequality holds on the Bayes-defined region. Understanding why learning nevertheless converges near strict PE\mathrm{PE} is the motivating question of this paper.

papers.title: Simultaneous 3D acoustic modulation and imaging of proton-induced nanodroplet vaporization for proton therapy monitoring
papers.abstract: Superheated nanodroplets exposed to ionizing radiation vaporize into echogenic microbubbles, enabling ultrasound-based radiation therapy monitoring and proton range verification. However, at body temperature, decafluorobutane nanodroplets are insensitive to primary protons, and vaporize only when traversed by rare heavy secondary particles, limiting the in vivo applicability of this concept. We previously demonstrated that acoustic modulation at pressures well below the Acoustic Droplet Vaporization threshold can transiently increase nanodroplet sensitivity to radiation, enabling vaporization by primary protons. However, as acoustic modulation was applied by a focused single-element transducer, sensitization was restricted to a small region of the irradiated volume, and monitoring required an additional imaging probe. Here, we introduce a compact implementation that combines wide-field acoustic modulation and volumetric imaging on the same large-element matrix array, enabling simultaneous nanodroplet sensitization to protons and vaporization monitoring across the entire irradiated volume. The resulting 3D vaporization maps were fitted to the proton stopping distribution to estimate beam position and width parameters. At body temperature and starting from acoustic pressures as low as 122 kPa, we observed a transition from a response dominated by secondary particles to a response dominated by primary protons. The resulting vaporization peak at the proton range enabled sub-millimeter range estimation and detection of a 1.05 mm range shift with both accuracy and precision below 0.2 mm. These results demonstrate proton range verification and 3D treatment monitoring with acoustically-modulated decafluorobutane nanodroplets and represent an important step towards the envisioned clinical application.

papers.title: A sufficient condition for the Liouville property of solutions to the Euler-Lagrange equations of variational integrals with nonstandard growth in terms of the ellipticity modulus near the origin
papers.abstract: We consider entire solutions $u$: $\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ of the Euler-Lagrange equation $\operatorname{div}(\nabla f(\nabla u))=0$ with convex density $f$: $\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ of nonstandard growth and nonuniform ellipticity. It turns out that the Liouville property can be characterized through the behavior of $D^{2}f(p)$ for points $p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ close to the origin: if, for example, $D^{2}f(p)$ behaves as $|p|^{\rho-2}\mathbf{1}$, $\mathbf{1}=\text{unit matrix}$, with exponent $\rho\ge2$ and for $|p|\le1$ then the validity of $n\le\rho+2$ together with the boundedness of $u$ implies its constancy.

papers.title: Status of Accelerator Automation in the Community: Classification, Survey Results, and the Role of AI and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of particle accelerators and the growing demand for operational efficiency have intensified the focus on automation in accelerator control systems. However, there is still a lack of a common language to describe and compare the level of automation across different facilities. This article presents a generic classification scheme for accelerator automation, defining five distinct levels ranging from basic operational assistance to full autonomy. To assess the current state of automation in the accelerator community, a structured survey was conducted during the 14th Workshop on Accelerator Operations (WAO 2025). Responses from major laboratories indicate that more than one third of accelerators currently operate at the lowest level 1 (operational assistance), and no facility has yet reached full automation. However, projections show a clear trend toward higher levels within the next decade. Key drivers include optimization algorithms for autotuning, finite-state machines, and closed-loop feedback systems. This study provides both a conceptual framework and a snapshot of current implementation practices, supporting a shared understanding of accelerator automation across the community.

papers.title: Hypervolume-based column-and-constraint generation for bi-objective two-stage robust mixed-integer programs
papers.abstract: Extending column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) for two-stage robust mixed-integer programs from the single-objective to the bi-objective setting is challenging: for a fixed first-stage decision and scenario, the second stage yields an entire nondominated set rather than a single objective value. We develop a C&CG algorithm that uses the hypervolume indicator - one of the most widely studied quality indicators in multi-objective optimization - to evaluate these sets and seeks a first-stage decision maximizing the worst-case hypervolume over a finite set of scenarios. To avoid the nonlinearities of an exact hypervolume formulation, we introduce a slab decomposition of the objective space that yields a linear mixed-integer master problem with an explicit bound on the discretization error. This bound enables a computable optimality-gap certificate and supports an adaptive algorithm that alternates between adding scenarios and refining the decomposition. We prove the correctness of the algorithm and establish sufficient conditions for its finite termination. Computational experiments on two-stage robust selection and assignment problems show that only a small number of scenarios need to be included in the master problem, even when the full scenario set contains 128 scenarios. Moreover, we identify the number of initial slabs as a key factor influencing the running time and develop a simple, instance-dependent rule for choosing the initial slab width that outperforms fixed choices on average for the selection problem and remains competitive for the assignment problem.

papers.title: Explicitly capturing demonstrator multi-modality for distillation into diffusion policies
papers.abstract: The diversity of a distilled diffusion policy's outputs matters beyond how it impacts the policy's success rate. In particular, downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement require exploration. Thus, we want to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies which reproduce their conditional action distributions. Standard data collection for behavior cloning applies a sliding window to demonstration episodes, which pairs unique observation histories with actions. These datasets can be fit by a policy that is either multi-modal, or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant to capture a diversity of actions seen at nearby observation samples. Prior work finds that diffusion policies trained on sparse data learn the latter, memorizing one action per observation. We adapt vine sampling to behavior cloning data collection to resolve this ambiguity: at some states the demonstrator visits, query it $k$ times from exactly the same observation. On a synthetic task, we study how the number of actions per observation, $k$, affects the learned policy, and find that larger $k$ yields a policy that better matches the demonstrator's conditional distribution, including its multi-modality and diversity. On a 2D truck unloading task, vine sampling likewise leads to a policy closer to the demonstrator and substantially improves both best-of-$N$ and expert iteration performance.

papers.intro:
Diffusion and flow policies trained with behavior cloning (BC) have proven effective on a range of challenging manipulation tasks [1, 2]. In BC, a policy is trained to imitate an expert demonstrator, such as a human teleoperator, a motion planner, or a scripted controller. In many applications, however, success rate is not the only metric of interest. The diversity of a policy’s action distribution, and in particular its multi-modality – that is, its capacity to take different actions in response to the same observation – is important when the policy is used for exploration by some downstream procedure. For instance, test-time search draws many candidate actions from a policy and selects the best with a verifier or value function [3, 4], and is limited when the policy’s samples are insufficiently diverse [5]. Expert iteration [6] and reinforcement learning (RL) post-training [7] similarly shift a policy toward higher-reward actions that it samples, directly or through a search it guides. Diversity also matters when a policy is used as a skill inside a task-and-motion-planning framework [8], where constraints may only become known at test time and a unimodal policy’s single approach may prove inadmissible.

These low-diversity policies follow from the way training datasets are constructed. Standard practice collects full episodes of the demonstrator solving the task, then applies a sliding window that, at each timestep, pairs an observation history with the demonstrator’s actions over the prediction horizon [10]. Each episode records a particular sequence of actions taken by the demonstrator. At each decision point, the demonstrator could have chosen differently, but the resulting dataset does not reflect these counterfactual actions (fig. 2). Because observations are often high dimensional and continuous, and reached states stochastic, other episodes never repeat exact observation histories.11 1 When the observation space is discrete and small, the same observation history may repeat across episodes, and the sliding-window dataset may contain explicit multi-modality. The demonstrator’s multi-modality is therefore not explicitly represented in the data [11]. At the same time, diffusion models at these dataset scales, given sufficiently expressive architectures and enough training, operate in or near the memorization regime (sec. 2). The standard pipeline therefore memorizes a dataset in which each observation is paired with a single mode; low policy diversity is an expected outcome. Some architectures may be better than others at nonetheless learning to generalize based on nearby observations paired with different action modes. Yet, these datasets themselves remain fundamentally ambiguous: the underlying demonstrator could be interpreted as multi-modal or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant. In this paper, we focus on disambiguating the dataset.

papers.title: Patchbay: a block model for the sonification of ADS-B aircraft data
papers.abstract: Patchbay is a design for turning the data that an ADS-B receiver collects into sound by wiring typed blocks together. ADS-B reports are the position and altitude messages that aircraft broadcast and that a small ground receiver can collect. We first describe what such a receiver reports: signals that differ in shape (continuous, stepped, circular, categorical), in resolution, in who produces them, and in how long they stay put, which runs from about ten seconds to the whole time an aircraft is in view. From this we derive a small model. Four kinds of connection carry an aircraft set, a value, an event or audio, and 27 blocks select aircraft, read fields, decide when a note starts, shape values and make sound. One of these blocks makes the receiver act as a radar: scanning by bearing it is a line that rotates about the receiver, and scanning by range it is a ring that grows from the centre or shrinks inward. Each aircraft sounds at the moment the scan reaches it, and the scan's period is set in bars of a beat clock. The model does not depend on a browser. Our reference implementation is a browser editor, contained in one HTML file, that replays two recorded captures and records both an audio take and a MIDI take, a file of the notes played rather than of the sound. We say what is not built and place the work beside the closest systems we found, among them a radar-sweep sequencer for tangible objects from 2006 and a range-ring sonification of ADS-B aircraft published in 2026. Sweeps that trigger sound, and typed connections, both exist in earlier systems. To our knowledge, none of the sources we reached carries the aircraft in view, with every field attached, as one kind of connection in an editor.

papers.intro:
Patchbay is a tool for making music from aircraft. It is the editor of Pitchaxis, our project for sonifying ADS-B data, and it takes its name from the panel of jacks and cables with which a studio routes signals between devices. It has two parts. The first is a design: what the tool takes an aircraft to be, what can flow between blocks, which blocks exist and what each takes and gives, and how a graph of blocks is evaluated against a beat clock. The second is a reference implementation, a browser editor contained in one HTML file, in which a user chooses one of two recorded captures of the air traffic seen from a receiver in central New Jersey and builds a patch, a set of blocks joined by cables, on a canvas. Patchbay is a tool for making music from aircraft. It is the editor of Pitchaxis, our project for sonifying ADS-B data, and it takes its name from the panel of jacks and cables with which a studio routes signals between devices. It has two parts. The first is a design: what the tool takes an aircraft to be, what can flow between blocks, which blocks exist and what each takes and gives, and how a graph of blocks is evaluated against a beat clock. The second is a reference implementation, a browser editor contained in one HTML file, in which a user chooses one of two recorded captures of the air traffic seen from a receiver in central New Jersey and builds a patch, a set of blocks joined by cables, on a canvas. Nothing in the design needs a browser. Section 6 says what another implementation would have to provide.

The data are not one signal. Section 2 characterizes what a receiver reports, signal by signal, because the choice of blocks depends on what the signals are like: how they are shaped, how finely they are resolved, how long they stay put and who produces them. Section 3 gives the model that follows from that: four kinds of connection, the rules for joining them and the reasons for those rules, and 27 blocks, with what each takes and gives.

The idea we most want to describe is the scan block (Section 4). A real radar turns a beam, and each aircraft is seen at the moment the beam passes it. papers.title: Solving Large Rubik's Cubes within a Factor of $2.37+o(1)$ of Optimal
papers.abstract: We design optimized algorithms to solve the $n \times n \times n$ Rubik's Cube within $30.5 n^2 / \lg n + o(n^2 / \lg n)$ moves. This upper bound is asymptotically within a factor of $2.37$ of the known lower bound, which applies to almost all instances. The constant $30.5$ is also the first explicit constant factor for the known upper bound of $O(n^2 / \lg n)$, where the implicit constant of the previous algorithm was $1.01 \cdot 10^{40}$ (ten duodecillion). Thus we improve the upper-bound constant by a factor of more than $3.30 \cdot 10^{38}$ (330 undecillion). Our algorithm runs in time linear in the input size $N = \Theta(n^2)$, and uses $O(\sqrt{N} \lg N)$ extra space (beyond the state of the cube). Our implementation is the first practical cube solver to generate solutions of length $O(n^2/\lg n)$. Our latest solver outperforms existing solvers for $n$ as small as $840$.

The Rubik’s Cube is perhaps the world’s best-known puzzle, which recently celebrated its 50th anniversary. The Cube has also fascinated a wide range of research communities, including mathematicians, computer scientists, and engineers [10]. In robotics, it serves as a benchmark for dexterous manipulation [2]. In machine learning, it is a testbed for graph algorithms [13, 1, 3]. In complexity theory, Demaine, Eisenstat, and Rudoy [5] proved NP-completeness of solving an n×n×nn\times n\times n Rubik’s Cube optimally from a given state.

A central question in cube theory is to determine the worst-case number of moves required to solve any configuration of the cube. In other words (by symmetry), what is the diameter of the configuration space, where vertices represent configurations and edges correspond to valid moves? For the 3×3×33\times 3\times 3 cube, Rokicki, Kociemba, Davidson, and Dethridge [15] computed this number (sometimes called God’s number) to be exactly 20 moves in the half-turn metric. papers.title: Scalable Neural Safety Certification via Monotonicity
papers.abstract: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.

papers.intro:
Dynamical systems provide a powerful mathematical framework for modeling and analyzing autonomous, engineered, and natural systems. They are widely used to describe complex behaviors arising in safety-critical domains such as self-driving vehicles, biological networks, and industrial process control. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to develop rigorous methods that can certify their safe operation over long or infinite time horizons. Barrier certificates provide a powerful inductive approach for this purpose: they reduce safety verification to the search for a scalar function that separates initial states from unsafe states and is preserved along system trajectories [42, 4]. When such a function exists, it serves as a formal certificate that the unsafe set is unreachable.

Although barrier certificates provide a clean inductive proof of safety, they remain difficult to compute for high-dimensional systems, especially in data-driven settings where the dynamics are unknown and only simulator-generated data or trajectories are available. Classical barrier-certificate methods construct certificates using linear programming [46, 58], sum-of-squares (SOS) optimization [42], or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) techniques [25]. These approaches have led to substantial progress and provide strong formal guarantees [41, 5, 55], but they often require explicit models, restrictive dynamics, or optimization procedures that scale poorly with dimension. Neural networks have recently emerged as a flexible representation class for learning barrier certificates from data [14, 63, 62, 45]. However, existing neural barrier frameworks typically rely on Lipschitz bounds, dense sampling, or expensive verification subroutines to obtain formal guarantees. As a result, their sample complexity and computational cost can grow rapidly with the state dimension.

Even when a system is not inherently monotone, controllers can often be designed to enforce monotonicity in the closed-loop dynamics, as in droop control for power systems [50], consensus protocols in multi-agent robotics [10], and structural control strategies in biological networks [9, 54].

papers.title: ALETHEIA: A Multi-Frequency Eddy Current Pulsed Thermography Dataset for Neural Operator Learning in Nondestructive Testing
papers.abstract: Learning neural solvers for spatiotemporal partial differential equations (PDEs) under real-world constraints remains a key challenge in scientific machine learning, especially for inverse tasks with sparse and noisy boundary observations. We present the Aletheia dataset, the first 3D benchmark for learning data-driven solvers in the context of nondestructive testing (NDT). The dataset simulates eddy-current-induced heating in conductive solids and models the resulting transient heat propagation governed by the heat equation. Aletheia contains over 4,700 high-resolution samples across 10 excitation frequencies (1-100,kHz), each providing volumetric heat source and temperature fields over time. It supports both forward prediction of temperature evolution and inverse reconstruction of internal heat sources or defects from surface infrared measurements. Real infrared thermography data from cracked rail specimens are included for calibration and comparison. We define four canonical tasks on both regular and irregular grids and benchmark them using various neural operators. Aletheia establishes a unified platform for evaluating neural PDE solvers under realistic NDT conditions, enabling progress in reliable, data-driven inverse modeling. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/sherlock-0327/ALETHEIA.

papers.intro:
Neural operator methods, such as the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [20, 19, 31, 40] and Transformer-based solvers [18, 38, 16], have emerged as a transformative approach for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from data. Unlike traditional methods, these architectures bypass mesh-dependent discretizations, enabling robust generalization across parameterized PDE families. However, they are typically evaluated on academic datasets (e.g., Darcy flow, Navier–Stokes) with fully observed fields and simplified geometries, which fail to capture the complexities of real-world inverse problems. In applications like nondestructive testing (NDT) [11, 41, 43, 9, 32], challenges such as sparse or noisy boundary observations, unknown source terms, and heterogeneous domains demand more robust benchmarks [26, 1].

However, they are typically evaluated on academic datasets (e.g., Darcy flow, Navier–Stokes) with fully observed fields and simplified geometries, which fail to capture the complexities of real-world inverse problems. In applications like nondestructive testing (NDT) [11, 41, 43, 9, 32], challenges such as sparse or noisy boundary observations, unknown source terms, and heterogeneous domains demand more robust benchmarks [26, 1].

In NDT, reconstructing hidden defects [23, 46, 29, 39] from surface temperature measurements, as in inverse heat conduction problems [27], is inherently ill-posed: distinct subsurface defects or excitation conditions can produce nearly identical surface temperature patterns [37], as illustrated in Figure 1. To address this, we employ multi-frequency pulsed induction heating, where different excitation frequencies probe the material at varying depths—lower frequencies penetrate deeper to capture internal defect responses, while higher frequencies reveal surface-level thermal behavior [22]. As shown in Figure 1, while some frequencies (e.g., 9 kHz) may yield similar surface temperatures for different defects, others (e.g., 25 kHz) reveal distinct patterns. This frequency-dependent response diversity breaks single-frequency ambiguity, enhancing defect discriminability.

To bridge this gap, we introduce the Aletheia dataset (Figure 2), a comprehensive 3D benchmark that integrates high-fidelity simulations with real infrared measurements from rail specimens with internal fatigue cracks. The dataset includes over 4,700 defect cases across 10 excitation frequencies (1–100 kHz), providing volumetric heat-source maps (eddy-current-induced Joule heating) and time-resolved temperature fields on both regular and irregular grids. papers.title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary. Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. On this protocol, SAEs reconstruct AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings better than every baseline at matched sparsity. Their features align with far fewer reference concepts than raw embedding dimensions (on AlphaEarth, 88% align with at most one of 20 concept groups, most with none, against a median of 12 per raw dimension). They also carry more of their variance at fine spatial scales (23 to 32% within a 640 m patch for BatchTopK and Matryoshka, against 9%). An SAE with a frozen random decoder shares both properties, which therefore follow from sparsity, whereas only a learned dictionary reconstructs the embedding accurately: on AlphaEarth, trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. We test the sparse code on two applications, discovering land-cover sub-concepts and detecting out-of-distribution pixels by area-of-applicability estimation. Both indicate how sparse features could be used, but neither is yet reliable enough for practical use. Together, these results are a step toward Earth observation models whose features can be inspected.

papers.intro:
Earth embeddings compress petabytes of satellite imagery into compact, reusable vector representations that capture the state of the land surface at any location and time [1]. Precomputed embeddings such as AlphaEarth [2] and Tessera [3], and open models such as OlmoEarth [4], already enable rapid global mapping from sparse labels. They have been used successfully in agriculture [5, 6, 7], forestry [8], meteorology [9], hydrology [10], development economics [11], disaster risk reduction [12], and environmental monitoring [13]. For the first time, the full Earth observation archives are within practical reach for downstream analysis.

These embeddings, however, remain largely opaque. Their intrinsic dimensionality is far lower than their ambient size [14], which suggests substantial redundancy. Some dimensions correlate with specific land-surface properties, but most mix several concepts [15, 16]. This entanglement undermines two properties that practitioners need. The first is interpretability, since scientists and decision makers must understand what a model has learned to trust its predictions and to discover new insights. The second is robustness under distribution shift. Downstream models are often trained on labels from one region and applied globally. If a dimension encodes deciduous forest in the training region but irrigated cropland elsewhere, the model transfers its forest mapping to cropland. Cropland pixels may then lie close to forest training pixels in embedding space, so a distance-based check for input shift [17] can miss the error [7, 18]. If forest and cropland activated different features, such a shift would become visible.

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a principled approach to this problem. The use of sparse, overcomplete representations has a long history in computational neuroscience [19] and has recently emerged as the dominant tool for mechanistic interpretability. By projecting dense activations onto an overcomplete dictionary, SAEs disentangle representations into approximately monosemantic features, each corresponding to a single interpretable concept [20, 21]. Originally developed for language models [22, 23, 24, 25, 26], SAEs have since been applied to protein language models [27], single-cell transcriptomics [28], biological foundation models more broadly [29], vision transformers [30, 31], weather and climate models [32, 33], and physics surrogates [34], consistently surfacing interpretable structure that remains invisible in the original dense activations of these large-scale foundation models. We bring this approach to Earth embeddings.

The main obstacle to using SAEs on Earth embeddings is evaluation. Current SAE evaluation protocols were developed for language models and commonly rely on LLMs to interpret features automatically, which is not established for Earth observation. An LLM can read the text on which a language-model feature fires, but the meaning of a pixel has to be read from maps of what is on the ground. In Earth science, moreover, concepts are spatially autocorrelated [35, 36] and vary on scales from single fields to biomes, so the scale at which a feature varies is part of what it represents. A further difficulty concerns SAEs in general: on language models, SAEs whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary nearly match trained ones on common interpretability metrics [37], and SAEs on randomly initialised transformers score about as well as SAEs on trained ones [38]. A good score alone therefore does not show that the SAE has learned meaningful features. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol tailored to Earth embeddings (Figure 1b). It scores any SAE on three criteria: reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with known concepts, and spatial scale. The known concepts come from a curated registry of reference maps, ranging from sub-metre roads to 500500 m land-cover grids, and every score is compared with that of an SAE with a frozen random decoder.

papers.title: Rules, Choice, and Chance: A Welfare Evaluation Framework for Student-School Matching
papers.abstract: Centralized student-school matching systems, adopted in the United States, Chile, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom, assign students to schools based on their submitted preference rankings and schools' priority policies. Yet welfare in these systems is typically measured through a narrow lens: a few aggregate statistics published by education authorities, such as the share of students unmatched or assigned to a top-ranked choice. A single aggregate cannot reveal how outcomes vary across students, or why. Welfare depends on three interacting forces: the rules policymakers set (algorithm, tie-breaking, list length limits); the choices students make (which and how many schools to rank); and chance (lottery draws and students' residential location). A rule that reduces unmatched rates may simultaneously lower top-ranked assignment rates for specific groups, and evaluating such trade-offs in advance is challenging because individual-level preference data are rarely available. We present Trace (Trade-offs in Rules, Agency, Chance, and Equity), an open-source framework that synthesizes individual-level preference profiles from aggregate data using mixtures of Mallows models and evaluates alternative rules across multiple welfare metrics, disaggregating outcomes by choice and chance. We apply Trace to two real-world systems: NYC high school matching, where we study minimum list length requirements, and Chilean school assignment, where we compare the current multiple tie-breaking rule with a counterfactual single tie-breaking rule. Both reveal substantial, heterogeneous welfare trade-offs, underscoring the value of simulation-based evaluation before implementing school choice reforms.

papers.intro:
Two-sided matching algorithms are used in many real-world settings, whether to match students to schools (Abdulkadiroğlu and Andersson, 2023), medical graduates to hospitals (Match, 2026), or refugees to locations (Strasser Ceballos and Kern, 2025). Particularly in the school setting, the use of these algorithms has gained considerable importance, prompting the replacement of traditional admission practices with centralized matching systems (Che et al., 2025) in the United States (Abdulkadiroğlu and Andersson, 2023), Chile (Correa et al., 2019), the Netherlands (Ruijs and Oosterbeek, 2019), and the United Kingdom (Terrier et al., 2026). These systems promise greater transparency and efficiency, as well as the potential to reduce educational segregation by enabling students to apply to schools beyond their local neighborhoods (Bellei et al., 2025; Abdulkadiroğlu et al., 2009).

These systems promise greater transparency and efficiency, as well as the potential to reduce educational segregation by enabling students to apply to schools beyond their local neighborhoods (Bellei et al., 2025; Abdulkadiroğlu et al., 2009).

Designing such systems, however, is far from straightforward. A natural starting point is the choice of the assignment mechanism itself (Abdulkadiroğlu and Andersson, 2023). Abdulkadiroğlu and Sönmez (2003) were among the first to formally study the design of school admission systems using matching theory. They analyzed and compared several mechanisms, including the Immediate Acceptance (IA) (Abdulkadiroğlu and Andersson, 2023), Top Trading Cycles (TTC) (Shapley and Scarf, 1974), and the Gale and Shapley Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm (Gale and Shapley, 1962). Based on this comparison, the authors identified the DA algorithm as a particularly suitable mechanism for school assignment, largely due to its two key theoretical properties: stability, meaning that no student-school pair would prefer to deviate from the assigned outcome, and strategy-proofness, meaning that students are best off ranking schools in order of their true preferences (Abdulkadiroğlu and Andersson, 2023). These properties motivated major reforms, with cities such as Boston and New York City (NYC) redesigning their systems in the early 2000s to adopt variants of the student-proposing DA algorithm (Abdulkadiroğlu and Sönmez, 2003).

papers.title: Martine: Benchmarking Multi-View 3D Surface Reconstruction Across Viewpoint Coverage, Resolution, and Lighting
papers.abstract: Controlled acquisition setups are widely used for high-accuracy multi-view 3D surface reconstruction, as they allow sensor configuration, image resolution, viewpoint distribution, and illumination to be specified. Yet benchmarking remains difficult, since reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on the reconstruction paradigm, object properties, and acquisition regime. Existing benchmarks often restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution, or illumination, which can bias comparisons towards methods suited to the chosen setting. Others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, limiting their use for metric surface evaluation. We introduce Martine, a benchmark for controlled 3D object surface reconstruction. Martine comprises 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views over a spherical cap under both single-light and multi-light regimes. It provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy quantified on test images, and 3D property masks for analysing errors by material properties, visibility, curvature and fine structures. Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction, and multi-view photometric stereo show that Martine enables regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The benchmark resolves sub-millimetric reconstruction differences, with a best observed Chamfer distance of 0.058 mm over the evaluated visible surface.

papers.intro:
3D surface reconstruction is a central problem in computer vision, with applications in cultural heritage preservation, industrial inspection, robotics, augmented reality, and digital content creation. Across these applications, the objective is often not only to recover a visually plausible shape, but to estimate surface geometry with sufficient accuracy for measurement, analysis, or downstream processing. Conversely, datasets designed for multi-view photometric stereo combine several viewpoints with multiple controlled illumination conditions, so that surface geometry can be inferred not only from multi-view consistency but also from shading variation. These datasets provide illumination conditions suitable for photometric reconstruction, but each covers the remaining benchmark dimensions only partially, such as viewpoint density, elevation coverage, image resolution, object count, or surface ground truth. DiLiGenT-MV [19] remains the standard benchmark for multi-view photometric stereo, but contains only five objects, each captured from 20 views at 612×512612\times 512 resolution. More recent datasets increase resolution or object count, but remain limited in viewpoint elevation coverage: LUCES-MV [18] contains 12 views at 2368×15522368\times 1552 resolution, and EvalMVX [21] contains 20 views at 2448×20482448\times 2048 resolution; all three acquire views at a single elevation. However, for surface-reconstruction benchmarking, its image-to-geometry alignment relies on object-dependent registration between the ground-truth scan mesh and a COLMAP [22] reconstruction. This can be unreliable when the COLMAP reconstruction is incomplete or geometrically inaccurate (see Figure 1), for example for transparent objects, thin structures, or challenging materials; yet the resulting alignment errors are not systematically quantified or reported. A related concern is addressed by NAVI [14] for in-the-wild object reconstruction, where 3D scanner ground truth is combined with manually verified 2D–3D alignment to obtain accurate object alignments. These results remain valuable, but they correspond to a hybrid setting, namely multi-light acquisition followed by single-light reconstruction. They therefore do not directly measure the performance of single-light reconstruction methods under a single-light acquisition regime. As a result, current benchmarks do not jointly provide broad object-centric viewpoint coverage, dense camera-mounted illumination, high-resolution imagery, accurately aligned 3D ground-truth scans, and acquisition regimes that allow single-light and multi-light methods to be compared under conditions designed for each paradigm.

papers.title: Unveiling a Concentration of Hard X-Ray Point Sources in the Nuclear Stellar Disk with XMM-Newton
papers.abstract: The Galactic Center is home to the largest known concentration of X-ray sources ever detected in our Galaxy, including a sizable population of accreting compact objects. Utilizing data from the XMM-Newton Galactic Plane Heritage Survey of the central $20^{\circ}\times2^{\circ}$ of the Milky Way, we investigate the varying source populations in the inner regions of the Galaxy. We identify for the first time a concentration of extremely hard X-ray sources within $|l|<1.3^{\circ}$ and $|b|<0.3^{\circ}$, a region that overlaps the nuclear stellar disk (NSD). We determine that this hardness is intrinsic to the sources and not a manifestation of high line-of-sight column density ($N_{\rm H}$). Unlike the "soft" X-ray sources, this population does not trace the stellar mass distribution, indicating an overabundance compared to the underlying stellar population. We simulate spectra for a variety of source types to model their X-ray hardness and compare their distributions to those we observed in our survey data. We find that a significant subset of the Galactic Center X-ray population may comprise intermediate polars (IPs) with massive white dwarfs, possibly formed through dynamical processes. Our study provides novel observational insights into the distribution of stellar remnants and other X-ray sources in the vicinity of our supermassive black hole, Sgr A*.

papers.intro:
More than 44 years ago, [83] discovered what would become known as the Galactic ridge X-ray emission (GRXE) – an apparently diffuse X-ray glow that seemed to trace the disk of the Milky Way. In the intervening decades, many studies have attempted to discern the origin of this emission. Some of the earliest efforts proposed that numerous unresolved faint point sources, such as cataclysmic variables (CVs) and active binaries (ABs), were responsible [82, 33, 61]. Others speculated that the source of the emission was indeed diffuse, proposing exotic mechanisms to supply or trap a sufficiently hot plasma bound to the shallow gravitational well of the Galactic disk [32, 87, 73, 13, 72]. [60] put an end to most of the speculation about the GRXE origin by showing that most of the observed X-ray emission can be accounted for by a population of faint point sources that were detected through deep Chandra observations of a low-extinction region (the “Limiting Window” [LW]). This was followed by [25], who showed that magnetic CVs (mCVs) dominated the population of faint sources in the LW – although this conclusion was disputed by [85], who argued for a majority contribution from dwarf novae (DNe) supplemented by ABs, based on the Fe line equivalent widths (EWs) and intensity ratios of those sources. The latter study was subsequently challenged by [64], who showed that ABs (like RS CVn systems) do not significantly contribute to the Fe emission and concluded that DNe and polars are the primary suspects. More recently, [8] has suggested that a population of symbiotic stars may comprise up to one-fifth of the GRXE emission overall, and an even larger fraction of the Fe XXV emission. An additional excess of neutral (or low ionization) Fe I-Kα\alpha emission (at 6.4 keV) has been attributed to the bombardment of molecular clouds by locally originating low-energy cosmic rays (LECRs) [89, 53].

papers.title: Toward Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms: An LLM-Driven Framework with a Case Study on Spatial Regime Discovery
papers.abstract: Geospatial algorithms have been developed through expert-driven discovery: a researcher spots a limitation, proposes a structural fix, and checks it by hand. With LLM-driven multi-agent systems becoming practical, much of the candidate-generation, evaluation, and selection work can now be largely automated, while the researcher's role shifts upstream toward problem formulation, evaluation design, and interpretation. We refer to this paradigm as Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA) and propose a framework with three required modules: a two-loop architecture with embedded geographic knowledge as the inner-loop engine; an automatic code formatter that converts any raw geospatial algorithm into the standardized triple required by the inner loop; and a simulation-driven training protocol, in which evolution runs only on synthetic data with known ground truth, and the discovered algorithm is applied unchanged to real data, keeping real-world results out-of-sample. We use spatial regime discovery as a case study, seeded with the Two-stage K-Models algorithm. Evolution uses the Rand Index against the ground-truth partition as fitness signal; the frozen algorithm is then evaluated on 150 simulated grids and 11 real-world datasets across climate, health, hydrology, and politics. The evolved algorithm outperforms its seed, knowledge-free baselines, and four classical regionalization methods. Ablations further indicate that the channel of geographic-knowledge injection, structured retrieval versus prompt-level hints, is itself load-bearing. In this case study, LLM-assisted search sped up the inner loop; whether it does so for other seeds and task families remains open. The geographer's role -- asking the right questions, designing trustworthy evaluation -- grows more central.

Geospatial modeling sits at the core of geospatial research, supporting tasks such as spatial partitioning (Anselin and Amaral, 2024; Duque et al., 2007; Assunção et al., 2006), prediction (Brunsdon et al., 1998; Fotheringham et al., 2002; Fotheringham et al., 2017), spatial dependence modeling (Anselin, 1988; LeSage and Pace, 2009; Anselin, 1995), and uncertainty quantification (Lou et al., 2025). The development of these models has typically grown out of an expert-driven process that brings together theoretical insights, empirical observations, and domain knowledge, often accumulating over decades of methodological refinement (Cressie, 1993; Goodchild, 2004). Such development can be characterized as expert-driven discovery: a researcher identifies a limitation, hypothesizes a structural improvement (e.g., adding spatial weights, restructuring a clustering objective, or proposing a new estimator), implements it, and validates it against established baselines. Each discovery step is conceptually rich but is also human-paced, costly in time, and naturally limited by the cognitive and institutional resources available to any single research group.

The rapid development of large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT (Singh et al., 2025), Gemini (Gemini Team et al., 2023), DeepSeek (Liu et al., 2024), and Qwen (Yang et al., 2025), together with the rise of LLM-based multi-agent architectures (Park et al., 2023), suggests that much of the routine engineering work of algorithm development can now be largely automated. Working in this complementary mode, the researcher delegates the work of generating candidate programs, evaluating them, and keeping the better ones to an LLM-driven system, while retaining responsibility for deciding what to optimize, setting up the evaluation, and making sense of what comes out. Working in this mode, researchers spend less time writing and debugging small algorithmic variants by hand, and more time on the upstream questions: what is a good solution to this problem, what fitness signal captures it, and what do the resulting algorithms tell us. The two modes are best seen as complementary: expert-driven discovery continues to mark out the design space and the objectives that matter, while LLM-assisted search systematically explores parts of that space that would be tedious to cover manually (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). Within geospatial science, the convergence of GeoAI (Janowicz et al., 2020; Mai et al., 2023) and LLM-based agents is opening up new directions for spatial analysis and knowledge discovery.

It is useful to distinguish at the outset between two complementary lines of LLM-based research now active in geospatial science. The first treats the LLM as an orchestrator of a fixed library of pre-existing geospatial tools and algorithms: the model interprets a user request, selects appropriate operations, and emits glue code that invokes them, while the underlying spatial algorithms remain entirely human-authored. We refer to this as the usage layer of the algorithm stack. The second treats the LLM as an author that proposes and mutates algorithm source code itself, generating new algorithmic logic rather than choosing among existing tools. We refer to this as the design layer. The present paper, together with the GeoEvolve framework it builds on (Luo et al., 2025), sits firmly at the design layer: the toolbox is the object that gets evolved, not the menu that gets chosen from. Section 2 reviews both lines in detail and identifies the specific inner-loop engines we adopt; here we only flag the distinction so as to keep the technical premise of the rest of the paper visible.

The central message of the present paper is that the combination of these two modes describes a noticeable shift in how geospatial algorithms can be developed, and that this shift deserves to be named and characterized as such. We refer to this LLM-assisted paradigm as Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA), denoting a structured, evaluation-driven search over the space of executable geospatial programs, in which candidate algorithms are continuously generated, evaluated, and selected by an LLM-powered multi-agent system. We propose a working hypothesis to guide its scope: if the optimization objective of a geospatial problem can be specified clearly enough for computational evaluation, the inner loop of algorithm development can be largely delegated to a multi-agent LLM system, while the outer loop of formulating the problem and interpreting the results remains the responsibility of the researcher. We do not claim that algorithm design has become trivial; rather, we observe that, given a well-defined objective, LLM-driven evolutionary systems can systematically explore parts of the design space that are difficult to traverse manually.

We do not claim that algorithm design has become trivial; rather, we observe that, given a well-defined objective, LLM-driven evolutionary systems can systematically explore parts of the design space that are difficult to traverse manually.

A natural starting point for realizing SEGA is the recently proposed GeoEvolve framework (Luo et al., 2025), which extends flat, single-loop, domain-agnostic evolutionary engines such as OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) by wrapping the inner LLM-driven code-evolution loop with an outer dialogue that retrieves geographic knowledge from a curated corpus and injects it into the next mutation. This two-loop architecture with embedded geographic knowledge is, in our view, the necessary substrate for any practical SEGA system, and we adopt it as the inner-loop engine of our framework without redesign. Two further extensions, however, are required before this engine can be used routinely on new geospatial problems. The first concerns the input side: raw geospatial algorithms are written in heterogeneous styles, and integrating each new seed by hand re-introduces a manual-engineering bottleneck that the inner loop is supposed to remove. An LLM-driven automatic code formatter that converts any raw geospatial algorithm into the standardized triple (evolvable program, evaluator module, configuration file) required by the inner loop is therefore needed to make the framework reusable across tasks. The second concerns the evaluation side: when evolution is driven directly by the algorithm’s performance on the very data on which its output will be reported, real-world metrics become both training target and evaluation target, and the resulting numbers tell us less than they appear to. A simulation-driven training protocol with a controlled data-generating process, in which evolution is run only on synthetic data with a known ground truth and the discovered algorithm is then applied unchanged to real data, is therefore needed to keep real-world results as out-of-sample evidence rather than direct optimization targets. The three pieces together, GeoEvolve’s two-loop architecture, an automatic code formatter, and a simulation-driven training protocol, constitute the conceptual framework developed in the remainder of this paper.

papers.title: ROS2MR: Connecting ROS 2 Motion Planning to Mixed-Reality Trajectory Visualization
papers.abstract: Mixed reality (MR) allows users to inspect planned robot motion within their physical surroundings, but displaying trajectories from robotics software requires converting their joint configurations and timing into a format the MR application can play back. This paper presents ROS2MR, an extension of the MR-Robotics LAB platform that converts YAML-serialized ROS 2 joint trajectories, including MoveIt motion plans, into the platform's existing JSON playback format. The converter validates the input, maps arm joints by name, and resamples the trajectory at a nominal rate of 30 Hz, using cubic Hermite interpolation when joint velocities are supplied and linear interpolation otherwise, while binary gripper commands are sampled separately using a zero-order hold. A Python export helper combines sequences of motion plans and gripper states into a single trajectory and checks positional agreement at segment boundaries. The MR application was also adapted for Apple Vision Pro in addition to Meta Quest 3. A technical evaluation showed that the converter preserved the normalized duration and endpoint configurations for dense, sparse, and irregularly timed inputs. With supplied velocities, the position RMSE was approximately 2.91x10^-5 degrees for all sampling patterns; without them, sparse input increased it to 0.85 degrees, and close positional agreement did not guarantee accurate velocity profiles. A pick-and-place sequence retained its open--closed--open gripper order, although off-grid transitions were shifted to the output sampling grid. The resulting file-based pathway enables inspection of ROS-generated trajectories in MR without a live ROS connection.

papers.title: Extending the reach of real-space real-time TDDFT: new developments in the Octopus code
papers.abstract: Octopus is an open-source package implementing time-dependent density functional theory in a real-space, real-time formulation. Here we report on the developments since our previous contribution to the Special Topic Issue on Electronic Structure Software [J. Chem. Phys. 152, 124119 (2020)]. New exchange-correlation functionals extend the range of systems that can be treated, while advances in relativistic and all-electron methods open the door to core-electron spectroscopy. New capabilities for lattice dynamics - stress-tensor calculation, geometry optimization, support for machine-learned force fields, and phonon calculations - enable a fully ab initio description of light-induced lattice dynamics in real time. We also present developments that move beyond the dipole approximation, capturing light-matter interaction more faithfully. Improved methods for exciton dynamics complement a set of algorithmic advances - new propagation schemes, imaginary-time evolution, and a refactored grid handling more than a billion points - that together substantially improve performance and scalability. Combined with technical improvements such as AMD GPU support and a modernized build system, these developments consolidate Octopus as a versatile, high-performance platform for exploring electronic excitations, light-matter interaction, and nonequilibrium dynamics in molecules, nanostructures, and extended systems.

papers.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
papers.abstract: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.

papers.intro:
Due to its recent democratization and versatility, AI can appear in a forensic investigation in various ways. It can be an asset to aid investigators, the target of an attack, or a medium for committing a crime. The digital forensics community has acknowledged the need to investigate AI systems (e.g., Dragonas et al. (2024); Jeong et al. (2025); Comeaux et al. (2026)). What is still missing is a structure that tells an investigator where to look for traces in an arbitrary AI system and that tells researchers which parts of the problem are already solved and which are not.

It can be an asset to aid investigators, the target of an attack, or a medium for committing a crime. The digital forensics community has acknowledged the need to investigate AI systems (e.g., Dragonas et al. (2024); Jeong et al. (2025); Comeaux et al. (2026)). What is still missing is a structure that tells an investigator where to look for traces in an arbitrary AI system and that tells researchers which parts of the problem are already solved and which are not.

To fill this gap, we developed a life-cycle model for AI systems which focuses on the artifacts that each stage in the life of an AI system leaves behind. We call it the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC). Because of its focus, FALC is both an artifact-centric life-cycle model and an artifact-centric reference model for forensic investigations. FALC provides a systematic way to enumerate questions that can arise during an investigation around an AI system and the artifacts available to answer them. Comparing those questions against the current state of forensic practice yields our second contribution: a classification of the fields of expertise that AI forensics requires into fields where existing methods transfer unchanged, fields where existing methods must be adapted, and fields where no adequate method exists yet. This last group marks where research is most urgently needed. In particular, our contributions are: • FALC, an artifact-centric reference model of the AI life cycle designed for forensic investigation rather than for process optimization. • A catalogue of forensic artifacts produced at each stage of the AI life cycle, together with where they can be expected to be found. • A collection of crimes and forensic questions associated with each stage, illustrating how AI can be involved in an offense. • A taxonomy of the forensic fields of expertise required by AI forensics, distinguishing directly applicable fields, fields requiring adaptation, and fields that do not yet exist.

papers.title: Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference without a Path
papers.abstract: We present a real-time method for reconstructing fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media under direct and ambient environmental illumination, using compact, low-cost scene features and statistics. Unlike Monte Carlo denoising pipelines for volumetric rendering, which depend on computationally expensive path-traced radiance estimates, our approach directly infers the final light-transport solution from inexpensive primary-ray and environment sample evaluations. We show that these features form a near-sufficient representation of the scene, enabling accurate reconstruction at substantially lower computational cost. Using an attention-augmented image-to-image network, we demonstrate that complete pixel radiance can be inferred directly from these auxiliary features, without requiring the original radiance signal. Operating in image space also provides a more stable computational cost as the camera zooms into or out of the volume, with substantially less dependence on volume density than approaches based on explicit multiple-scattering simulation. We demonstrate real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenarios.

papers.intro:
Monte Carlo (MC) path tracing achieves photorealistic rendering by simulating the full light transport pipeline, including emission, scattering, and absorption along importance-sampled light paths [Kaj86, Coo86, AK90, NGHJ18, PJH23]. For surface rendering, light paths terminate after a few bounces, yet each pixel still requires hundreds to thousands of samples to converge to a noise-free result. For volumetric media, the problem is substantially more severe: light scatters at every point along a ray, turning each sample into a recursive integration problem. Rendering a single frame of participating media such as clouds, smoke, or fog often requires seconds to minutes even on high-end GPUs, making real-time applications prohibitive.

papers.title: Enhanced Mid-Photospheric Heating Around a Solar Pore
papers.abstract: We present depth-stratified atmospheric reconstructions of a solar pore observed with the Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared SpectroPolarimeter (SCIP) aboard \textsc{Sunrise~iii}. Using spatially coupled NLTE spectropolarimetric inversions, we characterize the thermal, magnetic, and velocity structure of the pore and its surroundings from the photosphere to the chromosphere over approximately two hours. The inversions recover the canonical photospheric properties of pores: a cool umbra with strong magnetic fields dominated by the vertical component. Most photospheric velocities are subsonic, but localized downflows near the pore boundary reach transonic or potentially supersonic values around $\log\tau_{500}=0$. At higher atmospheric layers, the thermal contrast between the pore and its surroundings decreases substantially. We also detect localized mid-photospheric temperature enhancements forming a patchy, ring-like structure in the wings of the Ca\,{\sc ii} 8542\,{\AA} line, without a clear continuum counterpart. The temperature excess reaches approximately $300$\,K and corresponds to an excess thermal-energy density of up to $170$\,J\,m$^{-3}$. These regions coincide with an enhanced transverse magnetic-field component and the expanding magnetic canopy surrounding the pore. The structure is detected in all three rasters, although the cadence does not establish whether individual patches persist or repeatedly re-form. While the heating mechanism cannot be uniquely identified, the inferred magnetic topology supports an association with processes operating in the expanding canopy. These results demonstrate the value of pores for investigating the coupling between magnetic topology, convection, and atmospheric energy transport.

In some cases, this configuration is accompanied by a filamentary superpenumbral structure, as reported by Sobotka et al. [47] from Ca II IR observations, similar to superpenumbrae around sunspots. papers.title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

papers.intro:
As large language models (LLMs) have made substantial gains in reasoning and long-horizon task execution, a growing body of work explores deploying AI agents for scientific discovery [24, 11]. Existing studies demonstrate that AI agents can outperform the best human-designed solutions across a wide range of tasks, including mathematical proof [14], mathematical discovery [33], optimization [29], and a subset of scientific problems [57]. However, strong performance alone does not establish the creativity of the proposed methods. Prior work has identified limitations in the novelty of AI-generated proposals, including a tendency to explore incremental modifications or extensions of existing approaches [54, 15]. A key challenge is therefore to develop AI agents that can reliably generate proposals that are creative. Addressing this challenge requires both assessing creativity rigorously and developing methods to improve it.

papers.title: Measurement of the Neutrino Spectrum along the Galactic Plane with IceCube
papers.abstract: We present the first measurement of the variation of the high-energy neutrino flux along the Galactic plane using 10 years of neutrino-induced particle-shower data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. In this Letter, we fit both the neutrino flux normalization and the spectral index, in multiple regions along the plane, independent of model expectations. The neutrino flux per solid angle in the inner Galactic region ($\vert l\vert< 30^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) is approximately five times higher than in the outer Galactic plane ($\vert l\vert>60^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) at $E_\nu=5\mathrm{TeV}$. The spectral indices in the inner and outer region are $\gamma=2.76^{+0.18}_{-0.15}$ and $\gamma = 3.13^{+0.57}_{-0.37}$, respectively. Additionally, we compare the same region of Galactic emission measured in $\mathrm{TeV}$ gamma rays by LHAASO ($15^{\circ}<l<125^{\circ}$) to neutrinos, and conclude that the measurements are compatible within uncertainties, under the assumption of hadronic gamma-ray production.

papers.intro:
For many areas of astronomy, the Milky Way is the brightest region in the sky. It has been observed throughout the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays. Galactic plane (GP) gamma rays are produced either by astrophysical sources or by cosmic rays interacting with the interstellar medium. Both processes have hadronic and leptonic contributions [16]. Hadronic interactions produce neutral and charged pions. Neutral pions decay into gamma rays; the decay of charged pions results in neutrinos, which after oscillations are observed at Earth with a flavor ratio of approximately 1:1:1 [18].

Galactic plane (GP) gamma rays are produced either by astrophysical sources or by cosmic rays interacting with the interstellar medium. Both processes have hadronic and leptonic contributions [16]. Hadronic interactions produce neutral and charged pions. Neutral pions decay into gamma rays; the decay of charged pions results in neutrinos, which after oscillations are observed at Earth with a flavor ratio of approximately 1:1:1 [18].

Efforts to detect neutrinos from the GP have been undertaken for many years by the IceCube, ANTARES, and Baikal-GVD neutrino telescopes [2, 20, 21, 22, 24]. The first significant evidence came in 2023, when IceCube reported neutrino emission from the GP at 4.54.5σ\sigma [6]. This result has since been updated, reaching 5.75.7σ\sigma [12]. These searches are optimized to determine if the Milky Way as a whole is a neutrino source. Spatial and energy templates, based on model predictions that used GeV–TeV [16, 36] gamma-ray observations, were used to search for neutrinos. Given that neutrino emission from the Galaxy is now firmly established, we develop a different approach: we present a characterization of the neutrino energy spectrum in various parts of the GP (segments). In each segment, we describe the spectrum assuming a power law in energy, and we fit both the flux normalization and the spectral index, independent of neutrino emission models.

The diffuse GeV gamma-ray emission of the GP has been measured by the space-based Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) [16]. Ground-based observatories have measured diffuse Galactic gamma-ray emission in the TeV\mathrm{TeV} range, with imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, such as H.E.S.S. [15] and air-shower arrays such as HAWC [23], Tibet ASγ\gamma [25], and LHAASO [27, 28]. Many TeV gamma-ray sources in the GP have been found [14]. Galactic neutrino sources have not been detected [8], and the neutrino flux reported here includes both diffuse GP and source emission. The irreducible background for neutrino-source searches consists of atmospheric neutrinos and the isotropic component of the astrophysical neutrino flux. Their combined flux, measured by IceCube [10, 9], far exceeds that expected from any single source, making individual source detection challenging.

The CRINGE model [41] is fitted to recent Galactic cosmic-ray data, while also incorporating a model of unresolved sources, based on the pulsar-powered sources following [42].
