papers.title: Public, Identifiable, and Effectively Immutable: Ethical Lessons from Research on arXiv
papers.abstract: Ethical decision-making is central to safe cybersecurity research. Recent studies, one of which is our own, analyzing the source files of arXiv papers bring this challenge to light - arXiv publicly distributes the source files, to the surprise of many authors. Unique aspects reveal ethical challenges and dilemmas that extend beyond established ethical frameworks, institutional processes, and community best practices. In this work, we examine this case and provide insights for similar research on other public live resources, such as Zenodo or the Wayback Machine. While such empirical studies are particularly realistic, they must account for personally identifiable information, leaked secrets, and other sensitive details that could expose, shame, or otherwise negatively affect individuals, possibly leading to both reputational and practical harm. sDrawing on our collective experience and discussions among researchers, affected authors, and readers, we make three contributions: First, we define the ethical setting and highlight that even intentionally-public data with deliberate real-name attribution can raise ethical concerns when repurposed for empirical analysis. Second, we discuss the ethical issues surrounding the use of arXiv data and derive four higher-level dilemmas that researchers may face when working with similar data. Third, we derive practical guidance for ethically navigating such settings and, in doing so, distill four lessons for research on arXiv and similar public, live datasets: public availability should serve as the starting point of ethical reasoning; research should minimize the amplification it induces on exposed information; disclosure should be calibrated to the harm, confidence, and actionability of a finding; and effective immutability must be accounted for. Together, these contribute to community resources for ethically-sound cybersecurity experiments.

papers.intro:
Cybersecurity research often touches on issues that raise ethical questions [1]. Beyond empirical studies, researching and disclosing vulnerabilities arguably also benefits attackers who can use the information to compromise vulnerable systems. To that end, responsible disclosure practices have been established in the field [2] and are widely used [3]. In contrast, public datasets used in cybersecurity research can come with different trade-offs and warrant careful ethical considerations. Passwords leaked by hackers after data breaches are used in research, e.g., [4], despite profiting from malicious actors [1]. Similarly, data on Reddit [5] or GitHub [6], for example, is widely used in research, even though individuals contributing to these live datasets may not be aware that their data is used for research [7, 8] and that their consent is rarely, if ever, obtained [9, 10].

The arXiv preprint repository [11] represents one such public dataset and is an especially complex ethical case. On arXiv, researchers publish their work under their real names, resulting in trivial author identifiability. Prior work [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] extensively sourced this resource to understand citation dynamics, for example. Another peculiarity of arXiv is that authors must also upload their LaTeX source files [19] when posting preprints to foster research transparency. Yet authors might not be aware that the paper sources they upload will be fully openly available, including all comments and other artifacts they might have forgotten to delete before uploading. At the same time, arXiv intentionally does not permit the correction of information disclosed by accident in such source files [20, 21, 22]. Despite this situation, a growing body of literature has used these sources for empirical studies.

papers.title: Beating Rytter's Bound: All-Pairs CFL Reachability in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ Time
papers.abstract:
Context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition are fundamental problems in program analysis and language theory. Despite years of effort, the best algorithms for these problems run in time $O(n^3/\log n)$ on a word RAM model; they are based on an observation of Rytter in 1985 for 2NPDA which was adapted for CFL reachability by Chaudhuri in 2008. No better algorithm has been designed since.
  We give the first improvement to Rytter's algorithm. For both all-pairs context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition, we show a deterministic algorithm running in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ time and $O(n^{2+\epsilon})$ words of space for every fixed $0<\epsilon<1$ on a word RAM. Our improvement is based on a new data structure that reports set differences using batched maintenance of exact intersection counts, allowing saturation to skip regions that contain no new reachability information.

For a fixed context-free grammar 𝒢\mathcal{G} over an alphabet Σ\Sigma, and an input directed graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) whose edges are labeled with letters from Σ\Sigma, the all-pairs context-free reachability problem asks to output a relation RA⊆V×VR_{A}\subseteq V\times V for each nonterminal AA of 𝒢\mathcal{G} such that RA​(u,v)R_{A}(u,v) iff there is a path from uu to vv labeled by a word derivable from the nonterminal AA. CFL reachability has a classical algorithm based on saturation (Yannakakis, 1990; Reps et al., 1995): the algorithm records facts A⁡(u,v)A(u,v) saying that a walk from uu to vv has a label derivable from nonterminal AA. A production A→B​CA\to BC combines B⁡(u,z)B(u,z) with C⁡(z,v)C(z,v) and adds A⁡(u,v)A(u,v) to the set of facts. The algorithm terminates when no new facts can be derived. There are quadratically many possible facts for a fixed grammar but finding their consequences by scanning all third vertices takes cubic time; thus, naive saturation gives a cubic algorithm.

A related problem in language theory is 2NPDA recognition. Given a fixed 2NPDA and an input word ww of length ℓ\ell, it asks whether the (fixed) 2NPDA accepts ww (Gray et al., 1967; Harrison and Ibarra, 1968). An algorithm for 2NPDA recognition saturates paths in the automaton, its run time is again cubic. These problems include slicing, dataflow, heap-shape, points-to analysis, and set constraints (Reps, 1998; Chistikov et al., 2022; Balasubramanian et al., 2025; Kodumal and Aiken, 2004; Neal, 1989; Heintze and McAllester, 1997).

papers.title: PTC-IoU: CPU-Friendly Detection Quality Estimation for Edge Video Analytics
papers.abstract: An edge video analytics system must estimate the quality of local detections since there are no ground-truth labels available during runtime. Detectors usually provide confidence scores for their results, but these scores can not reveal every missed object or misplaced bounding box. So a quality estimator is necessary to provide a decision signal indicating which frame has potential detection failures that need to be escalated to a more powerful model in the cloud. Neural network based estimators add workload to the GPU already running detection, while CPU capacity may remain available. We present Predictive Temporal Consistency IoU (PTC-IoU), which moves this workload to CPU by compacting detection boxes histories to support deterministic result scoring. Comparing to neural counterparts, experiments on representative edge hardware, Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, show that our method reduced per-frame estimator latency from 10.3 ms for neural counterparts to 2.2 ms (4.7x faster), increased pipelined throughput by 13.6%, and cuts estimator energy consumption by up to 95%, while maintaining competitive final detection quality verified on multiple datasets.

papers.intro:
A roadside camera paired with a cloud server needs to detect vehicles continuously under limited compute and communication capacity. Fig. 1 demonstrates that a lightweight detector on edge devices can process each frame locally, while a stronger model in the cloud can assist with only the difficult images. The device therefore faces a second task alongside detection: deciding which results to keep or send to the cloud for stronger inference. This is called selective offloading.

Fig. 1 demonstrates that a lightweight detector on edge devices can process each frame locally, while a stronger model in the cloud can assist with only the difficult images. The device therefore faces a second task alongside detection: deciding which results to keep or send to the cloud for stronger inference. This is called selective offloading.

Selective offloading decision requires information that the detector does not directly provide. A detector returns object locations as bounding boxes, together with classes and confidence scores. Though a car may be confidently detected, this does not indicate whether another car was missed, or whether the detected box is accurately placed [1]. During runtime, there are no ground-truth labels against which to check the result. In selective offloading, quality estimators provide a decision signal for choosing only suspicious frames for cloud offloading before spending the communication and server-compute budget, to maximize the final detection quality while lowering the offload cost.

Producing this decision signal also consumes edge resources. A dedicated neural network head can reuse the detector’s features [1, 2], making GPU execution alongside detection a natural choice. As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), neural scoring adds a stage to the GPU already running detection. With detection and GFL quality estimation on the GPU, Fig. 3 shows lower average CPU utilization alongside a more heavily used GPU. This opportunity extends beyond Jetson: CoDL improves on GPU-only inference by sharing work with the CPU across Snapdragon and Kirin mobile SoCs [3]. This suggests a design opportunity and challenge: Fig. 2(b) proposes to move the quality estimator to the CPU, while keeping the GPU focused on detection. However, existing neural heads require matrix multiplications that are inefficient on the CPU. Constructing the estimation operations that the CPU can process efficiently is therefore necessary.

papers.title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
papers.abstract: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly integrated into scientific research since their emergence, supporting tasks ranging from scientific discovery to scientific writing [24, 16, 1, 7, 13, 15, 18, 20, 12]. Despite these advances, human researchers remained in control of the overall research process, while LLMs primarily served as assistants for individual tasks. With the development of harness-based agents, however, language models are increasingly being integrated into end-to-end scientific workflows [27, 23, 22]. We refer to such harness-based systems that autonomously carry out multiple stages of the research process as Auto Researchers. In these emerging systems, the traditional division of labor is substantially altered: auto researchers take a leading role in carrying out the research process, while human researchers increasingly provide guidance, feedback, and oversight [17, 28, 31]. This shift raises an important question of how the research produced by these systems should be evaluated. However, evaluating research independently generated by auto researchers is challenging: its novelty, scientific value, and potential for genuine breakthroughs are difficult to establish without extensive validation. A more tractable starting point is to use established human research as a reference for assessing how these systems formulate ideas, design experiments, and synthesize findings into papers. We therefore ask: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?

We refer to such harness-based systems that autonomously carry out multiple stages of the research process as Auto Researchers. In these emerging systems, the traditional division of labor is substantially altered: auto researchers take a leading role in carrying out the research process, while human researchers increasingly provide guidance, feedback, and oversight [17, 28, 31]. This shift raises an important question of how the research produced by these systems should be evaluated. However, evaluating research independently generated by auto researchers is challenging: its novelty, scientific value, and potential for genuine breakthroughs are difficult to establish without extensive validation. A more tractable starting point is to use established human research as a reference for assessing how these systems formulate ideas, design experiments, and synthesize findings into papers. We therefore ask: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?

Existing evaluation frameworks for LLM-based scientific research systems have largely focused on model-level capabilities, typically assessing performance on individual research tasks rather than the behavior of harness-based systems operating across the full research process [4, 25, 30, 26, 6, 5]. In this work, rather than evaluating auto researchers solely by whether they can complete predefined research tasks, we ask whether they can conduct research in ways that reconstruct the decisions and processes of human researchers. papers.title: Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance
papers.abstract: Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance is a key outcome of the AI Safety and Governance Program of World Internet Conference Specialized Committee on AI in 2026. Drawing on the latest developments in frontier AI capabilities and applications, the report systematically examines the evolving risk landscape, analyzing key risk areas, their severity and response priorities. Building on a review of existing global governance practices and an assessment of frontier AI governance readiness, it identifies key governance gaps and weaknesses and proposes directions and practical mechanisms for coordinated responses. The report provides a reference for government departments, international organizations, businesses, research institutions and other stakeholders. It aims to strengthen the international community's understanding of and consensus on frontier AI risks, enhance preparedness and collective response capacity, and advance the safe, reliable and responsible development of frontier AI to better serve the common well-being of humanity.

papers.title: Galilean Robots, Aristotelian Sensors: Joint Spatiotemporal Trajectory Estimation and Extrinsic Calibration
papers.abstract: Multi-sensor state estimation requires accurate spatial and temporal calibration between heterogeneous sensors. Existing spatiotemporal calibration methods typically represent sensor extrinsic parameters as a rigid-body transformation together with a scalar temporal offset, causing the spatial and temporal parameters to enter the estimation problem through separate mechanisms. While the spatial transformation composes directly with the robot pose, accounting for the temporal offset requires evaluating the trajectory at a shifted time, typically through motion compensation, interpolation, or a continuous-time trajectory representation. In this work, we formulate joint trajectory estimation and spatiotemporal calibration using the special Galilean group for the robot trajectory and the Aristotelian subgroup for sensor extrinsics. This representation incorporates the coupling between motion and temporal offset directly through the group structure, avoiding the need for a separately parameterized continuous-time trajectory. We develop twist- and IMU-driven motion priors, accommodate both ideal and non-ideal clocks, and evaluate the framework with camera, position, and range measurements. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate calibration and trajectory-estimation performance comparable to established methods across heterogeneous sensor configurations. Our simplified framework therefore offers a quality-of-life improvement over existing methods without compromising performance.

papers.intro:
Modern robotic platforms typically combine data from heterogeneous sensors, such as inertial measurement units (IMUs), cameras, lidars, and ranging radios. Fusing measurements from multiple sensors requires knowledge not only of their relative spatial configuration, but also of the times at which their measurements were acquired. Even when sensor clocks are synchronized, acquisition, processing, and communication delays can introduce temporal offsets between the reported timestamp and the underlying physical measurement event. Such offsets translate into spatial errors through the motion of the platform and can degrade the accuracy and consistency of state estimation [1, 2]. Consequently, spatiotemporal calibration, where inter-sensor spatial extrinsic parameters and temporal offsets are estimated jointly, is an important prerequisite for reliable multi-sensor fusion.

Existing approaches typically represent the extrinsic parameters as an element of \SE×ℝ\SE\times\mathbb{R} [1, 2, 3]: a rigid-body transformation together with a scalar temporal offset. Under this representation, the spatial and temporal components enter the estimation problem through fundamentally different mechanisms. The spatial transformation composes with the robot pose, whereas evaluating a measurement at a temporally shifted instant requires evaluating the trajectory away from the discrete state times, typically through motion compensation or interpolation between neighboring time instants [4]. Continuous-time approaches instead construct interpolants such as B-splines [5, 6] or Gaussian processes [7], and evaluate the measurement model at the shifted time. The widely used Kalibr toolbox [2] follows this continuous-time trajectory approach for camera–IMU calibration. These methods provide the temporal structure required for calibration by introducing an explicit continuous-time representation. However, this introduces additional representation choices, such as spline knot spacing and basis order, or GP kernel structure and hyperparameters.

papers.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
papers.abstract: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

papers.intro:
Temporal processing is fundamental to both biological and artificial intelligence, requiring systems to transform continuous inputs into structured internal representations. Effective training for temporal dynamics relies on accurate credit assignment over time, commonly addressed by backpropagation through time (BPTT, Werbos (2002)). However, BPTT requires storing and replaying full trajectories, limiting its applicability to online settings. In contrast, many natural and real-world systems operate continuously, where learning must occur in real time without access to stored past states, motivating the need for efficient online learning mechanisms. Prior research (Irie et al., 2024) suggests that online learning can also improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning settings.

Artificial neural networks typically employ instantaneous neurons, whose activations depend only on the current input. In contrast, leaky (integrating) neurons evolve according to continuous dynamics of the type τ​u˙=−u+W​r\tau\dot{u}=-u+Wr, where the membrane potential uu decays with time constant τ\tau while integrating presynaptic input rr through weights WW. These dynamics emulate biological membrane potentials and have therefore been widely adopted in computational neuroscience (Dayan and Abbott, 2005). Beyond biological inspiration, leaky neurons offer an intrinsic mechanism for temporal processing: each neuron implements a low-pass filter, and networks of such units naturally construct rich temporal kernels in an online manner. Unlike Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN, Bai et al. (2018)), which require access to full input sequences, leaky networks have the potential to process streaming data continuously while maintaining a distributed, multi-timescale memory, a power that has recently been demonstrated in models (Spieler et al., 2024; Ebato et al., 2024). Moreover, their dynamics align naturally with analog hardware, where voltage-based circuits exhibit leaky integration (Stoliar et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020).

Despite these advantages, online training of feedforward leaky networks remains fundamentally challenging. Due to temporal integration, activity at each layer influences future downstream responses, making the gradient depend jointly on spatial pathways and temporal dynamics, analogous to recurrent networks. In principle, exact gradients can be computed by BPTT or real-time recurrent learning (RTRL, Williams and Zipser (1989)). RTRL, while online, incurs prohibitive computational complexity of order 𝒪⁡(n4)\mathcal{O}(n^{4}), rendering it impractical beyond very small networks. Existing RTRL approximations either reduce complexity at the expense of gradient quality or fail to scale to deep architectures. As a result, investigating online learning in large and deep leaky networks remains challenging.

In this work, we introduce Kernel propagation (K-prop), a novel learning algorithm for feedforward leaky networks that achieves efficient, online, and accurate gradient approximation. The central idea is to express gradient contributions as a decomposition over exponential temporal kernels, and to propagate only their gain coefficients backward through the network. This transforms the combinatorial explosion of possible temporal pathways into a tractable, layer-wise computation analogous to standard backpropagation.

papers.title: ML Models Are Not Ciphers: Power Analysis for Weight Extraction Is Harder Than You Think
papers.abstract:
Can power-analysis techniques reveal secret weights of machine-learning models? Multiple recent works demonstrate proof-of-concept attacks that can partially recover such weights. To that end, these works build on techniques from cryptographic engineering, treating the model as a ``cipher'' and its secret weights as keys.
  We question the basic assumption behind such straightforward adaptations of cryptographic attacks and highlight the challenges arising when applying past techniques to fully recover all layers of deep neural networks. Unlike past works, which extract only a few weights, typically from shallow layers, we investigate the recovery of complete networks. Moreover, we target fully trained and functional models, rather than untrained, randomly initialized networks. To focus on fundamental challenges, we assume an unrealistically strong side-channel adversary that can directly observe the output of the leakage model without any added noise. With this adversary, we show that machine-learning models differ significantly from cryptographic implementations, giving rise to unique challenges that have not been observed in the prior art.
  We observe two main differences between machine-learning models and ciphers. First, in contrast to the high-diffusion nonlinear integer arithmetic prevalent in cryptographic schemes, machine-learning models tend to use limited-precision floating-point arithmetic and low-diffusion linear operations. We show that these operations introduce difficulties in weight recovery, often requiring an unexpectedly large number of traces, even under ideal channel conditions. Second, we observe that, unlike ciphers, which aim to increase the data entropy, machine-learning models aim to reduce it. This reduces data variability as the algorithm progresses, hampering weight recovery in deep layers of the model.

papers.intro:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have rapidly become the dominant approach for solving complex tasks such as object detection [38], image classification [54], audio processing [50], forecasting [67], and natural language processing [47]. Training these models requires carefully curated datasets, significant computational resources, and substantial human expertise. As a result, trained models, and particularly their learned weights, represent valuable intellectual property. The resources required to develop modern DNNs make their learned parameters a valuable asset, and consequently an appealing target for adversaries seeking to replicate or misuse proprietary models [30, 72]. This motivates a deeper examination of how such parameters may unintentionally leak.

This motivates a deeper examination of how such parameters may unintentionally leak.

In recent years, the machine-learning ecosystem has been undergoing a shift toward edge deployment [64]. To reduce latency, improve availability, and avoid transmitting sensitive user data to the cloud, many companies deploy trained models directly onto edge devices such as smart cameras, drones, and autonomous vehicles. In this work, we use the term edge GPU to refer to platforms, such as NVIDIA Jetson-class devices, designed for on-device inference in embedded robotics and Internet-of-Things (IoT) systems [15]. This deployment strategy prevents direct access to model weights, because they are not exposed through any accessible interface. However, it still places valuable models on devices under the physical control of potentially untrusted users. This creates an opportunity for physical side-channel attacks that bypass software-level protections.

Side-channel attacks extract information by observing incidental interactions between computation and the environment in which it takes place. A common example is Correlation Power Analysis (CPA), which correlates observed power consumption with hypothesized leakage models to recover secret values from computation [3]. In the past, side-channel attacks such as CPA mostly targeted cryptographic primitives [32, 3, 40]. However, more recently, multiple works have used CPA to extract weights from DNN implementations, targeting partial sums or the results of individual multiplications stored in registers. For example, CSI-NN [1] shows how to recover the hidden architecture and weights of multilayer perceptrons [18] and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [35]. Subsequent works target FPGAs [70, 36, 13, 69] and GPUs [23, 25] and use CPA-based techniques to extract model information such as architecture and weights. However, these works generally show the feasibility of CPA only on toy examples or, at most, on the first two layers of larger DNNs, and ignore error propagation. To the best of our knowledge, no prior attack has demonstrated parameter extraction of all the layers of a trained model, with realistic depth, parameter distributions, and architectural complexity, from edge devices.

In this work, we investigate the challenges of using side-channel attacks for such a full recovery of a DNN model. To facilitate the analysis, we focus only on intrinsic challenges that relate to the nature of leakage from DNN models, ignoring the challenges of physically measuring the leakage. To eliminate the effects of measurement limitations, such as interference, alignment, and device-specific behavior, we develop a simulation-based framework. Our framework uses the common Hamming weight (HW) and Hamming distance (HD) leakage models [3] and allows us to incorporate synthetic noise in the simulated measurements. Using this approach, we can systematically explore when, how, and to what extent correlation-based side-channel attacks can recover parameters from our target models.

Using this approach, we can systematically explore when, how, and to what extent correlation-based side-channel attacks can recover parameters from our target models.

Our main finding is that extraction of weights from DNNs presents new challenges that do not manifest in cryptographic attacks. We find that, in our setting, full key recovery of AES requires fewer than ten noise-free traces, whereas attacks on even simple DNNs may require more than 150,000 traces, often significantly more (Section 5.1). We analyze the causes of this stark difference and identify two fundamental differences between DNN models and cryptographic functions that contribute to it. The first difference is that, unlike cryptography, which aims to hide information and increase entropy, DNNs aim to extract information, i.e., reduce entropy. Consequently, as the computation progresses through the DNN model, the variability of the data tends to decrease [49]. However, CPA requires high data variability to distinguish between weight candidates. Hence, the decreased entropy hampers CPA attacks. We also find that we can increase the variability of the data in deeper layers by selecting data samples from the population that the model is designed to process, rather than selecting them uniformly at random, as is common in prior work [23] (see Section 4).

Floating-point computation behaves differently from the integer- or bit-vector-based computation typically used in cryptography. We further demonstrate that, due to properties of floating-point numbers, the Hamming distance model is inherently better suited than the Hamming weight model for CPA attacks on DNNs.

When attacking cryptography, the adversary aims to extract the exact secret. In contrast, when attacking DNN models, obtaining an approximate model is often sufficient. For example, an attacker might only need to reconstruct a model that achieves similar classification accuracy on benign samples, or one that is useful as a surrogate model for generating adversarial examples (Section 6). papers.title: More Papers, Not More Output: Collaboration and Publication Trends among Early-Career Researchers
papers.abstract: Concerns about publication pressure often assume that early-career researchers now produce more papers than comparable researchers did in the past. However, publication counts may give a misleading impression of individual publication output because research has become increasingly collaborative. Researchers can list more papers on their CVs not only by producing more work themselves, but also by working with more coauthors and sharing credit for the same papers. Whether the collaboration-adjusted output of early-career researchers has increased over time has rarely been examined empirically. This study addresses this gap by analysing publication records from more than 200,000 early-career researchers at Western research institutions across five major science, engineering, and health fields between 1996 and 2024. Recent cohorts appear on more papers than earlier cohorts, but they also work in much larger research teams. Once publication credit is divided among coauthors, collaboration-adjusted output remains stable or declines across all fields. These findings show that research evaluation metrics that ignore collaboration are increasingly poorly aligned with how scientific work is produced. Rising publication counts alone should therefore not be taken as evidence that early-career researchers are producing more individual publication output.

papers.title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
papers.abstract: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

papers.intro:
Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) plays an important role in many engineering applications in which the deformation of a structure affects the surrounding flow and, in turn, the resulting fluid loads influence the structural response. Examples arise in aerospace, wind energy, civil engineering, and other applications involving lightweight and flexible structures. In aeroelastic applications, for instance, structural deformations can significantly modify the aerodynamic loading, while the resulting fluid forces determine the structural response. The numerical prediction of this mutual interaction is therefore an important component in the analysis and design of flexible structures.

Examples arise in aerospace, wind energy, civil engineering, and other applications involving lightweight and flexible structures. In aeroelastic applications, for instance, structural deformations can significantly modify the aerodynamic loading, while the resulting fluid forces determine the structural response. The numerical prediction of this mutual interaction is therefore an important component in the analysis and design of flexible structures.

At early design stages, repeatedly resolving the complete three-dimensional structural geometry may be computationally expensive. Reduced-dimensional structural models are therefore particularly attractive for slender structures, as demonstrated by their widespread application in the aeroelastic analysis of aircraft wings [29, 40], helicopter rotor blades [33], and wind-turbine blades [17, 36]. In such applications, beam formulations can capture the dominant structural deformation mechanisms with substantially fewer degrees of freedom than shell or solid models.

In such applications, beam formulations can capture the dominant structural deformation mechanisms with substantially fewer degrees of freedom than shell or solid models.

Isogeometric analysis (IGA) provides an attractive framework for such beam formulations by employing spline basis functions, most commonly NURBS, to represent both the geometry and the unknown fields [22]. In addition to accurately representing curved geometries, spline-based approximations naturally provide higher inter-element continuity than standard displacement-based finite element discretizations. This property is particularly relevant for Bernoulli beams, whose bending kinematics require at least C1C^{1}-continuous centerline approximations. In the context of beam-based FSI, the continuity of the underlying approximation is also relevant to the reconstruction of the fluid interface, whose motion depends on both the beam centerline displacement and the orientation of its cross-sections.

Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) requires the satisfaction of kinematic and dynamic coupling conditions at the fluid–structure interface. Kinematic compatibility requires the fluid interface to follow the structural motion, while dynamic equilibrium requires the interface tractions exerted by the two fields to be in balance. These conditions can be enforced using either monolithic or partitioned solution strategies. In a monolithic approach, the governing equations of the fluid and structure are assembled and solved within a single coupled system [18, 21, 19]. In contrast, partitioned approaches solve the fluid and structural subproblems separately, exchanging interface quantities to satisfy the coupling conditions [14, 11, 12]. The latter strategy, adopted in this work, allows existing specialized solvers to be retained and combined within a modular framework [10].

Kinematic compatibility requires the fluid interface to follow the structural motion, while dynamic equilibrium requires the interface tractions exerted by the two fields to be in balance. These conditions can be enforced using either monolithic or partitioned solution strategies. In a monolithic approach, the governing equations of the fluid and structure are assembled and solved within a single coupled system [18, 21, 19]. In contrast, partitioned approaches solve the fluid and structural subproblems separately, exchanging interface quantities to satisfy the coupling conditions [14, 11, 12]. The latter strategy, adopted in this work, allows existing specialized solvers to be retained and combined within a modular framework [10].

For transient partitioned FSI, coupling must be addressed in both time and space. Temporal coupling determines how the individual solvers advance and exchange information within each time step, whereas spatial coupling concerns the transfer of kinematic and load quantities between the fluid and structural interface discretizations. When these discretizations are non-matching, suitable mapping operators are required to transfer interface quantities while preserving the relevant coupling properties [13]. This becomes particularly challenging when the structural model is represented by a one-dimensional beam and the fluid interface by a two-dimensional surface, as considered in this work.

Spatial coupling is already non-trivial when both fields provide surface discretizations, since the fluid and structural interface meshes generally do not coincide. Different resolution requirements and independent discretizations of the two fields naturally lead to non-matching interfaces. Consequently, considerable attention has been devoted to the transfer of motion and loads between non-matching meshes [13, 10]. Approaches include nearest-neighbor and projection-based interpolation, radial basis function methods, and mortar-type formulations. De Boer et al. [10] provided a comparative review of several such coupling methods, while Wang et al. [42] subsequently assessed nearest-element, standard mortar, and dual mortar mappings for non-matching meshes and geometries in computational FSI.

Besides interpolation accuracy, spatial coupling must ensure an appropriate transfer of motion and loads across the interface. Several approaches have therefore addressed conservation properties for non-matching discretizations, including consistent and conservative transfer strategies [13, 9], conservative load transfer across curved interfaces [23], and mortar-based coupling of isogeometric B-Rep and fluid discretizations [2]. These methods provide a general framework for non-matching interfaces, but typically assume that the interface geometry is explicitly represented on both sides of the coupling.

papers.title: Reconfiguring System-Level Protection Through Bounded Delegation in RISC-V MCUs
papers.abstract: MCU-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly require protection policies to change at runtime as resources, software, and system composition evolve. Yet widely used COTS MCU protection mechanisms are still largely designed around statically established policies. While they can restrict which domains modify protection primitives, they generally do not constrain what policy an authorized domain may create. As a result, domains may expand protection rules beyond their intended scope or interfere with boundaries established by other domains. We identify bounded configuration authority as a missing primitive for secure dynamic policy evolution and introduce an ownership-aware model in which explicit ownership and rule containment bound both configuration authority and recursive delegation. Changes to active protection-rule ranges are validated before commit, preserving protection boundaries without extending the normal access-checking datapath. We implement the model in an open-source RISC-V World Checker integrated into a CVA6-based SoC. Our FPGA evaluation shows no degradation in access latency or operating frequency, with 7.1% LUT and 1.2% FF overhead for eight rules. In an OTA update case study, direct reconfiguration under delegated authority reduces policy-transition latency by 89.5% over hypervisor mediation and 94.6% over trusted firmware mediation, while preserving established authority boundaries. All artifacts will be open-sourced to support the evolution of RISC-V specifications and system-level protection designs.

papers.intro:
Modern microcontroller (MCU)-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly consolidate heterogeneous and mixed-criticality workloads over shared memories, peripherals, and accelerators [12, 29]. Unlike application processors, these systems commonly rely on lightweight, physical-address, region-based protection mechanisms, traditionally configured statically by trusted firmware or a root of trust [2, 39, 14]. Emerging MCU systems, however, increasingly require resource assignments and their associated protection policies to evolve at runtime, driven by changing operating modes and evolving criticality requirements [15, 6, 51, 9].

A prominent example is an over-the-air (OTA) software update [31]. A communication domain (DCD_{C}) may receive an update image into a buffer (RbR_{b}) and use a hardware accelerator (HaH_{a}) to process the incoming data. Before installation, both the buffer and accelerator may need to be transferred to an isolated validation domain (DVD_{V}) for authentication and validation. Copying the image introduces additional memory traffic and latency, while permanent sharing prevents exclusive control. Instead, the protection policy can be updated in place by firmware to revoke DCD_{C}’s access and grant access to DVD_{V}. Identical transitions arise when shared buffers are resized, accelerators are reassigned across operating modes, or software components are incrementally deployed [13, 42]. However, retaining configuration authority in trusted firmware requires mediation for each handover, increasing policy-transition latency. This dependency also limits autonomy in hierarchical systems, where trusted boot firmware establishes the protection state and assigns selected resources to a real-time operating system (RTOS) or hypervisor [41, 21], which may then further partition and assign them among applications or guests [30, 23, 19, 51]. Without the ability to delegate configuration authority, these software layers still require firmware intervention to update protection policies. Direct hardware-supported delegation of configuration authority through these layers avoids repeated privileged software mediation [46], but introduces a fundamental challenge: configuration access alone does not bound policy authority.

Protection mechanisms used in mainstream commercial of-the-shelf (COTS) MCUs commonly expose memory-mapped configuration interfaces through which trusted software programs rules associating physical address ranges or resources with execution contexts and access permissions [1, 38]. Access to these interfaces may itself be restricted through additional protection rules [18], execution-domain identifiers [27, 25], or write-protection mechanisms [16, 34]. These mechanisms determine who may issue an update, but generally do not constrain what policy an authorized domain may create. Consider again the OTA update. The boot process delegates configuration authority over RbR_{b} to DCD_{C}, making DCD_{C} the only domain authorized to reprogram the corresponding protection rule. However, DCD_{C} may then expand that rule beyond the intended subregion (Figure 1). In mechanisms where multiple matching rules contribute to the effective policy, DCD_{C} may also create an overlapping rule that weakens protection over a region belonging to another domain. In both cases, DCD_{C} modifies only configuration state it controls, yet affects policy outside its intended authority. Existing mechanisms can therefore transfer configuration access without necessarily binding that authority to an enforceable policy boundary.

It allows protection policies to evolve at runtime with hardware enforcing who may modify each rule and which updates are valid. Our key observation is that this hierarchy does not need to be represented through a separate delegation hierarchy. papers.title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
papers.abstract: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.

papers.title: Residual-Based Spectral Submanifold Reduction of Constrained Multibody Systems on Matrix Lie Groups
papers.abstract: The parameterization method yields efficient and accurate reduced-order models for nonlinear dynamical systems, but existing procedures that compute them assume polynomial vector fields on vector spaces. Constrained multibody systems instead obey differential-algebraic equations on matrix Lie groups such as $\mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3)$ and $SE(3)$. Minimal parameterizations of these groups lead to non-polynomial equations that must be approximated or recast before reduction, and current implementations require the nonlinearities as explicit multilinear maps, which are cumbersome to construct for assembled multibody systems. This work develops a parameterization framework for constrained multibody systems on matrix Lie groups. Rigid and floating frame of reference bodies use rotation-matrix components or Euler parameters, while geometrically exact beam elements use an Euler-Rodrigues representation that eliminates the logarithmic map and expresses the exponential map polynomially, retaining screw-motion interpolation. The reduced-order models satisfy linear joint constraints exactly, and a rotation-preserving parameterization keeps the configuration on the Lie group to machine precision. The parameterization method is formulated directly in terms of the assembled residual, so that only residual evaluations and their derivatives are required. Truncated Taylor arithmetic delivers all Taylor coefficients of a given order from a single residual evaluation, and a non-intrusive coupling to codes with real-valued residuals is demonstrated with the multibody code Exudyn. Numerical examples show accurate prediction of backbone curves, forced response curves, and internal resonances at substantially reduced computational cost.

For instance, the exponential map, together with its tangent operator and its inverse, arises in the configuration update of Lie-group integrators [11, 30]. Li and co-workers [38] extended SSM theory and computation to mechanical systems with holonomic constraints formulated as differential-algebraic equations. papers.title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

papers.intro:
As Carl Sagan observed, “Science is a way of thinking much more than it is a body of knowledge.” Scientific discovery involves more than producing new hypotheses or accumulating findings. It unfolds through an iterative loop: scientific search generates and tests ideas, scientific understanding develops through the interpretation of the resulting findings, and this understanding guides subsequent search [1]. Researchers move within and between hypothesis and experiment spaces around a scientific question, proposing explanations, designing tests, and interpreting experimental, computational, or observational feedback [2]. Interpreting this feedback develops a working understanding of the problem: which judgments are supported, which conflicts remain unresolved, under which conditions findings apply, and which regularities may transfer across cases. As understanding changes, researchers revise hypotheses, reformulate questions, redesign experiments, and reassess which direction merits further effort. Classical problem-solving research describes how representations, operators, and heuristics organize this search and guide subsequent action [3, 4]. The central design question is how to retain the understanding developed during search and use it to select and adapt representations, operators, and heuristics, so that search experience informs subsequent research decisions.

Recent AI systems have extended one-shot idea generation into iterative scientific workflows. The AI Scientist connects ideation with experiments, analysis, and paper writing [5]; Co-Scientist organizes hypothesis generation, critique, and improvement [6]; and Robin combines multi-agent reasoning with experimental feedback [7]. Iteration alone, however, does not ensure that findings from different branches are retained with their evidence and applicability conditions, or that these findings affect later method selection. When iteration depends mainly on feedback from the current round, earlier failures, unresolved conflicts, and shared dependencies can be overlooked, leading to repeated errors or further search along unproductive paths. Search can also become overly responsive to recent outcomes, delaying recognition of key uncertainties or a change in targets, representations, or reasoning methods. A scientific agent therefore needs to preserve understanding across the search and use it to regulate what to investigate next and how to investigate it.

Often described as “thinking about thinking,” metacognition involves monitoring, and regulation of one’s own cognitive processes [8]. Nelson and Narens distinguish an object level that performs a task from a meta level that maintains a dynamic model of the object-level cognition and regulates its process through monitoring and control [9]. Prior work examines how artificial systems can monitor and adjust their own problem-solving processes [10], complementary research on strategy selection motivates matching reasoning methods to the task and current state [11]. Viewed through the lens of metacognition, object-level search develops scientific understanding, while the meta level selectively represents this understanding and assesses its implications for further search, guiding decisions about which premises to examine, representations to revise, methods to apply, or branches to stop. We adopt this functional distinction as architectural inspiration for explicit search regulation.

papers.title: Certified Zonotopic Reachability Analysis for Trajectory Tracking on Lie Groups
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles track planned trajectories close to obstacles. Unknown disturbances make them deviate from these trajectories. With a bound on the tracking error that disturbances can cause, a planned trajectory can be certified as safe before execution. Existing set-based methods bound the tracking error by one invariant ellipsoid for the whole trajectory or by intervals, which are both conservative. For aerial and space vehicles, the tracking error evolves on a matrix Lie group with nonlinear dynamics. However, for group-affine systems, the error dynamics are linear in Lie algebra coordinates when the vehicle receives the inputs of the reference. The control input and the disturbance enter through the inverse right Jacobian, a matrix that depends on the error. We propagate the linear part of the error dynamics with zonotopes and enclose the effect of the inverse right Jacobian on the disturbance in closed form. The resulting tubes are tight and provably contain all reachable tracking errors in continuous time. When some error components have no input, the inverse right Jacobian leaves unmatched nonlinear terms in the closed loop. None of the tested methods certifies such a closed loop. Hybrid coordinates make these terms matched, so that our controller cancels every nonlinear term that does not contain the disturbance. Our tubes give tighter bounds than the ellipsoid method in simulations of a planar aircraft and a fully actuated multirotor and in real flights of a quadrotor, where the tube contains every measured attitude error. Under larger disturbances and the same feedback gain, the ellipsoid method yields no valid ellipsoid, whereas our tubes remain valid.

We call the planned trajectory the reference and the deviation from it the tracking error. A planned trajectory can be certified before execution with a tube, a time-varying set that contains every tracking error that disturbances within given bounds can cause at every time instant (Chutinan and Krogh, 2003). If the region that the tube covers around the reference avoids all obstacles, the vehicle avoids them during execution. A tighter tube certifies trajectories that pass closer to obstacles.

Tubes around a reference trajectory are a standard tool for motion planning under disturbances. Tube model predictive control bounds the deviation of a linear discrete-time system from its nominal trajectory by a disturbance invariant set (Mayne et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2026). Funnel libraries precompute funnels along a set of maneuvers by sum-of-squares programming and compose them online (Majumdar and Tedrake, 2017). Control contraction metrics give tubes around every feasible nominal trajectory (Singh et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2022). FaSTrack (Chen et al., 2021) computes tracking error bounds that hold for every trajectory of a planner by Hamilton–Jacobi reachability. For quadrotors, geometric controllers on S​E​(3)SE(3) keep the tracking errors uniformly ultimately bounded under bounded disturbances (Lee et al., 2013). Zonotope reachability computes forward reachable sets of planned quadrotor trajectories with an approximation of the trajectory-dependent tracking error (Kousik et al., 2019). Our tubes are reachable sets of the tracking error in Lie algebra coordinates, computed for one given reference. They contain the tracking error at every time instant.

papers.title: AI-based characterization of lymphoid structures and the tumor microenvironment reveals lower mature tertiary lymphoid structures, lymph-node follicles, and plasma cells after neoadjuvant therapy in lung squamous cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: Mature, germinal centre-bearing tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) and mature lymph node follicles (secondary lymphoid structures, SLS) sustain the plasma cell response that shapes outcome and immunotherapy benefit in lung cancer. How this loco-regional axis differs between neoadjuvant-treated and therapy-naive tumors is poorly defined. We analyzed H&E whole-slide images of resected tumors and paired proximal and distal lymph nodes from matched neoadjuvant-treated (neoLUSC, n=20) and therapy-naive (naivLUSC, n=20) lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) patients. Aignostics Atlas H&E Tissue Analysis (HETA) models quantified cell densities per tissue compartment and cell-cell co-localization; a dedicated deep-learning model validated against pathologist annotations detected TLS and SLS and graded their maturity. Prognostic value was tested in an independent cohort (n=458; 46 treated). In neoLUSC tumors, stromal plasma cell density was 72% (p=0.004) and stromal lymphocyte density 48% (p=0.015) lower than in naivLUSC; macrophages and granulocytes did not differ significantly. Total and immature TLS did not differ, whereas mature TLS in the tumor (p=0.034) and mature SLS in the tumor-distal lymph node (p=0.003) were lower in neoLUSC patients. Peri-TLS plasma cell density correlated with tumor lymphocyte density in naivLUSC (rho=0.54, p=0.017) but not in neoLUSC tumors (rho=0.07). In the validation cohort, stromal plasma cell density (HR 0.69, p=0.011) and lymphocyte-plasma cell co-localization (HR 0.66, p=0.004) were associated with longer survival, and neoadjuvant status with shorter survival (HR 1.50, p=0.026). Neoadjuvant therapy is thus associated with fewer mature lymphoid structures and weaker coupling of the humoral compartment to the tumor rather than uniformly lower immune readouts. The stromal plasma cell/co-localization axis is a candidate prognostic biomarker.

papers.title: Search for a Dispersion Measure Excess Toward Nearby Galaxy Halos Using Fast Radio Bursts from the Second CHIME/FRB Baseband Catalog
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) probe foreground ionized baryons via their dispersion measures (DM). Using 1748 sub-arcminute-localized sources from the Second CHIME/FRB Baseband Catalog, we conduct a statistical stacking study of the circumgalactic media (CGM) of nearby galaxies by analyzing the DMs of FRBs whose sightlines intersect foreground halos. For galaxy halos within 50 Mpc, we measure a mean DM excess of $119\pm44$ pc~cm$^{-3}$ $(p = 0.0053; \sim 2.6\sigma)$ within one virial radius. Expanding to 150 Mpc (628 intersections), we find a tentative decline in the mean DM as a function of impact parameter $(p = 0.0046; \sim 2.6\sigma)$, which is predominantly driven by typical Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies $(10 \leq \log(M_*/M_\odot)\leq 11)$. We use this DM profile to constrain parameters of the CGM electron density distribution, $n_e^\mathrm{CGM}(r) \propto r^{-3\beta}$, finding an extrapolated central electron density in the range of $(1.7-21.1) \times 10^{-3}\mathrm{\,cm}^{-3}$, with a radial power-law index of $\beta = 0.68^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$, consistent with constraints from X-ray stacking studies of MW-like galaxies. At very low impact parameters, we detect a significant DM deficit likely due to cross-matching FRBs that originate from galaxies within our galaxy sample. By deriving the DM-galaxy cross-correlation function, we show that this deficit matches theoretical predictions if 20 FRBs originate from galaxies within 150 Mpc, indicating that CHIME/FRB detects a higher fraction of low-$z$ FRBs than previously thought. We forecast that $10^4$ FRBs with similar localization errors will provide a 5-$\sigma$ detection of the CGM, and that FRBs at intermediate redshifts ($0.4\lesssim z_\mathrm{FRB}\lesssim 0.75$) are ideal for studying intervening CGMs.

papers.intro:
Fast radio bursts [95, FRBs;] are incredibly useful probes of intervening plasma as they experience a variety of propagation effects whilst they traverse through astrophysical plasma. As FRBs propagate through plasma, they undergo a dispersive delay [72] such that lower frequencies arrive at a later time, and their transient nature allows us measure this dispersive delay. This time delay is proportional to the dispersion measure (DM), which is given by the integral of the free electron density along the observer’s line of sight (LOS): DM=∫0zne​(z′)cm−3​11+z′​d​ld​z′​pc​d​z′,\displaystyle\mathrm{DM}=\int_{0}^{z}\frac{n_{e}(z^{\prime})}{\mathrm{cm^{-3}}}\frac{1}{1+z^{\prime}}\frac{dl}{dz^{\prime}\mathrm{pc}}dz^{\prime}, (1) where nen_{e} is the free electron density in cm-3 and zz is the redshift of the source. Since nen_{e} traces the density of plasma, an FRB’s DM informs us about the total ionized plasma content between the observer and the source. Because the vast majority of the baryonic matter in the Universe is thought to exist as ionized plasma [63, 24, e.g.,], and since FRBs are the only known sources originating outside the Local Group with DMs, they serve as unique probes of the baryonic distribution of the Universe. In addition to dispersion, FRBs also undergo other propagation effects, such as Faraday rotation [139, 121, e.g.,], and scattering and scintillation [129], which can inform us about the magnetism [6, e.g.,] and turbulence [164, e.g.,] of plasma environments in the Universe, respectively.

The hot phase occupies the largest volume and mass fraction [116, 92, ≳99%\gtrsim 99\%; e.g.,] of the CGM; despite this, it remains poorly constrained due to its low density [58, e.g.,], which makes detecting it in X-ray emission difficult. Because of this, X-ray studies of the CGM of single galaxies have been limited to the CGM of the Milky Way [16, 94, MW; e.g.,]. To address this low X-ray photon count problem with single sources, statistical studies combining the emission of multiple galaxies as a function of virial radius have been recently conducted to constrain the baryon distribution in the inner CGM ≲100\lesssim 100 kpc [167, e.g.,]. In contrast, FRB DMs scale linearly with nen_{e}, making them uniquely sensitive to the diffuse, extended gas in the outer CGM. Thus, the distribution of baryons in the hot phase remains poorly understood and can be constrained with FRB DMs.

papers.title: Tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion in CeRh$_{2}$As$_{2}$
papers.abstract: CeRh$_{2}$As$_{2}$ is best known for its two superconducting phases, which are observed when a magnetic field is applied along the $c$ axis of its tetragonal unit cell. The emergence of superconductivity, with $T_{c} \approx 0.31$K, is preceded by an ordered state (phase I), with an ordering temperature $T_{0} \approx 0.46$K. The precise nature of the order parameter in phase I is still unknown, although evidence of dipolar ordering was found. To investigate a possible symmetry breaking at $T_{\textrm{0}}$, we conducted longitudinal thermal-expansion measurements along the crystallographic [100], [010], [110], and [1$\overline{1}$0] directions on a single-crystalline sample cut into an octagonal shape. Our results demonstrate the breaking of the fourfold in-plane symmetry below $T_{\textrm{0}}$, evidencing a small tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion (orthorhombicity $\delta \sim 10^{-7}$). The breaking of the tetragonal symmetry at $T_{\textrm{0}}$ might imply that the superconducting order parameter that develops within phase I cannot be multi-component. More generally, the distortion places restrictions on the possible order parameters for phase I.

papers.title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

papers.intro:
Agentic visual reasoning addresses the evidence-sparse bottleneck in perception-centered tasks by equipping vision-language models (VLMs) with tools to acquire fine-grained evidence. Related studies include think with images [32, 46, 48, 13, 33, 34, 25] and think with videos [45, 41, 12, 28]. However, invoking a tool does not guarantee that the model uses what it returns. We term this problem observation neglect, where a model acquires an intermediate observation but its subsequent reasoning is largely unaffected [37]. Alongside efforts to improve when tools are invoked [33, 42, 34], this raises a complementary question of how to train models to make effective use of the acquired observation.

Agentic visual reasoning addresses the evidence-sparse bottleneck in perception-centered tasks by equipping vision-language models (VLMs) with tools to acquire fine-grained evidence. Related studies include think with images [32, 46, 48, 13, 33, 34, 25] and think with videos [45, 41, 12, 28]. However, invoking a tool does not guarantee that the model uses what it returns. We term this problem observation neglect, where a model acquires an intermediate observation but its subsequent reasoning is largely unaffected [37]. Alongside efforts to improve when tools are invoked [33, 42, 34], this raises a complementary question of how to train models to make effective use of the acquired observation.

Meanwhile, most previous works focus exclusively on a single modality, while the few that simultaneously incorporate image and video tools rely on a mixed-data SFT-then-RL training paradigm. However, this often leaves the final unified model significantly lagging behind the one trained on a single modality. We argue that this is the combined result of the pattern conflict of off-policy SFT training and the supervision sparsity of RL. A more promising alternative is a densely supervised, predominantly on-policy training paradigm. On-policy distillation (OPD) serves as a foundational approach: by supervising the student’s own rollouts with dense token-level feedback, it bypasses both the sparse credit assignment of RL and the reference bias of off-policy imitation [1, 31]. Extending this paradigm, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [24] routes student-generated trajectories to domain-specialized teachers, and has been increasingly adopted by frontier models [23, 44, 14, 5, 4]. Subsequent works further refine it in terms of capability imbalance [11], heterogeneous convergence [2], behavioral drift under tool use [29], and cross-modal routing [20, 27]. However, existing paradigms primarily refine how supervision is delivered without intervening in rollout trajectories. This is a critical limitation for agentic visual reasoning since subsequent supervision is all conditioned on what tools returned.

Together, the two training stages enforce the two core properties for effective tool use: GD-GRPO makes the acquired observation necessary, while OG-MOPD keeps it valid. Furthermore, diagnostic analyses on observation dependence confirm that Reframe exhibits a markedly stronger causal reliance on tool-returned results than previous methods.

papers.title: A Computational Brainsphere Model for the Simulation of Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract:
Nowadays, there are different medical imaging techniques to collect data about the progression of
  Alzhei\-mer's disease in a patient's brain. These data describe different phenomena which are still
  not understood from a biological point of view.
  How can these data sets be combined in a mathematical model to simulate the evolution of such a
  neurodegenerative disease in a computer?
  In this snapshot, we present one possible approach to address this task with the help of graph theory
  and partial differential equations.

papers.intro:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a slowly progressing neurodegenerative disease causing the brain to shrink and brain cells to die. Much progress has been made in investigating the course and certain biomarkers of the disease. The perhaps largest attention is currently focused on two proteins that behave conspicuously in the brain of an Alzheimer’s patient: On the one hand, beta-amyloid peptides aggregate in the surrounding area of the neuronal network in the brain as plaques [8]. On the other hand, there are abnormally folded tau proteins which accumulate in the neurons in form of tangles and are believed to affect their functioning and, finally, to cause their death [9].

Much progress has been made in investigating the course and certain biomarkers of the disease. The perhaps largest attention is currently focused on two proteins that behave conspicuously in the brain of an Alzheimer’s patient: On the one hand, beta-amyloid peptides aggregate in the surrounding area of the neuronal network in the brain as plaques [8]. On the other hand, there are abnormally folded tau proteins which accumulate in the neurons in form of tangles and are believed to affect their functioning and, finally, to cause their death [9].

In the past, it was only possible to examine the brains of dead Alzheimer’s patients. The development of modern medical imaging techniques made it possible to visualize protein plaques in the brains of living patients as well (in-vivo data). PET scanners measure accumulations of tau and beta-amyloid, and functional MRI as well as DTI scanners provide indications of the structure and functioning of a human brain. Central goal of subsequent studies is the behavior of tau and beta-amyloid as well as the connectivity patterns in the brain.

A relatively new model for tau propagation is the transneuronal spread hypothesis. Transneuronal means that tangles travel from neuron to neuron, inducing tangles in neighboring neurons in a prion-like fashion. The word prion is a combination of “protein”, and “infection”, indicating that missfolded proteins can infect others. According to this hypothesis, the connectivity of neurons is a driver for tau pathology, i.e., highly interconnected neurons are more likely to receive pathology [7].

The crucial challenge is to analyze and combine the in-vivo data within in a mathematical framework. We propose a Computational Brainsphere Model for the Simulation of Alzheimer’s Disease which consists of three interacting parts: 1. A Brain Network Model to represent the human brain as a dynamical network, or, in mathematical terms, as a graph, and to investigate the effects of tau pathology on the connectivity patterns; 2. A Tau Distribution Model to simulate the spreading of tau proteins across the brain network; 3. A Beta-Amyloid Model to model the dispersion of beta-amyloid in the environment of the brain network. In the following, we will give a brief introduction to the Brain Network and the Tau Distribution Model. These have, as described above, a reciprocal dependency, i.e., the network structure influences the propagation of tau, and the presence of tau influences the structure of the network.

papers.title: Analysis of Solid Boron Injection for ITER
papers.abstract: Since ITER will now operate with a full tungsten divertor and first wall, the ITER Organization is considering boron wall conditioning schemes to getter oxygen and reduce tungsten sputtering to avoid excessive radiation to ensure that ITER can reach and sustain high- performance plasma operation. ITER has adopted Glow Discharge Boronization (GDB) in deuterated diborane (B$_2$D$_6$) as its main technique, which can only be performed in the absence of magnetic fields, but has also requested a study to determine how effective solid boron injection (SBI), which can be performed during plasma operation, using either an Impurity Powder Dropper (IPD) or a boron pellet injector, might be as a risk mitigation to achieving Q=10. Solid impurity injection has been used for decades as a wall conditioning technique on numerous tokamaks and stellarators around the world. The study presented here begins to assess SBI on ITER by first quantifying the boron source term across a particle size scan from 1 $\mu$m to 5 mm diameter and an injection velocity scan from 5 -- 200 m/s for several ITER plasma conditions: 1) Start of Research Operations (SRO) diverted L-mode, 2) Q=10 H-mode, and 3) low plasma current and low power limiter operation. Modeling of the ablation, transport, erosion and redeposition of solid boron is being carried out with the Dust Injection Simulator (DIS), the Neutral Gas Shielding (NGS), EMC3-EIRENE and WallDYN3D models. In the first steps presented here, the DIS and NGS models are compared for calculating the boron source term that is then used as input to EMC3-EIRENE and will later be used with WallDYN3D.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Acceleration of TRIMEG++ code using OpenMP for Gyrokinetic Simulations
papers.abstract: Turbulent transport largely determines the performance of magnetic-confinement fusion devices such as tokamaks, and gyrokinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations are a principal tool to predict it. Advancing up to hundreds of millions of markers and solving large sparse field systems at every time step makes whole-device simulations among the most expensive in plasma physics. GPUs can accelerate this workload, but porting a complex code requires restructuring its parallelism and memory traffic, ideally without a separate version per vendor. In this work, the gyrokinetic code TRIMEG-C1, whose unstructured triangular mesh and high-order finite elements cover both the confined core and the open-field-line edge of the plasma, is rewritten in C++ as TRIMEG++ and fully offloaded to GPUs with OpenMP target directives, so that one portable code base runs on both AMD and NVIDIA hardware. The particle-to-grid projection is offloaded in its standard and field-aligned formulations, the PETSc-based field solver runs on the GPU through the library's backends, and, together with the previously offloaded particle pusher, every stage whose cost scales with the marker count runs on the GPU. All speedups are node-to-node comparisons against a 256-core CPU node (2x AMD EPYC 9754). On the TCV-X21 tokamak reference case, the offloaded kernels reproduce the CPU results to a relative accuracy of 1e-11, and the full simulation runs 4.1-6.1x faster on a node with two AMD MI300A and 2.1-3.0x faster on a node with four NVIDIA A100, with the speedup growing with problem size. The MI300A, with shared CPU-GPU memory, needs no explicit data transfers, whereas the A100 needs them managed by hand. These results show that directive-based offloading can accelerate a complex gyrokinetic code across GPU vendors, making whole-volume tokamak simulations with hundreds of millions of markers practical on a single GPU node.
