papers.intro:
Nuclear fusion offers the prospect of a clean, virtually inexhaustible source of energy, and the central open problem on the path to a fusion reactor is confinement: the performance of a magnetic-confinement device such as a tokamak is largely set by the turbulent transport of heat and particles across the confining field. Because this turbulence cannot be fully diagnosed in experiments, numerical simulation is the principal tool for understanding and predicting it. The reference framework for this task is the gyrokinetic model, in which the fast gyromotion of the charged particles around the magnetic field lines is averaged out analytically, reducing the phase space from six to five dimensions while retaining the drift dynamics and parallel streaming that drive microturbulence (Lee, 1983; Fitzpatrick, 2014). Gyrokinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations remain nevertheless extremely demanding: a whole-device run evolves tens to hundreds of millions of marker particles over thousands of time steps, solving large sparse linear systems for the perturbed electromagnetic fields at every step. The majority of existing gyrokinetic codes restrict this calculation to the closed-flux-surface core of the plasma (Lin et al., 1998; Lanti et al., 2020; Kleiber et al., 2024), exploiting a structured mesh and a Fourier decomposition in the poloidal plane; this approach breaks down at the separatrix and cannot be extended across it, yet the scrape-off layer and the divertor govern the exhaust of heat and particles and are essential to predicting plasma-facing component loads in devices such as ITER. Reliable whole-device predictions therefore require a single, self-consistent simulation spanning the confined core and the open-field-line region (Hager et al., 2022; Michels et al., 2021), at a computational cost that is among the highest in plasma physics.

TRIMEG-C1 (TRIangular MEsh based Gyrokinetic code) meets this requirement by discretising the poloidal cross-section with an unstructured triangular mesh, which conforms to the separatrix without artificial periodicity and needs no poloidal Fourier filter (Lu et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2024). Higher-order C1C^{1} finite elements give the accuracy required for electromagnetic simulations across the full plasma volume, and the piecewise field-aligned finite element method (PFAFEM) has been developed on top of this mesh for the efficient simulation of individual toroidal harmonics (Lu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025c). This combination of unstructured geometry and high-order elements makes TRIMEG-C1 more complex, and hence considerably harder to port to a graphics processing unit (GPU), than a structured-mesh core code. Over the last decade the growth of supercomputing performance has come almost entirely from massively parallel accelerators rather than from faster CPU cores. The exascale machines that opened the current era, and an increasing share of mid-size academic clusters, deliver most of their throughput and power efficiency through GPUs. For an established scientific code such as TRIMEG-C1, this shift is both an opportunity, a potential order of magnitude in throughput, and a challenge, since exploiting a GPU efficiently requires exposing massive data parallelism and managing the host–device memory traffic explicitly. This must be carried out on hardware from vendors whose native programming models differ substantially, e.g., NVIDIA and AMD. Maintaining one portable code base across this heterogeneous landscape, rather than a separate version per architecture, is one of the central practical problems of current high-performance computing (HPC), and it is the problem this work addresses for TRIMEG-C1.

This paper reports the porting of TRIMEG-C1 to GPUs using OpenMP target directives, a directive-based, vendor-agnostic programming model that keeps a single source code for every platform. The code was first restructured in C++, which both modernises the software and gives OpenMP offloading a uniform compilation path across compiler toolchains. On this base, the two stages that dominate the cost of a time step are offloaded to the device: the particle-to-grid (P2G) projection, in both its non-field-aligned (Lu et al., 2024) and field-aligned (Lu et al., 2026) formulations, supported by a GPU-native evaluator of the equilibrium B-splines and a spatial sort of the markers; and the PETSc-based field solver, through the library’s Kokkos and CUDA GPU backends, with a rank-independent matrix restart format and a solver sub-communicator that decouples the rank count of the solve from that of the particle kernels. Combined with the particle pusher offloaded previously by Daneri (Daneri et al., 2026), these bring the whole time-stepping loop onto the device, leaving the host only the MPI reductions, the solver orchestration, and the diagnostics. Everything is developed and benchmarked on production HPC systems: the Viper-GPU cluster at the Max Planck Computing and Data Facility (MPCDF), built with 2 AMD MI300A accelerated processing units (APUs) with ∼\sim122.6 TFLOPS/s of peak double precision (FP64), the Raven cluster at MPCDF with 4 discrete NVIDIA A100 GPUs providing ∼\sim 38.8 TFLOPS/s of FP64, and the TOK CPU cluster at IPP Garching, whose nodes, each with two 128-core AMD EPYC 9754 (Zen 4c) processors, serve as the 256-core baseline, with an estimated peak FP64 performance of 25.4 TFLOP/s, calculated from 2 CPUs×\times128 cores×\times3.1 GHz×\times32 FLOPs/cycle, assuming two 512-bit FP64 FMA instructions per core per cycle. Running the same kernels on a unified-memory APU and on a conventional discrete GPU gives a direct measure of the architecture requirements and performance returns.

papers.title: What observations are needed to advance our theoretical understanding of galaxy formation at high redshift?
papers.abstract: Although significant progress has been made over recent decades, a comprehensive and predictive framework for galaxy formation remains elusive. Starting from cosmological initial conditions, current models cannot a priori accurately predict key galaxy properties such as their structure, size, star formation histories, chemical abundance patterns, or supermassive black hole mass. This challenge stems from the vast range of spatial scales involved, as numerical simulations must simultaneously account for sub-AU processes nearby stars and black holes in addition to Mpc-scale cosmological gas inflows/outflows and environmental effects. Consequently, simulations must rely on subgrid models and approximations. As a result, theoretical progress in galaxy formation remains fundamentally driven by observational data and the iterative testing of model predictions against empirical results. Here we highlight five key open problems in theoretical galaxy formation that require dedicated observations of the high-redshift Universe, beyond what can currently be achieved through GO programs.

papers.title: DMAJOR: A JWST Legacy Survey of Protoplanetary Disks
papers.abstract: We propose an infrared imaging survey of resolved protoplanetary disks spanning a range of galactic environments, directly mapping the 3D structure of planet-forming disks across the IR. DMAJOR (Disk Motions and Architectures JWST Observational Reference survey), our legacy survey, will deliver a benchmark sample to reveal structure and connection to environment. The exquisite stability of JWST allows us to probe for variability with a time-scheduled revisit strategy, while its sensitivity and resolution open a window on disks unobservable from the ground. A uniform sample will reveal how small grains and ice are distributed in protoplanetary disks, how scattered light structures relate to large-scale environmental features, and identify new companions. To achieve this, DMAJOR takes advantage of model-based data analysis using telemetry and mutual calibration to enhance processed data products while minimizing telescope overheads.

papers.title: Probing circumstellar interaction with spectroscopy of ZTF hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (H-rich SLSNe) are rare, exceptionally luminous transients. Most exhibit narrow Balmer emission and can be further classified as SLSNe-IIn, indicating interaction with dense circumstellar material (CSM). We present and analyse 304 optical spectra of 106 H-rich SLSNe observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). We examine their spectral evolution and Balmer-line properties, and model the H$\alpha$ profiles using Monte Carlo electron-scattering calculations. Of the 106 objects, 105 exhibit narrow Balmer emission consistent with SLSN-IIn classifications, including six with additional Ia-CSM-like characteristics and three with possible flash-ionisation features; the remaining one object exhibits only broad Balmer emission and is classified as a SLSN-II. Post-peak Balmer profiles range from approximately symmetric, exponential profiles to asymmetric profiles with prominent blue excesses or shoulders. Objects with Balmer line blue excess favour higher fitted photon-emitting shell velocities and tend to be fainter than those with persistently symmetric profiles. The H$\alpha$ pseudo-equivalent width (pEW) and FWHM of SLSNe-IIn overlap with those of lower-luminosity SNe IIn, while the pEW evolution is more diverse than in the broad-lined SLSN-II comparison sample. Our SLSNe-IIn sample's median Balmer decrement increases from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterwards, remaining consistently below that of the comparison Ia-CSM sample. We identify no Balmer-line morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn in the available comparison with lower-luminosity SNe IIn, although some SLSNe-IIn exhibit prolonged high-ionisation emission. Our results also support interaction with dense CSM formed through enhanced pre-explosion mass loss. We also highlight a possible hidden Ia-CSM population among luminous H-rich interacting SNe.

papers.intro:
Hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (H-rich SLSNe) are an observationally defined class of supernovae characterised by the presence of hydrogen in their spectra and peak optical absolute magnitudes of ≲−20\lesssim-20 mag (Smith et al., 2007; Ofek et al., 2007; Gal-Yam, 2012; Perley et al., 2016; Pessi et al., 2025a), reaching as bright as −22.6-22.6 mag in the most extreme cases (Kangas et al., 2022). These luminosities exceed those of ordinary H-rich core-collapse SNe by factors of 10–100, requiring an additional power source beyond the canonical radioactive decay expected in normal core-collapse explosions (Gal-Yam, 2012, e.g.).

Hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (H-rich SLSNe) are an observationally defined class of supernovae characterised by the presence of hydrogen in their spectra and peak optical absolute magnitudes of ≲−20\lesssim-20 mag (Smith et al., 2007; Ofek et al., 2007; Gal-Yam, 2012; Perley et al., 2016; Pessi et al., 2025a), reaching as bright as −22.6-22.6 mag in the most extreme cases (Kangas et al., 2022). These luminosities exceed those of ordinary H-rich core-collapse SNe by factors of 10–100, requiring an additional power source beyond the canonical radioactive decay expected in normal core-collapse explosions (Gal-Yam, 2012, e.g.).

The observationally defined class of H-rich SLSNe may encompass events with luminosities powered by different mechanisms. One proposed mechanism is the interaction between the SN ejecta and dense circumstellar material (CSM; Chevalier and Fransson 1994; Chugai 1997; Smith and McCray 2007) expelled by the progenitor system prior to the explosion. In this case, radiative shocks efficiently convert the kinetic energy of the ejecta into radiation. The presence of such dense CSM typically requires extreme pre-explosion mass loss, potentially through winds or eruptions associated with luminous blue variable stars (LBVs; Humphreys and Davidson 1994; Smith et al. 2008), eruptions with pulsational pair-instability origins (Woosley et al., 2007; Woosley, 2017; Lunnan et al., 2018; Gkini et al., 2025; Gkini et al., 2026), or mass transfer in binary systems (Petrovic et al., 2005; Langer, 2012; Ercolino et al., 2026). Alternative models have also been proposed, primarily in the context of H-poor SLSNe (SLSNe-I; e.g. Quimby et al. 2011), but efforts have been made to extend their applicability to the H-rich population. One class of models invokes a central engine that continuously injects energy into the expanding SN ejecta, such as a rapidly rotating magnetar (Ostriker and Gunn, 1971; Kasen and Bildsten, 2010; Woosley, 2010) or fallback accretion onto a newly formed black hole (Dexter and Kasen, 2013). Another model attributes the luminosity to the radioactive decay of large amounts of 56Ni (Smith et al., 2007; Gal-Yam et al., 2009, e.g.), with the required 56Ni masses generally expected only in pair-instability supernovae (PISNe) of very massive stars (Barkat et al., 1967; Woosley et al., 2002; Heger et al., 2003; Schulze et al., 2024).

(2018) presented the first study of a small sample of such events. Following these studies, we refer specifically to these broad-lined objects as SLSNe-II throughout this work. The 80% majority exhibit narrow Balmer emission lines resembling those seen in Type IIn SNe (SNe IIn; Schlegel 1990; Smith 2017; Nyholm et al. 2020), characterised by a narrow emission core (FWHM∼\mathrm{FWHM}\sim a few hundred km​s−1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}) together with exponential wings11 1 These wings are also commonly fitted phenomenologically with Lorentzian profiles. (generally with FWHM≤3000​km​s−1\mathrm{FWHM}\leq 3000\,\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}). For the dominant narrow-lined population, there is broad consensus that CSM interaction supplies a substantial fraction of the observed luminosity. The narrow Balmer components are generally interpreted as direct evidence for CSM interaction (Chevalier and Fransson, 1994; Chugai, 1997; Smith, 2017), as they originate from slowly moving, H-rich CSM that is ionised by shock breakout and subsequent ejecta–CSM interaction. Nevertheless, several key questions remain. One of the central issues, highlighted by both Perley et al. (2016) and Hiramatsu et al. (2024), is whether the objects referred to as SLSNe-IIn simply represent the luminous extreme of the SN IIn population. This question can be approached from both observational and physical perspectives. Observationally, one may ask whether there is a continuous distribution in the observed properties, such as peak luminosity, evolution timescale, and the duration and strength of narrow lines, across the full population of H-rich interacting SNe. Physically, one may instead ask whether the underlying progenitor and CSM properties form a continuum, including parameters such as CSM mass and extent, pre-explosion mass-loss rate, and even progenitor type.

Observationally, one may ask whether there is a continuous distribution in the observed properties, such as peak luminosity, evolution timescale, and the duration and strength of narrow lines, across the full population of H-rich interacting SNe. Physically, one may instead ask whether the underlying progenitor and CSM properties form a continuum, including parameters such as CSM mass and extent, pre-explosion mass-loss rate, and even progenitor type.

A second complication is that narrow Balmer emission and high luminosity do not uniquely identify a core-collapse SN. SNe Ia-CSM are thermonuclear explosions interacting with dense H-rich CSM and can produce luminous light curves and narrow Balmer-dominated spectra resembling those of SNe IIn (Silverman et al., 2013a; Leloudas et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2023). Early well-studied examples include SNe 2002ic (Hamuy et al., 2003, e.g.) and 2005gj (Aldering et al., 2006; Prieto et al., 2007), whose spectra were dominated by narrow Balmer emission with diluted SN Ia-like features, and PTF11kx (Dilday et al., 2012; Silverman et al., 2013b, SN 2011km;), which exhibited clearer SN Ia features with increasingly strong Balmer emission. However, in some cases (Benetti et al., 2006, e.g.), the thermonuclear nature of these Ia-CSM/IIn objects was ambiguous. Leloudas et al. (2015), using simulated composite spectra, argued that an underlying SN Ia can be hidden in interacting events as faint as MV=−20.1M_{V}=-20.1 mag, and that SNe Ia-CSM can span −21.6<MV<−19.5-21.6<M_{V}<-19.5 mag. This range substantially overlaps with H-rich SLSNe. A notable example of this complication is the H-rich SLSN 2006gy, for which a thermonuclear origin has also been proposed (Jerkstrand et al., 2020). Further classification ambiguities arise for transients projected near galaxy centres, where luminous interacting SNe, tidal disruption events (TDEs), and active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can share similar properties. For example, photometrically selected TDE candidate samples can include both SNe and AGN flares (Yao et al., 2023). Identifying such events is therefore essential before drawing population-level conclusions on H-rich SLSNe.

papers.title: The impact of MUSE sky subtraction on unresolved stellar population end products: Study cases of NGC 1097 and NGC 1433
papers.abstract: One of the main steps in data reduction for ground-based astronomy is sky subtraction. For extended objects, it is necessary to observe dedicated sky frames, usually with airmass values similar to the target's, using different pointing strategies. However, it is not well documented how different observing strategies can affect the science end product. In particular, with the use of the MUSE/VLT, this can yield distinct stellar population products, such as age, metallicity, and \alpha-enhancement. To address this, we considered two case studies seeking to investigate: (i) the sky stability in observations taken consecutively over a period of 2 hours with thin sky transparency and airmass values of 1.25-1.05, and (ii) the impact of different sky conditions on the same target. Among our main results, we find that for galaxies with 0.0014 < z < 0.0077, the sky line [NI] at \lambda 5200 coincides with the Mgb bandpass, which is essential for metallicity measurements, highlighting the need for proper sky subtraction. In addition, for regions with relative fluxes above 10 with respect to the sky in NGC1097, sky frames with variation up to ~18 % still retrieve consistent stellar population properties - in this case, this corresponds to flux values of >1500 x 10^-20 erg/s/cm^2 and Johnson-V ~19.0. In contrast, when comparing data from different nights for NGC1433, fainter regions suffer greatly from distinct sky conditions, especially in metallicity measurements, which range within +/- 0.2, strongly affecting the interpretation of stellar mass assembly and the origin of the gas (i.e., mergers might bring metal-poor gas, while an in-situ burst of star formation can yield metal-rich stars). This study is the first of its kind and highlights the importance of proper sky subtraction, providing insights regarding data limitations and observational strategies for future observations with MUSE.
papers.intro:
The Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE)11 1 https://www.eso.org/sci/facilities/develop/instruments/muse.html, at the Very Large Telescope (VLT/ESO), is an Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS) and represents a major milestone in the investigation of stellar mass assembly in nearby galaxies – e.g., TIMER (PI: Gadotti; Gadotti et al., 2019), PHANGS (PI: Emsellem; Emsellem et al., 2022), GECKOS (PI: van de Sande; van de Sande et al., 2024), and numerous other programs. It enables the investigation of the spatially and structurally dependent stellar population properties at a spatial sampling of 0.2” ×\times 0.2”, with a fairly large field of view (60” ×\times 60”).

The Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE)11 1 https://www.eso.org/sci/facilities/develop/instruments/muse.html, at the Very Large Telescope (VLT/ESO), is an Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS) and represents a major milestone in the investigation of stellar mass assembly in nearby galaxies – e.g., TIMER (PI: Gadotti; Gadotti et al., 2019), PHANGS (PI: Emsellem; Emsellem et al., 2022), GECKOS (PI: van de Sande; van de Sande et al., 2024), and numerous other programs. It enables the investigation of the spatially and structurally dependent stellar population properties at a spatial sampling of 0.2” ×\times 0.2”, with a fairly large field of view (60” ×\times 60”).

One of the crucial steps in achieving relevant results is data reduction, where many interventions must be considered, both to mitigate instrumental imperfections -- such as flats, biases, and darks -- and natural impediments, such as sky emission when observing from the ground. The pipeline provided by ESO22 2 https://www.eso.org/sci/software/pipelines/muse/ for MUSE is quite complex, since each pointing corresponds to thousands of spectra. To perform sky subtraction, the user can consider the sky around the target (for point-like sources) or a dedicated sky frame, which is the case for extended objects such as nearby galaxies, which can occupy the entire MUSE FoV. In the latter case, it is not clear, however, which dedicated sky pointing strategy results in the best sky subtraction, and different PIs consider different sequences, such as OSO, SOOS, OSOOSO, OOSOO, OOS (where O = object and S = sky). All these strategies assume that the sky background doesn’t change significantly between the science frame and corresponding sky frame and, ideally, one would like to take sky frames as few as possible. But this will result in a large time separation between the science and sky frames, and the above assumption may not hold. To date, the impact of this choice on the end products (such as age, metallicity, and α\alpha-enhancement) is difficult to constrain. Furthermore, many studies that built mosaics with MUSE (i.e., multiple pointings to cover a larger area) found jumps between frames in the values of derived properties (e.g., age, metallicity, dust), which can be at least partially attributed to different sky conditions and subtractions. Many of the dust maps of Emsellem et al. (2022) (Figure 23) present jumps between frames, while in Pessa et al. (2023), even with extensive additional processing, many maps still retain mosaic-correlated jumps. To mitigate the impact on dust maps, Kang et al. (2026) discarded most of the wavelength regime.

papers.title: Time-Delay Recovery in AGN Reverberation Mapping via Mutual Information
papers.abstract: Active galactic nuclei exhibit complex, nonlinear multiwavelength variability that standard cross-correlation techniques, sensitive only to linear covariance, may fail to capture fully. We apply time-lagged Mutual Information (MI) lag estimation, via the Kraskov-Stoegbauer-Grassberger $k$-nearest-neighbour estimator ($k = 5$) with a 150-iteration Random Subset Selection bootstrap, to the light curves of four Seyfert galaxies (Mrk 509, NGC 5548, NGC 4151, and NGC 4593) monitored across eight energy bands by Swift. In the UV/optical regime the MI estimator successfully reproduces the inter-band disc reprocessing lags established by the interpolated cross-correlation function, with performance degrading toward the optical where low variability amplitude produces poorly defined MI peaks. In the X-ray bands, where the physical X-ray/UV coupling is known to be weak, the estimator fails to recover consistent lags across the sample, with the notable exception of NGC 4593. Contextualising these outcomes within the multifractal characterisation of our previous work, we discuss how MI performance relates to the multifractal spectral width $\Delta\alpha$ of each band, and we propose $\Delta\alpha$ as a candidate diagnostic for anticipating where MI-based reverberation mapping is likely to succeed or fail in multiband datasets of active galactic nuclei.

papers.intro:
Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are among the most energetically extreme objects in the Universe, powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes at the centres of their host galaxies (Peterson, 1997; Netzer, 2013, e.g.). Their emission spans the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to hard X-rays (Ulrich et al., 1997; Shang et al., 2011), and varies on timescales ranging from hours to years (Vaughan et al., 2003). This variability encodes fundamental information about the geometry, kinematics, and physical conditions of the emitting regions surrounding the central engine (Ulrich et al., 1997). Understanding these regions, in particular the accretion disc and the broad-line region (BLR), is crucial for constraining models of black hole growth and AGN feedback across cosmic time (Kormendy and Ho, 2013; Heckman and Best, 2014).

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are among the most energetically extreme objects in the Universe, powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes at the centres of their host galaxies (Peterson, 1997; Netzer, 2013, e.g.). Their emission spans the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to hard X-rays (Ulrich et al., 1997; Shang et al., 2011), and varies on timescales ranging from hours to years (Vaughan et al., 2003). This variability encodes fundamental information about the geometry, kinematics, and physical conditions of the emitting regions surrounding the central engine (Ulrich et al., 1997). Understanding these regions, in particular the accretion disc and the broad-line region (BLR), is crucial for constraining models of black hole growth and AGN feedback across cosmic time (Kormendy and Ho, 2013; Heckman and Best, 2014).

Reverberation mapping (Blandford and McKee, 1982; Peterson, 1993) is one of the most powerful observational techniques for probing the inner structure of AGNs. Variations in the ionising continuum emission propagate outward and are reprocessed by surrounding gas and dust, producing delayed echoed signals arising from the finite travel time of light across the system, at longer wavelengths. By measuring the time lag, τ\tau, between a reference and a subsidiary band, one can infer the light-travel distance to the reprocessing region, mapping the spatial structure of the AGN on scales inaccessible to direct imaging (Cackett et al., 2021). In the scenario of thermal reprocessing of extreme UV/X-ray photons to optical/UV photons by the accretion disc (Cackett et al., 2007), the observed lags follow the characteristic wavelength-dependent scaling τ∝λ4/3\tau\propto\lambda^{4/3}, a direct prediction of the standard thin-disc model (Shakura and Sunyaev, 1973). This scenario is supported by X-ray reverberation lags observed in the Fourier domain of individual Seyfert galaxies (Uttley et al., 2014; Kara et al., 2016; Fabian et al., 2009), and by dedicated multiwavelength monitoring campaigns spanning X-ray, UV, and optical bands simultaneously (Edelson et al., 2015; Edelson et al., 2017; Edelson et al., 2019; McHardy et al., 2018b). These campaigns have provided tight constraints on the accretion disc structure and the geometry of the corona, while also revealing discrepancies between observed lag amplitudes and standard thin-disc predictions, pointing towards a contribution from the BLR and diffuse continuum emission to the observed lag amplitudes (Cackett et al., 2018).

The standard approach to measuring inter-band lags relies on the interpolated cross-correlation function (Gaskell and Peterson, 1987; Peterson et al., 1998, ICCF;) or its discrete counterpart (Edelson and Krolik, 1988, DCF;). More sophisticated methods, such as javelin (Zu et al., 2011), model the light curves as damped random walk processes and infer lags through maximum-likelihood fitting. While these approaches have yielded significant results, they share a common limitation: they are fundamentally based on second-order statistics, i.e., the linear covariance between bands. AGN Light Curves, however, are inherently non-Gaussian and nonlinear (Vio et al., 1992; Longo et al., 1996; Provenzale et al., 1994; Green et al., 1999), and exhibit complex temporal behaviour that includes intermittency (Chian, 1996) and non-linear variability signatures incompatible with simple stochastic models (Vaughan et al., 2003).

When this scaling exponent is approximately independent of qq, the spectrum collapses to a narrow range and Δ​α\Delta\alpha tends to, or equals, zero, indicating monofractal behaviour; when the scaling exponent instead varies with qq, multiple Hölder exponents emerge, characterising a multifractal behaviour (Kantelhardt et al., 2002; Souza et al., 2026b; Souza et al., 2026a). For q>0q>0, Fq​(s)F_{q}(s) is dominated by large fluctuations, whereas for q<0q<0 it is dominated by small fluctuations. A left-skewed spectrum indicates dominance of small fluctuations, a right-skewed spectrum indicates dominance of large fluctuations, and a symmetric spectrum indicates comparable contributions from both. This asymmetry is quantified by the parameter AA, with A>1A>1, A<1A<1, and A=1A=1 corresponding respectively to left-skewed, right-skewed, and symmetric spectra (Ihlen, 2012).

In parallel, information theory, originally formulated by Shannon (1948) in the context of communication systems, provides a natural framework for characterising statistical dependence in a model-free, nonlinear fashion. Unlike second-order statistics, information-theoretic measures capture any form of dependence between two variables, linear or nonlinear, without assuming a specific functional form or a particular noise model (Cover and Thomas, 2006). Practical estimation from finite, irregularly sampled data is made tractable by nonparametric density estimators that require no binning or bandwidth choice. Using such a measure as a lag estimator, by maximising it as a function of a trial time shift τ\tau, yields a natural generalisation of the Cross-Correlation Function (CCF) that imposes no linearity assumption.

papers.title: Studying the Fullerene Nest: JWST Observations of the Planetary Nebula Tc 1. II. A Spectroscopic and Spatial Study of C$_{60}$ and C$_{70}$ Emission
papers.abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the fullerene emission bands in JWST MIRI/MRS observations of the planetary nebula Tc 1. The observations reveal the emission features due to neutral C$_{60}$ and C$_{70}$ in unprecedented detail. The combined fullerene emission represents $\sim$2.6% of the total infrared output, suggesting that $\sim$0.6% of the carbon budget is locked up in fullerenes. We find no clear evidence for C$_{60}^+$, C$_{70}^+$ or C$_{60}^-$ in the spectrum. The high spectral resolution allows us to separate the fullerene bands from atomic emission lines for the first time, allowing for a much better characterization of the band profiles and yielding more accurate band ratios than previous observations. We see no spatial variation in the individual C$_{60}$ and C$_{70}$ band profile shapes across all pixels. The 17.4 and 18.9 $\mu$m C$_{60}$ bands show clear resolved ro-vibrational structure in their profiles, and similar structured emission is seen in the 12.5, 14.8, 17.7, and 21.8 $\mu$m C$_{70}$ bands, further establishing that all emitting fullerene molecules are in the gas phase. We report a higher 7.0/18.9 $\mu$m C$_{60}$ band ratio ($\sim$1.4-1.9) than previously reported ($\sim$1.3). We note that all bands, except the 8.5 $\mu$m band, contain a significant contribution from C$_{70}$, complicating the analysis. The fullerene emission is spatially concentrated in a thin, asymmetric shell at a radius of 5-6$''$ from the central star. The shell lies at the outer edge of the core of the nebula, which was ejected in a single, brief episode $\gtrsim$4,000 years ago.

papers.intro:
The Universe is rich in carbonaceous compounds (molecules and dust grains) that appear in a bewildering variety of sizes, structures, shapes, and chemical compositions, depending on the environment in which they reside [81]. About 15% of all carbon in the Universe is locked up in the form of large gas-phase molecules: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), fullerenes, and related compounds. These are widespread and abundant in space and set the Universe aglow with their characteristic infrared (IR) emission. Indeed, the characteristic spectral features of PAHs have been seen out to cosmological distances, including by recent JWST observations [34, 36, 3, e.g]. These molecules efficiently convert UV radiation to IR photons, drive key physical processes such as heating and cooling of the gas, and play an important role in interstellar chemistry. Consequently, they are major contributors to regulating large-scale processes in the Universe, including star and planet formation and the evolution of galaxies [80].

papers.title: Impact of the large scale environment on the baryonic scaling relations of disc galaxies: Insights from the GASP survey
papers.abstract: The Tully--Fisher relation (TFR) and the specific angular momentum--mass relation (SAMR) link the baryonic content of a disc to its kinematics and dynamics. Hence, these scaling relations should bear the imprints of any process removing baryons or altering their kinematics, such as those acting in clusters of galaxies. We test this using the MUSE survey "GAs Stripping Phenomena in galaxies" (GASP), which targets field, group, and cluster members at $z \approx 0.05$ and various stages of ram pressure stripping. For the 81 discs with favourable inclinations, we measure the distribution and kinematics of stars and ionised gas, and their specific angular momenta. Within their scatter, the stellar and baryonic relations show no significant dependence on the large scale environment: the TFRs have slopes $\alpha \approx 3.6$ and $\approx 3.5$ for any kinematic tracer, and the SAMRs have $\alpha \approx 0.65$--$0.75$, as predicted by tidal torque theory. The same holds for the ten S0-S0/as in our sample, consistent with the "faded spiral" formation scenario. Only the gas SAMR shows an environmental signature, with ram pressure stripped galaxies lying $\approx 0.16$~dex below unperturbed ones. This offset is mostly due to their enhanced star formation rate, and thus higher gas mass when inferred through the Schmidt-Kennicutt law, rather than to kinematic perturbations or disc truncation. Our results suggest that, within the area probed by MUSE ($\lesssim6$ disc scale lengths), these discs have preserved the angular momentum acquired at formation not only from cluster processes and pre-processing in filaments, but also from mergers and ejective feedback acting in any environment.

The dominant hydrodynamical mechanism is likely the ram pressure exerted by the intra-cluster medium (Gunn & Gott, 1972; Boselli et al., 2022, ICM;), which strips gas from the interstellar medium (ISM), most efficiently in the outer disc where the gravitational restoring force is weak. papers.title: Studying the Fullerene Nest: JWST Observations of the Planetary Nebula Tc 1. III. Tracing Fullerene-Linked Dust Variation
papers.abstract: We have observed the fullerene-rich planetary nebula Tc 1 with the MIRI/MRS on JWST. The mid-infrared spectra of this spatially resolved source reveal that the dust emission is not co-spatial with the fullerene emission. Three broad features can be distinguished: a 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $\mu$m plateau, a 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $\mu$m plateau and the 30 $\mu$m feature. The 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $\mu$m plateau does not change shape spectrally across the entire field of view, indicating it is produced by stochastically heated material. Spectral variations of the 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $\mu$m plateau reveal at least three distinct components, peaking at 9.5 $\mu$m, 11 $\mu$m and 12 $\mu$m respectively. SiC produces most likely at least the 11 $\mu$m component and we find evidence that the 12 $\mu$m component might be produced by SiC grains too. The variation in relative strength of these components across the field of view hints at dust processing taking place in Tc 1. The planetary nebula (PN, plural PNe) Tc 1 is exceptional because its infrared (IR) spectrum is dominated by ro-vibrational emission bands of fullerenes. Fullerenes are large carbonaceous molecules, constructed from hexagonal and pentagonal arrangements of carbon atoms, shaped like a hollow sphere or ellipsoid. The most stable molecule — and the archetype — of this family is C60, known as Buckminsterfullerene. Due to their stability against photo-dissociation, fullerenes can survive in the harsh conditions of the interstellar medium (ISM). Indeed, C60 has been found to be ubiquitous in the ISM, as several diffuse interstellar bands have been identified as C+60{}_{60}^{+} [21, 19, 15].

Tc 1 is the proto-typical planetary nebula to study C60, for two reasons: it does not contain significant emission from PAHs, which usually contaminates some of the IR active bands of C60. PAHs produce infrared emission features — referred to as “aromatic infrared bands” (AIBs) — through vibrational emission; the strongest features are located at 3.3, 5.25, 5.75, 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.2, 12.0, 12.7, and 13.5 μ​m\upmu\mathrm{m} [e.g. 49, and references therein]. C60 produces similar features at 6.5, 7.0, 8.5, 17.4 and 18.9 μ​m\upmu\mathrm{m} [33, 20, 10]. We also observe features at 8.8, 12.5, 14.8, 15.6, and 21.8 μ​m\upmu\mathrm{m} in Tc 1 (Giese et al. submitted), produced by C70 [38, 53]. Many of the infrared bands produced by C60 and C70 overlap with AIBs, thus the lack of AIBs in Tc 1 greatly simplifies the analysis of these fullerene bands. Secondly, Tc 1 is the closest known of such fullerene-dominated nebulae, which makes it easier to study spatial variations. It is resolved for large telescopes, in contrast to a number of other planetary nebulae that show a similar spectrum as Tc 1 but are located in the Magellanic Clouds [23, 22, 24]. This makes Tc 1 the ideal source to study not only the features of C60, but also the physical conditions that give rise to fullerene formation.

We study Tc 1 in detail to investigate in which conditions fullerenes are formed and how these molecules interact with their environment through chemical and physical processes. We present a series of papers “Studying the fullerene nest”, revolving around JWST observations of Tc 1. J. Cami et al. (2026, in preparation; hereafter Paper I) provides an overview of our MIRI/MRS observations of Tc 1. M. Giese et al. (2026, submitted; hereafter Paper II) focuses on an in-depth analysis of the fullerene features. In this paper, we study the broad emission features and the continuum emission to characterize the dust component of the environment.

papers.title: ALMA detection of continuum emission from GQ Lup B
papers.abstract: GQ Lup B is a massive (10-40 M$_{\text{Jup}}$) companion orbiting the young T-Tauri star GQ Lup A at a projected distance of $\sim$110 au (0.7''). It is outside the circumprimary disk in the submm continuum, but its ${\sim}\,63^\circ$ inclined orbit intersects the primary's gas disk twice per period. We report a 5.8$\sigma$ detection of continuum emission at the location of GQ Lup B, obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 0.89 mm (band 7). We associate this emission with a dusty disk around the companion, already detected by VLT/NACO and JWST/MIRI in the mid-Infrared. To date, this is the third disk observed at mm wavelengths around a companion spanning the brown dwarf and planetary mass regimes, following PDS 70 c, a gas giant embedded in the parent circumstellar disk, and SR 12 c, a planetary-mass companion at 1200 au from the primary. We retrieve a point source with peak intensity $54.5\pm9.4\,\mu\rm Jy\, beam^{-1}$, co-spatial with GRAVITY astrometry. The emission is spatially unresolved, placing an upper limit on the source radius of 2.3 au (from a synthesized beam of $\sim\,29\times25$ mas). For comparison, this is smaller than 1/3 of the Hill's radius (3-5 au for GQ Lup B, depending on the assumed mass), the theoretical upper limit for circum-planetary disks. Assuming optically thin thermal emission from mm-size grains in a disk-like structure, we infer a mass of 0.0032 M$_\oplus$, while the optically thick limit yields an emission radius of 0.2 au. Assuming a gas to dust ratio of 100, our results indicate a very low disk mass to accretion rate ratio, of the order of $\sim10^4$ years, analogously to the highest accretors in the stellar mass regime. In the case of GQ Lup B, this can be explained by its periodic crossings of the circumprimary disk, which could deliver a substantial amount of gas to the companion's disk over a long timescale.

papers.intro:
Typical tracers of an active planet formation process are observed at optical and infrared wavelengths. UV excess, Hα\alpha emission and near-IR hydrogen recombination lines trace ongoing accretion and shocks, (Zhou et al. 2014; Aoyama et al. 2021; Demars et al. 2023) while continuum excess, silicate features in the mid-IR and dust-induced polarization are linked to μ\mum-sized dust grains in the most irradiated surroundings of the protoplanet (van Holstein et al. 2021; Cugno et al. 2024; Choksi and Chiang 2025).

Typical tracers of an active planet formation process are observed at optical and infrared wavelengths. UV excess, Hα\alpha emission and near-IR hydrogen recombination lines trace ongoing accretion and shocks, (Zhou et al. 2014; Aoyama et al. 2021; Demars et al. 2023) while continuum excess, silicate features in the mid-IR and dust-induced polarization are linked to μ\mum-sized dust grains in the most irradiated surroundings of the protoplanet (van Holstein et al. 2021; Cugno et al. 2024; Choksi and Chiang 2025).

Observing these tracers requires high angular resolution and contrast, hence the most accessible targets are massive, bright and well-separated planetary mass companions (PMCs, Lachapelle et al. 2015; Bowler 2016). These are gravitationally bound objects with masses broadly in the range 1–30 MJupM_{\mathrm{Jup}}, at separations ≳100{\gtrsim}100 au from the star and outside the primary disk. Despite forming via pathways more characteristic of stars, their near-planetary masses suggest that they share properties with giant planets, including temperatures, surface gravities, and chemical compositions. PMCs also represent an excellent laboratory to investigate the physics of disks around substellar mass objects. Disks around planetary-mass companions could provide a valuable and more accessible comparison to Circum-Planetary Disks (CPDs) (Canup and Ward 2002; Ward and Canup 2010; Keith and Wardle 2014; Szulágyi et al. 2016; Maeda et al. 2024) around planets embedded in the primary disks, helping us to understand their physical properties and evolution, and how they affect planetary formation mechanisms.

For many PMCs rich observational datasets already exist, spanning direct imaging, accretion rate measurements and infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs), that could reveal the presence of a disk. (Santamaría-Miranda et al. 2018; Bowler et al. 2020; Martinez and Kraus 2022; Cugno et al. 2024; Cugno and Grant 2025; Darcis et al. 2026; Finley et al. 2026). However, none of these observations are suitable for investigating the bulk of a disk dust component, as the emission is likely optically thick and only probes the hottest layers of the disk, those near the surface and close to the central object. The main component of the dust reservoir instead is likely located in the colder region of the disk, in the midplane. It can be probed only by (sub)mm observations, which however may include contribution from free-free emission (Domínguez-Jamett et al. 2025). Detecting disks around PMOs and CPDs at millimeter wavelengths is extremely challenging and rare, as their typical dust mass seems to be lower than what can be probed by typical sensitivities of current surveys. Despite several ALMA campaigns targeting PMCs and embedded protoplanets (Bowler et al. 2015; Wu et al. 2017a; Wu et al. 2020; Jorquera et al. 2021; Facchini et al. 2026), only two sources have been detected: PDS 70c (Isella et al. 2019; Benisty et al. 2021), inside the primary’s disk, and SR 12 c (Wu et al. 2022), one of the widest-orbit PMCs known to date. With this paper we present the detection of 0.89 mm continuum emission at the location of the massive companion GQ Lup B.

GQ Lup is located in the Lupus star forming region, at a distance of 154.1 pc (Gaia Collaboration and others 2022). GQ Lup A is a T-Tauri star with spectral type K7V, an age of 2-5 Myr and a mass of 1.03 M⊙ (Donati et al. 2012; MacGregor et al. 2017). It hosts a circumstellar disk, whose dust component extends up to 59±1259\pm 12 au, with an inclination with respect to the line of sight of 60.5±0.5∘60.5\pm 0.5^{\circ} (MacGregor et al. 2017). Previous ALMA observations show signs of a dust gap at ∼10{\sim}10 au from the star (Long et al. 2020) and an asymmetric CO disk ∼ 200{\sim}\,200 au wide (MacGregor et al. 2017). Scattered light images with VLT-SPHERE show a single spiral arm in the southern region of the disk (van Holstein et al. 2021), likely caused by the interaction with the massive companion GQ Lup B. This 10-40 MJup object identified in 2005 (Neuhaeuser et al. 2005), is located at a projected separation of 0.7′′0.7^{\prime\prime} from the primary. Recent studies, based on almost twenty years of astrometry and precise radial velocity measurements, found that its orbit is inclined by 63+6−14∘{}^{+6}_{-14}{{}^{\circ}} with respect to the circumstellar disk, with a semimajor axis of 97 au (Venkatesan et al. 2025). This orbital configuration suggests that the companion punctures through the gas component of the primary disk twice per orbit, perturbing its kinematics and originating asymmetries in the disk morphology (Stolker et al. 2021). Other than with the circumprimary disk, the companion’s orbit is misaligned also with the stellar spin axis (relative inclination ∼ 52+19−24∘\sim\,52^{+19}_{-24}{{}^{\circ}} Bowler et al. 2023; Venkatesan et al. 2025 ) possibly implying that GQ Lup B formed outside of the primary disk, from the same parent cloud of the primary star. A similar CO12/13CO{}^{12}\rm CO/^{13}\rm CO ratio in the atmosphere of GQ Lup A (51−8+1051^{+10}_{-8}) and B (53−6+753^{+7}_{-6}) (Picos et al. 2025) indeed suggests they originated from a shared material reservoir. To complete the picture, there is a third object gravitationally bound to the system (Alcalá et al. 2020), GQ Lup C. It is a low mass star (0.15 M⊙) at a projected distance of 2400 au, which possibly participates in the intricate dynamical architecture of the entire system and may have played a role in determining the highly inclined orbit of GQ Lup B.

papers.title: Investigating the timescales traced by dynamical ages in young stellar systems
papers.abstract: Stars form in clustered environments, and then the stars may congregate into star clusters. The timescale on which individual stars form is not necessarily the same as the timescale on which star clusters assemble. Therefore, developing methods to probe these different timescales is a crucial part of understanding star cluster assembly and early evolution. Dynamical ages can be constructed from the kinematics of individual stars in clusters in the solar neighborhood using Gaia data. Using a star formation simulation, we test five different dynamical age methods. We divide dynamical ages into two approaches: methods which trace the size evolution of the cluster, and methods which trace the trajectories of individual stars. We confirm that size methods cannot accurately derive ages in bound clusters whereas methods tracing individual stars can be applied to both bound and unbound systems. We find that different dynamical age methods trace different epochs of star cluster formation and assembly: The method using stars with the oldest traceback ages provides an upper limit on stellar ages and the method using the median traceback ages is the best proxy for isochronal ages. Methods which trace the size evolution of the cluster best trace the onset of cluster expansion. Our work suggests that the median traceback time of stars moving away from the cluster provides the most reliable proxy for isochronal age, and that this method can be applied to any expanding system.

papers.intro:
Most stars form in clustered environments, from turbulent clouds of dense molecular gas [38, 36]. Star clusters and associations, seen observationally as local over-densities of stars may then assemble out of the structure in the collapsing cloud prior to the expulsion of the natal gas by feedback [37, 28, 13, 4]. These young clusters may be gravitationally bound or unbound, and may begin bound before becoming unbound at a later stage through dynamical interactions or changes in the local potential [36].

Most stars form in clustered environments, from turbulent clouds of dense molecular gas [38, 36]. Star clusters and associations, seen observationally as local over-densities of stars may then assemble out of the structure in the collapsing cloud prior to the expulsion of the natal gas by feedback [37, 28, 13, 4]. These young clusters may be gravitationally bound or unbound, and may begin bound before becoming unbound at a later stage through dynamical interactions or changes in the local potential [36].

Understanding the timescales on which star clusters assemble is key to understanding the population of star clusters we observe in the solar neighborhood. It is often assumed that star clusters form as simple stellar populations with a single age [8, 7]. Techniques to derive ages for observed clusters are usually based on properties internal to each star, and include isochrone fitting [5, 8, 43, e.g.], lithium depletion boundary [46, 60, 25, e.g.], gyrochronology [9, 42, e.g.], and asteroseismology [47, e.g.]. However, these methods can suffer from uncertainties inherent to model parameters [8, e.g. uncertain composition of the stars,], the adopted input physics [60, e.g. nuclear reaction cross-sections,], or systematic uncertainties in observational constraints [47]. The most common method for assigning an age to clusters is isochrone fitting. However, isochronal ages are especially uncertain for young clusters (<50<50 Myr) [29]. However, at present there is little consensus in the literature about what constitutes a dynamical age. Different works use different methods making it unclear what physical processes are measured by each unique dynamical age method. Techniques may be designed to trace the isochronal evolution of the star clusters, with the goal of tracing when the stars formed [51]. In contrast, detailed star cluster formation simulations can trace the evolutionary history of star clusters from the natal gas cloud to gas expulsion [27, 14, e.g.]. In this work, we apply five different dynamical age methods to a simulation of star clusters formed under conditions typical of the disk of the Milky Way [14]. Our goal is to understand how dynamical ages compare to each other, to the ages of the stars within the cluster, and to different stages of cluster assembly. We compute dynamical ages for clusters formed in a simulation where the formation and evolution of the cluster and its stars is known. Using a simulation allows us to test how dynamical ages evolve over time and investigate which dynamical age methods can quantify the signatures of star cluster formation and assembly in a meaningful way.

papers.title: AGN Feedback Turbulence in Cool-core Clusters: Evidence from XRISM
papers.abstract: The XRISM X-ray Observatory has revealed evidence for a "double-cascade" scenario in the Perseus cluster, in which active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback and mergers drive turbulence over distinct radial ranges and spatial scales. Whether this gas kinematic feature is common among cool-core clusters remains unclear. Here, we revisit XRISM observations of A1795 and A2029 to investigate the signatures of AGN feedback and their contribution to the gas velocity fields. In A1795, AGN feedback dominates the velocity dispersion in the core, similar to Perseus, and may provide turbulent heating at a rate comparable to radiative cooling. In contrast, we obtain only an upper limit on the AGN feedback contribution in A2029, where merger-driven motions dominate. Tailored simulations indicate that an off-axis minor merger $\simeq1.6$ Gyr ago displaced the central low-entropy gas in A2029, potentially suppressing AGN activity. This gas is now returning to the center, possibly facilitating the re-establishment of AGN feedback. We propose an evolutionary view of the double-cascade scenario, in which merger-driven motions dominate during and shortly after significant mergers, while feedback-driven turbulence re-emerges in cluster cores as systems relax. This framework provides a basis for interpreting XRISM kinematic measurements of (weak) cool-core clusters. Our findings highlight the importance of spatially resolved gas kinematics and detailed modeling for identifying double-cascade features and disentangling the contributions of AGN feedback and mergers.

papers.intro:
Galaxy clusters are assembled through merger and accretion of smaller structures from the cosmic web in the hierarchical structure formation scenario (see Kravtsov & Borgani 2012; Vikhlinin et al. 2014 for reviews). Both major mergers and significant minor mergers can substantially redistribute the cluster mass and energy content (Poole et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2011, e.g.,), in particular the baryonic component. They drive prominent shocks and strong turbulence during the first ∼1​Gyr\sim 1{\rm\,Gyr}, corresponding to their most violent phase. The merger remnants then undergo a relatively gentle evolution over the subsequent few Gyr until the next significant merger event. During this phase, the clusters relax and develop cool cores in their atmospheres through radiative cooling. Mergers can still have long-term impacts at this stage, often in the form of gas sloshing (Ascasibar & Markevitch, 2006, e.g.,), which gradually dissipates gravitational potential energy. Sloshing may partially offset radiative cooling losses at large radii (ZuHone et al., 2010; XRISM Collaboration, 2026a), but it is often insufficient in the very central region, where the gas density is high and the cooling timescale is short.

Radio-mode active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback provides a promising heating solution within the cool cores (Fabian, 2012; Werner et al., 2019). Energy released by the central supermassive black hole is injected into the surrounding medium through jets and inflated bubbles (Churazov et al., 2001; Churazov et al., 2002), which further drive shocks, sound waves, gravity waves, and turbulence (Fabian et al., 2006; Zhuravleva et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018, e.g.,). These processes leave observable imprints on both the thermal and nonthermal structures of the intracluster medium (ICM), many of which have been revealed by high-spatial-resolution X-ray and radio observations (e.g., Chandra, XMM-Newton, and LOFAR).

The recently launched XRISM X-ray Observatory provides unprecedented kinematic information on the hot atmospheres of galaxy clusters (Tashiro et al., 2021). Spatially mapping line shifts and line broadening allows us to directly characterize the kinetic energy injection, transport, and turbulent cascade associated with both AGN feedback and mergers (XRISM Collaboration, 2025a; XRISM Collaboration, 2026a; XRISM Collaboration, 2026b, e.g.,). From a theoretical point of view, mergers inject energy on large scales, of order hundreds of kpc or larger, comparable to the characteristic size of the infalling substructures and their orbital trajectories, whereas AGN feedback injects energy on much smaller scales and is more spatially concentrated in cluster cores. XRISM has provided the first observational evidence for this picture by revealing a significant enhancement of the ICM kinetic energy on small scales within a projected radius of ≃60​kpc\simeq 60{\rm\,kpc} in the Perseus cluster (XRISM Collaboration 2026a; see also Fig. 1). This finding implies that, in the Perseus cluster, AGN feedback efficiently drives turbulence within the cool core. XRISM Collaboration (2026a) proposed the “double-cascade” scenario, in which feedback and mergers drive turbulence predominantly at distinct spatial scales and different radii.

A natural follow-up question is whether this double-cascade picture is universal among cool-core clusters. Answering this question will provide critical insight into how AGN feedback distributes its energy and how efficiently that energy couples to the inner cluster atmosphere. Dozens of galaxy clusters, including several cool-core systems, have been observed by XRISM. However, isolating the contribution of AGN feedback to the observed velocity dispersion remains challenging because sloshing motions often coexist with feedback-driven structures in cluster cores. Perseus is a unique target for XRISM/Resolve due to its low redshift (z≃0.017z\simeq 0.017) and high X-ray surface brightness (Edge et al., 1990, e.g.,), which together allow the AGN-feedback-dominated region to be spatially resolved and the velocity measurements to extend significantly beyond it. The two dominant drivers can therefore be directly separated based on a simple scale argument (XRISM Collaboration, 2026a). Few other targets satisfy such conditions. Detailed analysis of their merger history is thus essential for characterizing the contribution of AGN feedback. For this reason, well-relaxed clusters that have not experienced significant mergers within the past few Gyr, or systems undergoing a single merger with a well-constrained configuration, are ideal targets.

A1795 and A2029 are among the most suitable systems in the current XRISM cluster sample for probing the kinematic signatures of AGN feedback. Both are well-known cool-core clusters with extensive multi-wavelength observations and a long history of X-ray studies. Their velocity radial profiles have been measured using multiple XRISM pointings (Sarkar et al., 2026; XRISM Collaboration, 2025d), enabling the characterization of merger-induced gas motions on large scales. In this work, we revisit the XRISM measurements of these systems by carefully modeling and separating the contributions from AGN feedback and merger-driven motions. We find that AGN feedback makes a dominant contribution to the velocity dispersion radial profile within ≃100​kpc\simeq 100{\rm\,kpc} in A1795, indicating a kinematic sphere of influence similar to that found in Perseus (XRISM Collaboration, 2026a). Despite large uncertainties, the feedback-associated heating rate of turbulence is comparable to the radiative cooling rate in both A1795 and Perseus, highlighting the significant role of feedback-driven turbulence in preventing catastrophic overcooling of the ICM. In contrast, the AGN feedback contribution is subdominant in A2029, suggesting that the cluster is in a transitional stage in which AGN activity has been re-established following recent merger-induced quenching, while merger-driven motions still make a substantial contribution to the observed kinematics. This interpretation is broadly consistent with the lack of cold gas despite the presence of newly launched radio jets with an estimated age of ∼100​Myr\sim 100{\rm\,Myr} in A2029 (Timmerman et al., 2022; Olivares et al., 2023). Based on these results, we propose a unified evolutionary picture for the interplay between mergers and AGN feedback, providing a framework for interpreting the kinematic properties of a broader sample of XRISM-observed clusters, such as A3571 (Aihara et al., 2026; McCall et al., 2026), Centaurus (XRISM Collaboration, 2025a), and Coma (XRISM Collaboration, 2025b; Gatuzz et al., 2026). We emphasize that the moderate velocity dispersions commonly found in the growing sample of XRISM-observed clusters (≃100\simeq 100–200​km​s−1200{\rm\,km\,s^{-1}}) can arise from complex and diverse dynamical processes. Detailed case-by-case modeling is therefore essential to interpret these measurements and disentangle the contributions of mergers and AGN feedback.

papers.title: Forward modeling linear variable filter data: High resolution PAH and Paschen-$\alpha$ maps from SPHEREx
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission is a powerful tool for the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in both Galactic and extragalactic contexts. It can reveal ionization state, radiation field, metallicity, composition, and ISM structure as sculpted by processes like turbulence and stellar feedback. Here we use NASA's SPHEREx to produce clean, high-resolution PAH maps at spectral resolution R $\sim$ 35 (compared to WISE at R $\sim$ 2). Prior treatments of the SPHEREx linear variable filter data seek to convert them to more conventional band-averaged maps that can leave striping artifacts associated with spatially variable wavelength sampling, especially at emission lines. In contrast, we deliver a scalable forward-modeling method capable of generating high-quality all-sky SPHEREx emission-line maps at 8.5 arcsec FWHM angular resolution (on 6.4 arcsec pixels), while naturally producing maps without visible striping. We reformat the data into a pixel-level database, mask stellar contamination, and infill missing pixels with a conditional, data-driven, anisotropic Gaussian process. We apply our method to produce 3.3 $\mu$m and 3.4 $\mu$m PAH and Paschen-$\alpha$ emission maps of a set of fields spanning a range of Galactic and extragalactic conditions including the Rosette nebula, the Corona Australis molecular cloud, M33, and M31. We demonstrate the quality and synergies of our SPHEREx 3.3 $\mu$m PAH maps by comparisons with other available gas and dust tracer maps and achieve sensitivities up to $\sigma(I_{3.3}) = 2.7 \times 10^{-8}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$. We estimate that a two-year extension of the SPHEREx survey, with modest modifications to the scanning strategy, would match or exceed the PAH sensitivity of WISE over the whole sky.

papers.intro:
The interstellar medium (ISM) is a chemically and dynamically rich environment. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are a ubiquitous class of interstellar organics that play an outsized role in the energetics of the ISM [104]. PAHs are stochastically heated by the interstellar radiation field, and produce prominent ro-vibrational emission lines in the mid-infrared that are widely used as tracers of interstellar physics, both in the Milky Way and extragalactically [9]. In the Milky Way, diffuse PAH emission is an exquisite tracer of high-angular resolution structure, enabling constraints on interstellar turbulence [75, 107], the relative orientation of density and magnetic field structures on small scales [22], and other physics that is encoded in the small-scale spatial structure of the ISM. These analyses require separating the diffuse PAH emission from other near-infrared emission, including from stellar and extragalactic sources. Meisner and Finkbeiner [74] produced 12 µm diffuse emission maps from Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE; Wright et al. 112) data that have been widely used as tracers of diffuse PAH emission. In nearby galaxies, spatially resolved maps of PAH emission can be used alone or in conjunction with other tracers to study the ISM properties, star formation, and the radiation field across galactic environments. Table 1 shows a selection of PAH features and the types of molecules predominantly responsible for the observed emission.

The Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) is a NASA Explorer satellite that is currently conducting an all-sky, near-infrared (0.75 to 5.0 µm) spectral survey [16]. These data present rich opportunities for ISM science: the SPHEREx spectral range encompasses the bright 3.3 µm aromatic PAH feature, as well as the 3.4 µm aliphatic hydrocarbon feature, hydrogen recombination lines, several ro-vibrational transitions of molecular hydrogen, and ice absorption features. In this work, we develop a method for forward-modeling the SPHEREx data that enables high-fidelity mapping of diffuse-emission spectral features, and apply our method to construct high-resolution maps of the 3.3 µm and 3.4 µm PAH features and Paschen-α\alpha. For simplicity, we refer to this method as LVFit throughout the paper.

SPHEREx uses linear variable filter (LVF) spectrometers, which gradually vary the spectral transmission across the surface of the detectors. This means that each pixel in the resulting spectral image corresponds to a slightly different wavelength and bandwidth. The SPHEREx team defines 17 bands for each of the 6 LVFs, which divides the data into 102 spectral channels [16, 100]. Much of the work on tracing PAH emission with SPHEREx to date has operated in this paradigm, by binning the measurements into spectral channel maps (see Section VI.3). [21] (see Section VI.3).

Here we produce large-area maps from many individual exposures using a forward-modeling method. Standard methods in optical astronomy for this kind of “mosaicing” or map-making traditionally involve interpolation and median (or similar) averaging of overlapping imaging; the current state of the art is drizzle [39]. These approaches are inappropriate here because the LVFs make it such that every pixel of the detector has (in principle) a slightly different spectral response. If images are made by binning pixels into spectral channels and combining by traditional methods, banding appears. Since the readout from any pixel of any detector in any good astronomical telescope is linearly related to the surface brightness on the sky, it is principled to make maps of the surface brightness by a classical “inverse problem” [12] or forward model, from which the map is found by optimizing an objective function based on a justified likelihood function.

These forward-model map-making methods have excellent properties: The output maps are linearly (or nearly linearly, depending on details) related to the input data, such that measurements made in the map are simply related to measurements made in the original raw data. The output maps can saturate the Cramér–Rao bound [91, 23] on the delivered image information. The input data can be arbitrarily heterogeneous in spatial structure, noise properties, and spectral response, provided that the likelihood function or forward model accounts for these properties correctly. Forward-model methods for map-making have had an extremely high impact in cosmic microwave background experiments (notably pioneered by Wright et al. 111, and used in different forms by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP; Bennett et al. 10), Planck (Planck Collaboration et al. 86), and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT; Naess et al. 79)). Recently these ideas have been introduced into optical imaging and spectroscopy [64, 96, 49].

One challenge or question with forward-modeling approaches is: Do we choose to deconvolve (in any sense) when we combine the raw data, or do we create a map at the native resolution of the raw data? Since a forward model is in play, the parameters of that model can be of the surface brightness field at any resolution (within reason), in either the angular or spectral sense. When the data and model are both good, the inverse problem can deliver a map at higher resolution than the raw data, at the cost of dependency on detailed assumptions. Here we use beliefs about the PAH and recombination lines to effectively perform only a light deconvolution of the SPHEREx data in the spectral direction. That is, we measure the PAH and recombination lines as precisely as possible given what we know about those line positions and shapes, and about the spectral response of each pixel of the SPHEREx hardware.

papers.title: Engagement Estimation in Human-Robot and Human-Human Interactions across Domain, Age and Culture: MultiMediate'26 Challenge
papers.abstract: Understanding engagement in human interaction is essential for modelling assistive and context-aware AI systems. Previously, the MultiMediate challenge has focused on estimating momentary continuous engagement values in adult conversation across cultures, achieving high levels of generalisability across domains. However, engagement can be measured in different metrics and manifest differently between children and adults. MultiMediate'26 therefore expands the evaluated domain set to include the PInSoRo dataset of Child-Child and Child-Robot play sessions in English. These sessions were annotated categorically with task and social engagement, diversifying engagement types, age ranges and interaction types. In this paper, we describe the MultiMediate'26 challenge and its goals, introduce the NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI, and PInSoRo datasets, showcase extracted multi-modal features, present our baseline model for engagement estimation across all domains, and discuss challenge submissions and approaches. In an effort to provide a transparent and welcoming challenge environment, baseline code, leaderboard, datasets, and extracted features are publicly available at https://github.com/hcmlab/MultiMediate_26.

Estimating the momentary degree of user engagement is crucial for AI systems that take part in and support social interaction. Consequently, a growing body of work proposed approaches for the automatic estimation of engagement in human-human and human-machine interactions.

Estimating the momentary degree of user engagement is crucial for AI systems that take part in and support social interaction. Consequently, a growing body of work proposed approaches for the automatic estimation of engagement in human-human and human-machine interactions.

Engagement in human-human interactions was predicted using gaze features (Bednarik et al., 2012; Nakano and Ishii, 2010) and multi-modal fusion approaches incorporating audio signals, gaze, eye contact, facial features and dialogue transcriptions (Ma et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025b). Human-agent and human-robot interactions were also analysed using backchannels (Rich et al., 2010), body posture (Sanghvi et al., 2011) and multi-modal transformer models (Lim et al., 2025). Research also showed success in predicting engagement in children (Rajagopalan et al., 2015), including interactions with artificial agents (Park et al., 2019; Jain et al., 2020).

MultiMediate is an expanding yearly challenge that focuses on human behaviour analysis in social interaction. It has addressed eye contact detection (Müller et al., 2021), backchannel detection (Müller et al., 2022), and backchannel recognition (Müller et al., 2023), while recent years have focused on the creation of engagement estimation approaches that are generalisable across cultures and conversational settings (Müller et al., 2024; Withanage Don et al., 2025). While these efforts have led to significant advances in engagement estimation, they remain constrained to a specific age group (adult), and a single notion of engagement (single overall magnitude per time point).

These sessions differ from the established estimation task in significant ways. First, they show interactions of children with each other and with robots with only sparse adult participation. Second, they are not conceived as conversations, but as free play interactions with varying amounts of speech. Finally, engagement was not annotated using a continuous scale, but through two sets of categorical annotation labels: task engagement and social engagement.

papers.title: On Relative Smoothness in Dually Flat Geometry
papers.abstract: We study the geometric meaning of relative smoothness on dually flat manifolds and its implications for the convergence analysis of mirror descent. Our main result yields one-sided counterparts of the classical Levi--Civita characterizations of Lipschitz Riemannian gradients, each equivalent to relative smoothness. We further investigate the stationarity of mirror descent iterates for possibly nonconvex objectives and show that relative smoothness alone does not guarantee convergence of the Riemannian gradient norm to zero. We identify a one-sided condition on the cubic tensor that ensures such convergence and yields an $O(1/N)$ stationarity bound. Examples based on the negative entropy potential illustrate the role of metric variation.
papers.intro:
The classical analysis of gradient descent assumes that the gradient of the objective function ff is Lipschitz continuous. Under this assumption, the error in the first-order approximation of ff at xx admits a quadratic upper bound in the Euclidean displacement y−xy-x. Relative smoothness replaces the squared Euclidean distance by the Bregman divergence associated with a convex potential φ\varphi [3, 9]. For twice differentiable ff and φ\varphi on an open convex domain MM, the condition is equivalent to the curvature comparison ∂2f⁡(x)⪯L​∂2φ⁡(x)∀x∈M.\partial^{2}f(x)\preceq L\partial^{2}\varphi(x)\qquad\forall x\in M. The choice of φ\varphi thus allows the upper bound on the curvature of ff to vary over the domain. Relative smoothness therefore accommodates objectives whose gradients are not globally Lipschitz continuous. Such objectives arise, for example, in maximum likelihood estimation for Poisson inverse problems [3, 8, 7] and in DD-optimal experimental design [9] The resulting bound on the first-order approximation error is fundamental to the convergence analysis of Bregman first-order methods, in particular mirror descent, as it yields a sufficient decrease estimate for a suitable choice of step size.

An early form of relative smoothness appeared in [4] in the analysis of Bregman gradient methods for Fisher markets. Relative smoothness was later systematically developed in [9, 3] as a generalization of Lipschitz gradient smoothness based on a convex reference function. These works established equivalent convexity, Hessian, and first-order characterizations of relative smoothness, providing a framework for the convergence analysis of Bregman first-order methods beyond classical Lipschitz gradient assumptions. The framework was extended to nonconvex optimization using the notion of LL-smooth adaptability (L-SMAD) in [5], with applications to quadratic inverse problems.

The main contributions of this work are as follows. (1) Geometric characterization of relative smoothness. (a) Equivalent formulations. We express the classical sufficient-decrease estimate [3, 9] through the symmetric Bregman divergence and show that the squared gradient norm in the metric averaged along the mirror step tends to zero; see Section 4.1. papers.title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
papers.abstract: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.
