papers.intro:
Variational principles are a cornerstone of physics: Fermat’s least time in optics, Hamilton’s stationary action in mechanics, and the Einstein–Hilbert action of general relativity all condense a physical law into the stationarity of a single scalar functional, and Feynman’s path integral recovers this stationarity in the classical limit. Over the past decade these principles have also proven valuable for developing numerical methods for physical phenomena [5, 6]: a variational problem is typically the most compact representation of a coupled multiphysics problem, and can be used to derive the weak form automatically for use with, e.g., the finite element method. For dissipative systems the picture is less settled [7], and two questions motivate the present work.

Variational principles are a cornerstone of physics: Fermat’s least time in optics, Hamilton’s stationary action in mechanics, and the Einstein–Hilbert action of general relativity all condense a physical law into the stationarity of a single scalar functional, and Feynman’s path integral recovers this stationarity in the classical limit. Over the past decade these principles have also proven valuable for developing numerical methods for physical phenomena [5, 6]: a variational problem is typically the most compact representation of a coupled multiphysics problem, and can be used to derive the weak form automatically for use with, e.g., the finite element method. For dissipative systems the picture is less settled [7], and two questions motivate the present work.

First, the extremal principles divide into two families that reflect the different scientific communities from which they arose. Minimum principles apply to nonequilibrium stationary states: Helmholtz’s minimum dissipation for Stokes flow [8], Kirchhoff’s for stationary currents [9], and Prigogine’s minimum entropy production [10]. They belong to thermodynamicists and chemists (Prigogine a chemist by training, Helmholtz a physician-turned-physicist), whose paradigm is the driven open system of chemistry and chemical engineering: reactants in, products out, entropy production minimized at the stationary state in between (Section 5.1.2). Maximum principles instead apply to relaxation in continuum mechanics and materials science: Ziegler’s maximum rate of dissipation [1], the principle of maximum dissipation in inelasticity, whose relation to dissipation potentials was clarified by Hackl and Fischer [2], and the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) of materials science [11, 12]. They belong to engineers and materials scientists, whose paradigm is inelastic material response (plasticity, creep, phase transformation) in a closed system releasing stored free energy at frozen state through rates that maximize the dissipation (Section 5.1.1). Onsager’s principle of least dissipation of energy [13] is, despite its name, not a stationary-state principle: it is an instantaneous principle for the rates, read as the maximum principle by Svoboda et al. [3], and the functional it minimizes is the Rayleighian functional that connects the two families (Section 2.1). That instantaneous maximization and stationary-state minimization of the entropy production are distinct statements has been noted before [14, 15], and for multicomponent diffusion the distinction has recently been made precise [3]: forces given and rates varied at an instant versus fields varied under fixed boundary data at the stationary state.

Beris and Edwards [4] recently pointed out that Rayleighian extremum principles remain restricted to cases where the kinetic energy is negligible, yet fluid mechanics routinely requires viscosity and inertia together. Hackl, Svoboda, and Fischer [16] proposed a coupling of the TEP with Hamilton’s principle in exactly this context, in which the Lagrangian is extended by a dissipation-force term; the present work follows a different route through the rate of the total energy (Section 4).

Both questions meet in a classical benchmark of fluid mechanics, the flow in a lid-driven square cavity [17], here computed with the unsteady Stokes equation, which neglects convection but keeps inertia through the time derivative. Figure 1 shows one computation in three phases. In phase (a) the lid is started from rest, and the dissipation decreases monotonically. In phase (b) the flow has become stationary: the power supplied by the lid is dissipated entirely, and by Helmholtz’s theorem this stationary dissipation is the smallest among all incompressible flows with the same lid velocity. In phase (c) the lid is stopped, and the stored kinetic energy is dissipated until the fluid comes to rest. The same equation thus produces a state of minimum dissipation and, after the lid stops, a decay that proceeds, as Section 5.1.1 shows, through the rates of maximal dissipation. Explaining why one functional yields both, with inertia present, is the subject of this work.

The present work is a contribution to the understanding of the TEP. We investigate its extremal properties and find the two families connected through a single convex functional, the Rayleighian, whose minimum appears as Ziegler’s maximum during relaxation and as the Helmholtz–Prigogine minimum at a driven stationary state (Section 5.1). Svoboda et al. [3] established the maximum and the minimum as two different extremization tasks for multicomponent diffusion; we extend this distinction to fluids and to systems with inertia and show that both tasks are two sides of one Rayleighian minimum. We further investigate the role of the Reynolds transport theorem, which turns out to be a useful tool: the choice of control volume fixes the energy rate the TEP requires and with it the structure of the resulting equations. The TEP is elegant for inertialess systems, where the driving forces are state functions. With inertia the driving force contains the acceleration and must be frozen during the variation, which is less natural. The same rule applies in Navier–Stokes flow and in Lagrangian mechanics, and writing ℱ˙\dot{\mathcal{F}} as rates times driving forces still delivers the correct equations, so that the TEP also covers dynamics that are not overdamped. An extremal statement survives whenever the frozen driving force does not depend explicitly on the varied rate: for unsteady Stokes flow and constant-mass mechanics the minimum persists directly, and for Navier–Stokes flow it is recovered by a change of perspective to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state; for configuration-dependent kinetic metrics only stationarity remains in the given coordinates. The argument is carried by the Navier–Stokes family of Section 3, that is, by Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier–Stokes flow in order of increasing complexity, and by dissipative Lagrangian mechanics (Section 4). Diffusion is deliberately left aside: there the TEP works well and has become an established tool, especially for multicomponent diffusion, where its use has been systematized in [5]; the scope here is fluids and mechanics, where inertia enters. Throughout, the dissipation is quadratic in the rates; Section 5.2 states what this restricts and shows that homogeneity of the dissipation in the rates already suffices for both extremal statements.

papers.title: Testing Models of Disk Formation and Gravito-Viscous Evolution Against Observations of Young Protoplanetary Disks
papers.abstract: Young protoplanetary disks have received increasing attention in recent years, due to observations revealing the presence of substructures in disks younger than one million years, suggesting that planet formation may begin earlier than previously thought. Other recent observations have provided new insights into the evolution of gas and dust in these early stages, enabling comparisons with evolved Class II disks. Yet the physical processes governing the earliest stages of disk evolution remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present two-dimensional thin-disk hydrodynamical simulations of the formation and early evolution of protoplanetary disks, under the influence of self-gravity and turbulent viscosity alone. We explore various properties of disks forming from the collapse of clouds with a range of initial masses and we compare our results with surveys of protoplanetary disks across multiple evolutionary stages. Our simulations broadly reproduce key observational constraints, including the mm fluxes of Class 0 disks and the dust disk radii of later stages. However, our models do not explain the observed gas and dust disk masses of Class I and II disks: while they account for the most massive observed disks, they fail to reproduce the least massive ones. We discuss that simulations incorporating the influence of the star-forming environment might be needed to resolve this discrepancy.

papers.intro:
Stars and protoplanetary disks form from the gravitational collapse of a molecular cloud. Protoplanetary disks are mostly composed of gas, but also contain a small portion of dust. This material can grow to form planets and other smaller bodies. Throughout their lifetime, young stellar objects (YSOs) undergo different evolutionary phases. In the initial phase, known as Class 0, the disk is still embedded in the molecular cloud and jets are usually present due to ongoing accretion from the envelope. This phase is quickly followed by the Class I stage, in which the disk is surrounded by a less dense envelope. The Class II stage begins when the envelope has finally disappeared and can last for several million years. The disk eventually dissipates to leave a planetary system (André, 2002).

This material can grow to form planets and other smaller bodies. Throughout their lifetime, young stellar objects (YSOs) undergo different evolutionary phases. In the initial phase, known as Class 0, the disk is still embedded in the molecular cloud and jets are usually present due to ongoing accretion from the envelope. This phase is quickly followed by the Class I stage, in which the disk is surrounded by a less dense envelope. The Class II stage begins when the envelope has finally disappeared and can last for several million years. The disk eventually dissipates to leave a planetary system (André, 2002).

The emergence of planetary systems from protoplanetary disks around young stars has now been observed directly in two systems, PDS 70 (Keppler et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2018; Haffert et al., 2019) and WISPIT2 (van Capelleveen et al., 2025; Lawlor et al., 2026). Exoplanetary systems (in which the disk has already dispersed) have been extensively observed in the last 30 years. As of today, more than 6200 exoplanets have been discovered, showing extreme diversity and demonstrating that planet formation in protoplanetary disks must be a common process. However, many aspects of this process are still unknown, including when planet formation may occur throughout the lifetime of a protoplanetary disk. The aforementioned PDS 70 and WISPIT2 systems are rather old (5-7 Myr), so they do not provide clear insights on how early their planets started to form.

The presence of substructures in protoplanetary disks can provide insight into the possibility of early planet formation. Substructures are quite ubiquitous in Class II disks (Andrews et al., 2018; Teague et al., 2025). Their appearance could be caused by various mechanisms (e.g. ice lines, instabilities, photoevaporation, magneto-hydrodynamic processes; see Bae et al. (2023) for a review), including the presence in these protoplanetary disks of already formed planetary companions. Therefore, the detection of substructures in Class II disks could indicate the presence of giant planets in these systems. However, substructures seem to be less common in Class 0 and I disks. The eDisk project inspected 19 Class 0 and I disks and found very few substructures in them (Ohashi et al., 2023). They concluded that most of the planet formation process should occur rapidly in between the late Class I and early Class II stages. However, recent surveys have shown that substructures are already common in Class I disks (Shoshi et al., 2025; Hsieh et al., 2025; Bhowmik et al., 2026), suggesting that the planet formation process may begin earlier, at the start of the Class I stage or even before. Moreover, Nazari et al. (2025) found that massive planets (≲102​M⊕\lesssim 10^{2}M_{\oplus}), even if already formed in Class 0 and Class I disks, would not be opening gaps in these early and warm disk phases. Therefore, even if they were present, young planets would be difficult to detect in the embedded stages. The suggestion of early planet formation is also supported by the "mass budget problem", whereby the dust content in Class II disks is insufficient for planet formation (Manara et al., 2018). Disks may be more massive than estimated due to their optical thickness. However, planet formation in earlier, more massive disk phases is still a possible solution to this problem, at least for forming the most massive planets.

The presence of substructures in protoplanetary disks can provide insight into the possibility of early planet formation. Substructures are quite ubiquitous in Class II disks (Andrews et al., 2018; Teague et al., 2025). Their appearance could be caused by various mechanisms (e.g. ice lines, instabilities, photoevaporation, magneto-hydrodynamic processes; see Bae et al. (2023) for a review), including the presence in these protoplanetary disks of already formed planetary companions. Observations of disks in the early stages are challenging, in particular because of the increased optical depth and extinction due to the envelope surrounding them. Nonetheless, several efforts have been made to constrain the disk properties. They include observing at longer wavelengths to mitigate high optical depth effects (Tobin et al., 2016), combining high- and low-angular resolution observations to distinguish the envelope from the disk emission (Ohashi et al., 2023), and detecting different combinations of molecular lines that allow tracing the gas disk masses (Zhang et al., 2025). These studies have allowed us to have the first observational evidence that a significant gas evolution has happened between the Class 0/I stages and the early Class II objects, slowing significantly during the later Class II phase (Zhang et al., 2025). Dust evolution might also start in early stages, suggested by the presence of substructures in various Class I disks, as discussed above, and by the small spectral index values found in the envelopes and disks of young stellar systems (Miotello et al., 2014; Cacciapuoti et al., 2023).

For this reason, it is essential to better constrain how disks form and evolve from the collapse of molecular clouds and to compare theoretical predictions with available observations. This would help to identify the key properties and physical processes that operate in the earliest evolutionary stages and shape the Class II phase, influencing the possible outcome of the planet formation process. Different previous studies have addressed the early phases of disk formation in cloud collapse simulations, focusing on different mechanisms driving protostellar accretion and disk evolution. Some examples include previous thin-disk or 3D works on the masses and sizes of embedded disks (Vorobyov, 2011; Machida et al., 2014; Hennebelle et al., 2016; Hennebelle et al., 2020; Vorobyov et al., 2024; Kobayashi et al., 2025, e.g.,), population synthesis of disks formed in hydrodynamical or magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of star forming clusters (Kuffmeier et al., 2017; Bate, 2018; Lebreuilly et al., 2021; Lebreuilly et al., 2024, e.g.,), studies considering semi-analytic models of envelope infall into the disk (Hueso and Guillot, 2005; Visser et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2016, e.g.,), and others focusing on dust dynamics and growth during these early stages (Lebreuilly et al., 2020; Tsukamoto et al., 2020; Appelgren et al., 2023; Vorobyov et al., 2025; Bate et al., 2026, e.g.,) However, only a few studies have numerically modeled gravito-viscous disks across different evolutionary stages. In particular, multi-dimensional simulations that couple gas and dust with self-consistent growth and drift from the embedded phases to Class II, and their statistical comparison with recent surveys, are still missing.

papers.title: Replication of Thermal Comfort Cohort Models: No Support for Improved Thermal Preference Prediction
papers.abstract: Cohort comfort models (CCMs) aim to overcome the extensive individual data requirements of personal comfort models (PCMs) by grouping occupants based on demographic and psychometric characteristics (cold start) or similar thermal preferences (warm start). We evaluated the validity of the reported CCM performance gains through (i) a methodological assessment of the original study, (ii) a replication using one of the two original datasets (DORN: 20 participants, 6 months) under a revised experimental protocol, and (iii) a replication using an independently collected dataset (PersonAI: 72 participants, 4 weeks). Classification performance was evaluated using F1-micro, as in the original study, and F1-macro to account for class imbalance. Under F1-micro, a trivial baseline that always outputs the majority class performed on par with cohort models. Under F1-macro, all cohort models achieved lower median scores than a simple baseline that makes random predictions based on the estimated distribution of thermal preferences. In our methodological assessment we identified the following key issues: Limited data per participant and per minority class, reliance on a metric insensitive to class imbalance, missing trivial baselines, inadequate cross validation strategy, and multiple occurrences of information leakage. Our findings challenge the original study's conclusion that CCMs improve thermal preference prediction. CCMs did not outperform simple class-distribution baselines. Future studies should improve experimental designs, including controlled thermal conditions, to obtain sufficient observations across thermal preference classes.

papers.intro:
Buildings face a dual and often conflicting challenge. They play a central role in global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for approximately 40% of worldwide energy demand Schweiger et al. (2020). At the same time, they must provide indoor conditions that support health, comfort, and performance, as people spend the vast majority of their lives indoors Klepeis et al. (2001). Over the past decades, researchers and standardization bodies have developed methods to predict indoor environmental quality and occupant comfort that are built on aggregated representations of how a typical occupant perceives the thermal environment Donkers et al. (2025). These aggregated representations are inherently limited because they estimate group averages and therefore often predict poorly for individuals. As a result, designing and operating buildings according to such models can fail to improve real occupant satisfaction and may instead encourage conservative HVAC sizing and scheduling, increasing energy use without reliably reducing discomfort Donkers et al. (2025). To address the limitations of aggregate models, data-driven Personal Comfort Models (PCMs) have been proposed. PCMs are a new approach to thermal comfort modeling that predicts individuals’ thermal comfort responses, instead of the average response of a large population and it can be applied to any HVAC system Kim et al. (2018a). The increasing availability of off-the-shelf wearable devices has strengthened this approach by enabling the collection of physiological measurements, such as skin temperature and heart rate, which have been shown to improve prediction accuracy. Yet collecting longitudinal field data remains costly and burdensome, as it requires repeated Right-Here-Right-Now (RHRN) surveys during daily activities and high-resolution environmental monitoring that is difficult to sustain at scale Tartarini et al. (2022). To address the scalability limitations of personalized models, Cohort Comfort Models (CCMs) have been proposed, exploiting similarities between occupants to estimate the thermal preferences of new individuals with little or no historical data Quintana et al. (2023). By estimating preferences based on similarities between occupants, CCMs combine the personalization of individual models with the data efficiency of aggregate approaches.

papers.title: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
papers.abstract: Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 $mK$ even at 50 $\mu V$ bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

papers.title: On maximum volume polytopes inscribed in the sphere
papers.abstract: We combine degree sequence bounds with a supporting tangent plane method to study maximum volume polytopes inscribed in the sphere $\mathbb S^2$. Building on the vertex-star estimates and combinatorial reductions in Wimmer's dissertation, we determine the exact maximum for ten vertices and the unique maximizing combinatorial type for eleven vertices. Moreover, using explicit computational certificates we identify a unique possible maximizing type for polytopes with thirteen and fifteen vertices, and two possible types for sixteen vertices; this approach also recovers Wimmer's fourteen-vertex combinatorial theorem. Finally, we derive a facial inequality which holds for every degree pattern, and prove that the maximum volume for polytopes with thirty-two vertices is $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{10(5-\sqrt{5})}$, attained precisely by an inscribed realization of the pentakis dodecahedron, which is the convex hull of the regular icosahedron together with its normalized facet centers. Wimmer had already determined this configuration and its optimality within its own combinatorial type. We also obtain a global degree sequence envelope and a universal affine volume bound.

papers.title: Fueling Inflation Risks: An Oil Shortage Scenario
papers.abstract: Central banks routinely use alternative scenarios to assess risks to the economic outlook, but these are usually generated from linear models that are unable to speak to the likelihood of extreme outcomes. We develop a nonlinear modeling framework that turns a narrative oil market scenario into a fully probabilistic assessment of the dynamics of oil and gasoline prices, aggregate inflation, and household inflation expectations. It combines an expert-based path for a tail event, a nonparametric model of the global oil market, and nonlinear Phillips curves for the energy, food, and core components of PCE inflation. We apply it in real time to quantify energy price and inflation risks of a severe oil shortage caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, modeled as a rapid drawdown of global petroleum inventories, using only information available in February 2026. Our analysis shows that once oil reserves hit rock bottom, oil and gasoline prices rise sharply, with risks tilted to the upside. Headline PCE inflation peaks near 4.8% in late 2026, and households expect inflation to rise by about 3 percentage points. Two years out, inflation is still highly likely to exceed the Fed's 2% target.

papers.intro:
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the wake of the US attack on Iran caused an unprecedented disruption of global oil flows. To offset the resulting supply shortfall, the International Energy Agency (IEA) swiftly acted to coordinate a release of 400 million barrels of crude oil and refined products from emergency stockpiles among its member countries, the largest intervention ever (see Baumeister, 2023, for an analysis of previous episodes). Together with record drawdowns from commercial inventories, supplies from storage initially kept a lid on oil prices. But the inventory buffer is finite. Once this shock absorber is exhausted, any remaining oil deficit has to be balanced by price adjustments, and the risk of extreme price increases rises sharply (Deaton and Laroque, 1992). A prolonged blockade of tanker traffic through the Strait therefore also poses an important upside risk to the inflation outlook. This raises the questions of how high oil prices, gasoline prices, and inflation could go if global petroleum inventories are drained to critical levels, and how likely such outcomes are. We address these questions with a scenario analysis that forms the basis for our real-time risk assessment.

We develop a flexible and transparent framework that maps an oil market scenario into probabilities of outcomes for gasoline prices, various measures of inflation, and household inflation expectations, enabling us to quantify tail risks for the inflation outlook. Our framework consists of three components. The first is an expert assessment of possibly severe developments in global oil markets that draws on a wide range of information to construct a path for global petroleum inventories over roughly the next two years. The resulting scenario postulates that both emergency reserves and commercial stockpiles are drawn down at record speed to their all-time low by the end of June 2026, remain at that operational minimum for one year, and then gradually recover to half of the pre-war level.

The second component is the nonparametric model of Baumeister, Huber, and Marcellino (2024), which combines a linear vector autoregression (VAR) with Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch, 2010, BART,) and factor stochastic volatility. This model was specifically designed to capture tail risks in global oil markets, including the risk of stockouts, and it has been shown to produce accurate tail forecasts of the real price of oil. We use this nonlinear model to generate predictive distributions of the real price of oil and other oil market fundamentals conditional on the predetermined inventory path and translate each simulated value for the oil price into US retail gasoline prices, nationally and for 474 metropolitan areas, using the rule of thumb of Hamilton (2012). We examine the conditional dynamics of gasoline prices because they are among the most visible and frequently observed prices for consumers, greatly influencing the formation of household inflation expectations, which in turn affect future inflation.

papers.title: PhysDNet: Physics-Driven Gradient Amplification for Real-Time Image Dehazing
papers.abstract: Modern dehazing networks are often computationally expensive and overfit to synthetic haze, limiting real-time deployment. This underscores an urgent demand for efficient, high-fidelity restoration methods that can operate on resource-constrained edge devices in practical, dynamic environments. We introduce PhysDNet, a lightweight multimodal architecture that fuses NIR imagery with sparse LiDAR depth and is trained with a physics-constrained dual-head objective. Differentiating through a fixed Koschmieder inversion induces density-adaptive gradient amplification, acting as an implicit resource allocation mechanism that concentrates learning on heavily degraded regions without increasing inference cost. PhysDNet delivers superior restoration with minimal capacity and enhanced training efficiency, facilitating real-time deployment on edge devices without increasing inference overhead. On the Seeing Through Fog benchmark, PhysDNet outperforms competitors by 1.67 dB at 5.2 times lower compute while recovering 54.9% of fog-induced detection loss. Ablations and cross-domain evaluations show that physics-guided training improves generalization, including under non-homogeneous haze that violates the Koschmieder assumption. PhysDNet further demonstrates compatibility with fixed-function NPUs, running at 29/45/99 FPS at <4 W across L/M/S variants. Code, deployment scripts and pre-trained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Heatdh/PhysDnet.

papers.title: Spin Conductivity: Insight From Perturbation Theory
papers.abstract: The investigation on the spin conductivity has now been blooming in burgeoning altermagnetic materials. Here, an alternative and elementary derivation for the spin conductivity expression is presented. This is done within the context of perturbation theory. It indicates that our derived expression for the $\mathcal{T}$-even ($\mathcal{T}$ for time reversal) spin conductivity agrees exactly with those derived from the Kubo linear response theory and quantum kinetic theory. In addition, the expression for the $\mathcal{T}$-odd spin conductivity in the clean limit is exactly consistent with those presented previously. We show that the $\mathcal{T}$-odd ($\mathcal{T}$-even) spin conductivity arises from the contribution of zeroth-order (first-order) wave function correction. Our work provides some physical insight into the spin conductivity from the perturbation theory and shines more light on the charge-to-spin conversion mechanism in magnetic materials.

papers.intro:
The charge-to-spin conversion enables all-electric generation of spin currents and plays a very important role in spintronics[1, 2, 3]. For example, the spin Hall effect (SHE) characterized by a transverse spin current in response to a longitudinal charge current is essential for many intriguing physical phenomena, such as the current-induced spin polarization[4, 5], the spin–orbit torque[6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], the spin Hall magnetoresistance effect[13, 14], etc. In particular, the spin-orbit torque exerted by a spin current enable the current-induced magnetization switching beneficial for high-speed and low-power spintronic devices[15, 16, 17, 18]. However, as enforced by the orthonormality relations between the charge current, the spin current and its spin polarization, the spin current generated by the conventional SHE typically reveals the in-plane spin polarization, which is not favorable to switch the perpendicular magnetization[15, 16, 17, 18]. Moreover, the charge-to-spin conversion efficiency is dominated by the strength of the spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is small compared to the magnetic exchange coupling. In this context, exploration of novel charge-to-spin conversion mechanism is desirable.

For example, the spin Hall effect (SHE) characterized by a transverse spin current in response to a longitudinal charge current is essential for many intriguing physical phenomena, such as the current-induced spin polarization[4, 5], the spin–orbit torque[6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], the spin Hall magnetoresistance effect[13, 14], etc. In particular, the spin-orbit torque exerted by a spin current enable the current-induced magnetization switching beneficial for high-speed and low-power spintronic devices[15, 16, 17, 18]. Moreover, the charge-to-spin conversion efficiency is dominated by the strength of the spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is small compared to the magnetic exchange coupling. In this context, exploration of novel charge-to-spin conversion mechanism is desirable.

papers.title: TRIAD: Multimodal Retrieval across Abstraction, Constraints, and State
papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval increasingly supports agentic systems, where user requests can involve cross-level relations, combine multiple constraints, and evolve across dialogue turns. In these settings, a highly similar result may still violate the user's requirements, while retrieved content may directly inform downstream actions without human screening. We introduce TRIAD, a multimodal retrieval benchmark for evaluating how well retrieval systems satisfy these complex, evolving requests. TRIAD comprises three tracks: abstraction, testing bidirectional retrieval between visual instances and concepts at different hierarchical levels; constraints, testing the joint satisfaction of positive and negative conditions; and state, testing the integration of requirements across dialogue turns and the updating of earlier conditions when users revise their requests. The benchmark contains six subsets, each with 1,000 queries and a fixed pool of 1,000 candidates per query, evaluated using a common multi-positive mean average precision (mAP) protocol. Simpler reference tasks and hard negatives grouped by the requirements they violate help characterize specific retrieval difficulties. We evaluate 20 configurations of 17 systems and find that no system leads across all six subsets. Performance declines with hierarchical distance, and negative-only queries generally underperform positive-only queries with the same number of constraints. Across paired tasks expressing the same final intent, multi-turn retrieval yields lower mAP in 39 of 40 configuration-domain comparisons. The benefits of explicit reasoning also vary across models and tasks. These findings highlight the gap between retrieving similar content and satisfying a complete request.

papers.intro:
Traditional multimodal search presents users with a ranked list of results in response to a text, image, or combined query. Embedding-based retrievers produce this ranking by mapping queries and candidates into a shared space and comparing their similarity, supported by advances in holistic image–text alignment and diversified multimodal embeddings (Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025d). Its traditional use, in which users inspect and filter results ranked primarily by approximate similarity, rests on three premises. The query is self-contained: the current input already expresses the full active intent, without requiring the system to determine which earlier requirements still apply. Overall similarity can stand in for relevance: candidates are compared mainly by degree of match, without hard requirements whose violation cannot be compensated for by similarity in other respects. Retrieval ends with human judgment: users can skip results that appear relevant but miss their actual needs.

In agentic settings, user requests become more detailed and complex and evolve through interaction, so these premises no longer generally hold. A request may seek concepts in a superordinate or subordinate relation, rather than simply similar content (Vendrov et al., 2016). For example, when retrieving a superordinate concept for a sparrow, biologically similar bird species may resemble the sparrow more closely in appearance or fine-grained semantics, yet cannot substitute for a superordinate concept such as bird or even animal. A request may also impose multiple constraints that must hold jointly: “like this scarf, but blue and not patterned” requires both inclusion and exclusion, together with preservation of attributes that were not requested to change. Similarity in other respects cannot compensate for violating these requirements. A request may further span multiple turns, requiring selective retention or updating of historical state: when a user first asks for orange and later changes to blue, the system must retain conditions from the history that remain valid while replacing the abandoned value with the new one, rather than assume that the latest turn is self-contained. Meanwhile, retrieved results may feed directly into subsequent reasoning or tool calls, without a user screening each result for errors. Relevance must therefore be judged against the user’s full current requirements, rather than overall similarity alone. Although existing benchmarks partially cover multi-constraint and multi-turn retrieval, a unified framework for evaluating these requirements and diagnosing specific model capability gaps is still lacking (Wu et al., 2019; Alhamoud et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2018). Our concern is not to replace similarity-based ranking, but to test whether the relevance it represents responds to the complete request: we define correct results from the request’s requirements, measure whether a model ranks them highly, and examine which requirements high-ranked errors violate.

papers.title: Towards Trustworthy Mobile Speech Interaction: Ensuring Voice Authenticity and Transmission Integrity
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of generative speech models has made high-fidelity voice cloning and editing cheap, fast, and widely accessible, weakening the security of voiceprint-based authentication in mobile speech interactions. Existing speech watermarking techniques focus on offline protection or watermarking synthetic speech, and thus cannot verify whether a live utterance originates from the genuine speaker at capture time. We present \textit{MoBiMark}, a real-time \textbf{mo}bile \textbf{bi}ologic speech water\textbf{mark}ing system that binds ultrasonic articulatory signatures to speech content and embeds a dynamic watermark during capture. MoBiMark emits a multi-frequency ultrasonic probe on commodity smartphones, extracts echo features from the vocal tract, and fuses them with a content-dependent speech embedding to produce a dual-layer dynamic watermark combining a persistent user identifier (UID) and a per-utterance speech identifier (SID), enabling both source authentication and propagation-time tamper detection. A jointly trained embedder and detector injects the watermark while preserving perceptual quality, and system-level optimization with INT8 quantization enables lightweight on-device deployment. Evaluated on 50 users across four smartphone models, MoBiMark achieves an average 99.79% accuracy in source and propagation attacks, with negligible impact on speech quality and intelligibility.

papers.intro:
Voice interaction has become a dominant interface for mobile assistants, smart speakers, and multimodal applications, yet the security of voice-based systems is increasingly fragile. Contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) generative models can clone a target speaker’s timbre from a short enrollment sample and synthesize fluent speech at scale, rendering voiceprint verification vulnerable to spoofing and content manipulation. Many voice-interactive intelligent agents are now capable of directly manipulating applications and accessing private data on users’ smart devices, yet they still rely on traditional voiceprint-based authentication mechanisms, posing significant privacy and security risks.

Large-scale anti-spoofing experiments demonstrate that even strong automatic speaker verification systems remain exposed to replay, conversion, and synthesis attacks across logical and physical access settings (Wang et al., 2020; Yamagishi et al., 2021; Tak et al., 2020; Park et al., 2021). Modern audio models built on neural architectures produce high-quality speech with low latency, while neural vocoders and end-to-end systems push naturalness closer to human recordings (van den Oord et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021).

Digital speech watermarking has emerged as a promising mitigation, with decades of work on imperceptible and robust audio watermarking (Swanson et al., 1998; Hua et al., 2016; Al-Haj, 2014; Cox et al., 2002). Recent learning-based watermarking frameworks improve robustness under compression and filtering (Pavlovic et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Roman et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025a), but they still lack broad applicability. In the face of advanced voice cloning, a watermark can be removed, replayed, or replaced by attackers. Existing methods predominantly operate offline, focusing on protecting user-generated content after creation or verifying AI-generated output. As AI-powered speech forgery capabilities grow increasingly sophisticated, applying watermarks to protect speech at the moment of utterance emerges as a more logical and urgent approach. There is currently no work that focuses on using digital watermarking to protect user speech online in real time. A watermarking system operating on a device still cannot verify that the input speech originates from a real user, which remains one of the key factors limiting wider adoption.

We observe two core limitations of existing speech watermarking systems. First, content-only watermarks cannot verify the physical source: attackers can remove or regenerate watermarks using private models, or replay and re-edit captured speech to bypass detection. Second, most designs use static watermarks and lack reliable biometric binding in online settings, where registration requirements and device-specific keys limit deployability. A practical system must bind a watermark to the user’s biometric characteristics during capture, operate without specialized hardware, and remain robust under common signal processing attacks.

The reflected echoes encode signatures of articulator motion, which are fused with speech content to produce a biometric-dependent dual-layer watermark. As shown in Fig. 1, MoBiMark emits an inaudible multi-frequency ultrasonic signal via the phone earpiece and captures its reflections through the built-in microphone. Although our system shows great promise, several key challenges remain to be addressed: First, how to effectively perform feature transformation and watermark encoding to ensure user speech protection throughout propagation. We propose a dual-layer dynamic watermark encoding method combining a system-assigned static UID with a speech-correlated dynamic SID. This ensures that tampered or forged speech can be reliably detected. By integrating the source user’s biometric information and security mechanisms, a closed-loop security framework is formed from the source to the propagation process. Second, how to effectively embed the generated watermark into the original speech and achieve reliable detection, ensuring that the watermark remains detectable and supports accurate discrimination after embedding. In the embedding scenario, we enhance watermark robustness against benign modifications by adjusting the speech frame ordering strategy. Furthermore, through security-oriented analysis, we incorporate an external stabilizer to perform denoising and enhancement on both the encoded speech information and the input at the detection end, thereby ensuring the stability of the generated speech features and the watermark. Finally, how to build a universal and high-accuracy system on real-world mobile smartphones, enabling online real-time use on resource-constrained edge devices. Benefit to the widespread availability of microphone hardware required for ultrasonic signals, our system inherently possesses hardware universality. Combined with our carefully designed lightweight model, which employs efficient modules and incorporates quantization to maximally compress the original system while preserving accuracy, we successfully deploy the system on mobile devices, achieving a truly universal, secure and accurate solution.

papers.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Biometric Watermarking Against Face Video Deepfakes
papers.abstract: Currently, artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) poses a severe threat to facial video deepfakes, and many AIGC companies employ video watermarking to mitigate unauthorized fake video usage, but its effectiveness is limited due to watermark tampering and private-model forgery. Additionally, some schemes actively add watermarks to user videos. However, current approaches focus primarily on the quality of watermark embedding in offline scenarios, and no existing work offers a solution for protecting human facial videos in real-time online applications. To fill this gap, we propose, to the best of our knowledge, a novel biometric video watermarking method, UltraGuard, for the first time. It uses the smartphone's built-in speaker and microphone to emit ultrasonic signals and capture biometric features, which are then fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into videos in real time, enabling dynamic, content-aware watermarking throughout transmission and propagation. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that UltraGuard can effectively defend against malicious attacks such as forgery and editing, both at the source and during propagation, proving the system's efficacy. In the future, it can be deployed on users' mobile devices to provide real-time protection for users' facial videos, thereby preventing security and privacy breaches caused by various malicious attacks.

papers.intro:
With the widespread adoption of high-speed mobile networks, online video communication, such as video conferencing and real-time video calls, has become integral to modern information exchange. In many practical scenarios, these interactions involve legal archiving and business decision-making, which makes complete and trustworthy video records increasingly important. At the same time, the security and authenticity of video content become more difficult to guarantee (Zhang, 2022). To counter highly deceptive Deepfake and malicious tampering techniques, existing defenses increasingly shift from traditional passive detection to data-driven deep learning methods (Passos et al., 2024). However, these approaches often show limited generalization when they face unseen cross-domain attacks or complex transmission distortions (Khan and Dang-Nguyen, 2023). Furthermore, we note that with the recent advancement of AIGC, representative models such as Sora (OpenAI, 2024) and Seedance (Gao et al., 2025) can generate forged facial videos that are increasingly difficult to distinguish from real ones. The latest face-swapping algorithm (Flynn et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026) focuses specifically on modifying target faces, which will make forgery detection increasingly challenging in the future, posing a significant threat to user privacy and security. Against this backdrop, digital video watermarking emerges as a promising direction for proactive provenance tracking and content authentication (Zhang et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2025). However, the mainstream solution adopted by current large model vendors is to embed watermark information into forged videos. However, this approach is easily removed by attackers or circumvented by privately trained generative models. A better facial anti-spoofing solution is to proactively embed watermark information into all genuine human face videos of users, such that any video with an incorrect watermark or without a watermark is regarded as an attacker-forged video.

Furthermore, a closer look at prior work reveals fundamental security limitations in existing video watermarking schemes. Most of them are designed as static watermarking solutions for offline settings (Zhang et al., 2011; Fernandez et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025b), treating the watermark as a post hoc tag rather than a source-authenticating signal at capture time. As a result, they cannot verify whether a video truly originates from a live, legitimate source. This weakness leaves them vulnerable to replay attacks, allowing pre-recorded forged videos to obtain valid watermarks and be accepted as trusted content (Aberna and Agilandeeswari, 2024; Asikuzzaman and Pickering, 2017). Moreover, because most video watermark extractors are publicly accessible, attackers can reverse-engineer the extraction model, infer static watermark features, and reconstruct them for injection into tampered videos. This can mislead the verifier into returning a valid decision, thereby enabling highly stealthy forgeries.

Most of them are designed as static watermarking solutions for offline settings (Zhang et al., 2011; Fernandez et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025b), treating the watermark as a post hoc tag rather than a source-authenticating signal at capture time. As a result, they cannot verify whether a video truly originates from a live, legitimate source. This weakness leaves them vulnerable to replay attacks, allowing pre-recorded forged videos to obtain valid watermarks and be accepted as trusted content (Aberna and Agilandeeswari, 2024; Asikuzzaman and Pickering, 2017). Moreover, because most video watermark extractors are publicly accessible, attackers can reverse-engineer the extraction model, infer static watermark features, and reconstruct them for injection into tampered videos. This can mislead the verifier into returning a valid decision, thereby enabling highly stealthy forgeries.

To make matters worse, existing methods address these threats in isolation. Video forgery detection approaches (Qian et al., 2020; Tariq et al., 2018; Corvi et al., 2023) focus solely on identifying post-hoc forgeries but provide no proactive protection at the source. Face authentication methods (Zhao et al., 2003; Schroff et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019) verify user identity at capture time but fail to protect video content once it enters the propagation channel. Neither approach provides an end-to-end security guarantee covering both generation and propagation. This fragmentation creates a critical gap where a video that passes authentication at capture can still be manipulated during transmission without detection. The growing deployment of video communication in high-stakes domains—such as remote judicial proceedings, telemedicine consultations, and executive business negotiations—further amplifies the urgency for a comprehensive solution that provides verifiable provenance from capture through the entire video content lifecycle.

In this paper, we present UltraGuard, a secure online dynamic watermarking system that leverages biometric information and facial content to defend face videos against deepfake attacks during both generation and propagation, as shown in Fig. 1. The key insight is that source-side online dynamic watermarking is more secure by design than post-generation watermarking, because it grants valid watermark protection only to videos from authenticated live users and exposes unauthenticated or incorrectly watermarked videos as forgeries. Our system offers two key advantages over traditional video watermarking systems. First, our system is the first to leverage wireless reflections to capture face-related biometric information for secure online video watermarking, enabling live-user verification and preventing replay attacks that inject valid watermarks into forged videos at the source. Second, our system is the first to introduce dynamic biometric video watermarking for secure video propagation, leveraging the uniqueness of facial changes within a time window to jointly encode user identity, facial motion dynamics, and biometric information, thereby significantly reducing the risk of malicious video tampering.

papers.title: Nemotron 3 Diarization: Advancing the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier in Streaming Speaker Diarization
papers.abstract: Streaming Sortformer introduced an arrival-order speaker cache to maintain speaker identities across chunks in end-to-end streaming speaker diarization, with a single model supporting configurable latency profiles spanning offline operation to ultra-low-latency streaming. Nemotron 3 Diarization addresses the original model's four-speaker limitation by extending support to eight speakers while improving both accuracy and computational efficiency. The previous FastConformer-Transformer stack is streamlined into a pure Transformer encoder. A learned upsampling layer then maps the encoder's coarse 80-ms representations to 10-ms resolution, enabling fine-grained predictions. Training leverages large-scale simulated mixtures and adds activity and phantom-speaker losses to the standard Sortformer objectives. Despite doubling speaker capacity over its predecessor, the new architecture reduces training memory by a factor of 2.8, makes training $2.2\times$ faster, and delivers up to $6.4\times$ higher inference throughput. Nemotron 3 Diarization establishes a new state of the art in DER on DIHARD III and CALLHOME. When used to condition DiCoW, it also achieves state-of-the-art tcpWER on the single-microphone conditions of AMI and NOTSOFAR-1. Training code is open source, and model weights are released under the permissive OpenMDW-1.1 license.

papers.intro:
Speaker diarization remains a core capability for meeting transcription and multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR), even as speech large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate speaker-attributed transcripts directly. Recent systems and benchmarks explore unified prediction of lexical content, timestamps, and speaker labels [28, 34]. Yet these developments do not eliminate the need for explicit diarization: DM-ASR [24] uses diarization as an explicit structural prior for an LLM, while a recent comparative study [43] found unified models competitive in two-speaker conditions but less robust than modular pipelines as speaker count and overlap increase. Accurate diarization therefore remains valuable both as a standalone capability and as a component of systems built around speech LLMs.

End-to-end neural diarization (EEND) replaces multi-stage diarization pipelines with direct prediction of joint speaker activity and naturally represents overlapping speech [11]. Extensions based on encoder-decoder attractors accommodate an unknown number of speakers [15], while EEND with vector clustering combines overlap-aware local predictions with global embedding clustering to handle long recordings and arbitrary speaker inventories [21]. This local-to-global design underlies widely used systems such as Pyannote [1] and DiariZen [13, 14]. By contrast, Sortformer [33] follows a fixed-capacity EEND approach, combining permutation-invariant loss (PIL) with arrival-time-sort (ATS) supervision to assign speakers to output channels according to their order of first arrival. Because densely annotated real conversations are scarce, EEND relies heavily on simulated mixtures. Large-scale pre-training improves performance [2], but its effectiveness depends on turn-taking statistics, source diversity, acoustic augmentation, and how simulated and real data are combined [37].

Most of this progress targets offline processing. Importantly, streaming diarization must preserve identities across chunks despite bounded right context, overlapping speech, and newly arriving speakers. Prior online systems address this problem through limited-context encoders, speaker-tracing buffers, or blockwise speaker detection and representation [12, 48, 17, 6]. Streaming Sortformer [27] adds an arrival-order speaker cache (AOSC) to maintain channel ordering across chunks, allowing one model to serve multiple latency profiles. Its released model, however, is limited to four speakers and produces predictions only every 80 ms. This leaves a gap for an open model that combines competitive accuracy in both offline and low-latency streaming settings with support for more speakers, precise boundaries, and high computational efficiency.

These requirements are tightly coupled. Within the AOSC design, supporting more speakers requires a larger cache to retain sufficient evidence for each identity, which directly increases inference cost. Additional output channels also remain unused in typical recordings, increasing the risk of phantom-speaker activations. Meanwhile, running the encoder at a 10-ms frame step to improve boundary precision would greatly increase sequence length and attention cost. The model must also remain robust across latency profiles that provide different amounts of future context. These trade-offs motivate a design that supports more speakers and finer temporal resolution without sacrificing streaming efficiency.

This work introduces Nemotron 3 Diarization11 1 https://hf.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization, an open-weight model addressing these constraints. Our contributions are threefold. First, we redesign the architecture to efficiently increase speaker capacity and output temporal resolution. Second, we introduce an activity loss that models overall speech activity and a phantom loss that suppresses false activations in unused speaker channels. We pair these objectives with mixed-data and variable-context training to support both offline and streaming operation. Third, we analyze these choices through ablations of the backbone, initialization, temporal resolution, objectives, augmentations, and training data. We evaluate diarization accuracy across latencies and benchmark training and inference efficiency. We also assess downstream speaker-attributed ASR in offline and streaming settings.

papers.title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons
papers.abstract: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. Here we show that a stationary localized state containing an Ising wall first becomes a fixed breather and then develops finite chirality and drift motion through a spontaneous non-equilibrium Ising-Bloch transition. Stability analyses identify the modes responsible for the breathing and the motion, revealing controllable dynamics of polarization cavity solitons.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?
papers.abstract: Can a large language model (LLM) write the parameters of a medical image classifier from medical knowledge alone, without any training data? Such classifiers normally require labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable. We investigate this question through weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM writes or adapts the weights and biases of a neural network directly, without optimisation on training data. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra each generate the parameters of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use and without access to any image. We compare these networks against zero-shot MedSigLIP and against the same architecture trained on labels using the Adam optimiser, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities: chest X-ray, breast ultrasound and abdominal CT (all from MedMNIST), and pelvic MRI (SynthUterus). The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with a mean test AUC of 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both models outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. However, the same network trained with Adam on only 256 labelled images achieves a higher AUC on every MedMNIST task (mean AUC 0.828). On SynthUterus, Opus attains an AUC of 0.764, whereas Astra falls below chance (AUC 0.136) owing to a systematic error. These results show that LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but that they do not yet replace training data. We release the protocol, logs and all generated weights at https://github.com/MaximilianLindholz/weight-space-programming-medical.

Neural networks are usually programs that are not written but found by an optimiser on labelled data [20]. Takehi et al. recently introduced weight-space programming [39], which asks whether frontier LLMs can now operate in the other direction, reading a network’s weights and writing new ones directly. Setting weights without gradient descent is not new in itself: hypernetworks have generated weights since 2016 [12, 19], but they are trained predictors. In WSP, the predictor is a general-purpose LLM that writes weights from knowledge stated in natural language.

papers.title: Misorientations in dislocation cell structures: Modelling and statistical analysis
papers.abstract: Dislocation pattern formation is accompanied by the emergence of lattice rotations and concomitant misorientations across dislocation walls (cell boundaries). Recent advances in mesoscopic modelling of dislocation patterns enable for the first time a systematic simulation study of this phenomenon. We present simulation results for lattice rotation and misorientation patterns in crystals with face-centered cubic and rocksalt lattice structure. Statistical analysis of the orientation changes across cell walls reveals a transition associated with a symmetry-breaking bifurcation in slip system activity: Below the bifurcation, statistical tests indicate the presence of a single population of misoriented walls whereas, above the bifurcation, two sub-populations of 'incidental' and 'geometrically necessary' dislocation walls are present. Our data analytic approach demonstrates that this distinction does not require prior image segmentation and emphasizes the statistical robustness of the distinction between two types of dislocation walls.

papers.intro:
Dislocation microstructure evolution is characterized by the spontaneous emergence of heterogeneities in dislocation flow, which lead to the growth of dislocation density fluctuations and ultimately to the formation of a cell structure consisting of dislocation-depleted cell interiors separated by dislocation-rich dislocation walls [20], for an excellent recent study by in-situ X-ray microscopy, see [29]. Spatial heterogeneities in dislocation flow, and thus in the local shear strain rates on individual slip systems, necessarily lead to the emergence of lattice rotations. The phenomenology of dislocation cell structures indicates that these rotations are closely correlated with the dislocation patterns, in the sense that the lattice orientation within a cell volume is approximately constant whereas orientation changes (’misorientations’) occur mainly across the cell walls. Moreover, after an initial stage, the cell structure adopts a two-scale morphology where two types of walls are present [16, 14, 15]. This morphology is characterized by the presence of cell blocks consisting of approximately equi-axed cells which are separated by ’indidental boundaries’ (IDBs), i.e. dislocation walls of low misorientation. Slip system activity differs significantly between cell blocks, and therefore the ’geometrically necessary boundaries’ (GNBs), which separate cell blocks, carry much larger misorientations. An illustration of such a two-scale microstructure is provided in Figure 1.

Slip system activity differs significantly between cell blocks, and therefore the ’geometrically necessary boundaries’ (GNBs), which separate cell blocks, carry much larger misorientations. An illustration of such a two-scale microstructure is provided in Figure 1.

Based on the observed basic morphology, quantitative microstructural analysis of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) images has focused on the statistics of microstructural parameters including boundary type, crystal orientation with respect to deformation axes, boundary plane, spacing, misorientation angle, and width. Hughes and co-workers [16, 14, 14] report that the statistical distributions of GNB and IDB misorientations exhibit a scaling form which can be approximated by Gamma distributions with strain dependent mean value. At low to intermediate strains, the mean GNB misorientation increases about linearly whereas the mean IDB misorientation increases roughly in proportion with the square root of strain, indicating a different physical mechanism: Whereas the growth of IDB misorientations is a stochastic process driven by random fluctuations in local slip activity [27], the growth of GNB misorientations is the consequence of a bifurcation in slip activity between adjacent cell blocks where different slip systems locally dominate. Similar scaling laws have also been reported for spatial features such as the spacings of GNBs and IDBs, which decrease with increasing strain in rough agreement with the ’law of similitude’ which imposes the characteristic length of dislocation patterns to scale in inverse proportion with the stress at which they have been formed.

In view of the nature of the phenomenon, it is clear that models of cell structure formation must be based on an adequate description of dislocation transport, either in terms of discrete dislocation dynamics or in terms of density-based formulations (’continuum dislocation dynamics’) [26, 12, 9] (for a recent discussion of different flavors of continuum dislocation dynamics, see [1]). Although discrete dislocation simulation gives access to embryonic stages of dislocation cell formation [4] and has recently been used to study the formation of single GNBs [8], the method is still limited to the investigation of individual features and specific mechanisms and remains far from reaching the spatial scales and strains required for a statistical analysis of multiscale dislocation patterns. Continuum dislocation dynamics, on the other hand, has in the past decade been used by several authors to study dislocation pattern formation considering both two- and three-dimensional models [26, 10, 24, 25, 30], and has recently been shown by Zhang et. al. to give access to the emergence of two-scale dislocation patterns [30] and the associated lattice rotations [31] in a fully 3D setting. We therefore use the approach of Refs. [30, 31] as the starting point for our present investigation of misorientations in cell structures.

papers.title: 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
papers.abstract: This paper describes the set-up of a segmentation competition for automatic and semi-automatic extraction of the liver from computed tomography scans and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI data. This competition was held in the form of a workshop at the 2007 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference. The rationale for organizing the competition is discussed, the training and test data sets for both segmentation tasks are described and the scoring system used to evaluate the segmentation is presented.

papers.intro:
In 1986 Keith Price wrote a highly amusing article [1] in which he complained that “computer vision suffers from an overload of written information but a dearth of good evaluations and comparisons.” He asks the question: “How do you evaluate the works of others when you do not have their programs? You can look at their results in the papers, but that leaves many questions unanswered.” And he concludes, after a brief literature survey: “One area where ‘non-result’ papers are valid (and are lacking) is in a detailed analysis and comparison of various approaches to the same type of problem.” Although much has changed in two decades and researchers in medical image analysis nowadays have to take evaluation seriously in order to get their work published in high ranking journals, Price’s musings still sound all too familiar to many of us.

Rule-based systems building upon classical image processing techniques remain popular, level-set frameworks are ubiquitous, there is a large variety of methods that learn models of the shape and appearance of objects from training data and can fit these models to unseen data, elastic registration is proving to be a powerful tool for segmentation through atlas matching, classification techniques from pattern recognition and machine learning are attracting a growing number of proponents, and this enumeration is far from complete. To facilitate a comparison between a wide range of segmentation techniques we have organized a competition for two important segmentation tasks. The first is liver segmentation from CT scans. This is important for surgery planning, monitoring of therapy, and several other clinical applications. The second is the extraction of the caudate nucleus from brain MRI. The delineation of brain structures such as the caudate is essential for disease understanding, diagnosis, treatment monitoring and functional analysis of the brain. Both tasks are challenging and have been the subject of a range of published papers, but in clinical practice they are routinely segmented completely manually by human experts.

papers.title: From Prompt Engineering to Programmatic Prompting: Toward a Software Engineering Discipline for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The practice of instructing large language models (LLMs) through natural-language prompts has, in the span of a few years, migrated from an interactive curiosity to a load-bearing component of production software. Yet the vocabulary, tooling, and mental models of the field remain anchored in its interactive origins: we still speak of "prompt engineering" as though the crafting of a single well-worded instruction were the central problem. This paper argues for a categorical distinction. Prompt engineering, we contend, is an interaction technique - a human-computer interaction skill for eliciting desired behavior from a model in a conversational or exploratory setting. Programmatic prompting, by contrast, is an engineering discipline governing the behavioral interface between software systems and language models: the construction, composition, versioning, testing, and maintenance of prompts as first-class software artifacts embedded in larger systems. Conflating the two has produced brittle applications, unrepeatable evaluations, and an accumulation of prompt debt. We make three contributions: (1) a definition of programmatic prompting; (2) a systematic differentiation of programmatic prompting from prompt engineering, prompt tuning, fine-tuning, and general LLM application development; and (3) an account of prompt debt that distinguishes the self-admitted debt measurable in code from the silent debt that surfaces only as incidents, and identifies its economic cause. Our thesis is simple to state and consequential to accept: prompt engineering is an interaction technique; programmatic prompting is an engineering discipline.
papers.intro:
Every computing abstraction that has mattered has passed through a phase in which its practitioners mistook interaction for engineering. Early programming was “coding” in the literal sense—the manual translation of algorithms into machine instructions—until the software crisis of the late 1960s forced the community to recognize that constructing large, long-lived programs was a fundamentally different activity than writing individual routines, and the discipline of software engineering was born [1]. That history marks a fork every interactive practice reaches when it outgrows its origins: it either develops an engineering discipline or pays permanently for the absence of one.

We argue that prompting large language models is at precisely this juncture. The term prompt engineering entered common use around 2021–2022 to describe the craft of phrasing inputs so that a model produces desired outputs [2, 3]. Its rise had an economic logic: Brown et al. had shown that in-context instruction could approach the performance of task-specific fine-tuning at zero training cost [6], making the prompt the cheapest route to specialized model behavior—adjustable at inference time, by anyone, without a training pipeline. The term was apt for its moment: practitioners were exploring what models could do, and the unit of work was the individual prompt, iterated by hand in a playground or chat interface. But the moment has passed. Prompts today are embedded in retrieval pipelines, agent loops, multi-model routing systems, and customer-facing products. They are concatenated from templates, populated with untrusted user input, chained across dozens of model calls, and expected to behave consistently across model versions the developer does not control. The individual prompt is no longer the unit of work; the prompt-based system is.

The vocabulary has not kept pace, and the consequences are not merely terminological. When an organization believes its LLM problems are prompt-engineering problems—problems of wording—it staffs, tools, and budgets accordingly: a clever writer, a playground, an afternoon of iteration. When the problems are in fact engineering problems—problems of specification, composition, regression, and drift—this response fails in characteristic ways, and the failures are now in the public record. Prompts are edited in production without version control: in May 2025, one unreviewed change to the system prompt of xAI’s Grok bot pushed politically charged content into thousands of unrelated conversations, and the announced remedy—published prompts and mandatory review of prompt changes—was, precisely, version control [23]. A wording change that fixes one behavior silently breaks three others, and no test suite exists to notice; an unevaluated support chatbot invents a refund policy, and a tribunal holds the company to it, as Air Canada learned in the first such ruling [24]. A model provider ships an update and an application’s behavior shifts overnight, with no baseline against which to measure the shift—a drift measured in the field when GPT-4’s accuracy on one fixed task fell from 84% to 51% between its March and June 2023 versions, both versions meanwhile acquiring formatting habits that broke previously executable code output [25]. Evaluation, where it exists at all, consists of a developer eyeballing a handful of outputs—a practice documented among non-experts by Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. [4], confirmed among professional developers by Liang et al. [21], and shown by Shankar et al. to be unreliable even when done carefully [5].

This paper’s thesis is that the field is already implicitly developing two distinct activities, and that their separation—still blurred in practice under shared vocabulary—should now be made explicit:

Prompt engineering is an interaction technique. Programmatic prompting is an engineering discipline.

The first is a skill of human-computer interaction: knowing how to phrase, decompose, and iterate on instructions to elicit desired behavior from a model, in real time, with a human in the loop to judge the result. It is genuinely valuable, genuinely learnable, and genuinely not engineering—in the same way that skilled use of a search engine, a calculator, or a REPL (read–eval–print loop, the interactive console in which programmers try out code line by line) is valuable to an engineer without being engineering itself. The second is the discipline of treating prompts as software: artifacts with specifications, interfaces, tests, versions, dependencies, performance characteristics, and failure modes, embedded in systems that must operate without a human judging every output. Its relation to the operational tooling now marketed as LLMOps is that of software engineering to DevOps—complementary, never substitutable: dashboards and cost tracking can show that a monitored system’s behavior changed, but without specifications and evaluation baselines they cannot say whether it is correct.

papers.title: Creative Priming: Decoupling Process from Product to Escape the Creative Paradox
papers.abstract: Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response.
papers.intro:
Even as benchmark after benchmark and test after test have fallen to LLMs in recent years (Rein et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025; Patwardhan et al., 2025; Arora et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Center for AI Safety et al., 2026; Merrill et al., 2026; Sajadieh et al., 2026), creativity remains an unconquered frontier (Padmakumar and He, 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Mizrahi et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026). Perhaps that is why many of the most compelling motivational framings for the future of AI point to creative endeavors: we will discover new cures, invent new technologies, find solutions to our most pressing problems, and imagine new art forms (Amodei, 2024; Altman, 2024). All of these looming triumphs involve fundamentally creative acts.

All of these looming triumphs involve fundamentally creative acts.

As AI continues to extend its dominance across an increasingly wide set of domains, the question of when this creative renaissance will begin in earnest becomes increasingly central. The focus on creativity is already reflected in scientific domains, with efforts for models to generate hypotheses, formulate research plans, anticipate scientific insights, and act as autonomous researchers (Liu et al., 2026a; Goel et al., 2025; He-Yueya et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Lupidi et al., 2026; Nathani et al., 2025). To be sure, there are some domain-specific signs of AI creativity, yet perhaps there should be more evidence after billions of dollars spent and seemingly superhuman capabilities in mathematics (Das, 2026; OpenAI, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026a). Where are the cured diseases, the revolutionary new technologies, the solutions to our energy challenges, the new genres that change the world?

Margaret Boden’s influential conception of creativity imagines a continuum from weaker to stronger forms, from the more prosaic combinatorial and exploratory creativities to the more profound transformational version (Boden, 2004). One potential hope is that models are slowly climbing this ladder as they become more generally capable, and are just now bumping against the lower rungs of transformational creativity. However, studies of scientific ideation find that model-generated ideas remain less original than human ideas and tend to stay close to familiar scientific directions (Chen et al., 2026b; Bao et al., 2026; Antoniades et al., 2026). These findings give reason to believe that creativity is unique within the intelligence landscape and cannot be learned through conventional means like other aspects of intelligence.
