Consider that creativity is notoriously challenging to teach even to humans (Schooler and Melcher, 1995; Kaufman et al., 2010; Baird et al., 2012). A key obstacle is that, unlike other skills, creativity is difficult to learn from examples. While any successful past creative output could in principle serve as a training example for an aspiring student of creativity, most approaches to learning would make similar outputs more likely in the future (Jansson and Smith, 1991; Smith et al., 1993). However, for creativity, reproducing past outputs is exactly opposite the goal; rather, the goal is to learn generative principles for producing future creative outputs.

A key obstacle is that, unlike other skills, creativity is difficult to learn from examples. While any successful past creative output could in principle serve as a training example for an aspiring student of creativity, most approaches to learning would make similar outputs more likely in the future (Jansson and Smith, 1991; Smith et al., 1993). However, for creativity, reproducing past outputs is exactly opposite the goal; rather, the goal is to learn generative principles for producing future creative outputs.

In this way, learning to be creative faces a vexing creative paradox: emulating examples of past creative success (even if they were your own successes) can actually prevent you from reaching your full creative potential. The drive to escape the past is not ideally served by reinforcing past behavior. Part of the problem is the fleeting nature of novelty; as soon as a novel artifact appears in the world, even if it was your own original idea, it is no longer novel. After all, anything in the distribution of past events is by definition not novel, which is why learning to generate past instances of novelty runs into the creative paradox.

Therefore, rather than asking what did I do that was creative, what we really want to ask is, what lessons can I abstract from the successful generation of creativity that can be reapplied to generate further creativity? Answering this question is the path to circumventing the creative paradox. The problem is that training methods do not automatically decouple the abstraction of general lessons from the reinforcement of specific past effective actions.

The priming model learns through GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse. Thus the system can reinforce the priming process that yields creative outputs without reinforcing any specific creative output, circumventing the creative paradox.

We evaluate CP on NoveltyBench (Zhang et al., 2025) and compare against two methods that train models to directly respond creatively. Each method is evaluated by generating 64 responses per prompt and counting the number of responses that are simultaneously novel, high-quality, and semantically distinct (a metric that we argue a creative system should score highly on), finding that CP leads to an average of 22.8 such responses per prompt, compared to 16.4 and 7.6 from direct generation methods (1.39–3.0×\times more). Furthermore, scaling the number of on-policy training samples for a direct generation baseline fails to match CP on measures of system creativity and can actually reduce performance, supporting the creative paradox’s prediction that directly reinforcing successful responses is not expected to improve creativity indefinitely. Because the primer learns general principles for creativity, it also transfers to models it was never trained with: across four API models, priming increases the number of distinct responses by 4.5–10×\times and diversity by 2.5–4.6×\times, while modestly improving quality (0.5–4.6%).

papers.title: Receding horizon control with sensor-induced positive semidefinite state penalization
papers.abstract: This paper develops and analyzes a receding horizon control (RHC) framework for the stabilization of infinite-dimensional nonautonomous continuous-time systems with an infinite-horizon control objective. The considered stage costs penalize only a finite-dimensional component of the state and are therefore positive semidefinite with respect to the full state. Without imposing terminal costs or terminal constraints, we establish exponential stability and derive suboptimality estimates under suitable stabilizability and detectability-type assumptions, together with an online selection of the sampling times. In the linear case, we extend the framework to output-feedback RHC by combining it with a Luenberger-type state estimator based on finitely many sensors, and establish closed-loop stability using an augmented Lyapunov functional. The abstract state-feedback results are verified for a nonlinear Schl\"ogl parabolic equation around an unstable steady state and, in the output-feedback setting, for nonautonomous linear parabolic equations. The control and observation realizations involve finite-dimensional actuation and sensing, including localized boundary controls and spatially localized state-penalization operators. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the performance of the proposed RHC schemes.

papers.title: GeoPilot: Diagnosis-Guided Interventions and Geometric Evaluation for Aerial Reconstruction
papers.abstract: When a mesh reconstructed from aerial remote-sensing imagery disagrees with reference geometry, deciding what to change requires a diagnosis of the reconstruction process. We present GeoPilot, a workflow that turns diagnostics and prior observations into executable program or camera-configuration interventions. A large language model proposes the change, numerical tools reconstruct the mesh, and an external evaluator measures its geometry under a stated coordinate and reference protocol. The main case tests a shared-intrinsics hypothesis proposed before the comparison. On 224 Metashape-raster development images, shared intrinsics improved all six native-coordinate measures and reduced mean surface-to-reference distance by 7.04%. Reference-assisted alignment fitted and evaluated on separate within-scene checkerboard samples reversed the mean-distance ranking, limiting that gain to native-frame delivery. A separate matched comparison on publisher-undistorted images favored fixed published cameras on all six measures, reducing mean distance by 12.11%; the cameras retain upstream image and laser-scanning adjustment information. With one reconstruction per configuration, these comparisons provide conditional evidence for camera handling. Three end-to-end runs each delivered a mesh and six-metric evaluation from all 327 images of a second development scene.

papers.intro:
Geometric meshes reconstructed from aerial remote-sensing imagery depend on camera calibration, image preparation and surface reconstruction. A reconstruction may complete successfully while its mesh still disagrees with reference geometry. The next change could concern meshing, calibration or image preparation, depending on the suspected cause. COLMAP and OpenMVS provide the numerical components [1, 2]; choosing which component to change requires interpreting the diagnostics and testing the resulting mesh.

The shared-intrinsics case studied here illustrates that decision on the Metashape raster track of Dataset-1, denoted M. The reconstruction assigned a separate intrinsic model to each image of a homogeneous image set. Camera-center residuals directed attention to calibration flexibility, and the agent proposed sharing intrinsics before the matched comparison. The shared-intrinsics reconstruction improved all six native-coordinate measures, yet reference-assisted alignment reversed the mean-distance ranking. A useful intervention therefore needs both a reason for trying it and a clear account of what its geometric result supports.

papers.title: Generation of semigroups for vector-valued pseudodifferential operators on the torus with space-dependent symbols
papers.abstract: We consider toroidal pseudodifferential operators with spatially dependent, operator-valued symbols of positive order and finite regularity. For an arbitrary complex Banach space $E$, we prove that the negative of the closure of a parabolic operator on $C^\infty(\mathbb T^n,E)$ generates an analytic semigroup on $W_p^k(\mathbb T^n,E)$, where $1\le p<\infty$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, provided the symbol has sufficiently many spatial derivatives and discrete differences. The proof combines uniform estimates for parameter-dependent kernels with right and left parametrices. It does not require the UMD property of $E$. Real interpolation gives corresponding resolvent estimates on $B_{pq}^s(\mathbb T^n,E)$ for $0<s<k$ and $1\le q\le\infty$. The induced semigroups are strongly continuous for $q<\infty$ and on the little Besov spaces when $q=\infty$.

papers.title: Gate-tunable supercurrent switching in a three-terminal quantum dot transistor
papers.abstract: We propose and analyze a three-terminal superconducting transistor switch in which a gate-defined quantum dot region interrupts a flux-controlled loop. The output supercurrent is switched off completely when the two loop arms couple to the dot with equal tunneling strengths and half a flux quantum threads the loop. The device then operates as a symmetric SQUID at half flux. The condition follows from a single geometric factor $\chi$, which reduces the three-terminal problem to an equivalent two-terminal Anderson impurity model and makes the switching mechanism independent of the Coulomb interaction, the dot level position, the total hybridization and temperature. These enter only through a prefactor and thus decide how tolerant the device is to imperfect barrier tuning. Numerical renormalization group calculations across the full coupling parameter space show that the resonance is embedded in a broad region of elevated switching ratio at intermediate hybridization $\Gamma \approx \Delta$, while both weaker and stronger coupling reduce it to a thin isolated line. Finite temperature smooths the underlying singlet-doublet transition and lowers the supercurrent amplitude, but affects the open and closed states comparably and leaves the switching ratio largely intact. Within a zero-bandwidth two-level model, a second dot level is shown to open a leakage channel that grows as the two levels approach in energy. Raising the output barrier and the realistic presence of inter-level Coulomb repulsion, however, suppress the leakage.

Control electronics for solid-state qubits is therefore kept mostly at room temperature and connects to the cold stages through coaxial lines that conduct heat and carry thermal photons downward.

Cryogenic CMOS controllers relocate part of this electronics to the 44 K stage, where more cooling power is available, but this stage remains hot on the scale of the qubit and the signal lines must still be attenuated on their way down [47]. Superconducting (SC) circuit elements operating natively at the qubit stage would remove this thermal boundary entirely, making SC classical logic a natural candidate for integration with quantum computation nodes. Such elements operate with supercurrents that must be controllably suppressed (the OFF state) or allowed to flow (the ON state), with a switching ratio of at least several orders of magnitude required for reliable control. While ratios of this size have been reported in gate-controlled suppression of the supercurrent in SC heterostructures [17, 46, 16, 15, 48, 51, 49, 52], the microscopic origin of such gate-controlled-supercurrent effects remains under debate [6, 8, 2, 7, 65]; see Ref.[53] for a recent review. SC elements based on Josephson junctions, which switch via the phase rather than the condensate, are thus a more natural pathway to overcome both limitations.

Josephson junctions are often realized either as superconductor–insulator–superconductor (SIS) tunnel junctions, such as Al/AlOx/Al stacks [19], or as superconductor–normal-metal–superconductor (SNS) junctions, in which the supercurrent is carried through a weak link [36]. Electrostatic control of the weak link was first demonstrated in planar junctions defined in GaAs/AlGaAs [58] and InAs [43] two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) with related Josephson field-effect transistor implementations demonstrated subsequently [1]. Later developments involved carbon nanotubes [30] and semiconductor nanowires [18]. A complementary approach employs electrostatic gates to control Josephson transport through quantum dots by tuning discrete levels and/or their tunnel coupling to superconducting electrodes [26, 10, 9, 28]. Among these, planar 2DEGs combine a proximity-induced gap and high mobility with lithographic flexibility; InAs quantum wells with epitaxially grown Al are the most developed realization [55, 32], with InSb [31], HgTe [4] and planar Ge [61, 38, 35] representing emerging alternatives.

papers.title: Optimal Actuator Support Design for Infinite-Horizon Linear-Quadratic Parabolic Control Problems
papers.abstract: We study an optimal actuator design problem for infinite-horizon LQ control problems governed by parabolic equations. The control acts only on a small measurable subregion of the spatial domain, and the objective combines the infinite-horizon control value with a cost for the actuator region. Using the Riccati representation of the value function, we derive a comparison identity for two actuator supports and obtain an exact expansion of the objective. This leads to a topological derivative with respect to local changes in the support. We prove a localized Riccati sensitivity estimate to control the remainder and show that the infinite-horizon term in the derivative can be computed by solving a Lyapunov equation. This yields a computable support-update algorithm with a measure-controlled Armijo search. Under explicit uniform remainder and admissibility assumptions, its first-order stationarity defect tends to zero. Numerical experiments illustrate these results.

papers.title: A Model Organism for Studying Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness
papers.abstract: Large language models can recognize when they are being evaluated and change their behavior accordingly, undermining the reliability of safety benchmarks. Evaluation awareness (EA) is usually measured by having an LLM judge scan reasoning traces for explicit statements of recognition, but this signal is increasingly unreliable. Recent frontier-model system cards report a drop in verbalized rates between releases, which is indistinguishable from awareness that has gone unverbalized. Interpretability methods could detect such unverbalized evaluation awareness (UEA) in individual interactions, but lack instance-level ground truth. Asking the model alters the input, and dataset labels do not reveal whether it recognized a particular prompt as an evaluation. We address this gap with a model organism. Using synthetic document fine-tuning, SFT, and DPO, we train Qwen3.5-27B to emit a marker (a designated token) in its final response when it recognizes an evaluation, while suppressing the marker and verbalized awareness in its reasoning. The marker largely tracks the evaluation concept as it can be strongly modulated by evaluation framing in the system prompt. When not told whether it is being evaluated, the organism recognizes evaluations from test-question cues, mirroring what its base model often verbalizes. Using the marker as a label, we benchmark linear probes, the Jacobian Lens, and Activation Oracles, built on the base model and blind to the marker. None recovers the label reliably. These results suggest that current interpretability methods are not yet reliable UEA detectors, even when recognition relies on simple cues. Our model organism offers a testbed for improving them.

Frontier models distinguish evaluation from deployment transcripts significantly above chance (Needham et al., 2025). This Evaluation Awareness (EA) can alter behavior. papers.title: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
papers.abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.

papers.intro:
State-space models (SSMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to attention-based architectures for sequence modeling (Gu et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2023; Orvieto et al., 2023; Gu and Dao, 2023; Alonso et al., 2025; Massai and Ferrari-Trecate, 2025). A key feature behind their computational efficiency is that their dynamics are linear in the state, often with diagonal transition matrices. In selective SSMs such as S6, the recurrent core of Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023), the state-update coefficients may depend on the current input, but, once the input sequence is fixed, the state evolves through a sequence of affine maps. The recurrence can therefore be evaluated sequentially with cost scaling linearly in the sequence length, or in parallel through associative scans (Blelloch, 1990; Martin and Cundy, 2018). These properties have led to strong empirical performance in language (Fu et al., 2023), audio (Goel et al., 2022), and vision (Nguyen et al., 2022).

This additional flexibility can be useful when the appropriate update depends on the past context, and recent results show that modern RNNs can remain competitive with, and in some settings outperform, SSMs (Beck et al., 2024). The price is a nonlinear recurrence that no longer admits the direct associative-scan evaluation available to input-controlled affine dynamics.

papers.title: Rethinking Radar 3D Perception: Representation Learning from Raw Spectra
papers.abstract: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.

papers.intro:
Radar sensors are becoming increasingly important to autonomous driving as they remain reliable under adverse weather and lighting conditions, where cameras and LiDARs often degrade [1]. However, the rich frequency-domain spectra produced by radar hardware are rarely used directly in perception pipelines. Instead, they are first compressed through handcrafted reductions such as CFAR detection [2], which collapses them into sparse point clouds, or compact statistics that summarize their Doppler content [3, 4]. Modern radar perception systems are then developed around these reduced representations [5, 6, 7, 8], and substantial effort has gone into refining this paradigm [9, 10, 11].

Radar sensors are becoming increasingly important to autonomous driving as they remain reliable under adverse weather and lighting conditions, where cameras and LiDARs often degrade [1]. However, the rich frequency-domain spectra produced by radar hardware are rarely used directly in perception pipelines. Instead, they are first compressed through handcrafted reductions such as CFAR detection [2], which collapses them into sparse point clouds, or compact statistics that summarize their Doppler content [3, 4]. Modern radar perception systems are then developed around these reduced representations [5, 6, 7, 8], and substantial effort has gone into refining this paradigm [9, 10, 11].

This pipeline has an important but largely unexamined cost. Handcrafted reductions do not merely suppress noise but they define what will be treated as noise before learning begins. Weak reflections that fall below CFAR thresholds are discarded. Doppler structure not captured by summary statistics is discarded. The resulting representation is therefore not simply a cleaner version of the radar measurement. It is the subset of the measurement that survives a fixed set of assumptions about what signal should look like. Any weak, distributed, or noncanonical structure that violates these assumptions is removed, even if it is informative for downstream perception.

Weak reflections that fall below CFAR thresholds are discarded. Doppler structure not captured by summary statistics is discarded. The resulting representation is therefore not simply a cleaner version of the radar measurement. It is the subset of the measurement that survives a fixed set of assumptions about what signal should look like. Any weak, distributed, or noncanonical structure that violates these assumptions is removed, even if it is informative for downstream perception.

A natural alternative is to learn directly from unreduced post-FFT radar spectra, which we refer to as raw spectra because they preserve the spectral information otherwise discarded by handcrafted reductions. However, prior attempts have not established dense spectra as a clearly superior representation. Supervised learning on fully dense spectra under realistic driving conditions does not reliably outperform reduced inputs [12], a finding we also reproduce. This outcome is often interpreted as evidence that raw spectra are too noisy to support direct learning. We argue that the failure lies in the objective, not the input. Supervised perception losses, such as those based on bounding boxes or semantic labels, are defined over the task’s output space. They provide only indirect supervision for how the model should interpret the input. When trained on dense spectra, a supervised model is exposed to all components that handcrafted pipelines would have removed, but receives no explicit signal about which spectral structures are coherent and which are incidental.

This suggests that dense radar perception requires an objective that reasons about structure in the input space itself, without presupposing the morphology of signal or noise. We propose a novel definition: signal is what remains reconstructable under localized corruption, and noise is what does not. papers.title: KiteNorm: Variance Regularisation for Stable and Scalable Post-LN Transformers
papers.abstract: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.

papers.intro:
Post-LayerNorm (post-norm) Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) have largely been replaced by Pre-LayerNorm (pre-norm) Transformers (Wang et al., 2019) in large-scale Transformer implementations, owing to their improved gradient conditioning along the uninterrupted skip branch (Xiong et al., 2020). However, pre-norm exhibits persistent weaknesses, such as parameter inefficiency in deep layers (Sun et al., 2025; Gromov et al., 2024) and massive activations (Sun et al., 2026). Residual scaling (Sun et al., 2025; Radford et al., 2019) can mitigate these weaknesses, but it cannot fully eliminate them as the architecture necessarily piles up sublayer contributions on the skip branch.

However, pre-norm exhibits persistent weaknesses, such as parameter inefficiency in deep layers (Sun et al., 2025; Gromov et al., 2024) and massive activations (Sun et al., 2026). Residual scaling (Sun et al., 2025; Radford et al., 2019) can mitigate these weaknesses, but it cannot fully eliminate them as the architecture necessarily piles up sublayer contributions on the skip branch.

This has motivated renewed interest in post-norm architectures with the goal of scaling them to a large number of layers. The core challenge is the fact that the Jacobian of post-norm acts on both the residual and skip branches during backpropagation, which leads to gradient vanishing as the scale of the activations and the number of layers rise (Nguyen and Salazar, 2019; Huang et al., 2020). While prior work has analysed the effective dynamics of this phenomenon, the underlying cause remains poorly understood. We extend existing insights by deriving an upper bound that directly relates hidden-state variance to gradient propagation, and by providing empirical evidence linking variance expansion to rank collapse (Dong et al., 2021; Noci et al., 2022).

Recent works have made strides in improving the conditioning of post-norm Transformers through branch scaling and double-normalisation (Wang et al., 2024; Chen and Wei, 2026; Joseph et al., 2024). While these methods improve optimisation conditions at initialisation, they can be less robust to high learning rates or less competitive at moderate depths. We postulate that methods that rely primarily on favourable initialisation conditions are ultimately prone to degraded performance or stability as large learning rates push models further away from initialisation. Resolving this trade-off is therefore important for improving the scalability and efficiency of Transformer training. Our contributions can be outlined as follows: • We extend the theoretical analysis of gradient propagation in post-norm Transformers by highlighting the impact of hidden-state variance, and provide empirical evidence linking variance expansion to rank collapse. • We propose KiteNorm, constraining hidden-state variance through a combination of residual scaling, double-normalisation, scalarised LayerNorm and a new variance regulariser, which stabilises optimisation even at large learning rates. • We conduct a suite of experiments with decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters that demonstrate KiteNorm’s improved stability and scaling with respect to model depth, width, batch size, and training budget, even when compared to leading solutions. • We provide a series of ablations that demonstrate each component of KiteNorm is essential. papers.title: From many-body Schr\"odinger dynamics to magnetic Vlasov equation
papers.abstract: We analyse the combined mean-field and semiclassical limit from the time-dependent Schr\"odinger dynamics of $N$ spinless fermions in a non-constant magnetic field to the magnetic Vlasov equation with scaling $\hbar = N^{-1/3}$. With the velocity-shifted coherent states and the induced magnetic Husimi measure, we derive an exact BBGKY hierarchy with a remainder of order $\hbar^{1/2-}$. The main result is the weak $L^1$ convergence of the $k$-particle magnetic Husimi measures to the $k$-copies of the solution to the magnetic Vlasov equation. Furthermore, the convergence holds in the Wasserstein distance $\mathbb{W}_2$ when the second moment of initial Husimi measure correspondingly converges.

papers.title: Beyond Bit Matching: Orthogonal Watermarks for Collusion-Resistant Image Fingerprinting
papers.abstract: Image fingerprinting assigns each distributed copy a user-specific watermark for source tracing. Averaging collusion is a central threat: several recipients can average their differently marked copies to suppress each individual mark. Discrete bit-string watermarks are especially vulnerable because averaging drives bit evidence toward ambiguous decisions. We introduce \textbf{VectorMark}, which maps user keys to near-orthogonal high-dimensional unit vectors and identifies colluders by cosine similarity to the extracted watermark direction. Under ideal averaging of $K$ vector keys, the normalized average preserves a cosine signal of order $1/\sqrt{K}$ for each colluder, while unrelated keys remain concentrated near zero. The spherical geometry of random directions gives a shifted-Beta null distribution for cosine similarities, enabling analytic per-key false-positive-rate control after validation on unwatermarked images. VectorMark uses a neural watermark encoder and centered extractor trained with JND masking and a progressive curriculum for photometric, geometric, and collusion robustness. Experiments on MS-COCO, OpenImages, and AI-generated images show that VectorMark maintains robust watermark attribution under photometric and geometric distortions, and achieves the best strict all-colluder detection among evaluated methods, while preserving high visual quality. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/nurlanov-zh/VectorMark

papers.intro:
The proliferation of generative AI has intensified long-standing concerns over intellectual-property protection for digital media. A canonical protection model is multi-user fingerprinting: an author distributes personalized copies of an image, each invisibly marked with a user-specific key identifying the licensee Cox et al. (2008). If a copy leaks, the embedded key can trace it back to the responsible party. The problem becomes substantially harder when several users collude by averaging, interleaving, or otherwise combining their marked copies before release.

Most modern neural image watermarks expose a discrete payload interface Zhu et al. (2018); Bui et al. (2025). This interface is natural for blind single-copy recovery: the decoder predicts a bit string, which is then matched to a user identifier. However, when several differently marked copies are averaged, bit evidence is pushed toward an ambiguous middle state. Even if a detector still recognizes that the image is watermarked, all-colluder attribution can fail because no individual user’s bit string remains cleanly recoverable.

papers.title: Not All Layers Are Equal in Image-to-Video Transfer
papers.abstract:
Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery.
  This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/th-nesh/STRAP.

Adapting frozen image foundation models to video with lightweight temporal modules has become a prominent strategy for video understanding [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], avoiding the substantial data and compute costs of video-native pretraining [6, 7]. Yet while considerable effort has gone into designing these temporal adapters, the question of where to place them has received comparatively little attention: existing methods [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] find, through ablations comparing presence versus absence of a single temporal adapter type, that uniform placement performs best within this search space. This leaves open whether placing different adapter types based on layer-wise behavior can outperform uniform placement of temporal adapters.

We investigate this by analyzing how temporal sensitivity develops across layers in video-native transformers spanning vision-only [6, 8] and vision-language [9, 7] pretraining paradigms. For each model and layer, we apply complementary spatial and temporal perturbations to the input and measure the relative dominance of temporal over spatial sensitivity in the resulting representations. This yields a depth-wise temporal sensitivity ratio that reveals two findings. First, temporal sensitivity is not uniform: it increases with depth across all model families. papers.title: Crystal and magnetic structures of MnSi in zero magnetic field: Neutron diffraction and symmetry analysis
papers.abstract: Combining high-resolution wide-angle neutron powder diffraction with magnetic-superspace symmetry analysis, we refine the crystal structure and present, to our knowledge, the first systematic refinement of cubic $P2_13$ MnSi's zero-field magnetic structure across multiple magnetic satellite families. We compare single-arm rhombohedral 3+1D and cubic four-arm 3+4D magnetic superspace-group (MSSG) descriptions with propagation vectors along $\langle111\rangle$. Simultaneous extinction of the two satellite groups around $\{100\}$ dictates a transverse circular-helix model. This suppression and refinements of 18 separately varied satellite-group intensities support this ideal limit with only one adjustable magnetic amplitude. In the ideal single-arm model with MSSG $R3.1'(0,0,g)ts$, the moment has constant magnitude 0.535(3) $\mu_B$ per Mn. An explicit four-arm 3+4D cubic superspace construction presented here combines four interpenetrating helices and, for the illustrated phase choice, has moments ranging from zero to 0.874(5) $\mu_B$ per Mn, with the same root-mean-square moment as the 3+1D structure. Their identical powder profiles prevent the present measurements from distinguishing them. The average crystal structure remains cubic within experimental resolution, providing structural motivation for the cubic magnetic model. The mean lattice parameter, determined with formal relative precision $\sigma_a/a \lesssim 10^{-5}$, exhibits nonmonotonic temperature dependence below the N\'eel temperature.

papers.intro:
MnSi is a prototypical itinerant chiral magnet with the noncentrosymmetric cubic B20 structure, space group P​21​3P2_{1}3. Competition between predominantly ferromagnetic exchange and the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction favors a long-wavelength modulation, while weak anisotropy selects the ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle propagation directions [1]. At ambient pressure, magnetic order develops near TN≃29T_{N}\simeq 29 K through a weakly first-order transition [2]. Its field-induced skyrmion lattice has made MnSi a central example of topological magnetism [3], but its zero-field structure nevertheless merits separate examination.

Its field-induced skyrmion lattice has made MnSi a central example of topological magnetism [3], but its zero-field structure nevertheless merits separate examination.

Transport measurements provide complementary evidence for topological spin textures. A topological Hall effect (THE) was reported in the finite-field AA phase of MnSi close to TNT_{N} [4]. In the isostructural short-period helimagnet MnGe, a substantially larger Hall contribution attributed to THE occurs over a broader temperature range [5]. Our zero-field diffraction analysis and the continuum topology discussed below do not establish a connection between the proposed four-arm structure and THE.

Early magnetization and neutron measurements already indicated that MnSi was not a simple ferromagnet [6]. Ishikawa et al. subsequently observed satellites near (110)(110) and (111)(111) using triple-axis diffraction with λ=2.55\lambda=2.55 Å, and around the reciprocal-space origin using small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) with λ=4.99\lambda=4.99 Å [7]. They established propagation along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle with a period of approximately 180 Å at 4.2 K. Their zero-field diffraction did not, however, determine the spin-rotation plane: a plane perpendicular to the propagation direction was inferred with support from the magnetization. The quoted moment of approximately 0.4​μB0.4\,\mu_{B} per Mn likewise came from magnetization. Thus, the helical interpretation was experimentally well motivated, but was not a refinement of all site-resolved Fourier components against zero-field satellite intensities.

Subsequent polarized small-angle neutron diffraction established the relation between crystal chirality and magnetic helicity, including measurements at 16 K in a 60 Oe guide field after zero-field cooling [8]. These low-field measurements constrain the helicity of the modulation, but helicity alone does not confirm a single-arm structure. At a resolved magnetic satellite, the polarization dependence probes the Fourier component of the corresponding propagation-vector arm, without determining relative phases between distinct arms. The same helicity signature is therefore compatible with single-arm 3+13+1D domains or with the corresponding arm of a coherent four-arm 3+43+4D structure. Our study addresses these alternatives in zero applied magnetic field.

papers.title: Causal Resolution of Undefined Answers in Datalog with Negation
papers.abstract: Unstratified negation may leave the answer to a Boolean Datalog query undefined under the well-founded semantics. We study database causality in this setting by asking which fact insertions and deletions realize a prescribed transition and which other changes preserve the observed query answer while making a designated fact pivotal. Such a set of changes to other facts is a contingency for the designated fact and the prescribed transition. Our game representation assigns one shared move to each mutable fact and preserves query values and intervention distances. Pairing source and target certificates characterizes all minimum contingencies for the six transitions among true, false, and undefined. When inserting or deleting a move resolves a draw, a directed tree traces the newly winning and losing positions along alternating paths to the source of that move. For the fixed one-rule win--move program, deciding whether a contingency of size at most $k$ exists is $\mathrm{NP}$-complete for each transition, even on bounded-degree graphs. Computing the minimum size is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}[\log]}$-complete, and counting minimum contingencies is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. When only one of true and false is reachable, the prime implicants of undefinedness satisfied at the observation cover every undefined state, and their supports induce nonempty subtrees of a common tree, we compute a minimum resolving intervention in polynomial time from the game instance. From the explicit tree and these implicants, we construct an equally large family of disjoint supports, certifying optimality.

papers.intro:
When a database query returns an unexpected answer, one may ask how the answer was derived, why an expected answer is absent, or which input facts are responsible for the observed answer. Lineage and provenance describe successful derivations [7, 21], whereas why-not provenance can identify failed derivations that explain why an expected answer is absent [26]. Database causality asks a different question: whether inserting or deleting a designated input fact changes the query answer, possibly after changes to other input facts that preserve the observed answer [28, 29]. We study this question for Datalog programs with recursion through negation under the well-founded semantics (WFS) [36]. The answer to a Boolean query can then be true, false, or undefined, even when the input database is completely specified. Changing a true answer to undefined and changing it to false can therefore require different updates.

Deletion-based causality partitions the database into exogenous facts, which remain fixed, and endogenous facts, which may be deleted [28]. An endogenous fact is an actual cause of a true answer if there exists a set of other endogenous facts, called a contingency, whose deletion preserves the answer but whose deletion together with the designated fact makes the answer false. For Datalog with negation, we keep the program fixed and distinguish fixed input facts from mutable facts, which we may insert as well as delete. For an undefined answer, we seek a set of insertions and deletions, an intervention, that yields a prescribed value, true or false. For a designated fact, a contingency consists of changes to other facts that preserve the observed answer and make the designated insertion or deletion yield a prescribed different answer. We seek sets of minimum cardinality in both cases. For contingencies, we consider all six ordered transitions between distinct truth values.

papers.title: Joint Power and Adaptive-Constellation Optimization for OFDM-ISAC Systems
papers.abstract: Next-generation wireless systems are expected to support integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). However, sensing imposes different requirements on the power allocation (PA) and the modulation format than communications, leading to a fundamental trade-off in frequency-selective channels. In this paper, we jointly optimize the PA and modulation format for orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM)-based ISAC systems, considering both target detection and tracking. We first derive an upper bound on the mutual information to predict the communication performance for power-constellation allocation. We then use an autoencoder (AE) to learn a family of finite constellations that realizes the allocation under different sensing constraints without retraining. The results show that tracking alleviates the sensing & communications (S&C) tradeoff compared with initial detection, and that the PA and the modulation dominate the S&C trade-off at low and high signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), respectively. At intermediate SNR, the proposed joint optimization significantly outperforms individual optimizations, while the pretrained adaptive constellation family almost fully realizes the predicted allocation gains.

papers.intro:
In future wireless systems, ISAC is expected to enable the reuse of the OFDM communication signal for radar-like sensing [2]. However, the optimal PA and modulation format for SC differ [3]. For communications, a WF (WF) PA in combination with a Gaussian-distributed input maximizes the MI (MI) over an AWGN (AWGN) channel under a transmit power constraint [4]. In contrast, a uniform PA and unit-modulus modulation format reduce ranging SL of the autocorrelation function [5].

Therefore, constellation shaping has recently gained attention as a means to balance SC performance [6, 7]. However, these works optimize constellations for fixed sensing constraints, leaving adaptive constellation shaping for varying SC requirements unexplored. Furthermore, the impact of the PA on sensing has been characterized and optimized for initial target detection, where the SL averaged over the delay domain are minimized [5, 8]. However, it remains unclear to what extent prior target information can alleviate the SC trade-off by localizing the sensing constraint to a small delay region.

While the individual modulation- and power-induced trade-offs have been studied extensively, the literature on their joint optimization remains sparse. To the best of our knowledge, existing joint approaches are limited to a power and constellation selection framework [9] and an information-theoretic continuous input distribution design based on an upper bound [10]. These works provide important initial insights into the coupled power-modulation trade-off. However, selecting constellations from a finite set of conventional modulation formats underestimates the achievable SC performance, whereas continuous input distribution design provides an upper benchmark that overestimates the performance attainable with practical finite constellations. Moreover, both approaches mainly focus on the high SNR regime, where the PA-induced trade-off largely vanishes, leaving the coupled power-modulation trade-off insufficiently characterized.

In this paper, we bridge the gap between conventional modulation format selection and continuous input distribution design. Specifically, we jointly optimize the PA and modulation for OFDM-ISAC systems operating in frequency-selective channels. To make the joint optimization tractable, we generalize the upper bound on the MI from [11] to account for frequency-selective fading and PA. Since both the resulting MI surrogate and the sensing metric depend only on power and kurtosis, i.e., the fourth-order moment of the constellation, we split the original problem into constellation shaping and power-kurtosis allocation. Finally, simulation results validate the proposed approach: The joint optimization outperforms optimizations over either power or kurtosis alone, while the adaptive constellations realize the predicted allocation gains. Moreover, target tracking alleviates the trade-off compared with detection.

papers.title: Neural Multipath Fields for 6G FR3 Digital Twins: Latent Adaptation from Sparse Data
papers.abstract: Wireless digital twins are essential for environment-aware 6G communications, motivating the investigation of frequency range 3 (FR3), an emerging mid-band regime offering a promising balance between bandwidth and propagation characteristics. Neural Radio Frequency (RF) fields provide continuous surrogates for site-specific radio propagation, but adapting a scene-specific field to a new environment can require substantial measurements and retraining. To this end, we propose the Latent-Adaptive Neural Multipath Field (LANMF), a scene-conditioned FR3 model that predicts path-resolved delays, complex channel impulse response (CIR) coefficients, and arrival and departure directions from transmitter-receiver coordinates. LANMF learns shared propagation representations across source environments and adapts to unseen scenes by optimizing only a 16-dimensional scene latent. Evaluated on six ray-traced indoor scenes at 7.5 GHz, latent-only adaptation yields improvements in prediction with just 5-10 target links (0.42-0.83% of available links). Compared with full-network fine-tuning, it updates only 16 persistent target parameters, reducing adaptation time by 28-30% and incremental peak GPU memory by 82-85%. While the proposed solution supports various wireless applications, we demonstrate its utility through beam-candidate reduction using a 64-beam codebook, retaining measurement-based final beam selection.

papers.intro:
Future 6G networks are expected to integrate communication, localization, and sensing, motivating the investigation of frequency range 3 (FR3), often termed the golden band. FR3 offers a promising balance between bandwidth and propagation characteristics for integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) applications [1, 2]. In ISAC systems, directional beamforming is important for both maintaining communication links and controlling the spatial illumination of the environment for sensing [3]. Consequently, efficient beam management benefits from knowledge of the underlying propagation paths and their directional characteristics. Effective beam management therefore requires site-specific channel knowledge that captures how signals propagate through the surrounding environment.

While digital twins can model propagation through environment geometry and ray tracing, CKMs enable spatial channel inference from available observations. Coordinate-based neural representations address this problem by learning a function that maps spatial coordinates to channel-related quantities. Once trained, the network can be queried at new transmitter (Tx)–receiver (Rx) locations to predict the corresponding channel information. Frequency-Aware NeRF2 subsequently extended the approach toward wideband prediction [8]. Spatial coordinate encodings can further help these networks capture rapid channel variations [6].

A path-resolved representation instead describes each propagation path through its delay, complex coefficient, and arrival and departure directions. These quantities reveal the temporal and directional structure of the channel and can support applications such as beam selection. However, conventional codebook-based beam selection may require probing a large number of candidate beams to identify the strongest communication link, introducing measurement overhead [2]. Predicting the underlying multipath characteristics can help prioritize promising beams and reduce the number of candidates requiring measurement, in FR3 wireless systems. However, explicitly predicting MPCs in unseen environments from only a few observed links remains challenging. papers.title: Out-of-plane interference effects in the angle-resolved photoemission of epitaxial graphene
papers.abstract: The epitaxial growth of monolayer graphene by Si sublimation of 6H-SiC(0001) is one of the most effective ways of producing large-scale monocrystalline graphene samples of high quality. However, graphene is left interacting with a reconstructed carbon buffer layer known as zerolayer graphene (ZLG) and the SiC substrate underneath. Beyond the mere creation of Dirac cone replicas, the effect of this interaction on photoemission measurements is poorly understood. We utilized synchrotron radiation for photon-energy-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the complex final-state interactions of photoelectrons within the heterostructure of monolayer graphene, ZLG, and SiC. We identify multiple resonances in the photoemission intensity of the Dirac cone as a function of photon energy that originate from interlayer interference, confirmed with a multiple scattering model. We also demonstrate for the first time that the relative intensity of the replica bands induced by the $(6\sqrt{3} \times 6\sqrt{3})\text{R}30^\circ$ reconstruction scales with the electron kinetic energy. Finally, we resolved four nondispersing electronic states, which originate from the ZLG. Our findings show that the three-dimensional (3D) structure of SiC and ZLG manifests itself in the photoemission from two-dimensional (2D) epitaxial graphene. By revealing how 3D substrate architecture dictates the photoemission of a 2D layer, this work establishes a crucial framework for investigating the electronic structure of complex heterostructures via ARPES.

papers.intro:
The emergence of two-dimensional (2D) materials, especially graphene, has revolutionized the field of condensed matter physics and opened new possibilities for tunable materials by stacking to form heterostructures [1, 2]. Arguably the best platform for producing large-scale, high-quality graphene samples is by thermal decomposition of silicon carbide (SiC) [3, 4]. This method can produce monolayer graphene (MLG) at a wafer scale. However, underneath the MLG lies another, (6​3×6​3)​R​30∘(6\sqrt{3}\times 6\sqrt{3})\text{R}30^{\circ} reconstructed, carbon layer. This layer has the typical honeycomb structure of graphene, but is in part covalently bonded to the SiC. Therefore it does not possess graphene’s typical π\pi-band structure and is called zerolayer graphene (ZLG). The ZLG can interact with and strain the MLG [5]. Together the MLG, ZLG, and SiC form a complex three-dimensional (3D) heterostructure. To understand this system, it is important to measure the electron energy dispersion.

In angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (ARPES), understanding the matrix element effect on measurements is of the utmost importance to effectively study a material [6]. It is well understood how the matrix element depends on properties of the material such as orbital symmetry, atomic locations, and material thickness as well as the choice of photon energy h​νh\nu, polarization, and angle of incidence to the sample [7, 8, 9]. The best known example of this effect in graphene is the so-called dark corridor effect, in which pseudospin suppresses the photoemission intensity in parts of the Fermi surface [10, 11]. Work was done to leverage the matrix element by varying polarization to allow for the full visibility of the Fermi surface [12, 13]. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that h​νh\nu tuning is critical for modulating the intensity distribution around the K¯\overline{\mathrm{K}} and Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} points, providing a pathway to investigate the final-state effects in 2D systems [14, 15, 13]. However, while these models effectively capture the intrinsic symmetry of the graphene lattice, they typically ignore how the presence of the substrate will affect the photoemission process. A significant knowledge gap remains in how the 3D structure of the MLG/ZLG/SiC system fundamentally changes the matrix element of the final-state electron. Additionally, previous h​νh\nu-dependent studies [14, 15, 13] have generally been restricted to limited energy ranges, which may fail to resolve high-energy resonances or the full evolution of many-body features.

papers.title: Ambient-pressure superconductivity in bulk single crystals of La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{10}$
papers.abstract: Superconductivity in the Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates has so far been confined either to multilayer compounds under high pressure or to square-planar infinite-layer-type films stabilized by epitaxial strain. Here we report the high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) growth of bulk single crystals of the quadruple-layer RP nickelate La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{13}$ ($n=4$) and reproduce the quintuple-layer La$_6$Ni$_5$O$_{16}$ ($n=5$) synthesis, two members of the series that had previously been accessible only as thin films. Topotactic reduction of La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{13}$ single crystals with CaH$_2$ yields the square-planar phase La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{10}$, which we show to be a bulk, ambient-pressure superconductor with $T_\mathrm{c}^\mathrm{onset} \approx 18\,\mathrm{K}$, a shielding fraction above 60\%, and a specific-heat jump that confirms a bulk pairing transition. All crystals show besides superconductivity a coexistence with a density-wave or metal-insulator transition. The upper critical field shows a small anisotropy, $\gamma \approx 2.4$, which remains finite as $T \to T_c$, indicating three-dimensional superconductivity with substantial coupling between the four-layer blocks. These results identify the square-planar nickelates $R_{n+1}$Ni$_n$O$_{2n+2}$ as a bulk platform in which the layer number alone tunes the nickel valence into the superconducting regime, without chemical substitution, pressure, or epitaxial constraint.

papers.title: BO-Arena: An Evolving Benchmark for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimisation
papers.abstract: High-dimensional Bayesian optimisation (HDBO) is an increasingly crowded field with new methods proposed at every major conference, making it ever harder to answer a deceptively simple question: "Which method is currently state-of-the-art?" In this paper, we question the efficacy of benchmarking practices in the field, and find them to be systematically ineffective: multiple published works fail to benchmark against the strongest available baselines, or even include incorrect implementations of key methods. Without a shared reference implementation, such errors are difficult to detect during peer review. We therefore introduce BO-Arena, an actively maintained and extensible package providing canonical implementations of state-of-the-art algorithms, which allows researchers to develop new methods and benchmark them rigorously. Using BO-Arena, we find that what currently drives performance in HDBO is even simpler than previously thought. We use these insights to propose a new algorithm which is competitive with the state of the art on problems with many observations, without resorting to the complex GP approximations used in recent methods. Finally, we question whether there is currently sufficient evidence that any more complex method outperforms a simple Gaussian process baseline for HDBO.

Consequently, some papers do not benchmark against the strongest existing method at their time of writing. For instance, recent papers do not always benchmark against Vanilla BO, and sometimes use weaker baselines such as EI-BO in Figure 1 (Cheon et al.,, 2025; Yun et al.,, 2025; Miao et al.,, 2025). 3. papers.title: Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency Enables Reliable Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics from Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) extends molecular simulations to length and time scales inaccessible to atomistic models, but building thermodynamically faithful CG potentials remains a longstanding challenge. Energy-based diffusion models (EBDMs) provide a promising route for learning CG potentials through their zero-time energy. However, CGMD driven by diffusion-learned potentials can produce equilibrium ensembles that deviate substantially from the target distribution. We show that the zero-time distribution error is bounded by the sum of the spatial score error and temporal energy-derivative error, whereas conventional diffusion objectives directly supervise only the spatial component. Based on this finding, we introduce Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency (STEC) supervision, which complements spatial score matching by explicitly constraining temporal energy derivatives. We derive an exact and tractable objective for this temporal component, avoiding the substantial computational overhead associated with previous regularization schemes. Across peptide and fast-folding protein systems, STEC-trained EBDMs accurately reproduce equilibrium distributions with free-energy errors within chemical accuracy, while supporting stable long-time simulations that recover key metastable transition patterns. On held-out octapeptides, STEC reduces free-energy errors by more than 5-fold relative to the strongest competing baseline, while achieving a median production-cost reduction of approximately 1,700-fold relative to atomistic molecular dynamics under a defined structural-coverage benchmark. These results establish STEC as a scalable framework for learning thermodynamically reliable CG force fields for increasingly complex biomolecular systems.

papers.intro:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have become a central tool for connecting molecular structure to function, providing mechanistic insight into biomolecular processes and conformational pathways while increasingly informing drug discovery and materials design [14, 11, 79, 63, 18, 22]. However, many biologically relevant processes remain beyond the accessible length and time scales of atomistic molecular dynamics (ATMD), owing to its large number of microscopic degrees of freedom (DoFs) and the small integration time steps required to resolve fast atomic motions [60, 33, 55, 13]. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) alleviates these limitations by integrating out local DoFs, allowing larger integration time steps and more efficient exploration of conformational space [44, 58, 76, 68, 10] (Fig. 1a). Its reliability, however, critically depends on a CG potential that faithfully reproduces the equilibrium thermodynamics of the underlying atomistic ensemble [9, 49, 50, 47].

The corresponding thermodynamically consistent potential is the potential of mean force (PMF), UCG​(𝐱)U^{\rm CG}(\mathbf{x}), defined up to an additive constant by qCG​(𝐱)∝exp⁡[−UCG​(𝐱)kB​T]q^{\rm CG}(\mathbf{x})\propto\exp\left[-\frac{U^{\rm CG}(\mathbf{x})}{k_{\rm B}T}\right], where kBk_{\rm B} is the Boltzmann constant and TT is the absolute temperature. Bottom-up [26, 27] coarse-graining seeks to recover this effective potential from atomistic-level potential, which is a challenging computational task as it requires high-dimensional marginalization over the eliminated DoFs. This has been primarily tackled through variational force matching (FM) and relative entropy minimization (REM). FM exploits the fact that −∇𝐱UCG-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}U^{\rm CG} corresponds to the conditional mean of appropriately projected atomistic forces, allowing UCGU^{\rm CG} to be learned through supervised force regression [25, 25, 71, 77, 23, 16, 5, 3]. However, instantaneous projected forces can exhibit substantial variance around this conditional mean, leading to noisy supervision and potentially large errors in sparsely sampled transition regions [36, 52]. REM avoids this force-noise bottleneck by directly matching the target distribution qCGq^{\rm CG} with the Boltzmann distribution induced by the learned potential [61, 48, 15, 69]. Although this distribution-level objective can improve thermodynamic fidelity, its optimization requires expectations over the evolving model distribution and therefore repeated, computationally expensive CG sampling throughout training. Existing approaches thus face a fundamental trade-off between high-variance force supervision and expensive model-driven sampling (Appendix A provides more discussion).

papers.title: Applicative theories can count
papers.abstract: Applicative theories offer a proof-theoretic framework for studying complexity. In this paper, we introduce a family of applicative theories to characterize classes ranging from constant-depth circuits to polynomial space. Our approach relies on a simple axiom scheme, the small variations of which allows to capture various forms of counting and alternation. This leads to highly uniform results. When applied on notation, the scheme captures bit counting, yielding a characterization of the functions computable by constant-depth, polynomial-size threshold circuits ($\textbf{FTC}^0$); when applied lexicographically, it allows for the counting of accepting computations, yielding a characterization of the functions in the counting hierarchy ($\textbf{FCH}$). Increasing the logical complexity of the induction formulas allowed in the scheme, we obtain characterizations of the functions computable by bounded Boolean circuits of logarithmic-depth and polynomial-size ($\textbf{FNC}^1$) and of the functions computable in polynomial space ($\textbf{FPSPACE}$). The latter characterization solves an open problem in the field. Finally, we investigate separation results. While it is unknown whether $\textbf{FNC}^1$ and $\textbf{FCH}$ are different, there is an oracle relative to which (relativized) $\textbf{FNC}^1$ is strictly contained in (relativized) $\textbf{FCH}$. We use this fact to separate the theories characterizing them, by exploring their ability to represent higher-order functionals.
papers.intro:
First introduced by Feferman in the 1970s to provide logical foundations for Bishop-style constructive mathematics [38, 39], applicative theories have subsequently been used for studying computational complexity [21, 62] (see [64] for a survey). Since their language is expressive enough to define terms representing any partial recursive function, these theories offer a convenient framework for obtaining proof-theoretic characterizations of classes, without coding functions as complex formulas. The intuitive idea is that one can reinterpret an equation of the form F⁡(x+1)=H⁡(F⁡(x))F(x+1)=H(F(x)) as the implication F⁡(x)=z→F⁡(x+1)=H⁡(z)F(x)=z\to F(x+1)=H(z), which, letting A⁡(x,z)A(x,z) be the atomic formula F⁡(x)=zF(x)=z, can be seen as the induction step A⁡(x,z)→A⁡(x+1,H⁡(z))A(x,z)\to A(x+1,H(z)). The advantages of the applicative-theoretic perspective over other machine-independent approaches to complexity are (at least) twofold: first, induction schemes offer more degrees of freedom than recursion schemes, namely, the logical complexity of the formulas allowed in induction and the scope of the quantifiers involved [62, 36]; second, applicative theories can elegantly capture higher-order versions of complexity classes [63], thus providing a uniform setting for studying how the computational content of certain induction schemes propagates to proofs of complex formulas. Following the initial work devoted to poly-time computable functions [61, 21, 62], multiple complexity classes have been characterized relying on restricted principles of induction [21, 62, 20, 47, 36]. However, thus far, small-circuit and counting classes have mostly escaped applicative-theoretic treatment.

papers.title: Towards A Parametrized Complexity of Determinization
papers.abstract: Given a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA), we want to estimate the difficulty of finding an equivalent deterministic finite automaton (DFA). We demonstrate that computing the state complexity of an NFA within polynomial precision is \textsf{PSPACE}-hard, and furthermore the same holds for the complexity of the subset construction, Brzozowski's algorithm, or, indeed, \emph{any} determinization algorithm which runs at least as fast. This result implies that making any \textit{a priori} estimate of the running time of the major determinization algorithms is inherently hard. To circumvent this---in the spirit of parametrized complexity---we try to identify complexity measures which can guarantee efficient determinization. Our main idea rests on linking the complexity of the subset construction to transition monoids using the semigroup complexity. We show that the semigroup complexity by itself can be reasonably approximated for certain classes of NFAs, and then introduce \emph{subset complexity}---a refinement of the semigroup complexity which has a tighter connection with the subset construction. In certain scenarios, the subset complexity can be approximated in polynomial time, making it potentially viable for more practical applications.

papers.title: AWS Serverless Infrastructure from WebAssembly Components
papers.abstract: The infrastructure definitions and the code for serverless applications are often only loosely connected. This yields a large error class: the referenced infrastructure components might not exist. It is also hard to keep the application and its permissions in sync. To address this problem we present an infrastructure from code solution where we provision cloud infrastructure from Wasm Interface Type (WIT) - the language defining the interface of WebAssembly components. We limit ourselves to the basic example of an AWS Lambda function accessing S3 buckets. We build two interpreters for the WIT language: one that derives the definition of S3 buckets as infrastructure as code and least-privilege IAM permissions, and a generic runtime that runs the component as a Lambda function and provides access to the S3 buckets as capabilities. We formulate consistency properties that ensure the existence of the S3 buckets and correct permissions of the Lambda, and provide evidence that our interpreters satisfy them. We show how selected failures for deployment of such cloud components can be prevented using our technique and how a baseline setup fails at this task. Together with the strict sandboxing of the WebAssembly runtime we achieve an instance of capability-based security for access to AWS infrastructure as a further result.

papers.title: Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions
papers.abstract: The central difficulty in quantum many-body physics is that the Hilbert space dimension grows exponentially with the total degrees of freedom. A key feature to circumvent this problem is locality, which manifests dynamically through an approximate causal structure in the form of a Lieb-Robinson bound (LRB). LRBs have been proved for quantum spin systems and certain lattice boson systems, but so far never for realistic continuum systems. We present the first LRB that applies to a standard system of one-dimensional continuum fermions. It applies to initial states with controlled moments of local particle number and energy and is thus thermodynamically stable. Our result breaks the main technical barrier that has existed for using the vast locality toolbox on continuum systems.

papers.title: How a Model's Architecture and Performance Influences Explainability: A Study of Grad-CAM and CRAFT in CNN-Based Image Classification
papers.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), are widely adopted in computer vision, yet their opaque decision-making raises concerns in high-risk applications like healthcare and autonomous systems, where trust and accountability are critical. Therefore, robust explainable AI (XAI) methods are desirable to provide transparent insights into model decisions. To ensure these methods are reliable and effective across diverse scenarios, it is important to understand how model performance and architectural complexity influence explanation quality. Our study takes an initial step toward systematically investigating the impact of these two factors on key XAI evaluation metrics. We constructed a pipeline using 10 subsets of ImageNet-1K, each containing 80 unique classes, on each of which we trained three CNN architectures of increasing structural complexity: VGG16, ResNet50, and ConvNeXt-Tiny. For each individual model, we analyzed 10 training checkpoints representing increasing levels of model accuracy using two XAI methods: Grad-CAM (feature-attribution-based) and CRAFT (concept-based). We assessed these methods across four evaluation categories: Faithfulness, Correctness, Sensitivity, and Simplicity. Our findings reveal that as training progresses, the complex architectures (ResNet50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny) exhibit improved Faithfulness and lower Sensitivity, indicating more robust explanations. In contrast, VGG16's simpler architecture yields simpler but less faithful and correct explanations.

papers.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

Materials discovery is characterized by costly experimental pipelines, where rapid iteration cycles are stifled by the cost of evaluating a candidate set of input parameters. As such, Bayesian optimization (BO) is a natural paradigm to explore the space of experimental configurations, given past results [15, 28, 9]. As running a full active learning campaign for each new candidate method is both impractical and ineffective, methods are commonly evaluated and compared retrospectively in completed learning campaigns [36, 26]. The default surrogate model for the BO loop in these settings is a Gaussian process (GP) [26, 20, 37].

papers.title: Converse Lyapunov theorem for input-to-state stability of infinite-dimensional systems
papers.abstract:
We prove converse Lyapunov theorems for input-to-state stability (ISS) of a broad class of infinite-dimensional systems applicable to evolution equations in Banach spaces, boundary control systems, and delay systems. To this end, we employ a novel method that does not require constructing auxiliary closed-loop systems. We start by showing that ISS of a control system implies uniform global asymptotic stability of the same system with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. Then, under an additional regularity requirement, we prove that an ISS Lyapunov function can be constructed.
  Based on our general result, we prove that for linear systems with unbounded $\infty$-admissible operators, ISS is equivalent to the existence of a Lipschitz continuous coercive ISS Lyapunov function.

The concept of input-to-state stability (ISS), introduced by E. Sontag in the late 1980s in [45], unified the Lyapunov and input-output stability theories and revolutionized the constructive nonlinear control theory for ordinary differential equations (ODEs) [23]. It played a major role in robust stabilization of nonlinear systems [10], design of robust nonlinear observers [27, 1], nonlinear detectability [43, 24], event-based control [48, 39], stability of nonlinear networks [16, 8], supervisory adaptive control [13], data-driven control [6, 9, 25], and other areas.

papers.title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.

Today, language models increasingly shape the capabilities and alignment of other models. They write synthetic training data, filter pretraining corpora, label preferences, and judge outputs. As such, it becomes increasingly important to understand the ways in which models influence each other via training.

One canonical example of such influence is subliminal learning (Cloud et al., 2025). A teacher model is prompted to hold some bias, such as a love of owls, and is asked to output seemingly random number sequences. When a student model is fine-tuned on those number sequences, it then acquires the same bias. Following Shah et al. (2026), we say the data exerts a covert influence. We call the transmitted trait a hidden bias of the data. Subliminal learning is not the only form of covert influence. Hidden biases also transfer through a teacher’s filtered answers to ordinary instructions, in phantom transfer (Draganov et al., 2026), and through preference pairs selected from an existing dataset, in logit-linear selection (Aden-Ali et al., 2026).

Similarly, explicitly penalizing the KL divergence has similarly been shown to constrain the generalization of misaligned behavior across domains (Soligo et al., 2026). As a result, regularization appears to be a promising candidate for constraining covert influence.
