papers.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
papers.abstract: Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in emergent misalignment. We discover a surprising "on-the-line" phenomenon in persona generalization: in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates across various fine-tuning hyperparameters follow an approximately probit-linear relationship, and the specific probit-linear relationship is surprisingly shared even across model families and model sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Training choices that leave the set of trainable parameters unchanged, such as learning rate, weight decay, and training duration, largely move models along the same line, reducing transfer mainly by weakening in-domain learning. Changing which layers are fine-tuned, however, can change the slope. For unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields shallower slopes, retaining strong in-domain learning while reducing out-of-domain misalignment. This "on-the-line" phenomenon unifies unexpected, isolated observations of persona generalization within a quantitative framework for predicting and controlling behavioral transfer.
papers.intro:
Fine-tuning a language model on data from a narrow domain can cause emergent misalignment, where unsafe advice, excessive sycophancy, or other undesirable behavior transfers to a different domain (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025). Such changes are often described as a change in the model persona: a pattern of behavior consistent with a personality description across tasks (Chen et al., 2025). This OOD generalization can be surprising: truthfulness fine-tuning improves accuracy outside the training domain (Joshi et al., 2024), and subliminal learning transfers behavior through number sequences generated by another model (Cloud et al., 2025). Safe and reliable deployment requires that we can predict and control misaligned behavior beyond the training domain (OpenAI, 2026; Greenblatt et al., 2026). The unintuitive nature of persona generalization poses a real safety problem, especially when otherwise high-quality fine-tuning data can contain unintentionally misaligned behavior. This motivates the central question of this work: Do these observations follow a common structure, and can training choices control how far a learned behavior transfers?

We find a surprising “on-the-line” phenomenon in persona generalization: for each domain pair, full-model fine-tuning follows approximately the same slope across model families, sizes, common hyperparameter sweeps, and regularization. In particular, the frequency of persona behavior in one domain follows an approximately probit-linear relationship with its frequency in another. For each domain pair, this line is largely consistent across model families, model sizes, hyperparameters, and regularization when updates are applied across all layers in the network (full-model fine-tuning). For example, after training on medical questions, the rate of unsafe responses on these questions tracks the rate on DIY questions along the same line across models (Figure 1.a). This extends prior work on classification accuracy, which similarly found a consistent probit-linear relationship between in-domain and out-of-domain performance across models and training configurations (Miller et al., 2021). Once calibrated, the OOD misalignment rate of a subsequent model can be predicted from its in-domain misalignment rate alone.

This relationship suggests a second question: can we change the slope of the line? We often want to learn the target in-domain behavior while limiting the transfer of misaligned behavior. The obvious candidate for limiting generalization is to tune the hyperparameters and regularization, as is standard practice for controlling learning and generalization. These choices indeed affect how strongly behavior is learned in-domain and out-of-domain. However, in the tested full-model settings, the probit-linear relationship between learning and OOD generalization implies that merely tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization generally cannot limit OOD generalization without simultaneously limiting the learning of the desired fine-tuning behavior. The prior work on classification finds that the same line can remain fixed across changes in architecture, regularization, training duration, and dataset size (Miller et al., 2021; Baek et al., 2022). This suggests that standard training choices may offer limited control over transfer at a fixed level of in-domain learning.

This gives us a way to control how far a learned behavior transfers by choosing where learning takes place, without simply reducing in-domain learning.

papers.title: A Simple Computer-Assisted Proof of the 5/6-Bound for Real-Period Pinwheel Scheduling
papers.abstract: In pinwheel scheduling with real periods, an instance consists of $n$ tasks with real periods $1\le a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n$. The goal is to find a schedule that assigns one task to each day indefinitely such that, for every task $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every positive integer $\ell$, task $i$ occurs at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil\ell a_i\rceil$ consecutive days. Given an instance $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)$, its dimension is $n$, its density is $\sum_{i=1}^n1/a_i$, and its potential is $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1/a_i$. We prove that every real-valued instance of density at most 5/6 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $4\cdot2^n$. For integer periods, the 5/6 density bound was a long-standing conjecture settled by Kawamura using a computer-assisted proof [STOC 2024, PNAS 2026]. Our result confirms the real-period conjecture of Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi [DMTCS 2026]. Our computer-assisted proof builds on Kawamura's ideas while using fewer explicit schedules. It combines dimension reduction by folding with nine satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks over linear real arithmetic. A set of 14287 explicit periodic schedules contains a schedule for every instance of dimension at most 8 and density at most 5/6, and for every instance of dimension 9 and potential at most 5/6. Folding is used to reduce every instance of larger dimension and potential at most 5/6 to an instance of dimension 9 and the same potential bound. We also prove that every real-valued instance with minimum period at least 4 and density at most 17/20=0.85 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $19\cdot2^n$. The density bound 17/20 is tight and improves the 0.84-bound of Mishra, Rho, and Kleinberg [arXiv 2025] for integer periods. It also resolves the $a_1=4$ case of Kawamura's 2025 conjecture that integer-valued instances of density at most $1-(a_1-1)/(a_1(a_1+1))$ are schedulable.

In the classical pinwheel scheduling problem, we are given nn tasks and a positive integer period aia_{i} for each task i∈[n]={1,2,…,n}i\in[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. papers.title: Semantic Synthesis over Brute-Force Search: LLM-Guided Transformation Design for Efficient Learning
papers.abstract: Data transformation pipelines shape the training distribution in computer vision, but designing them is a computationally expensive problem. We investigate whether large language models can enable efficient discovery by synthesizing executable transformation programs outside predefined augmentation spaces. We compare nine strategies under a unified training protocol, including standard augmentation policies, brute-force search, direct code generation with two LLMs, and performance-guided generation using LLMs fine-tuned on accuracy-ordered transformation pairs. When the best candidates are retrained for 20 epochs, LLM-generated transformation programs lead on every dataset, reaching 0.8877 accuracy on CIFAR-10, 0.5825 on CIFAR-100, and 0.9588 on SVHN, surpassing brute-force search over 6,000 candidates. The best transform on CIFAR-10 and SVHN comes from a fine-tuned generator using 270 candidates, while the best on CIFAR-100 comes from an off-the-shelf generator using only 10. This needs 22x fewer candidate evaluations in the generation step and 600x fewer for off-the-shelf generations, relative to brute-force search. Beyond transformation discovery, we analyze the reliability of the reduced-budget evaluation commonly used for augmentation search. Correlating one-epoch selection scores with 20-epoch outcomes reveals strong, weak, and absent predictive relationships depending on the dataset and architecture, with correlations ranging from 0.756 to near zero. A positive control indicates that range restriction alone is unlikely to explain the low correlations. Our results indicate that semantic synthesis with code LLMs provides an efficient alternative to search-based transformation discovery and highlight the importance of validating evaluation fidelity when optimizing data transformations.

papers.intro:
A neural network’s accuracy depends on its architecture and on how its training data is preprocessed. Which augmentation pipeline to use for a given task has no settled answer, so practitioners choose among strategies that differ by orders of magnitude in cost: fixed policies such as RandAugment [15] and TrivialAugment [46] that require no search; meta-learned assistance that recommends preprocessing for a given algorithm [8]; automated search such as AutoAugment [14], whose policy space is large enough that reinforcement learning was needed to traverse it; and, recently, code generated by large language models [16, 18].

A transformation program is a curated data artifact. Viewed at the level of the training set rather than the model, a transformation program belongs with pruning, distillation, and synthetic data generation, and occupies a distinct position among them. Pruning removes existing samples; distillation learns a small synthetic replacement set; generative synthesis adds samples from a learned model. A transformation program does none of these: it edits the preprocessing distribution applied to every sample of an existing set, and only the code is produced and stored. The asymmetry is severe. The programs here are under 22 kB of source each, against 153.6153.6 MB for CIFAR-10 as uint8 and 1.21.2 to 6.16.1 MB for a distilled set at 1010 to 5050 images per class in float32 — three orders of magnitude below distillation and five below the raw set, while acting on all 50,00050{,}000 samples. What such a program does commit to is a search procedure, and that procedure is what we examine here.

Search requires scoring thousands of candidates; full training runs are too expensive to repeat thousands of times, so candidates are scored by a cheap proxy: train for a few epochs, or one epoch, and rank by validation accuracy. This proxy is standard practice in AutoML, but augmentation search inherits the practice without inheriting the validation that the pruning literature performs on its own proxies [13].

papers.title: Atomically Sharp Magnetic Domain Walls beyond Micromagnetics
papers.abstract: Atomically narrow magnetic domain walls can arise in ultrathin magnetic films, van der Waals magnets, and systems with reduced effective exchange stiffness due to competing exchange interactions. As their width approaches the atomic lattice spacing, the continuum approximation underlying micromagnetics becomes increasingly unreliable. We investigate the structure and stability of such domain walls in a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor J-K-D spin-lattice model incorporating Heisenberg exchange, uniaxial anisotropy, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). In the absence of DMI, we demonstrate analytically a continuous transition to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall at the critical exchange-to-anisotropy ratio J/K = 3/2, characterized by the softening of a localized Hessian mode. Atomistic spin-dynamics simulations confirm this transition and reveal that fitting discrete wall profiles with the conventional micromagnetic solution, as commonly done in experimental analyses, underestimates the exchange interaction and overestimates the anisotropy. Finite DMI removes the perfectly collinear wall as a stationary configuration, replacing the transition by a smooth crossover toward a strongly localized but canted wall that approaches the collinear easy-axis configuration only asymptotically in the strong-anisotropy limit. We derive an analytical expression for the DMI-induced canting in this regime and demonstrate its strongly enhanced canting response near the critical ratio. These findings establish the limitations of micromagnetic descriptions of atomically narrow domain walls and suggest opportunities for controlling their structure through anisotropy and DMI.

papers.intro:
In a typical ferromagnet, the magnetization is distributed in ferromagnetic domains of different, typically energy equivalent magnetization directions separated by magnetic domain walls. Although metastable, these domain-walls can have very long lifetimes and are of scientific and technological relevance. In the context of information technology, understanding the nature of domain walls in magnetic nanostructures has become an important issue. The field of spintronics [9] offers current induced controlled and quick transport [8] of domain walls from input to output devices. This provides an interesting basis for building both low-power logic [4, 35, 22] and memory [27, 26, 32] domain-wall devices that can open a path to in-memory and beyond John von Neumann computing [12]. Domain walls (DW) in magnetic nanostructures and thin films arise from the interplay of the quantum-mechanical exchange interaction, described in the continuum limit by the spin stiffness, the magnetocrystalline anisotropy caused by the relativistic spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and the classical long-range magnetostatic contribution. The experimental characterization of the domain-wall profile provides information about these quantities [29, 30, 36]. In ultrathin films and multilayers, surface and interface contributions to the magnetic anisotropy often dominate over bulk contributions at film thicknesses below approximately 2 nm, frequently favoring an out-of-plane magnetic easy axis. Although the magnetostatic dipole-dipole interactions are intrinsically non-local and long-ranged their contribution in ultrathin films can often be approximated by a local effective anisotropy term [16].

In general, the rotation of the magnetization across a domain wall has no preferred handedness, and walls with clockwise and counterclockwise rotational sense are energetically equivalent. In ultrathin films, multilayers, and heterostructures, however, broken inversion symmetry together with spin–orbit coupling gives rise to the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), characterized by the strength D\pazocal{D} [16]. In general, the rotation of the magnetization across a domain wall has no preferred handedness, and walls with clockwise and counterclockwise rotational sense are energetically equivalent. In ultrathin films, multilayers, and heterostructures, however, broken inversion symmetry together with spin–orbit coupling gives rise to the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), characterized by the strength D\pazocal{D} [16]. As domain walls become increasingly narrow, however, this fundamental assumption eventually breaks down. The experimentally observed reduction of domain-wall widths toward only a few lattice constants, together with the occurrence of DMI-induced chiral walls in ultrathin magnetic systems, therefore motivates a description in terms of discrete atomic spins.

In this work, we investigate how the competition between exchange and magnetic anisotropy determines the structure and stability of domain walls at the atomic scale, and how this behavior is modified by DMI. We find that the discrete exchange–anisotropy (JJ–KK) model exhibits a continuous transition at J/K=3/2J/K=3/2 to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall (EAS), in which all spins are aligned parallel or antiparallel to the easy axis and the magnetization reverses abruptly between two neighboring lattice sites. The transition is characterized by the vanishing of the lowest eigenvalue of the energy Hessian. Near the critical point, fitting the magnetic domain-wall profile with the continuum model leads to underestimation of the exchange interaction and overestimation of the magnetic anisotropy. A finite Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), however, removes the stationary easy-axis state, lifts the soft mode, and replaces the transition by a smooth crossover. The paper is organized as follows. First, we introduce the conventional micromagnetic and discrete spin-lattice models and derive the critical exchange-to-anisotropy ratio at which an infinitely long chain undergoes a continuous transition from a canted domain wall to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall. We then compare numerically relaxed configurations of a 100-spin chain, obtained with Spirit [33, 23] with the continuum domain-wall profile. This comparison yields apparent continuum parameters and exposes the energetic and profile errors of the continuum approximation near the atomically sharp-wall transition. Finally, we investigate the effects of finite DMI on the structure and stability of the domain wall through an analysis of the Hessian spectrum, the minimum out-of-plane magnetization, and the linear response of the wall in the strong-anisotropy regime.

papers.title: Contrasting one- and two-particle excitations in cuprate strange metals
papers.abstract: In unconventional superconductivity, the pairing mechanism remains one of the central unresolved problems in solid-state physics. Moreover, the normal state shows strong deviations from conventional Fermi-liquid behavior, most notably a scattering rate that is linear in energy and temperature. Here we study the momentum dependence of the energy and damping of collective excitations in optimally doped cuprates in the normal state. In particular, we analyze existing Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS) data of Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 [Phys. Rev. B 44, 7155 (1991)] and new analogous optical plasmon data of Bi2Sr2Ca2Cu3O10. Furthermore, we reanalyze similar Resonant Inelastic Xray Scattering (RIXS) acoustic plasmon data [Phys. Rev. R 6, 043184 (2024)] of La1.84Sr0.16CuO4 and La1.84Ce0.16CuO4. We contrast these two-particle excitation results with one-particle excitations measured by Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES). Most of the plasmon behavior can be described well by combined self-energies of a hole and an electron. The dispersion of optical plasmons at high energy is only weakly determined by correlation effects, indicating resilient quasiparticles. The damping of the optical plasmons at low energy, however, is strongly influenced by the reduced scattering rates described in the marginal Fermi liquid model for "strange-metal" behavior. In addition, the same model describes the linear-in-energy damping of acoustic plasmons. Contrary to some theoretical predictions, we see no overdamped optical plasmons below the classical Lindhard critical wave vector.

papers.intro:
Understanding how strong electronic correlations govern charge dynamics remains one of the central challenges of condensed-matter physics and a major obstacle to identify the mechanism of high-TcT_{\rm c} superconductivity. In the normal state, cuprate superconductors exhibit pronounced deviations from conventional Fermi-liquid behavior, most notably a “strange-metal” phase characterized by a resistivity that is linear in temperature over a broad range and persists even beyond the Mott–Ioffe–Regel (MIR) limit. Within a Drude picture, this limit corresponds to a mean–free path comparable to the lattice spacing [58, 41, 18]. Such anomalous transport behavior signals the breakdown of the quasiparticle paradigm and points to enhanced low-energy excitations and eventually to an unconventional continuum of low-energy electronic excitations, as captured phenomenologically by the marginal Fermi-liquid theory [86].

papers.title: A Game-Theoretic MPC Planner for Cooperative and Adversarial Drone Coordination
papers.abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.

papers.intro:
Coordinating multiple drones requires planning trajectories that account for both vehicle dynamics and the motion of other drones. Cooperative inspection and environmental monitoring motivate such planning in shared airspace [1, 2]. In cooperative goal reaching, each drone seeks its assigned position while maintaining separation from the others [3]. In adversarial pursuit–evasion, the drones have opposing objectives: pursuers seek to approach evaders, while evaders seek to avoid them [4].

Model predictive control (MPC) provides a way to plan motion using a dynamics model and state and input constraints [5, 6]. It optimizes future control inputs over a finite horizon and repeats the optimization after executing the first part of the plan. In this work, MPC serves as a trajectory-planning layer that supplies predicted positions and velocities to a tracking controller.

The interaction costs and separation constraints can make the game nonconvex. Computational cost depends on the number of drones, prediction horizon and control parameterization. We therefore investigate how to implement the planner, how to evaluate its solutions and whether their computation fits the available planning period.

papers.title: CRAFT-AI: Capability and Requirement Alignment for Flexible Manufacturing through Agentic AI
papers.abstract: One of the fundamental needs for reaching resilient production infrastructure is flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing production requirements into implementable system configurations. This paper introduces \textbf{CRAFT-AI}, an agentic AI approach combining natural language (NL) requirement interpretation, Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-based capability descriptions, and reusable engineering knowledge from existing manufacturing configurations. A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach is demonstrated using a Factory I/O prototype with twelve reference scenes and five illustrative manufacturing tasks of varying complexity, providing an initial feasibility assessment of the proposed AAS-enabled, system-level generative engineering approach. For the four valid user task descriptions, proper requirements, correct references to the relevant engineering knowledge, correct components and lastly a valid Factory I/O scene are generated. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, the user is informed about which requirements of the scene generation lack domain knowledge and also which sensor is not compatible with the selected raw material by the user with link to the related documentation. After fixing the task description, the correct scene is seamlessly generated. \textbf{CRAFT-AI} highlights the importance of safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation model-driven solutions.

papers.intro:
Manufacturing systems increasingly operate under changing product requirements, smaller batch sizes, and disruptions that demand rapid reconfiguration of production resources. Beyond product customization, supply-chain disturbances can require manufacturers to reconsider both the resources employed and the configurations in which they operate. The ability to safely and reliably reconfigure production resources in response to changing demands and disruptions is therefore a fundamental prerequisite for resilient manufacturing infrastructure (Puchkova et al., 2020; Kechagias et al., 2026). In that regard, Manufacturing-as-a-Service (MaaS) has been investigated as one mechanism for improving flexibility and resilience across production networks (Chen et al., 2023; Sidorenko et al., 2026). At the factory level, however, responding to new demands still entails the engineering task of translating often informal objectives into resource selections and implementable system (re)configurations (Keddis et al., 2015; Elbasheer et al., 2025).

Capability-based engineering addresses part of this challenge by decoupling required functions from specific manufacturing resources. In the product–process–resource perspective, a required capability, also referred to as requirement, describes what a production task demands, whereas an offered capability, also referred to as capability, describes a function an arbitrary resource can provide. Moreover, the capability–skill–service literature further distinguishes capabilities as implementation-independent functional descriptions from skills, which in the related literature is referred to as their executable implementations (Eichenwald et al., 2024; Wagner et al., 2025).

papers.title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet-V2.

Its original instantiation, however, realizes only a fraction of the paradigm’s potential. The inward reference splits the image into a grid of patches and stacks them along the channel dimension: every convolution response mixes content from grid cells that lie far apart in the image, and pixels adjacent across a patch border land at opposite spatial edges of the rearranged tensor, so the locality the reference aims to preserve is destroyed before any convolution sees it. The injection is moreover ungated, admitting raw texture everywhere with equal weight (Fig. 2(c)). The outward reference, meanwhile, supervises its boundary head with an image-Laplacian target scaled by an unbounded intermediate logit rather than gated by a foreground probability, and applies the result as a bare single-channel rescaling that modulates all feature channels uniformly. These are not isolated defects to be patched, but symptoms that the paradigm has never been instantiated with its core requirements—locality, selectivity, and focused supervision—taken seriously.

papers.title: The Radicalization Pipeline: Characterizing and Predicting Online Misogyny
papers.abstract: Social media platforms are known to shape and polarize user opinions and, increasingly, facilitate pathways toward ideological extremism. Among these trends, online misogynistic communities associ- ated with the incel (involuntary celibate) ideology have received growing scholarly attention. Previous work has primarily focused on ideological narratives and linguistic content within incel communities them- selves. However, much less is known about how user behaviors evolve over time, particularly before and after their engagement with incel spaces, and whether early signals can anticipate such transitions. In this study, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of Reddit users who participated in the r/incels community on Reddit. Our results show that engagement with the incel community is associated with a substantial in- crease in toxicity in both posts and comments, while hate increases particularly in posts after engagement. These changes extend beyond explicitly ideological communities: users who engage with the r/incels sub- reddit display elevated toxicity and hate speech even in subreddits related to leisure, entertainment, and everyday interests. In parallel, user activity shifts away from recreational and support-oriented communi- ties toward subreddits focused on social issues, indicating a broader reorientation of online participation. Finally, we show that future incel users can be identified with high accuracy prior to engagement using supervised machine learning models trained on linguistic, contextual, and interaction-based features. These findings suggest that online misogynistic radicalization follows detectable behavioral trajectories and diffuses across the broader social media ecosystem.

papers.intro:
Social media platforms serve not only as channels for communication, but also as digital spaces in which users actively construct identities, negotiate social norms, and interpret their social realities [4, 29]. These processes are also shaped by the affordances of specific platforms, such as hashtags on Twitter/X or the community-based architecture of Reddit, which encourage users to connect with like-minded others and cluster around shared interests [36, 12]. While the creation of these groups can facilitate social support and community belonging, the same sociotechnical mechanisms that connect users around shared experiences also restrict their informational environments, isolating them from other perspectives. In this scenario, users are increasingly exposed to homogeneous viewpoints, reinforcing polarization and, in some cases, accelerating pathways toward radicalization [11, 7, 33].

A growing body of research has examined how digitally networked spaces can serve as incubators for extremist ideologies by enabling sustained interaction, identity reinforcement, and the normalization of radical beliefs. Within this literature, particular attention has been paid to the misogynistic subcultures collectively referred to as the “Manosphere” [14, 25]. The Manosphere is not a single unified movement, but rather a series of online communities connected by antifeminist sentiment and a shared perception that masculinity is under threat. It includes groups such as Men’s Rights Activists (MRAs), Pick-Up Artists (PUAs), and Men Going Their Own Way (MGTOW), which interact through overlapping discourse and membership [16, 35, 32].

Among these groups, the incel (involuntary celibate) community has emerged as the most extreme. The term “incel” was originally coined in 1997 to describe an inclusive support network for people of all genders struggling with dating and intimacy [21], known as “Alana’s Involuntary Celibacy Project.” At this early stage, involuntary celibacy functioned primarily as a descriptive category rather than an ideological identity, and incel forums were used largely as peer-to-peer support spaces centered on shared vulnerability.

As online culture evolved in the early twenty-first century, however, these communities increasingly reflected the norms of participatory platforms such as 4chan and Reddit, where visibility and engagement were often driven by provocative and transgressive expression. Although incel forums were dispersed across multiple online spaces rather than confined to these platforms, their discourse gradually adopted similar stylistic conventions. Practices such as trolling and “shitposting” blurred the boundary between irony and sincerity, allowing expressions of frustration to escalate into increasingly hostile and exclusionary narratives [18]. Over time, these dynamics contributed to the transformation of incel spaces from support-oriented communities into sites of ideological radicalization [22]. Indeed, the incel ideology promotes a form of biological determinism in which physical appearance is seen as genetically fixed and treated as the primary determinant of social and romantic worth. Those who fail to meet rigid beauty standards are considered irrevocably excluded from intimacy and social success [15, 27, 18].

Scholars have described “being incel” in multiple dimensions: as a social identity (self-identifying as incel), as an ideology (adopting misogynistic beliefs consistent with incel views), and as group membership (belonging to incel communities) [26]. At the same time, these spaces often function as informal peer-support networks for individuals experiencing significant psychological distress. Empirical studies suggest that many users are drawn to incel communities due to depression, social anxiety, autism spectrum traits, and chronic isolation [8, 28]. Yet, rather than alleviating distress, community dynamics frequently encourage co-rumination [13, 9], whereby users repeatedly externalize blame. Over time, personal vulnerability is reframed as collective injustice, increasing hostility toward women and society at large [10, 9]. This process not only intensifies mental health struggles but also serves as a cognitive bridge to ideological radicalization [34], contributing to the amplification of hateful discourse and the normalization of violence against women [20].

These dynamics have important implications for how individuals come to enter and participate within incel spaces. As incel communities became increasingly associated with misogynistic extremism and offline violence, platforms decided to intervene and, in 2017, Reddit banned its largest incel forum, r/incels. Although such interventions aim to curb hate speech and reduce harm, research on platform governance suggests their effects are mixed. Studies of deplatforming indicate that while bans disrupt established communities, they often incentivize users to migrate to alternative subreddits or less regulated platforms such as 4chan and dedicated forums, where extremist discourse may proliferate with fewer constraints [6, 19, 1]. At the same time, recent evidence from the European Parliament suggests that these communities are not only displaced to fringe platforms, but also increasingly emerge within mainstream social media environments such as X, contributing to the broader normalization and diffusion of misogynistic narratives [3].

papers.title: Complementarity without ground truth?
papers.abstract: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.

papers.intro:
Since the early 2020s, complementarity has become an increasingly investigated performance measure in human–AI interaction (HAI) research (Bansal et al., 2021b; Bansal et al., 2021a; Donahue et al., 2022; Cabitza et al., 2023; Vaccaro et al., 2024). In prediction tasks, a human assisted by an AI system achieves complementarity when the resulting human–AI team performs better than both the human and the AI alone. This generalises human augmentation, where AI improves human performance, and AI reliance, where the human adopts AI output (Schemmer et al., 2023; Grote et al., 2024).

Since the early 2020s, complementarity has become an increasingly investigated performance measure in human–AI interaction (HAI) research (Bansal et al., 2021b; Bansal et al., 2021a; Donahue et al., 2022; Cabitza et al., 2023; Vaccaro et al., 2024). In prediction tasks, a human assisted by an AI system achieves complementarity when the resulting human–AI team performs better than both the human and the AI alone. This generalises human augmentation, where AI improves human performance, and AI reliance, where the human adopts AI output (Schemmer et al., 2023; Grote et al., 2024).

The conceptual simplicity of complementarity has, however, exposed a few theoretical and empirical limitations (Vaccaro et al., 2024; Ferrario et al., 2026). In this work, we focus on one structural assumption: the dependence of complementarity on ground truth. In prediction tasks, complementarity is evaluated relative to labelled datasets: the predictions of the human, the AI system, and the human–AI team are compared against common reference labels, i.e., the ground truth labels, through a loss function or an equivalent label-based performance measure (Donahue et al., 2022; Ferrario et al., 2026). Thus, this comparison presupposes a reference label intended to represent which relevant state of affairs obtains and against which the predictions can be scored.

Thus, this comparison presupposes a reference label intended to represent which relevant state of affairs obtains and against which the predictions can be scored.

While this setting is appropriate for prediction tasks, HAIs also concern tasks for which this procedure is less natural. Prominently, in the medical field, a clinical AI system may support the management reasoning paradigm (Cook et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2019), recommending one treatment among several alternatives, ranking therapeutic options, suggesting escalation or discharge, or supporting the evaluation of competing decision alternatives. Here, the relevant question is whether an AI-assisted action is adequate within a specific decision context and given several adequacy criteria, such as treatment efficacy, effectiveness, toxicity, and quality of life. However, none of these dimensions alone determines which treatment should be selected. While these practical judgments still may depend on truths about the world, their evaluation is not exhausted by adequacy with respect to a to-be-predicted state of affairs.

In this work, we address the ground-truth limitation of complementarity through a four-step approach. First, following Högberg et al. (2026), we distinguish ground truth from ground truthing, the process through which ground truth labels are defined, collected, and validated as references to states of affairs, and we characterise ground truthing as a key component of the reference construction procedure for prediction tasks. Second, using medicine as a source of motivating use cases, and diagnosis and treatment selection as illustrative cases, we generalize this procedure to AI-assisted practical decision-support tasks, exemplified by the management reasoning paradigm in medicine (Cook et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2019). We argue that such tasks can also admit labels, but that these encode adequacy relative to contextualised evaluative standards rather than correspondence to a state of affairs. Third, we use these adequacy labels to extend complementarity to practical tasks, making the normative commitments involved in defining adequate outputs explicit within the evaluation procedure. Finally, drawing methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism (CR) (Durán, 2025), we identify factors relevant to supporting adequacy-label construction and examine robustness across admissible reference constructions. The paper makes four contributions: 1. it characterizes the reference construction procedure underlying complementarity in HAIs; 2. it generalizes this procedure to practical decision-support tasks through the construction of adequacy labels; 3. it extends complementarity functionals to these labels while making their evaluative commitments explicit; and 4. it provides a CR-inspired account of evidential support for reference construction and a robustness criterion for complementarity across admissible reference constructions.

papers.title: SU(2) Yang-Mills: Spectral Bounds, Vacuum Concentration, and Criteria for the Continuum Limit
papers.abstract: A continuum mass-gap argument must preserve nonzero renormalized states and a positive spectral estimate while the spatial cutoff is removed and physical volume grows. We develop quantitative results that separate these requirements. Gauge reduction, reflection positivity and attributed strong-coupling estimates give physical-transfer bounds with nontrivial local sectors. At fixed spatial cutoff and positive coupling, we construct subsequential infinite-volume physical-time dynamics from local history correlations, with nonconstant gauge-invariant observables. For finite spatial boxes, explicit bounds apply to the entire physical vacuum complement; finite-matrix criteria include all omitted representations. Vacuum concentration gives extensive entropy bounds, quantitative fidelity obstructions for hard electric cutoffs, and necessary growth of retained representation spaces. A sharper local comparison yields complete bounds on fixed discarded-link sectors, while collective projection and Schur estimates isolate the additional input needed for a volume-uniform gap. The work also certifies a finite three-link conditioning functional through Wilson coupling 0.354, with its physical interpretation conditional on the stated block-comparison hypotheses. Exact blocking, corrected effective-potential theorems and a representation-by-representation two-dimensional benchmark clarify which approximations preserve the relevant observables. Published glueball measurements retain their original attribution; their reanalysis and the reproduced winding-channel and replica studies have explicitly statistical scope. Complete derivations and reproducible calculations support a set of certified benchmarks and continuum transfer criteria. A nontrivial four-dimensional spatial-cutoff construction and a positive spectral bound along it are not established; no exact continuum mass is asserted.

papers.title: Ultrafast Liquid Jet X-ray Total Scattering
papers.abstract: X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide the temporal resolution needed to extend total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to investigate structural dynamics on femtosecond-to-picosecond timescales. We recently demonstrated that high-quality total scattering data and PDFs can be obtained from individual XFEL pulses; here, we take the next step towards time-resolved studies of structural dynamics in solution. Using the Materials Imaging and Dynamics (MID) instrument at the European XFEL, we obtain total scattering data up to $Q_{\max} = 16.4\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$ from both conventional capillary samples and, critically, from samples delivered by a liquid jet. Despite the large air and solvent backgrounds inherent to this setup, PDFs suitable for quantitative structural analysis are recovered from liquid dispersions and molecular clusters in solution. We further demonstrate pump-probe total scattering from $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_3$ nanocrystals in a liquid jet, resolving a fluence-dependent photoinduced isotropic lattice strain. Additionally, empirical potential structure refinement (EPSR) of XFEL total scattering data from an aqueous Keggin cluster reveals site-specific hydration environments and enables three-dimensional mapping of the surrounding solvent structure. Together, these advances open the door to tracking not only ultrafast structural changes in solution, but also the evolving solvent environments that govern molecular behaviour and reactivity.

papers.title: Benchmarking Real-World Robotic Manipulation through Stochastic Challenges
papers.abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.

papers.intro:
Reliable comparability between robotic manipulation methods is a common bottleneck in current robotics research. Manipulation is an inherently interactive task: the same model can produce different outcomes on the same physical setup, and different model outputs can lead to the same outcome, so evaluation on static datasets cannot capture method quality. Existing alternatives each carry limitations. Centralized competitions such as RoboCup require physically transporting robots to a single site. Simulation benchmarks [23] provide scale and repeatability but exhibit physical realism gaps. Real-world benchmarks built around fixed object sets [4] have driven important progress, but a single hand-picked setup risks overfitting.

Recent efforts have identified the same problem and proposed real-world distributed benchmarks [1, 6]. However, both rely on standardizing either the robot embodiment [1] or the task [6], and both constrain themselves to tabletop scenarios. This prevents precisely the comparisons that matter as manipulation systems scale to deployment: comparing different platforms - humanoids, wheeled mobile manipulators, quadrupeds, on real tasks that require both mobility and interaction with real scenes.

We address this gap with stochastic challenges, a benchmarking framework that standardizes a distribution of scenes and tasks rather than a fixed test set. This extends the idea of YCB [4] from a fixed object set to a sampled distribution: any lab can reconstruct any specific scene from a seed, but participants see only a small fraction of all possible scenes and do not know the correct response to a challenge in advance, similar to the test set of a dataset benchmark. This allows evaluation instances to be sampled only at test time, unlike a fixed paired test set. A system must therefore be prepared for the broader task distribution even though only a small subset of configurations is evaluated in practice. This reduces the opportunity to overfit to a known physical test set. We hypothesize that, if tasks and scenes are sampled from the same distribution, sufficient samples allow methods to be compared at a chosen statistical confidence level independent of the robot platform, software stack, or policy used.

papers.title: Done Is Not Correct: Measuring Silent Failures and Self-Verification Calibration When LLM Agents Take CAD Actions
papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent writes parametric CAD code from a natural-language specification, syntactic success decouples from semantic correctness. We release a benchmark and harness that measure this gap directly: 13 specification tasks whose every requirement maps to machine-checkable properties of the produced B-rep, measured by the kernel against published tolerance bands, with reference solutions and the full graded attempt corpus. The exact, self-audited oracle isolates two quantities no prior CAD benchmark reports: the silent-failure rate (a valid, renderable solid, an explicit completion claim, and at least one failed semantic check) and completion-claim calibration. Across four models from four vendors (156 attempts per architecture), single-shot agents claimed completion on 98% of attempts and were silently wrong on 14.1%; a tool-use loop that enforces measure-then-claim cut silent failures to 3.2% and raised claim precision from 64% to 96%, and a four-model ablation attributes the change to the claim contract rather than the feedback. A planner-coder-checker pipeline matched that precision at lower coverage with no success gain. Stated confidence was miscalibrated single-shot (ECE 0.32) and became informative under verification for three of four models. Hardening our own oracle flipped 18 of 519 regraded verdicts from pass to fail and none in reverse; a blind expert audit overturned 3 of the 18 silent failures outside the one ambiguously specified task; and fourfold scaling of every tolerance band leaves the contrast intact.

papers.intro:
LLM agents increasingly act rather than advise: they write and execute code, call tools, and report back [Yao et al., 2022, Schick et al., 2023]. Software engineering already has execution-grounded benchmarks for this regime [Jimenez et al., 2023], and a growing body of evidence that agent evaluation systematically overstates reliability: graders admit false positives [Yu et al., 2025, Zhu et al., 2025], headline accuracy hides inconsistency [Yao et al., 2024, Kapoor et al., 2024], web-agent progress shrinks under rigorous re-evaluation [Xue et al., 2025], and agents asked to estimate their own success are grossly overconfident [Kaddour et al., 2026].

Mechanical computer-aided design (CAD) is the next domain in this trajectory; it is also, we argue, the best instrumented one for studying agent reliability. A wave of recent work generates parametric CAD from text [Khan et al., 2024, Xie and Ju, 2025, Wang et al., 2026], increasingly with agentic feedback loops over a CAD kernel [Mallis et al., 2024, Yuan et al., 2026, Barkley et al., 2026, Ocker et al., 2025], and surveys now map the area [Zhang et al., 2025]. Yet evaluation in this literature measures generation quality: Chamfer distance or IoU to a reference solid, execution success, or judge scores [Zhou et al., 2025, Alrashedy et al., 2024]. None of it asks the reliability question that determines whether an engineer can delegate: when the agent says the part is done, is it, and does the agent know?

Crashes are cheap to catch: a spec that fails to execute announces itself. The expensive failure is a part that builds and renders plausibly while its bolt circle sits on the wrong pitch diameter, delivered with “done, confidence 0.97.” Companion work by the first author [Rodrigues, 2026] defines context drift in multi-agent LLM pipelines, a divergence between agents’ working beliefs that we also measure here (Section 3); people relying on AI advice often fail to rely on it appropriately [Schemmer et al., 2023]; and the self-correction literature explains why the agent’s own check is not to be trusted without external feedback [Huang et al., 2023, Kamoi et al., 2024, Gou et al., 2023]. CAD supplies what those settings lacked: exact measurement. The produced B-rep can be measured (dimensions, feature counts and extents, hole positions, mass properties, volume), so agent-side overclaiming can be separated from grader inadequacy to a degree execution-graded software benchmarks cannot [Yu et al., 2025]; we audit and quantify the residual grader risk rather than assume it to be zero.

It is released with every graded attempt (final code, measured properties, verdicts under both oracle versions, transcripts for the fixed-protocol runs), the grader, the harness, and a 3D viewer (Section 7). (2) A claim-conditioned, self-auditing exact-oracle silent-failure rate coupled to completion-claim calibration. The silent-failure rate is the conjunction of (i) valid renderable geometry, (ii) an explicit agent completion claim, and (iii) failure of at least one semantic check, graded by an exact kernel oracle that we audit against ourselves; it is coupled to completion-claim calibration measured as ECE, reliability diagrams, AUROC, and Brier score [Guo et al., 2017, Tian et al., 2023, Kaddour et al., 2026]. Conditioning on the agent’s own claim and on a self-audited exact oracle is what separates this from the generation- and repair-quality scores of CADSmith [Barkley et al., 2026], the finite-element requirement-pass rate of Son et al. [2026], and the assembly-structure, interface and functional scores of MUSE [Dong et al., 2026]; we do not claim to be first to measure geometric correctness. We also report which of our pre-specified predictions the data did not support (Section 8).

papers.title: Data-Driven Precision Control of Soft Helicoid Robots
papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.

papers.title: Accelerated Reinforcement Learning for Soft Robotics: Hours Instead of Years
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.

papers.title: Lagrangian tori in the three-dimensional quadric and mirror symmetry
papers.abstract:
In the three-dimensional quadric, we study the Oakley--Usher torus and its Chekanov counterpart as defined by the authors in the companion paper \cite{OU1}. Computing the versal deformation of the $\Psi$-invariant of Shelukhin--Tonkonog--Vianna, we find that the Chekanov Oakley--Usher torus is knotted in a strong sense: it is not Hamiltonian isotopic to the Biran-lift of any Vianna torus in the two-dimensional quadric. Furthermore, we investigate enumerative properties of the Oakley--Usher torus in $Q^3$ and prove its non-displaceability, settling an open question asked by Oakley--Usher. We relate this to mirror symmetry by proving a split-generation result for the monotone Fukaya category of $Q^3$. This should be viewed as the analogue of a result by Abouzaid--Diogo after compactifying. Interestingly, in the compactification, the monotone copy of the $(S^1 \times S^2)$-generators of Abouzaid--Diogo becomes displaceable. On the other hand, the Oakley--Usher torus still appears as a generator.
  In the appendix joint with Soham Chanda, we give an alternative construction of the Chekanov Oakley--Usher torus using a double solid torus mutation. This allows us to compute its disk-potential using wall-crossing results.

papers.title: A Note on the Hardness of Partially Dynamic Max Flow
papers.abstract: We study the fine-grained complexity of partially dynamic max flow in capacitated graphs. Assuming the combinatorial 4-clique hypothesis, combinatorial algorithms require $\Omega(n^{2-o(1)})$ amortized update time. Thus, recomputing max flow after each update is optimal up to subpolynomial factors for combinatorial algorithms in dense graphs. The previous conditional lower bound was $\Omega(n^{1-o(1)})$ amortized update time under SETH or the OMv hypothesis and applies to all algorithms [Dah16].

papers.title: Strong Connectivity Oracle for Multiple Failures via Rooted Flow-Augmentation
papers.abstract:
We present a significantly improved $k$-fault-tolerant strong connectivity oracle, one of the most basic data structures on a directed graph $G$ that, given any set $F$ of failed edges of size $|F|\le k$, answers whether $G \setminus F$ is strongly connected. For every constant $k$, our oracle only uses $n^{1+o(1)}$ space and $n^{o(1)}$ query time. No prior result can achieve $o(n^{2})$ space and $o(n)$ query time, \emph{even when $k=2$}. Previous oracles either require $\Omega(n)$ query time [BCR18], or $\Omega(n^2)$ space [vdBS19].
  Our main technical contribution is a \emph{rooted} version of the highly successful flow augmentation technique, which may be of independent interest. Given a directed graph $G$, an integer $k$, and a source vertex $s$, we can sample a set of edges $A$ such that each minimal $s$-rooted cut of size at most $k$ becomes an $s$-rooted min-cut in $G + A$ with probability $2^{-poly(k)}n^{-o(1)}$.

papers.title: Randomized Greedy MIS Is Fast at Every Node of a Tree
papers.abstract: The Randomized Greedy MIS (RGMIS) algorithm computes a maximal independent set (MIS) by processing the vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily adding each vertex to the independent set whenever possible. Despite its simplicity, this algorithm has proved effective in a range of parallel, distributed, and dynamic settings. For sufficiently small maximum degree, Nguyen and Onak (FOCS~'08) and Yoshida, Yamamoto, and Ito (STOC~'09) showed that a recursive simulation of RGMIS can be used to estimate the sizes of matching and vertex cover in sublinear time. The key subroutine in their approach is the following local query procedure: given a vertex $v$, to determine whether $v$ belongs to the MIS, recursively evaluate the neighbors of $v$ that precede $v$ in the random order. If any such neighbor is found to belong to the MIS, the procedure immediately concludes that $v$ is not in the MIS; otherwise, it concludes that $v$ is in the MIS. For graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$, Nguyen and Onak showed that, in expectation over the random ordering, this procedure makes $O(\exp(\Delta))$ recursive calls from a worst-case starting vertex. No better upper bound is known even for trees. We prove that on trees, from \textit{any} starting vertex, this recursive RGMIS procedure makes $\mathrm{poly}(\Delta)$ recursive calls in expectation.

papers.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
papers.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

Perhaps the central idea in recent neural network quantization strategies is the change of basis. To compute the matrix product between an input and a weight matrix, we may transform the input by a matrix PP and apply the corresponding inverse transform to the weights, leaving the product unchanged. If PP is chosen wisely, the transformed inputs and weights can be substantially easier to quantize.

If PP is chosen wisely, the transformed inputs and weights can be substantially easier to quantize.

Two types of transform are widely used to ease quantization. First, activations and weights may be rotated into a different basis using an orthogonal matrix MrotM_{\mathrm{rot}}. The Hadamard transform is especially popular because it can be applied in O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N) operations and tends to produce approximately Gaussian-distributed outputs (4). Second, individual channels may be rescaled using a diagonal matrix MdiagM_{\mathrm{diag}} (29, 18, 21), thereby suppressing outlying channels and balancing the quantization difficulty of activations and weights.

One potential downside of such a change of basis is that, although the weight-side transform can be absorbed into the weights at quantization time, the corresponding input transform ostensibly needs to be applied online. Prior work often avoids this cost by propagating the input transform through the network and absorbing it into preceding layers. This approach is widely used because it can eliminate the explicit runtime transform (1). However, it also introduces dependencies between layers: applying the transform to one linear layer may require modifying its normalization parameters, preceding projections, residual branches, or other connected operators.

MACaQ confines every transform and quantization decision to a single linear layer. No neighboring layer is modified to compensate for its quantization, and no basis transform needs to be propagated through the network. Eliminating these inter-layer dependencies allows each linear layer to be calibrated, transformed, and quantized independently. This simplifies application to new architectures, enables layers to be loaded and quantized one at a time, and leads to substantially faster quantization. Furthermore, all linear layers can benefit from online basis transforms, where in some architectures not all layers can have absorbed basis transforms.

papers.title: A Bayesian oriented exploration and reinforcement learning in continuous-time mean-variance portfolio optimization
papers.abstract: We propose a new reinforcement learning (RL) framework for the continuous-time mean-variance portfolio optimization with unknown market parameters. To better reflect the impact of improved information of the unknown drift on the degree of exploration, we consider a novel randomization based on continuous-time stochastic filtering. Specifically, we construct a continuous-time analog to Thompson Sampling by treating the unknown drift as a random draw from a generalized sampling distribution parameterized by the filter's posterior mean and variance. The new learning objective measures the tradeoff between the wealth performance and the weighted KL divergence between the policy and the true Bayesian posterior, which transforms the classical feedback control into an information guided stochastic policy. As a result, the degree of exploration endogenously depends on the Reward-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimation that decays with the shrinking filter's variance. This allows us to devise an efficient model-based learning algorithm in the mean-variance portfolio optimization with theoretical guarantee and superior learning performance.

papers.intro:
Mean–variance portfolio selection provides an intuitive way to balance the expected terminal wealth against risk, which has been widely used in practice since the seminal work of Markowitz (1952) and its dynamic extensions in Li and Ng (2000) for multi-period model and in Zhou and Li (2000) for the continuous-time model. The endogenous linear-quadratic structure brings the favorable tractability in the dynamic control problem, however, relying crucially on the precise information of model parameters. In practice, the asset drift is unobservable and particularly difficult to estimate using the history data (Merton, 1980), leaving possibly large errors in implementing the theoretical optimal solution using the inaccurate drift (Best and Grauer, 1991). A common response in the literature is to adopt the identify-then-optimize procedure used in adaptive control (Bielecki et al., 2019; Kumar and Varaiya, 2015; Faradonbeh et al., 2020). Once the resulting estimates are treated as the true parameters, the remaining parameter uncertainty is hidden. Consequently, when the estimated model is substituted directly into the complete-information feedback policy, estimation errors might be further amplified (Best and Grauer, 1991; Kan and Zhou, 2007).

Within this framework, Wang and Zhou (2020) study the precommitted mean–variance problem and show that the optimal stochastic policy is Gaussian, which leads to a structured and implementable learning method. In all aforementioned studies, although the entropy regularization provides a tractable way for the policy randomization, its induced exogenous noise in the randomized policy cannot reflect the agent’s improving uncertainty on unknown model parameters along the learning. Intuitively, when the agent continues to learn, he would gain more information of the unknown environment and employ less randomness for the purpose of exploration. In addition, how to choose the temperature parameter in the standard entropy regularization to balance the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation in RL algorithms is still an open problem. On the other hand, Bayesian filtering quantifies that reduced unknownness through a posterior updated from observed prices, providing a statistical basis for calibrating exploration. The use of posterior beliefs to inform investment decisions is well established in portfolio optimization with partial information (De Franco et al., 2019; Xiong and Zhou, 2007). Lakner (1995) derives optimal investment and consumption decisions when only prices are observed, while Sass and Haussmann (2004) use a filter for a hidden Markov-chain drift to characterize the terminal-wealth optimizer. Bismuth et al. (2019) extend Bayesian learning to portfolio-choice, liquidation, and transition problems with unknown expected returns. In these models, the filter carries information of both the estimated parameter and its remaining uncertainty along the investment horizon. The economic relevance of retaining that uncertainty is illustrated by Rogers (2001), which reveals that the welfare cost can exceed the cost of infrequent portfolio review.

For an unknown constant drift, Au (2026) combines Bayesian filtering with action-space entropy regularization and shows that the mean allocation remains the deterministic Bayesian feedback, while entropy changes the allocation variance. In these formulations, the randomness in the stochastic policy still comes exogenously from the entropy regularization. The filtered belief can affect the optimal allocation variance, but a positive entropy weight can sustain the randomization in the stochastic policy even when parameter uncertainty vanishes, as illustrated by the known-drift limit in Au (2026). For a small investor whose trades do not affect market prices, randomized policy does not change the return observations available to the filter and therefore does not provide additional information to improve the knowledge of the unknown drift. Such randomization can generate different wealth outcomes for policy evaluation, but it also incurs the cost of trying unnecessary suboptimal policies (Szpruch et al., 2024).

papers.title: BRACE: Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control for Safe Navigation under Unknown Disturbances
papers.abstract: Disturbances encountered during autonomous navigation generally vary across space, often discontinuously, as obstacles redirect wind and changing terrain alters traction. Tracking controllers typically assume sufficient control authority to mitigate disturbances and maintain safety; the regime where this assumption fails remains underexplored. We present Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control (BRACE), a hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) framework for reach-avoid navigation under unknown, bounded, spatially varying disturbances. BRACE infers a disturbance belief from model prediction errors and uses that to condition a high-level policy that adapts the reference trajectory. The policy combines a nominal and a belief-guided residual term, trained jointly with a likelihood-ratio advantage reweighting heuristic. Autonomous robots operating in the real world must act safely under unknown, spatially varying disturbances, such as wind fields for aerial vehicles [1]. Such disturbances can cause deviations from planned trajectories, making safe navigation particularly challenging in cluttered environments, where feasible corridors may be narrow. The dominant paradigm for handling disturbances operates at the trajectory-tracking layer through robust and adaptive control methods [2, 3, 4, 5]. These tracking-layer methods can improve tracking of a given reference, but cannot necessarily resolve reference infeasibility under disturbances and actuation limits. This limitation motivates adapting reference trajectories at the planning level.

papers.title: Dual Model Predictive Control through Sampling-Based Belief Propagation
papers.abstract: We propose a sampling-based dual model predictive control (MPC) approach that combines belief propagation with parameterized feedback policy optimization. By sampling uncertain dynamics and process noise, we approximate the evolution of the hyperstate over the prediction horizon, allowing future control decisions to adapt to anticipated observations and belief updates. This enables the controller to account for the future value of information without explicit exploration incentives. We establish almost-sure uniform convergence of the sample-average objective to the finite-horizon expected objective over a compact policy class. The approach is specialized to Bayesian linear regression and evaluated on stochastic systems with constant and time-varying uncertain dynamics. We compare our approach to certainty equivalent control, and an MPC that optimizes over open-loop control sequences rather than feedback policies, demonstrating the benefits of our method in terms of both control performance and information gain.

papers.intro:
Dual control addresses the problem of simultaneously regulating a dynamical system and learning its uncertain dynamics. As originally recognized by Feldbaum [1], control actions influence both the physical state and the information available for future decisions. The optimal Bayesian control policy accounts for this dual effect by balancing immediate control performance against the future benefits of improved model knowledge [2, 3]. However, computing this policy requires solving a stochastic dynamic program over the posterior distribution of the physical state and of the unknown dynamics, the so-called hyperstate, which is generally computationally intractable [4].

However, computing this policy requires solving a stochastic dynamic program over the posterior distribution of the physical state and of the unknown dynamics, the so-called hyperstate, which is generally computationally intractable [4].

Model predictive control (MPC) can provide a tractable approximation of the optimal control problem, typically by an open-loop input sequence over a finite prediction horizon [5]. By optimizing over feedback policies and closed-loop predictions the controller can anticipate how current decisions affect future observations, belief updates, and subsequent control decisions. This enables the value of information to influence the control policy, thereby capturing the dual effect. Motivated by this idea, we propose a tractable sampling-based dual MPC approach that optimizes parameterized feedback policies over sampled state and belief trajectories.

We propose a sampling-based dual MPC formulation that optimizes a shared sequence of parameterized hyperstate-feedback policies. In contrast with other sampling-based approaches, the computed policy is actually an implementable feedback law that can be rolled out for any uncertainty realization and does not rely on hypothetical realizations. papers.title: Graphene: A Lightweight Transformer with Ising Mean-Field Refinement for Image Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution architecture with two complementary feature refinement mechanisms: Ising-model-inspired local feature refinement using an Ising Refinement Block (IRB) and stage-history-based feature refinement using a History Attention (HistAttn) module. The IRB reuses attention output features and pre-softmax attention logits to construct signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates, and refines features through a gated residual correction. These signed couplings allow alignment and opposition between latent spins to modulate local feature refinement. HistAttn attends over the current stage output and earlier representations at the same token position and adaptively blends the current stage output with a history-weighted feature aggregate without adding spatial pairwise attention. On Urban100 at $\times4$, Graphene and Graphene-light improve over IET and IET-light by 0.24 dB and 0.38 dB, respectively, with 34.3%/13.7% fewer parameters, 44.8%/44.4% fewer FLOPs, 78.4%/71.5% lower latency, and 76.0%/85.5% lower peak memory. Real-world SR comparisons further show that Graphene recovers fine details and preserves textures across diverse degradations. Code and reference checkpoints are available at https://github.com/skethz/Graphene

papers.title: FESOM2.8 in single precision: climate fidelity over six decades and performance on CPUs and GPUs
papers.abstract: Halving the floating-point precision of an ocean model can make it substantially faster, but whether the rounding errors stay negligible over climate time scales has rarely been tested. We implement single precision in the global ocean-sea-ice model FESOM2 and compare 60-year hindcasts with double-precision controls. A first implementation lost salt steadily, accumulated a heat-content deficit of 129 ZJ, and shifted major ocean fronts. Controlled experiments trace the drift to the tracer update: small increments added to a large salinity value are rounded away, and the increments themselves are biased. Accumulating tracer tendencies and layer thicknesses in 64 bits, and carrying the rounding error of each tracer update into the next, removes the drift for at most 8% additional runtime. Single- and double-precision simulations then differ in heat content and mean state about as much as two double-precision runs with slightly perturbed initial conditions, sea ice differs by at most 0.2%, and he salinity difference is four orders of magnitude smaller than before. In the coupled model AWI-ESM3, single precision adds no detectable heat source or sink over 60 years. Single precision speeds up the 60-year hindcasts by a factor of 1.35, and the model by up to 1.66 on meshes of up to 5 km resolution; on GPUs, a C++/Kokkos version runs up to 1.27 times faster and needs 43% less memory. Whether reduced precision is safe for climate integrations is decided by long-term budgets, not by short tests.
