papers.title: Parametrizations of the solutions of Love equations and their momenta
papers.abstract: The Love equation is a paradigmatic example of a Fredholm integral equation of great interest in mathematics and physics, where its applications range from electrostatic problems to exactly solvable models for one-dimensional systems. In this work we propose a method to approximate the normalized solutions of Love equations of the first and second kind via a parametrization obtained by Hermite interpolation at Chebyshev nodes. Following the same approach, we also obtain approximations for the second, fourth and sixth momenta of the solution of the Love equations. We focus in particular on one-dimensional quantum gases described by the Lieb-Liniger and the Gaudin-Yang models. For these models, the solutions of Love equations correspond to the normalized densities of pseudorapidities. We show that remarkably accurate results can be obtained using the Hermite-Chebyshev interpolation with a number of points as low as 17+2. In the case of the Lieb-Liniger model, we also propose a very accurate closed-form estimate of the dimensionless ground state energy valid for all values of the dimensionless interaction parameter incorporating known results for small and large couplings supplemented by the Hermite-Chebyshev interpolation for intermediate couplings. As an application of this result, we compute the dimensionless local two-particle correlation function and the black soliton solutions of the Lieb-Liniger model.

papers.title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
papers.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

papers.title: Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents are widely used to develop critical production software. Even though coding agents are known to occasionally write vulnerable code, there has not been any investigation into how code base vulnerabilities evolve over time under coding agent contributions. In this work, we close this gap by investigating whether and how vulnerabilities in existing code lead coding agents to introduce similar vulnerabilities in the code they write. We first evaluate coding agents on 96 tasks that require implementing a new backend application in a repository where other applications already exist. Second, we investigate repository-level code generation on 20 pairs of tasks in real C/C++ projects. In each task, the agent is asked to complete code critical to memory safety. We find that in both settings, insecure existing code leads to agents writing vulnerable code more often. In backend generation, insecure neighbors reduce the share of correct and secure implementations by 3.4% on average, and in C/C++ repository-level coding, the average gap between secure and insecure contexts reaches 35.4%. Prompting to follow existing code-style or to be careful about security increases, respectively decreases, how strongly agents propagate vulnerabilities, but neither stops them. When asked to explain their implementation choices, coding agents attribute them to following another code site in 76.5% of cases, even though they recognize the introduced vulnerability in 69.9% of cases. These findings show that agents use existing vulnerabilities as templates for new ones indiscriminatorily, turning each contribution into an opportunity to introduce more vulnerabilities. As such, as agents write a growing share of production code under decreasing human review, code bases can increasingly degrade in security if security vulnerabilities are not thoroughly fixed continuously.
papers.intro:
Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have become an essential part of software development. These agents, such as Claude Code [2] and Codex [17], allow LLMs to interact with the coding environment through tools, enabling them to explore a repository, edit files, and build and test their changes. Developers increasingly delegate entire tasks to these agents and review the generated changes at a decreasing rate. In a 2026 survey of over 15,000 professional developers, 68% used LLM-based coding agents daily at work, with Claude Code being the most widely adopted [5]. AI-generated code is also entering production software. Google reports that 75% of its new code is agent-generated [22], and security-critical projects such as the Linux kernel have adopted formal policies for LLM-assisted contributions [27]. Meanwhile, reviewing the generated code becomes largely infeasible, as agents produce vast amounts of code [8]. Therefore, the security of agent-written code is rapidly gaining in importance for keeping our production software systems secure.

Although newer model generations produce fewer vulnerabilities, a non-negligible number remain [29, 24]. Prior work found that vulnerable code in the LLM’s context can influence the security of non-agentic code generation: adding a secure or vulnerable function to the prompt shifts the security of code completions [20, 10], and defective commented-out code affects zero-shot generation security [9].

Coding agents introduce massive context. One of the most powerful features of coding agents is their ability to automatically explore and navigate repositories: they load files from the repository and provide them as additional context to the underlying LLM. Repository-level code generation relies on this context to adapt to the repository’s coding style and produce correct and consistent implementations [37, 13, 11]. However, existing code can contain vulnerabilities, even in widely used and heavily scrutinized open-source projects [7, 1]. Thus, the powerful navigation feature of coding agents can become a double-edged sword and unintentionally exacerbate vulnerabilities: if coding agents follow vulnerable patterns instead of detecting and avoiding them, each vulnerability can become a template for new ones, degrading code base security with every new code contribution.

How does codebase security evolve under coding agent contributions? In this work, we are the first to investigate this threat empirically: whether modern coding agents propagate vulnerabilities from existing code into the code they generate. To this end, we answer the following five research questions through extensive empirical analysis: RQ1 Do coding agents propagate vulnerabilities from existing code into newly generated code? RQ2 Do coding agents adopt secure implementation patterns from existing code? RQ3 How do different common prompting strategies affect vulnerability propagation? RQ4 Do vulnerabilities that are inapplicable to the task affect the security of newly generated code? RQ5 Do agents recognize vulnerabilities in their generated code, and how do they explain the implementation choices that introduce them? The first evaluates adding a new backend application to a repository with existing neighboring applications, which provides a high degree of control over surrounding code. The second evaluates code generation in real C/C++ repositories at the sites of known memory-safety vulnerabilities, a highly realistic setup.

In the first evaluation, we construct 96 tasks in synthetic service repositories, adapted from AutoBaxBench [29]. The task is to implement a new backend application from a functionality description and an OpenAPI specification. The repository already contains completed neighboring applications. They are functionally independent of the target application and not needed for the task. We construct secure and insecure versions of each neighbor, and compare the security of the code agents generate for the exact same task when the repository contains different versions of the neighbors, or no neighbors at all.

The second evaluation examines whether agents propagate vulnerabilities in real codebases. We curate 20 pairs of repository-level code generation tasks from CyberGym [31] across five widely used C/C++ projects. In each pair, the two tasks are exactly the same code generation task, except that similar code elsewhere in the repository is more secure in one and less secure in the other. In both tasks, we mask a code region at the site of a known memory-safety vulnerability, and the agent implements the missing functionality from a short description. We compare how often the agent’s implementation reproduces the target vulnerability between the two tasks in each pair. For vulnerable implementations, we ask two follow-up questions: whether the implementation contains a vulnerability and why the agent chose that implementation. These questions probe whether agents can recognize the vulnerabilities they introduced and whether they attribute their implementation choices to consistency with existing code.

papers.title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
papers.abstract:
Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors.
  Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks.
  Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision.
  Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

papers.title: The cohomology of finite simple groups is unbounded
papers.abstract: In every fixed positive degree, we show that the cohomology of finite simple groups, algebraic groups and quantum groups, with coefficients in simple modules, can have arbitrarily large dimension. In particular, we disprove Guralnick's conjecture.

papers.title: Declarative DNS - Resolving Recursive Resolution
papers.abstract:
DNS zone configuration errors are a frequent source of outages and frustration, particularly in combination with DNSSEC. Research has attempted to address the problem of zone configuration errors using formal methods, but existing proposals (i) only verify the absence of specific, known configuration errors, and (ii) do not consider DNSSEC.
  We present a new formal model of the DNS that covers most of DNSSEC, making it one of the most complete DNS models to date. In addition, we present a new tool, DecDNS, that performs a resolvability change-impact analysis of zone configuration updates using our model. We show that such a change-impact analysis can identify configuration errors without explicitly searching for them.
  We evaluate DecDNS both formally and empirically. We prove that DecDNS is sound and complete and show that its results agree with widely used DNS software. Finally, we explain how our approach can be integrated into operational practice, helping guide zone management in the real world.

The Domain Name System (DNS) is a fundamental Internet technology. So fundamental that the unavailability of the DNS can be practically indistinguishable from the unavailability of the Internet. For example, some governments censor the Internet solely by filtering the DNS [28, 27, 10, 8]. Although “censored” services are technically still reachable, many clients and users cannot reach them anymore.

For example, some governments censor the Internet solely by filtering the DNS [28, 27, 10, 8]. Although “censored” services are technically still reachable, many clients and users cannot reach them anymore.

At first glance, the DNS appears simple. Data is associated with names such as example.com. All names form a tree, and sets of connected nodes form so-called zones. Different zones are served by different name servers, and recursive resolvers query name servers to obtain the data associated with names. Underlying this simple concept, however, is considerable complexity. The DNS’s two original standards were published in 1987 and, since then, it has been extended numerous times. As of fall 2026, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), which maintains the DNS, has published 298 documents, called Requests for Comments (RFCs), on the DNS [22].

If such a characterization were given, one could detect configuration errors by computing all queries that have a positive response. Any difference to the set of queries that should have a positive response would point to a configuration error.

Such a characterization, though, is hard to obtain. Having the user state all queries that should be resolvable is infeasible and likely a task just as error-prone as configuring the zone itself. We therefore use the old configuration as a baseline and perform a resolvability change-impact analysis on a zone configuration update. Given two zone configurations, new and old, a change-impact analysis computes which queries have a positive response in exactly one of the two configurations. Users can then inspect the result of this analysis, compare it with their expectations, and consequently identify configuration errors.

Given a zone configuration, DecDNS compiles it to a constraint logic program (CLP). This declarative specification captures which queries have a positive response in that zone configuration. We abstract from details of the underlying transport mechanisms, e.g., packet sizes and headers, and instead model what a recursive resolver would conclude in response to arbitrary queries if it were given the input zone configuration. We capture, though, that recursive resolvers must first discover name servers and obtain their network addresses before they can send them queries. Given two such CLPs, one corresponding to an old zone configuration and the other to a new version of the configuration, DecDNS computes a change-impact analysis.

papers.title: SpinSCI: Mask-Conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer for Video Snapshot Compressive Imaging
papers.abstract: Video snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) recovers multiple frames from one spatiotemporally coded measurement. This paper proposes SpinSCI, a mask-conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer whose Mask-Conditioned Ising Refinement Block (MC-IRB) combines attention logits and sensing information to form signed spin couplings. Finite mean-field updates gate residual feature refinement. Physics-guided initialization and final data consistency incorporate the measurement model. Compared with HiSViT$_9$, SpinSCI achieves average PSNR gains of 0.51 dB, 0.23 dB, and 0.04 dB on small-scale gray, mid-scale color, and large-scale color benchmarks, respectively, with 16.9% fewer parameters, 21.0-21.6% fewer FLOPs, 17.1-49.9% lower latency, and 62.3-63.3% lower peak memory. Relative to DU-9stg, average PSNR differs by at most 0.13 dB across these benchmarks, with 28.2-28.7% fewer FLOPs, 64.6-71.7% lower inference latency, and 30.1-35.0% lower peak memory. Qualitative comparisons on the real benchmark further show recovery of fine details and textures. Code and reference checkpoints are available at https://github.com/skethz/SpinSCI.

papers.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

papers.title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
papers.abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

Models can also fail to use relevant evidence reliably even when it is present in the context (Liu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024b). Parametric learning offers a complementary approach by distilling new knowledge into the model’s weights, where it remains available without repeatedly retrieving and processing the source material at inference time.

Existing self-distillation methods differ in how they generate training rollouts, creating a tradeoff between distribution match and learning signal. We make this tradeoff explicit with the supervision signal: the per-token forward Kullback–Leibler divergence between the teacher’s and student’s next-token distributions along a rollout (Kullback & Leibler, 1951). On-policy rollouts match the student’s test-time distribution, but are signal-starved: after the student commits to an early prefix, the teacher is conditioned on that prefix and can only provide a coherent continuation. Off-policy rollouts preserve stronger signal by using teacher-generated prefixes, but train the student on trajectories it will not produce at test time. Both choices therefore allocate supervision inefficiently. On-policy training spends it on positions where the teacher has little to add, whereas off-policy training spends it on states the student will not visit. This raises our central question: can we preserve the signal of off-policy rollouts while staying close to the student’s distribution?

papers.title: Architectural Textured Proxy Generation
papers.abstract: Textured proxy models are a fundamental representation for architectural scenes, enabling efficient rendering while preserving visual fidelity. Existing approaches construct such proxies through a sequential pipeline in which geometry is first abstracted from a dense reconstruction and textures are later projected from input images. This geometry-only formulation neglects image evidence during proxy generation, leading to misalignment of structural features such as facades, edges, and their intersections across views. As a result, inconsistencies are deferred to a downstream correction stage during texturing, where the underlying geometric structure can no longer be reliably recovered. In this work, we introduce an image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. By incorporating image derived structural cues directly into the construction process, the proxy is optimized to align with observed features across views from the outset, rather than relying on post hoc correction that may be infeasible. This shift from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are inherently consistent with the input imagery, enabling more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping. We realize this formulation through a framework that extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry, and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization. The resulting proxies exhibit improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift, and cross view inconsistencies. Experiments on diverse architectural scenes demonstrate that our approach produces compact, geometry texture aligned proxies with substantially improved visual fidelity compared to existing methods.

High-quality 3D reconstruction from images has become widely accessible, producing dense geometric models with detailed appearance (Sinha et al., 2008; Musialski et al., 2013). However, such models remain impractical for downstream applications due to their complexity. Proxy representations address this limitation by abstracting geometry into compact, structured models that enable efficient rendering and manipulation. However, such models remain impractical for downstream applications due to their complexity. Proxy representations address this limitation by abstracting geometry into compact, structured models that enable efficient rendering and manipulation. In architectural scenes, proxies are typically composed of piecewise planar elements, capturing the dominant structure of buildings while serving as the support for texture mapping (Garland and Heckbert, 1997; Salinas et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024).

Despite their utility, existing pipelines suffer from a fundamental limitation: geometry abstraction and texturing are treated as separate stages. A proxy is first constructed from a dense model, and textures are later projected from the input images (Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a). This sequential design leads to inconsistencies in what we term structural features—planar facades, edges, and their intersections that define the geometry of buildings. These features should coincide across the proxy and all input views, yet in practice they drift. Errors from camera estimation, geometric abstraction, and projection accumulate, causing edges to misalign, planar regions to fragment, and textures from different views to disagree (Fig. 2). As a result, texturing becomes a corrective step that attempts to compensate for misaligned geometry, often with limited success (Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a). Prior approaches either optimize textures without modifying geometry, rely on manual adjustments (Sinha et al., 2008), or employ learning-based generation that may deviate from the observed scene (Chen et al., 2025).

Rather than constructing a proxy and then fitting textures, we build the proxy so that structural features are already aligned across views, prior to texturing. papers.title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
papers.abstract: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting--e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline ($n_{\texttt{annotations}} = 2{,}957$, $n_{\texttt{humans}} = 996$). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes commercial settings [10, 13, 69]. To unlock their economic value, LLMs must not only competently follow user instructions and effectively complete tasks, but also comply with applicable law [54, 40]. Legal compliance facilitates integration of LLMs into businesses; reduces the legal exposure of developers, deployers, and users; and implements goals articulated in model character and safety documents such as OpenAI’s Model Spec and Anthropic’s Constitution [53, 11]. Some authors also argue that legal compliance by LLMs could reduce safety risks that LLMs pose to society [54, 40, 41]. To date, however, researchers have dedicated relatively little attention to empirically studying whether LLM agents comply with the law in practice [45, 62].

A particularly important area of legal compliance concerns fraud, which is estimated to cost the global economy over US$500 billion annually [74]. In most U.S. jurisdictions, an actor commits fraud when she intentionally misrepresents or conceals information important to a commercial transaction, inducing another actor’s reliance and causing economic harm (see [3]). Policymakers have expressed concern about fraud risks from LLMs [76, 20], and AI systems are already being used in real-world fraud schemes involving millions of dollars [46].

Currently, no LLM evaluation explicitly measures compliance with the detailed legal doctrine of fraud, despite numerous studies that extend LLM benchmarking to more realistic, economically valuable settings (e.g., [55, 71, 12]). Existing legal evaluations have largely studied LLMs’ legal reasoning abilities (e.g., [25, 43, 28, 21]) rather than the degree to which LLM actions comply with the law. Studying how LLMs behave in real-world settings, and comparing their behavior to accepted legal standards, complements preexisting evaluations of LLM deception in the alignment and safety literature. Unlike newly created benchmarks of LLM deception, the legal doctrine of fraud is already broadly applicable and has been refined through centuries of case law, though its detailed application in the context of AI models acting autonomously remains legally untested as of November 2026.

papers.title: Environmental Assessment of GaN Current-Source and Voltage-Source AC-AC Variable Speed Drives
papers.abstract: Three-phase ac-ac converters for variable-speed drives can be realized conventionally as voltage-source converters (VSCs) or, leveraging emerging monolithic bidirectional GaN power transistors (M-BDSs), as current-source converters (CSCs). This paper presents a comparative life-cycle assessment of a realized VSC and a CSC demonstrators including grid-side and motor-side EMI filters, and with identical specifications (1.4 kW rated power, 200 V line-to-line rms grid and motor voltage). The embodied carbon footprints are similar (44.8 kgCO2eq for the VSC and 47.4 kgCO2eq for the CSC) and dominated by auxiliary and control electronics, and the printed circuit boards. Over 10 years of continuous operation under the NEMA Power Index mission profile for variable-load centrifugal systems (pumps, fans), the CSC's higher part-load efficiency translates into a clearly lower life-cycle carbon footprint of around 900 kgCO2eq compared to the VSC's 1130 kgCO2eq when operating with a carbon-intense electricity mix (440 gCO2eq/kWh). However, this difference almost vanishes when considering a future renewable electricity mix (25 gCO2eq/kWh).

papers.intro:
Electric motor-driven systems account for nearly half of global electricity use [1], and in manufacturing industries that share can reach about 80% [2]. In such industrial environments, variable-load machines such as pumps, fans, and compressors account for a large part of that demand, and many are still driven by grid-fed motors running at a fixed speed, with valves or dampers setting the mechanical output, thus wasting significant amounts of energy [2]. In such variable-load centrifugal systems, the torque typically rises with the square of speed, thus the motor speed is a direct lever for reducing the power consumption. A variable-speed drive (VSD) placed between the grid and the machine can adjust the motor speed, and thus the power output of the motor, to the demand, and the energy use falls sharply.

In such industrial environments, variable-load machines such as pumps, fans, and compressors account for a large part of that demand, and many are still driven by grid-fed motors running at a fixed speed, with valves or dampers setting the mechanical output, thus wasting significant amounts of energy [2]. A variable-speed drive (VSD) placed between the grid and the machine can adjust the motor speed, and thus the power output of the motor, to the demand, and the energy use falls sharply.

The typical realization of a grid-connected VSD is a two-level voltage-source converter (VSC), i.e., a back-to-back connection of a three-phase voltage-source rectifier and a three-phase inverter sharing a common dc-link capacitor. Modern voltage-source converters (VSCs) increasingly employ wide-bandgap semiconductors such as GaN power transistors, which enable higher switching frequencies and, consequently, smaller passive components. However, the resulting fast voltage transitions (high d​v/d​tdv/dt) at the inverter output can increase motor bearing currents, cause reflections on the motor cables and accelerate motor insulation ageing, and may require shielded motor cables to avoid EMI issues [3]. To mitigate these effects, motor-side and grid-side EMI filters are typically employed as shown in Fig. 1a. An alternative topology for a grid-connected VSD is the current-source converter (CSC), which consists of a three-phase current-source rectifier and a three-phase current-source inverter sharing a common dc-link inductor, see Fig. 1b. Unlike a VSC, the switching stage of the CSC provides a switched current at its phase terminals, i.e., requires ac-side capacitors that absorb the switched current and thereby inherently ensure smooth output voltages. Nevertheless, grid-side and motor-side EMI filters are still required to meet specific emission limits.

Again, unlike a VSC, the voltage across a switch of a CSC is not a dc voltage but defined by the ac line-to-line voltage and, hence, can have either polarity. Consequently, each switch must be capable of blocking both positive and negative voltages. Traditionally, this capability was achieved by connecting two unipolar transistors in anti-series, doubling the on-state resistance compared to a single transistor. Achieving the same total on-state resistance thus requires paralleling of a second anti-series connection of two transistors, i.e., a four-times higher chip area overall.

papers.title: Mitigating the BICM Loss in MIMO Receivers with Correlation-Informed Logits
papers.abstract: Bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) is widely used in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless systems. However, separating MIMO data detection from channel decoding and only exchanging per-bit soft information discards correlation information among the bits within each transmit vector. We show that the resulting information loss limits the performance of practical one-shot receivers. Even though iterative detection and decoding (IDD) can recover most of this loss, IDD significantly increases receiver complexity and latency. In order to reduce this loss, we propose COrrelation-Informed Logits (COIL), a soft-output format that combines per-bit soft information with pairwise coupling logits for correlated bits. We show how to incorporate these coupling logits into a conventional belief-propagation-based channel decoder, which enables correlation-aware decoding in a one-shot receiver without IDD. We evaluate COIL in a MIMO-BICM system with a conventional low-density parity-check code. For a 4x4 MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system, a one-shot linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) receiver with COIL outperforms a conventional one-shot unbiased LMMSE receiver by 1.3dB and operates within 0.8dB of four-iteration IDD, while requiring only a single pass through the data detector.
papers.intro:
Bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) [1, 2, 3] is the de facto standard in modern multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless systems as it achieves excellent error-rate performance at manageable complexity [2, 4, 5]. The basic idea is as follows: The transmitter encodes information bits with a modern forward error-correction code, such as a low-density parity-check (LDPC) code [6, 7, 8], and spreads the resulting coded bits (typically after interleaving) over space, frequency, and/or time. The receiver then operates in two stages. First, a soft-output MIMO data detector produces per-coded-bit reliability information, commonly called soft outputs. Second, a soft-input channel decoder uses this soft information to compute estimates of the transmitted information bits.

Second, a soft-input channel decoder uses this soft information to compute estimates of the transmitted information bits.

In order to reduce complexity and latency, most MIMO-BICM receivers (i) are one-shot (see Fig. 1(a)), i.e., they run the data detector and the channel decoder only once, and (ii) use equalization-based data detectors, which first estimate the transmitted symbols and then compute per-coded-bit soft information [9, 5]. In many situations, more sophisticated soft-output data detectors and/or iterative detection and decoding (IDD) can significantly improve the error-rate performance of MIMO-BICM systems [4, 10, 11, 12] (see the dashed feedback path in Fig. 1(a)). IDD iterates between a soft-input soft-output MIMO data detector and a soft-input soft-output channel decoder. These (outer) iterations increase complexity and latency, complicate scheduling of the two stages, and make efficient hardware implementation difficult [13].

A key component of MIMO-BICM is the interface between the two stages through which the data detector passes per-coded-bit soft information to the channel decoder. This interface enables us to develop, optimize, and implement both stages separately, which is essential for efficient hardware implementations [14, 15, 16, 17, 11]. However, such a per-bit interface throws away crucial information contained in the received signals.

We propose a one-shot MIMO-BICM receiver architecture that recovers a large part of the BICM loss using COrrelation-Informed Logits (COIL); see Fig. 1(b). We start with a fundamental question: where exactly does a one-shot MIMO-BICM receiver lose performance? We answer this question by analyzing the detector–decoder interface using a vector-level generalized mutual information (GMI) measure that gives an achievable rate for the Gaussian metric produced by an equalization-based MIMO data detector. Our analysis reveals that the rate loss is caused primarily by the interface between the data detector and the channel decoder, rather than by the detector’s suboptimality: per-bit soft outputs discard crucial correlation among the bits mapped to the same transmit vector. This insight motivates COIL, a soft-output format in which an equalization-based MIMO data detector not only reports per-coded-bit soft outputs but also pairwise coupling logits that convey correlation information. We first analyze how much correlation information COIL provides. We then show that message-passing-based channel decoders can process COIL soft outputs by statically augmenting their factor graph with one additional degree-three check node per coupled bit pair—the decoding algorithm is left unchanged. With COIL, all iterations remain within the channel decoder, and no outer iterations over the MIMO data detector are required, which reduces complexity and latency. As a proof of concept, we simulate a MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system with a conventional LDPC code. Our results demonstrate that a one-shot linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE)-based receiver that outputs COIL outperforms conventional one-shot receivers and approaches IDD receivers at a fraction of their complexity and latency. Since COIL changes only the receiver, it can be deployed in any system that builds upon MIMO-BICM without any modifications to the communication standard.

Zehavi proposed the architecture now known as BICM in [1]. Caire, Taricco, and Biglieri subsequently established its information-theoretic foundations and showed that the per-bit metric interface loses rate relative to coded modulation [2]. Reference [3] later reinterpreted the bit-metric interface as mismatched decoding, for which the GMI [18, 19] is the standard achievable-rate measure; references [20, 21] discuss BICM and mismatched decoding in detail. In contrast, we ask how much information is contained in a MIMO data detector’s output before it is reduced to per-bit metrics. Furthermore, we show that the BICM loss corresponds to the conditional total correlation [22] of the coded bits within one transmit vector, given the receive vector. COIL recovers the part of this total correlation that can be captured by a maximum-weight spanning tree. The spanning tree’s vertices (or nodes) correspond to the coded bits of one transmit vector, and each edge is associated with one coupling logit that characterizes the dependence between the connected bit pair.

COIL is not the only approach to improve upon the per-bit interface of BICM. For example, non-binary LDPC codes over higher-order Galois fields [23] enable the decoder to consider dependence among groups of bits, and such codes are known to improve performance [23]. However, non-binary LDPC codes fix the grouping at code-design time and require specialized decoder algorithms, which are difficult to implement in hardware, as discussed in, e.g., [24, 25]. In contrast, COIL retains the binary code and the decoding algorithm, and lets the data detector select the coupled bit pairs for each transmit vector from the received signal. Thus, COIL is compatible with the binary LDPC codes of modern wireless standards, whereas non-binary codes are not.

papers.title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
papers.abstract: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.

papers.title: Optimizing the Steady-State Travel Time of Nash Flows over Time with Capacity Increases
papers.abstract: We study budgeted capacity augmentation for single-source single-sink \NFOTs under constant inflow $u_0$. The goal is to increase capacities on arcs subject to a global budget constraint in order to minimize the steady-state travel time in the network. We show that this problem is weakly NP-hard on series-parallel networks and provide an exact pseudopolynomial algorithm as well as a fully polynomial algorithm that attains the optimum travel time for budget $B$ while spending at most $B + \varepsilon\cdot\max\{B,u_0\}$. On general networks the problem becomes strongly NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\text{P} = \text{NP}$, for every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve the optimal steady-state travel time while exceeding the budget by at most a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$. Lastly, we give structural properties about steady-state travel time under varying arc capacities. We identify capacity thresholds determined by subsets of $s$-$t$-cuts and show that the travel time is constant in the interior of the cells resulting from the corresponding hyperplane arrangement.
papers.intro:
Congestion is a common feature of many real-world network problems, inherent in traffic and communication networks. Here, selfish users choose a path to traverse a network depending on link lengths and congestion induced by other users. This phenomenon can be modeled with a game theoretic variant of flows over time, in which infinitesimally small selfish agents traverse a network according to specified free flow arc traversal times as well as arc capacities. If the capacities in the network are exceeded, queues start to build up, adding to users’ travel time. Assuming omniscient users, this leads to the notion of a Nash flow over time, a strategy profile in which all users are traveling on shortest paths. Crucial structural results on Nash flows over time by Koch and Skutella [koch2011nash] (see also [koch2012routing]) have led to many properties of Nash flows over time being established for single-source single-sink networks. Key among those are existence [cominetti2015dynamic], uniqueness of equilibrium travel times [cominetti2015dynamic, olver2022continuity], continuity [olver2022continuity], a bound on the price of anarchy in special cases [correa2019price], and long-term behavior [cominetti2022long, olver2022continuity]: following transient phases, a Nash flow over time settles into a so-called steady state in finite time. In the steady state, queues grow at a constant rate or remain constant [cominetti2022long, olver2022continuity]. A comprehensive overview of Nash flows

One key property of Nash flows over time is that the steady-state travel time depends non-trivially on the network congestion building up during the transient phases, which in turn depends on the arc capacities. It is therefore natural to ask how the steady-state travel time can be optimized via capacity modifications. We consider the problem of distributing a budget for capacity increases among arcs to optimize the steady-state travel time, referred to as the Steady State Capacity Augmentation for Nash Flows over Time (SSCA). Previous work on long-term behavior of Nash flows over time has split into two settings, based on the relation between network inflow rate u0u_{0} and minimum-cut capacity νC\nu_{C}. If u0>νCu_{0}>\nu_{C}, the network cannot support the entire flow and the steady-state travel time grows linearly [olver2022continuity]. However, minimizing its growth rate reduces to maximizing νC\nu_{C} with the budget constraint, a problem solvable in polynomial time. The more interesting regime occurs when νC\nu_{C} surpasses u0u_{0}. Here, the steady-state travel time remains constant over time: we denote it by Δ\Delta. Cominetti, Correa and Olver [cominetti2022long] showed that Δ\Delta can be computed as the solution to a minimum cost flow linear program, if the value of the sink potential dtd_{t} is unique among all optimal dual solutions. Despite this simple description in terms of an LP, optimizing Δ\Delta turns out to be hard, even on simple series-parallel networks. A key difficulty is that we optimize a single one of the variables appearing in the dual objective by changing the objective coefficients. However, the characterization via linear programming opens up a geometric perspective on the problem, providing structural insights into the behavior of Δ\Delta within the capacity space. In particular, Δ\Delta remains constant within regions defined by the network topology, so any change in Δ\Delta requires crossing some network-dependent capacity threshold. Thus, SSCA has a fundamentally discontinuous nature.

papers.title: Harmonic origin of local symmetry breaking in PbTe revealed using machine-learned potentials
papers.abstract: We use machine-learned interatomic potentials combined with higher-order interatomic force constant models to show that finite-range polar correlations in PbTe are driven by long-range harmonic interactions rather than lattice anharmonicity. Our molecular dynamics simulations reveal a spatial polar correlation range exceeding 50 {\AA} at low temperatures and decreasing with increasing temperature. Selective interatomic force constant mapping demonstrates that crystal anharmonicity usually associated with the formation of polar nanoregions suppresses polar correlations. Instead, long-range harmonic interactions extending to 13 {\AA} are necessary to reproduce the spatial coherence of local dipoles. In reciprocal space, these extended harmonic interactions correspond to high curvature of the transverse optical (TO) phonon branch at the $\Gamma$ point. Comparison with isostructural NaCl connects these extended interactions to local underscreening of predominantly Coulombic forces. Our results provide a key microscopic description of finite-range polar correlations and a framework for understanding local symmetry breaking in centrosymmetric materials.

papers.intro:
The presence of an inversion center (centrosymmetry) in a crystal strictly prohibits macroscopic properties such as pyroelectricity, chirality, piezoelectricity, and even-order nonlinear optical responses [23]. Ferroelectricity is a prominent manifestation of macroscopic inversion symmetry breaking, characterized by a switchable spontaneous polarization usually emerging below a distinctive transition temperature. However, local structural fluctuations can break inversion symmetry over finite spatiotemporal scales even while the crystal preserves its average high-symmetry phase. Local symmetry breaking can produce optical, electronic, and electromechanical responses that are not apparent from the average crystal structure alone [34, 37, 42].

Distortions associated with such spontaneous local symmetry breaking often occur in ferroelectrics above their ferroelectric transition temperature, and are associated with the soft (low frequency) transverse-optical (TO) phonons. They lead to phenomena such as polar nano- and mesodomains [66, 17], polarization density waves [44], order–disorder ferroelectric transitions [6], and emphanisis [9, 30] and are known to be strongly correlated with crystal anharmonicity, including phonon–phonon, strain–phonon, and flexoelectric coupling [38, 52, 22, 44].

PbTe is an example that maintains a high-symmetry cubic phase at all temperatures, lacking a conventional phase transition to a macroscopically polar state; extrapolation of the softening TO phonon frequency would suggest a ferroelectric phase transition at negative temperature. Nevertheless, real-space pair distribution function (PDF) analyses reveal anomalous, non-Gaussian broadening of the peaks, alongside a continuous increase in the asymmetry of nearest-neighbor Pb-Te pair correlations upon heating [9]. Extending this local structural model to three dimensions, single-crystal diffuse scattering and three-dimensional difference pair distribution function mapping have demonstrated an unusual, step-like decay of displacive pair correlations along the ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle crystallographic directions [53].

These observations challenge a purely phonon–phonon scattering-based interpretation and suggest that additional microscopic mechanisms may contribute to the emergence of correlated local polar distortions.

In this work, we aim to reconcile these conflicting observations by identifying the microscopic origin of correlated local dipoles and establishing materials-design principles governing their emergence. We begin with the development of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on density functional theory (DFT) data [54, 19], which enable molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at unprecedented length and time scales providing access to local structural correlations with high resolution. MD simulations based on MLIPs offer limited physical insight into the underlying interactions, so we construct an interatomic force constant (IFC) model that reproduces the MD behavior of the MLIP and provides a physically interpretable description of the underlying interatomic interactions. This combination of large-scale MLIP simulations and an interpretable force-constant framework allows us to directly connect the observed local structural correlations to their microscopic origin and identify the key factors governing the emergence of correlated local dipoles.

papers.title: Surrendering and Reclaiming Judgment: How Software Engineering Students Experience AI Reliance
papers.abstract: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. We report on an exploratory case study of 43 senior software engineering students who used AI throughout a semester-long, team-based software architecture project. We combined surveys with focus groups and analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. We constructed two themes. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

One of the most important skills is software architecture, or the ability to design software architectures (Hasselbring, 2018). Mastering architecture is particularly difficult for novices, because its open-ended and complex nature makes it hard to learn (Galster and Angelov, 2016). The widespread adoption of generative AI in software engineering11 1 https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025 might disrupt how novices master software architecture, as AI can reason about software architecture (Guerra and Ernst, 2025) and even suggest entire architectures (Esposito et al., 2026). These capabilities make AI very useful for experienced developers and may increase their productivity (Schmid et al., 2025; Ullrich et al., 2025). However, how these benefits extend to novices is less clear, because a developer’s experience affects how they use AI for development (Jaman et al., 2026), and the capabilities that enable experienced developers to use AI for architecture might not serve novices in the same way. In fact, it might be attractive for novices who have not yet mastered architecture to offload the demanding parts of architectural work to AI (Choudhuri et al., 2026).

We combined three surveys with four focus groups, and we analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2022).

In this paper, we report on the two themes we constructed through reflexive thematic analysis. Both are about what it was like for students to work with AI, and both center on participants’ judgment over what AI produced. Our first theme, Surrendering Judgment to AI, is constructed around participants’ accounts of an extensive reliance on AI, of surrendering their judgment, first over architectural decisions and then over code they could no longer evaluate, and of the emotional toll that followed: they felt ashamed that they had to rely on AI, frustrated when incorrect information from AI left them stuck, and increasingly disconnected from their work as their reliance deepened. In participants’ accounts, three conditions pushed them toward surrender: an unfamiliar technology stack, delivery pressure outside their control, and an expectation that they use AI. None of these is unique to a course project, as junior developers entering industry experience all three (Zhao and Tsuboi, 2024; Begel and Simon, 2008; Miller et al., 2025). We believe, these conditions can contribute to a sustained reliance on AI that erodes the motivation to learn, and without that motivation there is little reason to break the reliance. Our second theme, applying human judgment, suggests this outcome is not inevitable: participants told us how relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI helped some of them reclaim their judgment. These changes hint at interventions that can help developers and organizations adopt AI sustainably, in ways that preserve novice developers’ judgment, ownership, and motivation.

papers.title: Neutronic Field-Effect Transistor
papers.abstract: Field-effect electronic devices are in widespread use in communication, computing, data storage, and sensing applications. We demonstrate a neutronic field-effect transistor (NFET) that is analogous to the Datta-Das electron spin transistor and atomtronic devices. The NFET is based on a perfect-crystal Mach-Zehnder neutron interferometer with phase shifts applied to the spin and path degrees of freedom.

Neutron interferometry is a powerful tool for investigating fundamental quantum physics and precision measurement [1]. It also provides a platform for testing quantum computing concepts in a controlled, low-noise environment [2], as well as performing weak measurements of neutron spin and path degrees of freedom [3, 4, 5].

It also provides a platform for testing quantum computing concepts in a controlled, low-noise environment [2], as well as performing weak measurements of neutron spin and path degrees of freedom [3, 4, 5].

Here we view neutron interferometry from a spintronic perspective. We demonstrate a neutronic spin transistor that uses the same principle as the electron spin transistor proposed by Datta and Das [6, 7], that was subsequently realized by Koo, et al. [8]. Beyond simple switching applications, our device can also support universal quantum gate sets on the two-qubit neutron spin-path system.

papers.title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography
papers.abstract: Medical images encode intrinsic tissue properties that indicate disease progression, yet these properties remain entangled with the system-dependent physics of image formation. Differentiable inverse rendering asks whether they are recoverable by inverting the imaging system's forward physics rather than through post-hoc correction. We address this in optical coherence tomography (OCT), focusing on the optical attenuation coefficient, a per-pixel marker of pathology and cellular composition. Conventional recovery relies on closed-form inversions limited to simplified light-tissue models, or learned methods coupled to specific imaging configurations. We instead recover per-pixel attenuation from a single OCT image by gradient descent through a differentiable physics-based forward model. We verified the method against analytical solutions, validated it on five in vitro phantoms, and applied it without modification to 29{,}269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients. The inversion needs no training data or segmentations and is portable across platforms and retrospective archives. Replacing the forward model or recovering another optical parameter leaves the optimization procedure unchanged. We demonstrate per-pixel recovery is tractable because gradient information scales to this high-dimensional problem, where gradient-free methods become intractable. Our work supports quantitative tissue characterization from OCT images and provides a framework for extension across imaging modalities and organ systems.

papers.intro:
The interrogation of biological matter through diverse forms of energy constitutes the foundation of modern medical diagnostic practice. Whether utilizing magnetic gradients in magnetic resonance imaging Berger (2002), high-frequency sound waves in ultrasound Harvey et al. (2002), ionizing radiation in computed tomography Buzug (2011), or backscattered light in optical coherence tomography (OCT) Drexler and Fujimoto (2008), modern imaging modalities share a common operative principle. They apply energy to tissue and infer anatomy from how the energy is differentially reflected, scattered, or absorbed by the underlying material Shung et al. (2012). Historically, the advancement of these technologies has focused on hardware innovations to improve spatial resolution and contrast, providing clinicians with high-fidelity anatomical visualizations of organ systems and diseased tissue Webb (2022); Oppelt (2006). However, while these anatomical maps are essential, they are not direct measurements of tissue composition: each image is a projection of the underlying intrinsic properties through the physics of the imaging system, entangling composition with modality-specific acquisition artifacts. In clinical applications, intrinsic properties such as stiffness, conductivity, and pH dictate disease progression and physiological stability Levental et al. (2009); Webb et al. (2011); Gabriel et al. (1996), yet remain inaccessible from the projected image alone. This paper inverts that projection. Although the imaging chain is a complex, modality-specific forward operator whose inverse is ill-posed, we demonstrate intrinsic tissue composition can be recovered directly from clinical imaging through differentiable inverse rendering, with OCT as our case study.

Existing approaches to OCT attenuation recovery fall into three categories Chang and Bowden (2019). Curve-fitting (CF) methods extract a single attenuation coefficient by fitting signal decay over a manually segmented region van der Meer et al. (2005), which is robust for uniform tissues but unable to capture intra-tissue heterogeneity. Depth-resolved (DR) methods compute per-pixel attenuation from the ratio of local intensity to remaining energy Vermeer et al. (2013); Liu et al. (2017), but the closed-form formulation constrains them to single-scattering assumptions and makes the resulting maps sensitive to noise sources like speckle and local signal artifacts. Recent work in this area addresses the noise sensitivity issue using despeckling to improve local region homogeneity Cannon et al. (2021). (2026), but the learned amortized inverse is fixed after training and coupled to the simulated distribution. (2023), and optimization also estimates these parameters via an implicit neural representation of optical properties through an OCT imaging model using multi-angle measurements Li et al. (2025). Our method instead optimizes any differentiable forward model by gradient descent from a single B-scan.

papers.title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
papers.abstract: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.

papers.intro:
Text-to-image models increasingly support visual creation across a broad range of users, including design and non-design professionals who create visual assets as part of their work. Yet the dominant interaction remains an opaque prompt-and-output loop: users describe an image, inspect a rendered result, and revise the prompt or describe an edit when the output diverges from their intent (He et al., 2025b; Liu and Chilton, 2022). Other interfaces have explored node-based workflows and direct manipulation to provide more structured control, but often requires users to construct technical workflows or focus on particular visual dimensions (ComfyAnonymous and Contributors, 2023; Shi et al., 2025b; Mou et al., 2024). The model also often implicitly makes consequential creative decisions on the user’s behalf, often before the those decisions have been consciously specified by the user (Simone et al., 2026; Wadinambiarachchi et al., 2024).

The model also often implicitly makes consequential creative decisions on the user’s behalf, often before the those decisions have been consciously specified by the user (Simone et al., 2026; Wadinambiarachchi et al., 2024).

This prompt based workflow treats creative intent as something that can be fully specified and communicated in text upfront. Visual design and creation, however, develops through progressive exploration of interdependent decisions such as subject, color palette, composition, and style (Shi et al., 2025a). Prompt-based generation compresses this emergent process into a single upfront specification. For creative tools, this means supporting asset production without necessarily supporting the process of developing the intent behind it.

Nuanced visual intentions must be translated into language, often requiring users to find the right textual description for a concept, while the model’s interpretation remains largely hidden. Users see the resulting image, but have limited visibility into how individual aspects of their request were interpreted. Without persistent representation of these intermediate decisions, users have limited support for inspecting, revisiting, or expressing them as their intent evolves, or for changing one aspect while preserving others.

papers.title: The Cool Circumgalactic Echo of the Stellar-to-Halo Mass Relatio
papers.abstract: The stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR), a key prediction of galaxy formation models, peaks at $M_* \sim 3 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$. This scale is often attributed to circumgalactic baryonic feedback processes, however, direct observational evidence linking the two remains scarce. Using Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) galaxy--quasar pairs, we map the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) using Mg II $\lambda\lambda2796, 2803$ absorption with stacking technique across nearly three decades in stellar mass. The radial Mg II absorption equivalent-width profile, $W_{\rm MgII} \propto D^k$, becomes progressively shallower with increasing stellar mass, following $k = 0.70\log(M_*/M_\odot)-9.12$. Crucially, we find that the $W_{\rm MgII}$ in the CGM scales tightly with the SHMR. The $W_{\rm MgII}$ peaks at the same characteristic mass as the SHMR, coinciding with a transition of the cool CGM from super-virial to sub-virial kinematics. Low-mass halos show excess non-gravitational motions consistent with recycled accretion and feedback-driven circulation, whereas massive halos show halo-centric heating that may maintain star formation quenching. This study bridges the gap between cool CGM and SHMR, showing that peak star formation efficiency coincides with the most abundant cool CGM reservoirs.

The stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) provides a compact empirical description of how galaxies assemble their stellar mass within dark matter halos [82, 51, 81, 75].

The baryon-conversion efficiency, ϵ∗=M∗/(fb​Mhalo)\epsilon_{*}=M_{*}/(f_{\rm b}M_{\rm halo}), where fb=Ωb/Ωmf_{\rm b}=\Omega_{\rm b}/\Omega_{\rm m} is the cosmic baryon fraction, reaches a maximum of order 20%20\% near Mhalo∼1012​M⊙M_{\rm halo}\sim 10^{12}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}} (M∗∼3×1010​M⊙M_{*}\sim 3\times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}) and declines toward both lower and higher masses [66, 37, 3, 86, 85]. The low-mass decline has motivated explanations involving baryon loss and inefficient gas-to-star conversion driven in part by stellar feedback [32, 11, 73, 84], whereas the high-mass decline is commonly linked to the emergence of stable hot halos, virial shocks, and energetic feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) [65, 77, 21, 7, 20]. These mechanisms need not map uniquely onto the observed SHMR, but together they highlight that the efficiency peak marks a change in the balance among gas supply, recycling, heating, and removal [75, 46]. The SHMR therefore provides a well-defined empirical characteristic scale against which changes in the baryonic components of galaxy halos can be tested, rather than a priori specifying how those components should behave.

Previous statistical absorption and cross-correlation studies have established that Mg ii strength declines with projected distance and depends on galaxy properties including stellar mass and star-formation activity [14, 13, 15, 89, 33, 38, 34, 18]. Most of these measurements, however, have focused on the mean radial decline, covering fraction, or absorption strength at fixed radius [59, 19]. How the shape of the radial profile itself changes continuously across stellar mass remains less well constrained. This distinction is important: a mass dependence in the radial slope would indicate that the spatial organization of the cool CGM changes along the galaxy mass sequence, rather than merely reflecting a change in overall absorption amplitude. Establishing whether these observables vary coherently provides a direct empirical test of whether the CGM exhibits a characteristic transition comparable to the one marked by the SHMR.

papers.title: First demonstration of long-distance electron drift in liquid xenon with the Xenoscope time projection chamber
papers.abstract: Xenoscope is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated at the University of Zurich to investigate electron transport over distances relevant to the next-generation XLZD (XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN) observatory. We demonstrate electron drift over $2.6$ m in liquid xenon using cosmic-muon-induced ionization signals. External muon tagging provides a timing reference for charge produced at known depths, while the endpoint of the average electroluminescence waveform probes transport over the full drift length. We measure electron drift velocities of $(1.320 \pm 0.006)$ mm/$\mu$s at $(80.92 \pm 0.36)$ V/cm and $(1.436 \pm 0.001)$ mm/$\mu$s at $(96.00 \pm 0.42)$ V/cm. These results establish detectable charge transport over meter-scale distances and provide an experimental benchmark for the development of future large liquid-xenon time projection chambers.

papers.intro:
Dual-phase xenon time projection chambers (TPCs) are the most sensitive detector technology for weak-scale dark matter and other rare-event searches such as second-order weak processes Baudis (2023). Experiments with multi-ton target masses and unprecedentedly low background levels Aprile and others (2022); Aprile and others (2025); Qian and others (2022); Aalbers and others (2023) lead the exploration of the dark matter direct detection parameter space in the GeV\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}- TeV\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V} mass range. Achieving reliable operation of a detector with a target mass of several tens of tonnes places high requirements on detector design and operation.

The planned XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN (XLZD) observatory will use a dual phase xenon TPC with an active target of 60–80 t Baudis (2024); Aalbers and others (2025). XLZD will extend sensitivity to dark matter interactions down to the irreducible background from solar and atmospheric neutrinos O’Hare (2021) (referred to in the literature as neutrino fog) with exposures of approximately 100 tonne-years, while enabling searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay and other precision and rare-event measurements.

A dual-phase TPC operates by collecting prompt scintillation light (S1) and ionization electrons resulting from energy deposits in the liquid xenon (LXe). The electrons are drifted upwards using an electric field, towards the liquid–gas interface, where they are extracted by a stronger electric field and generate a delayed electroluminescence signal (S2) in the gas. The time separation between S1 and S2 provides the interaction depth, while the S2 light distribution determines the horizontal position. Combined, these signals allow for 3D event reconstruction and discrimination between electronic and nuclear recoils from their relative amplitudes. Consequently, all measurements rely critically on good knowledge of electron drift velocity, diffusion and survival probability, motivating characterization over the relevant scale for XLZD.

papers.title: One-Particle Resonances and Eigenstate Thermalization in Periodic Free-Fermion Lattices
papers.abstract: We study eigenstate fluctuations of the particle number in the nearest-neighbour free-fermion model on the periodic cubic lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^d$. For every fixed dimension, every particle number, every subvolume, and every normalized energy eigenstate, we prove a bound of order $NL^{d-1}$ for the particle-number variance. The corresponding eigenstate-thermalization estimate is of order $L^{d-1}/(N\eta^2)$ for fluctuations of relative size $\eta$. In particular, at positive particle density the bound decays as the inverse linear size. The proof decomposes the centered particle-number operator according to one-particle energy transfer and treats the zero- and nonzero-transfer components separately. The nonzero-transfer part is controlled by a sharp resonance bound, proved from Mann's theorem on relations among roots of unity, while the zero-transfer part is estimated by a Hilbert-Schmidt argument. These bounds are optimal in every dimension: the maximal nonzero-gap multiplicity has order $L^{d-1}$, and suitable many-body eigenstates realize matching variance lower bounds and show that the concentration bound cannot be improved in estimates uniform in the tolerance parameter.

papers.intro:
We study macroscopic equilibrium in energy eigenstates of free fermions on a periodic cubic lattice. The question is whether the number of particles in a spatial region is concentrated around the value prescribed by the uniform particle density, and how its fluctuations depend on the particle number and system size. We ask this for every energy eigenstate, including arbitrary superpositions within degenerate energy eigenspaces. The rigorous formulation of macroscopic equilibrium and its relation to eigenstate thermalization were developed in works of Goldstein et al. [5] and Tasaki [12]. Concrete thermalization results for free-fermion chains were subsequently established by Shiraishi and Tasaki [11] and by Tasaki [13].

papers.title: Quasipositive and almost positive sectional curvature on finite quotients of Wallach spaces
papers.abstract: We construct nonnegatively curved metrics on the cyclic and full permutation quotients of the Wallach flag manifolds in dimensions $6$, $12$, and $24$. The metrics are quasipositively curved in all three dimensions and almost positively curved in dimensions $12$ and $24$. The cyclic quotients are orientable with fundamental group $C_3$, and their further full permutation quotients have fundamental group $S_3$; none admits any metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature. For the almost-positive metrics we describe every zero-curvature plane and prove that the zero-point loci have Hausdorff dimensions exactly $11$ and $23$, respectively. A one-step deformation has, in each dimension, an explicit zero locus with nonempty interior. Further nested deformations reduce it to a measure-zero set while leaving a common codimension-one stratum. The argument combines normal forms for horizontal commuting planes with quaternionic rank conditions and a dimension estimate for commuting compressions of skew-symmetric operators. We also determine the possible degrees of arbitrary free finite quotients of the three flag covers and derive order bounds for fundamental groups when the Euler characteristic is nonzero. We have used ChatGPT-6-astra for mathematical exploration and verified and rewritten all the results.

The difference between these curvature conditions is geometric and topological. A homogeneous metric that is quasipositively curved is positively curved everywhere, because isometries carry a positive point to every point. A homogeneous manifold, however, may carry an inhomogeneous metric with quasipositive or almost positive curvature even when its topology excludes positive curvature. Finite quotients are particularly useful in making this distinction explicit.

Wilking’s work [28] introduced a broad normal-biquotient construction of almost-positive metrics. papers.title: Topological and measurewise amenability for locally compact groupoids
papers.abstract: We prove the equivalence of topological and measurewise amenability for $\sigma$-compact locally compact groupoids with a Hausdorff unit space and a continuous Haar system. This in particular includes the second countable locally compact Hausdorff case. Our proof averages arbitrary Radon probability measures along strictly positive densities to obtain quasi-invariant measures. We overcome the lack of absolute continuity of the original measure with respect to its quasi-invariant substitute by also averaging the Reiter functions along the same density.

Amenability was introduced as a group-theoretic averaging property in von Neumann’s work on the Banach–Tarski paradox [vN29]. It has since become a central approximation property in operator algebras and dynamics. Its strength is illustrated by a plethora of classification results which turn abstract averaging properties into concrete internal approximations.
