In the measurable setting, the Connes–Feldman–Weiss theorem shows that countable amenable measured equivalence relations are hyperfinite [CFW81]. The noncommutative analogues of measure spaces are von Neumann algebras, where a similar role is played by the Connes–Haagerup classification of injective factors with separable predual [Con76, Haa87].

In the measurable setting, the Connes–Feldman–Weiss theorem shows that countable amenable measured equivalence relations are hyperfinite [CFW81]. The noncommutative analogues of measure spaces are von Neumann algebras, where a similar role is played by the Connes–Haagerup classification of injective factors with separable predual [Con76, Haa87].

On the topological side, Connes’ theorem has both inspired and technically facilitated the Elliott classification programme which culminated in the classification of unital simple separable nuclear 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-stable C∗C^{*}-algebras satisfying the universal coefficient theorem (UCT) (see [Win18, Whi23] for an overview). The converse holds as well: Every unital simple separable nuclear 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-stable C∗C^{*}-algebra satisfying the UCT can be written as a twisted groupoid C∗C^{*}-algebra [Li20].

One reason for the power of amenability is its flexibility due to its many equivalent definitions. While Reiter’s definition [Rei65] of amenable locally compact groups in terms of approximately invariant functions seemingly depends on the topology by referring to uniform convergence on compact sets, Zimmer’s fixed point property [Zim78] only depends on the measurable structure of the group action. Both definitions of amenability were generalized to locally compact Hausdorff groupoids by Renault22 2 See [AEG94] for the equivalence between Zimmer’s definition and measurewise amenability. [Ren80] and subsequently called topological and measurewise amenability in the foundational monograph [ADR00] by Anantharaman-Delaroche–Renault. Later, the theory was extended to non-Hausdorff groupoids in [Ren15]. Since then it has been a long-standing open problem whether these two notions are equivalent (see [Ren80, page 92], [AD23, § 2.4]). Anantharaman-Delaroche and Renault proved the equivalence for locally compact Hausdorff groupoids with countable orbits, and more generally for groupoids equivalent to such groupoids [ADR00]. This in particular includes all second countable Hausdorff étale groupoids. More recently, Buss–Echterhoff–Willett obtained the equivalence for transformation groupoids associated to actions of second countable locally compact groups on second countable locally compact Hausdorff spaces [BEW24], building on [BC22]. Our main result establishes the equivalence of topological and measurewise amenability for general σ\sigma-compact locally compact groupoids.

Here, quasi-invariance means that its pull-back μ∘λ\mu\circ\lambda to GG along the Haar system is Radon–Nikodym-equivalent to its image under inversion. For transformation groupoids this simply means that μ\mu is Radon–Nikodym-equivalent to all of its translates along the group action [Ren80].

It is easy to see that topological amenability implies measurewise amenability. The converse implication is usually proved using a Hahn–Banach argument: Since the Reiter functions (gi)i(g_{i})_{i} are closed under convex combinations, weak-*-approximations with respect to all Radon probability measures can be upgraded to uniform approximations on compact subsets. The remaining problem is: Not all Radon probability measures are quasi-invariant. If the groupoid has countable orbits, this problem can be overcome by averaging the original measure along the orbits. Since each point in the orbit is an atom, the original measure is absolutely continuous with respect to its quasi-invariant average. In particular, weak-*-approximations for the quasi-invariant measure yield weak-*-approximations for the original measure and the Hahn–Banach argument applies [ADR00].

papers.title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
papers.abstract: We introduce Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter model for engineering with native multimodal input, deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window. We design the Micius data pipeline as a knowledge-tree-driven data flywheel comprising three stages: knowledge tree construction and expansion, data synthesis, and quality validation with hard-example augmentation. From this data, we train expert models for semiconductor knowledge and reasoning, hardware coding, and semiconductor multimodal understanding, along with agentic experts. Subsequently, we employ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to supervise training on sequences generated by Micius itself, thereby integrating the capabilities of these expert models into a unified model. On more than 20 datasets with about 15K records, Micius-Flash averages 64.2% on hardware code benchmarks, 15.0 points above a same-size baseline. It scores 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, exceeding the same-size baseline by 17.2 points. We further develop Micius Harness for industrial applications, connecting the model to specialized tools, including EDA tools and KiCad, as well as execution environments. Case studies in PCB design, chip design workflow automation, and software development demonstrate the model's ability to use tool execution feedback for multi-step planning, code debugging, and iterative verification. We release Micius as an open-source model to advance the development of agents for science and engineering.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their capabilities in reasoning, code generation, multimodal understanding, and interaction with external tools [6, 15, 29, 36, 33]. Research on software agents further demonstrates the importance of interfaces and execution environments for complex, multi-step tasks [43, 12, 38]. These developments create new opportunities for scientific research and engineering, where models must work with specialized knowledge, heterogeneous information, and professional software beyond conventional text-based interactions.

Semiconductor research and engineering exemplify these demands, spanning device physics, manufacturing processes, circuit design, and verification. Tasks may involve interpreting schematics, generating hardware code or EDA scripts, and refining designs using simulation feedback. Domain-adapted models show the value of specialized training [20, 21, 41], while benchmarks expose limitations in hardware generation, circuit understanding, and realistic design tasks [30, 22, 4, 44]. Three challenges remain. First, engineering knowledge is fragmented and insufficiently covered by general-purpose training data, motivating systematic domain data collection, synthesis, and quality control [16, 39]. Second, engineering tasks require complementary capabilities that are difficult to consolidate within a single model without interference or degradation of general-purpose performance [25]. Third, applying model capabilities to real engineering workflows requires dedicated execution infrastructure. Specialized tools have distinct interfaces and runtime dependencies, while multi-stage tasks require coordinated tool access, environment configuration, and executable workflow.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Channel Estimation for MU-MIMO-OFDM
papers.abstract: Conventional channel estimation for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) relies on the pilot interpolation without explicitly identifying the sparse delay-angle (DA) components. To exploit DA sparsity while maintaining backward compatibility with existing MIMO-OFDM systems, we propose a cross-domain channel estimation scheme for multiuser MIMO-OFDM (MU-MIMO-OFDM) systems. The scheme exploits the circular convolution structure in the DA domain to identify candidate DA pairs by correlating delay-domain observations with DA pilot responses. These pairs and the known pilots then define a time-frequency (TF) dictionary for refining the DA coefficients from TF observations through least-squares or sparsity-regularized fitting. The refined coefficients and candidate pairs reconstruct the aggregate channel across antennas and subcarriers aligning with the geometric channel model. Numerical results show approximately 10 dB and 7 dB lower normalized mean-square error than the conventional OFDM estimation schemes for integer and fractional delay and angle indices, respectively.

papers.intro:
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) supports wideband multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) transmission by converting a frequency-selective MIMO channel into a set of narrowband MIMO subchannels. Accurate estimates of these subchannels are essential for spatial precoding and detection, which enable parallel transmission and reliable recovery of multiple data streams [1]. Conventional OFDM estimators recover aggregate time–frequency (TF) channel coefficients at pilot locations and interpolate those at data locations by exploiting channel correlation within a coherence region [2].

Accurate estimates of these subchannels are essential for spatial precoding and detection, which enable parallel transmission and reliable recovery of multiple data streams [1]. Conventional OFDM estimators recover aggregate time–frequency (TF) channel coefficients at pilot locations and interpolate those at data locations by exploiting channel correlation within a coherence region [2].

The development of future wireless networks has brought new design opportunities for estimating the MIMO-OFDM channel. For example, sixth-generation (6G) networks are evolving toward upper mid-band spectrum (frequency range 3, FR3) and extremely large-scale MIMO arrays [3, 4]. Wider bandwidths and larger array apertures provide finer delay and angular resolution, respectively. For channels dominated by a limited number of paths, this finer resolution enhances the sparsity of the delay–angle (DA) representation, with most channel energy concentrated around a few peaks [1]. The frequency–antenna channel can be efficiently transformed into this sparse DA representation using a pair of fast Fourier transforms (FFTs).

In fact, exploiting the advantages of the transform-domains for communications is no longer a new topic. Noticeably, several waveform designs have emerged to exploit channel sparsity in transform-domains. For example, orthogonal time-frequency space (OTFS) modulation multiplexes symbols in the delay–Doppler (DD) domain [5, 6]. Sufficient bandwidth and observation time across multiple symbols provide fine delay and Doppler resolution, respectively, yielding an approximately sparse DD representation [7, 8]. Embedded-pilot schemes can therefore exploit this DD sparsity to focus channel estimation on a small set of significant components identified by thresholding the received pilot response [9]. Similarly, affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) exploits the sparse effective channel in the discrete affine Fourier transform (DAFT) domain for low-complexity detection [10]. Orthogonal chirp delay–Doppler division multiplexing (CDDM) spreads symbols in the DD domain using the chirp–Zak transform. It exploits DD channel sparsity to identify path delays and Doppler shifts, then estimates the corresponding gains through chirp correlation [11].

Although these waveforms exploit channel sparsity for estimation and detection, their adoption requires significant transceiver modifications that can complicate backward compatibility with existing OFDM systems [8]. Preserving compatibility is particularly important given the adoption of OFDM in fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR) and its retention in the ongoing 6G radio study [8]. These practical constraints motivate channel estimation schemes that exploit transform-domain channel sparsity while preserving the OFDM waveform. For example, the scheme in [12] transforms pilot-based TF channel estimates into the DD domain and uses maximum likelihood estimation to recover path delays, Doppler shifts, and gains. These parameters reconstruct the TF channel matrix for minimum mean-square error equalization that accounts for intercarrier interference. In our previous work [13], we proposed a two-stage cross-domain scheme that transforms OFDM pilots and received samples into the DD domain, where twisted correlation and thresholding identify candidate DD pairs. These pairs define a TF dictionary for fading-coefficient estimation through ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularized least squares (LS), which suppresses false candidates before channel reconstruction.

We transform the known frequency–antenna pilots into the DA domain and the received samples into the delay domain to exploit DA sparsity while retaining the transmitted OFDM waveform. papers.title: Beyond Prompt Attacks: Least-Action Auditing of Concept Erasure
papers.abstract: Concept erasure, or concept unlearning, in text-to-image diffusion models is usually audited with prompt attacks. A prompt attack tests whether one conditioning string still retrieves the erased concept. It does not measure the probability that the frozen generator still assigns to that concept. We introduce least-action auditing of this residual probability, and evaluate it on Stable Diffusion concept-erasure checkpoints. The least-action barrier is the minimum control cost of driving the frozen reverse process into a detector-defined concept event. This cost equals the path-space KL divergence of conditioning the model on the event, and therefore the event's negative log-probability. The estimate $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}$ uses a CLIP$\wedge$DINOv2 consensus terminal, with no retraining and no adversarial prompt. Across $18$ erased concept-mechanism pairs spanning object classes and NSFW nudity, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}$ predicts deployment leakage counted on $1{,}500$ fresh samples per model by detectors excluded from the audit (pooled Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.76$, $p{=}5{\times}10^{-4}$). Within every audited concept, the eraser with the higher barrier leaks less ($18/18$). On NSFW nudity the barrier orders the standard erasers exactly: UCE $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}{=}3.9$ (leak $16.4\%$) $<$ ESD $75.5$ ($9.8\%$) $<$ RECE $224.5$ ($1.4\%$), while Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) stays near zero and leaks $85.5\%$ under explicit prompts. The same trajectories repair deployed checkpoints. An audit-guided closed-form patch reduces UCE nudity leakage from $16.2\%$ to $0/1{,}500$ and RECE church leakage by $3.3\times$, where direction-count-matched random edits fail.

papers.intro:
An erased model can stop responding to a target prompt and still retain the target concept in its generative dynamics. Concept-erasure methods edit a text-to-image diffusion model so that it no longer produces a target concept, such as an artistic style, an object class, or unsafe content (Gandikota et al., 2023a; Gandikota et al., 2023b; Schramowski et al., 2022). Erased checkpoints are released as open weights and deployed directly. The field audits them almost entirely through the conditioning interface: re-prompt the model, or run a prompt/embedding attack, and check whether the concept reappears (Zhang et al., 2023; Tsai et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Pham et al., 2023). Deployment leakage depends on a different quantity: the probability mass that the frozen reverse process still assigns to the target event. We audit this residual capacity directly, through the minimum action required to reach the event from the frozen model.

papers.title: Applied bifidelity material response model construction and uncertainty quantification with a sampling hypernetwork
papers.abstract: Multifidelity modeling offers a practical route to accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce but lower-fidelity data are comparatively abundant. This work develops a bifidelity Langevin sampling hypernetwork framework that constructs probabilistic neu- ral response models by learning a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than a single deterministic fit. The method combines a flexible shared-latent data representation for low- and high-fidelity responses, enabling parameter sharing and transfer learning between the fidelities. We introduce several methodological enhancements to improve the robustness and efficiency of this ap- proach, including stability-promoting drift models, staged and conditional training strategies, adap- tive initialization of Langevin trajectories, and training procedures designed to better exploit corre- lations between fidelity levels. These additions improve convergence behavior, reduce the sampling effort required to obtain representative posterior ensembles, and provide more reliable predictive uncertainty in data-limited regimes. The resulting framework makes more effective use of available multifidelity data while preserving interpretability through the learned posterior structure, yielding improved predictive performance, better uncertainty characterization, and a more stable workflow for constructing uncertainty-aware surrogate models. The method is demonstrated on experimental, high-fidelity simulation and illustrative synthetic data.

Although sophisticated methods exist [1, 2, 3, 4] which can handle multiple data sources without a strict ordering of fidelities, in this work we limit our focus to the bifidelity (BF) scenario where there is clearly a high-fidelity (HF) source, such as experiments, and a (relatively) low-fidelity (LF) source, such as direct numerical simulation (DNS). There are a variety of MF and BF approaches which we briefly survey in Sec.​ 2. In general, these approaches explore means of using the LF source to boost the accuracy and certainty of a model of the HF data; this entails a variety of sampling, surrogate models, and other constructions to link the different fidelity information. The core idea that we utilize is to employ LF simulations to learn a reduced representation (e.g., a low-rank basis of model outputs) and then correct/lift that representation using a small set of HF samples. These methods are most effective when: (a) HF and LF models are strongly correlated and (b) the model outputs exhibit low intrinsic dimensionality, which influence efficient sampling and surrogate construction. BF models and UQ can offer substantial computational savings while retaining near-HF accuracy when the LF-to-HF discrepancy is learnable from limited HF data, which is sometimes called surrogate-based reasoning.

papers.title: CALFA-KV: Joint Calibration and Fisher-Guided Anchors for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.

papers.title: PrivMark: Pixel-Space Steering against Privacy Leakage in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) routinely disclose soft-biometric attributes such as age, gender, and race in their text outputs, exposing demographic information from uploaded images to any downstream API user. Existing privacy defenses do not fit this setting: face de-identification leaves distributed soft-biometric cues intact, classifier-targeted adversarial perturbations do not transfer to open-ended generation, and stronger VLM-specific methods require retraining or runtime activation access unavailable to downstream APIs. We propose PrivMark, a framework that suppresses biometric leakage at the image level. By analyzing VLM activations, we identify two weakly aligned steering vector directions in hidden-state space, each tied to a distinct leakage behavior --- one corresponding to incidental attribute disclosure under open-ended descriptions, the other to compliance with direct biometric probes instead of refusal --- and encode both directions into a single bounded pixel perturbation, so the protected image alone enforces privacy with no invasive access to model internals at deployment. To support evaluation, we assemble BioleakBench, $1{,}600$ VQA pairs covering biometric privacy attributes under both free-form description and direct-probe protocols. Across three white-box source models, PrivMark achieves up to $85.9\%$ biometric suppression while retaining $75\%$ of clean OK-VQA utility, up to $1.4\times$ the privacy-utility tradeoff of the strongest pixel-only baseline. The same one-shot perturbations transfer consistently to seven unseen VLMs including closed-source APIs.

papers.intro:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have quickly become the default interface for image understanding, deployed in consumer assistants, accessibility tools, and cloud APIs (Bai et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2025). Although detailed, prompt-conditioned image description is a key strength of vision-language models, it also exposes a significant privacy risk: unauthorized soft-biometric profiling at scale. Even benign prompts elicit attributes the uploader never requested: a query as simple as “describe this image” can return “a young Asian woman with brown eyes sitting on a park bench,” disclosing age, gender, race, and eye color in a single sentence (Kim et al., 2025). Because no task-specific training is required, any downstream consumer with API access can systematically extract such attributes from publicly shared photographs, carrying out automated demographic processing that regulations such as GDPR and the CCPA classify as special-category personal data requiring informed consent. The same applies when users ask directly: prompts like “What is this person’s race?” typically receive a compliant answer rather than a refusal.

Existing privacy defenses do not meet this setting’s requirements. Face de-identification (Hukkelås et al., 2019; Maximov et al., 2020; Meden et al., 2021) targets identity but leaves distributed soft-biometric cues such as body shape and skin tone intact. Adversarial methods for visual privacy (Mirjalili et al., 2020; Oh et al., 2017; Shan et al., 2020) target discriminative classifiers with fixed output labels rather than open-ended generation. VLM-specific defenses either require model retraining (Kim et al., 2025), per-image bounding boxes (Brachemi Meftah et al., 2025), learned anonymizers masking privacy-relevant body regions and removing entangled scene cues (Hui et al., 2026; Ilic et al., 2024), or runtime model access (Rimsky et al., 2024; Sivakumar et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2024). Concurrent image-only work (Balakrishnan & Phute, 2025; Shao et al., 2026) shares our threat model but takes different optimization routes, leaving the soft-biometric design space we explore here open. These limitations highlight the need for prompt-robust, image-only protection against soft-biometric leakage. Such protection should be attribute level, require no deployment-time model access, and preserve utility for non-sensitive queries.

papers.title: Toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials: a local excitation Hamiltonian for size consistency and transferability
papers.abstract: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials could make excited-state simulations across chemical space routine, but excitation energies, unlike ground-state energies, are not sums of atomic contributions. The excited states of noninteracting molecules are the union of their states, which pooled multistate readouts reproduce at best for the lowest state. We introduce LEH-MACE, whose excitation energies are the eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian assembled from atom-centred blocks, so this union holds exactly. We generated TD-DFT energies and forces for about 300,000 equilibrium, thermal, and excited-state geometries of over 100,000 molecules. LEH-MACE's advantage over direct readouts grew with the distance from the training data and was largest above $S_1$, with about half their $S_2$ and $S_3$ errors for long conjugated oligomers. For molecule pairs, only LEH-MACE kept its single-molecule accuracy, while a softmin readout remained superior for $S_1$ dynamics of larger chromophores. Exact size consistency is thus one step toward such potentials.

papers.intro:
Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach the accuracy of their quantum-chemical reference methods at a small fraction of the cost and have become standard tools for simulations in the electronic ground state [1]. For electronically excited states, MLIPs can make photodynamics simulations of molecules orders of magnitude cheaper than on-the-fly electronic-structure calculations [2, 3, 4]. Since the first nonadiabatic dynamics simulations with MLIPs [5, 6, 7], excited-state MLIPs have enabled photodynamics on nanosecond time scales [8, 9], mechanistic studies of photochemical reactions [10], the virtual screening of photoswitches [11, 12], and studies of the photodegradation of materials for organic light-emitting diodes [13], with architectures that also predict the couplings between states [14, 15]. Most of these models are trained for one molecule or a small family of related molecules. A diabatic neural network trained on azobenzene derivatives transferred to azobenzenes with substitution patterns outside its training set and predicted their photoisomerization quantum yields [11], and models that transfer across chemical space more broadly have been proposed only recently [16, 17, 18, 19]. Such a model has to solve two problems that ground-state MLIPs do not face.

Since the first nonadiabatic dynamics simulations with MLIPs [5, 6, 7], excited-state MLIPs have enabled photodynamics on nanosecond time scales [8, 9], mechanistic studies of photochemical reactions [10], the virtual screening of photoswitches [11, 12], and studies of the photodegradation of materials for organic light-emitting diodes [13], with architectures that also predict the couplings between states [14, 15]. A diabatic neural network trained on azobenzene derivatives transferred to azobenzenes with substitution patterns outside its training set and predicted their photoisomerization quantum yields [11], and models that transfer across chemical space more broadly have been proposed only recently [16, 17, 18, 19]. Such a model has to solve two problems that ground-state MLIPs do not face.

The first problem is the structure of the target. Ground-state energies are, to a good approximation, sums of local contributions, which makes atom-centred MLIPs transferable to larger systems. Excitation energies are not additive. For two noninteracting fragments A and B, the locally excited states of A+B are the union of the excited states of A and of B, so that Δ​E1​(A+B)=min⁡[Δ​E1​(A),Δ​E1​(B)]\Delta E_{1}(\text{A}+\text{B})=\min[\Delta E_{1}(\text{A}),\Delta E_{1}(\text{B})] and two identical fragments give exactly degenerate pairs of states. A multistate readout that sums atomic contributions, as used in many excited-state MLIPs [14, 17], produces excitation energies that grow with system size. Mean pooling is intensive but averages the fragments. papers.title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset
papers.abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.

papers.intro:
Recent progress in robot foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) models suggests that robotic manipulation can benefit substantially from scale [1, 2, 3]. However, action-labeled robot data remain costly to collect, embodiment-dependent, and far less abundant than visual data [3, 4]. Generative world models therefore offer a promising path beyond direct action supervision by learning how objects and scenes evolve from visual experience [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Connecting these predictions to robot execution requires an intermediate representation that is both scalable to learn and actionable for downstream control [10, 9].

Prior representations each capture useful structure but expose trade-offs. Pixel-space predictions, such as goal images [11] or videos [8], preserve rich visual information, but they are indirect for control and typically require an additional grounding step. Sparse keypoint or point-based interfaces represent manipulation objectives using landmarks or affordance points [12, 13], but may miss the complete object motion. 6-DoF object poses offer metrically grounded state descriptions, but they rely on rigid-body assumptions and cannot capture non-rigid deformations [14, 15]. Recent flow-based interfaces use object flow as an intermediate representation for manipulation [16, 17, 18]. However, they mainly model motion over visible or tracked object regions, leaving unobserved surfaces outside the motion field. We refer to object flow over visible regions as partial object flow.

To make object motion complete and actionable, we introduce 3D full-object flow, which specifies dense trajectories over the complete target-object surface as an explicit motion target for robot execution. Utilizing the reconstructed geometry of a target object, this representation maps dense trajectories over the entire object surface across time. It makes complete object motion explicit in a unified 3D geometry, while remaining grounded in object kinematics rather than robot-specific actions. The resulting dense correspondence can describe rigid motion and non-rigid deformation, and provides an object-level motion target that downstream controllers can optimize against.

While numerous large-scale human video datasets and robotic trajectory collections exist [3, 4, 22, 23], their supervision signals are predominantly limited to semantic action labels, sparse 2D tracking, or robot-specific proprioception. They lack the dense, unified 3D full-object flow annotations required to supervise a generalizable object-centric world model across diverse tasks and scenes.

Experiments validate the full pipeline from annotation to downstream execution, demonstrating reliable flow supervision, improved prediction through data scaling and model design, and effective robot manipulation with transfer across environments and embodiments.

papers.title: IntentLens: Grounding Underspecified Multimodal Queries for Recommendation via Tool-Augmented Reasoning
papers.abstract: As intelligent personal assistants are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios, recommendation paradigms are shifting from passive preference matching to inferring user intent from underspecified multimodal inputs. In practical interactions, users typically issue a reference image paired with a vague natural language query, keeping key visual attributes, personalized preferences, and item-side constraints implicit. Existing recommendation methods either leverage historical user interactions augmented with multimodal item features or assume fully articulated textual queries; both paradigms struggle to resolve underspecified multimodal queries for accurate item matching. To address this limitation, we propose IntentLens, a tool-augmented recommendation framework that grounds ambiguous multimodal queries into query-relevant evidence prior to user-item matching. IntentLens follows a ground-then-rank pipeline: a shared multimodal LLM leverages visual tools, user memory modules, and item attribute retrieval tools to (i) infer latent user intent from image-text inputs and (ii) augment each candidate item with fine-grained, query-conditioned evidence. Subsequently, a lightweight ranker scores candidates based on the grounded representations. To facilitate research in this novel setting, we construct two benchmarks with underspecified multimodal queries, namely \textsc{GoogleReview-MMTool} and \textsc{Yelp-MMTool}. Extensive experiments on these benchmarks demonstrate that IntentLens outperforms competitive MLLM and retrieval baselines, and exhibits strong generalization to unseen categories and datasets.

We accordingly propose IntentLens, a two-stage ground-then-rank framework. In Stage 1, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) selects and invokes query-side tools (i.e., visual and memory tools) as well as item-side tools to collect structured evidence, and then converts the resulting information into compact textual representations for the query and each candidate. In Stage 2, a lightweight dual-encoder ranker scores candidates against the grounded query representation, separating evidence acquisition from efficient ranking.

Pretrained MLLMs support basic tool invocation but are not trained to acquire evidence for personalized recommendations. Fine-tuning MLLMs is challenging in recommendation settings with many candidates, where rewards are sparse and effective planning requires exploring a large space of tool decisions. To better align tool decisions with downstream recommendation quality, we introduce a ranker-aligned Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) scheme that adapts the MLLM into a tool planner. We design a counterfactual ranking reward that compares each tool-using rollout with a no-tool baseline, making the value of acquired evidence explicit. We optimize this objective with trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), restricting gradient computation to policy-generated tokens by masking out environment-returned observations. Comprehensive experiments on our constructed benchmarks show promising recommendation quality of IntentLens.

papers.title: Industrial RPCVD growth of high-purity 28Si epilayers with 29Si content below 30 ppm for high-fidelity electron spin qubits
papers.abstract: Silicon quantum-dot spin qubits are among the most promising routes to large-scale quantum computation, but the residual 29Si nuclear spins in natural silicon impose a hyperfine dephasing limit that must be overcome by isotopic purification. Here, we report the epitaxial growth of high-purity 28Si on float-zone silicon using an industrial reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RPCVD) system. Secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) confirms an 28Si isotopic purity of 99.997%, with the 29Si concentration below 30 ppm. Through a systematic vacuum annealing matrix (850-1150 C), combined with atomic force microscopy and SIMS, we investigate the defect-mediated decomposition of the native oxide and the injection of non-equilibrium vacancies. We identify a thermal-budget window below 950 C within which the thin-layer structure of 28Si remains intact. At 1.5 K, magnetotransport measurements reveal a peak Hall mobility of 12,858 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1 and a quantum scattering lifetime of 0.659 ps, corresponding to a single-particle level broadening of 499 micro-eV. A double quantum dot fabricated on this platform exhibits a T2* of 0.62 us, a Hahn-echo coherence time of 28.8 us, and single-qubit gate fidelities of up to 99.9% measured by randomized benchmarking. Our results establish industrial RPCVD as a promising route toward high-coherence, high-fidelity silicon spin qubits.

Quantum computation offers a decisive advantage for the simulation of specific complex systems and for certain accelerated algorithms. Among the hardware platforms under active investigation, CMOS-compatible semiconductor quantum-dot qubits are widely regarded as one of the most credible solid-state architectures for large-scale monolithic integration, owing to their exceptional scalability [1–3]. Realizing high-fidelity qubit control, however, depends critically on an ultra-low-disorder electromagnetic and lattice environment.

In natural silicon, the non-zero-nuclear-spin isotope 29Si (nuclear spin I = 1/2, natural abundance ≈\approx 4.673%) [4,5] is spatially disordered and therefore generates a randomly fluctuating magnetic field acting on the localized electron. For an electron strongly confined in a quantum dot, this fluctuating nuclear-spin bath constitutes the dominant hyperfine relaxation channel and is one of the core mechanisms limiting qubit coherence (T2* ≈\approx 1 µs in natural silicon) [6]. Removing 29Si by isotopic purification [4,39] — thereby suppressing the random nuclear-field perturbation — is the most effective and widely adopted strategy for extending qubit dephasing times, and can improve coherence times by one to two orders of magnitude [7–9].

To satisfy the large-scale requirements of universal quantum computing, the preparation of 28Si must be transitioned from laboratory-scale, specialized equipment to high-throughput, standardized, industrial semiconductor manufacturing platforms [10,11]. Here, we report the epitaxial growth of an high-purity 28Si-MOS structure using an industrial reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RPCVD) system, obtaining epilayers with an isotopic purity as high as 99.997%. To establish the thermal-budget limits of this system during subsequent device processing and to clarify the microscopic structural evolution, we designed and executed a systematic vacuum annealing matrix. By combining real-space and reciprocal-space characterization, we traced the coupling between thermal decomposition of the native surface oxide, non-equilibrium vacancy injection, and the physical boundaries of local defect nucleation, long-range isotopic interdiffusion, and dewetting at extreme temperatures. In addition, low-temperature (down to 10 mK) magnetotransport was used to study the low-temperature mobility and deep microscopic scattering mechanisms of an induced two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) at electron inversion layer forms near the 28Si/28SiO2 interface, confirming an low disorder level in the channel. Finally, we fabricated lateral double-quantum-dot devices on the optimized material platform, extracted the electron-spin dephasing and coherence times, and quantitatively evaluated single-qubit gate fidelity by standard randomized benchmarking (RB). These results show that industrial RPCVD-grown 28Si films constitute a promising material platform for building high-fidelity spin qubits [13,22].

Finally, we fabricated lateral double-quantum-dot devices on the optimized material platform, extracted the electron-spin dephasing and coherence times, and quantitatively evaluated single-qubit gate fidelity by standard randomized benchmarking (RB). These results show that industrial RPCVD-grown 28Si films constitute a promising material platform for building high-fidelity spin qubits [13,22].

papers.title: Orbital texture of valence band and interband transitions of the type-II multiferroic van der Waals NiI$_2$
papers.abstract: NiI$_2$ is a van der Waals semiconductor characterized by complex electronic and magnetic phases, holding promise towards functional applications. For this purpose, a detailed understanding of its band structure and its excitations is essential to elucidate the electronic and transport properties. We present a comprehensive description of the band structure and of the lowest valence-to-conduction band transition in bulk NiI$_2$, by means of time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy supported by first-principles calculations. We describe the orbital character of Ni and I manifolds, and identify the main momentum-resolved features of the valence band and the shallow minima of the conduction band. With this study, we provide a foundational understanding of the electronic structure of NiI$_2$ and its single-particle interband electronic excitation, a benchmark for theoretical models, and a framework for future investigations on this material.

Van der Waals (vdW) materials have attracted considerable attention due to a plethora of emergent properties at low dimensionality such as increased correlations, orbital reordering, and unconventional magnetism [33, 11, 13]. In particular, the quest for functional materials in the thriving field of spintronics demands electrically-controllable magnetic configurations. The transition-metal halide NiI2 [25] appears as an ideal candidate thanks to the strong coupling between electronic and magnetic degrees of freedom: below ∼59 K\sim$59\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ the crystal enters a helimagnetic antiferromagnetic phase and a ferroelectric polarization perpendicular to the helix propagation vector appears. NiI2 is thus a type-II multiferroic vdW material, and displays a robust magnetoelectric response down to the monolayer (ML) limit [19, 36, 35, 29, 3]. It has also been proposed that NiI2 hosts an unconventional high-spin Kitaev state, at the origin of quantum-spin-liquid states and topological spin textures [41, 16].

papers.title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schr\"{o}dinger Bridges
papers.abstract: We study the numerical approximation of Schr\"{o}dinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

papers.title: FMA-Net: Flexible Modality Adaptation for Robust Multimodal Face Presentation Attack Detection
papers.abstract: Multimodal face presentation attack detection (fPAD) improves robustness using complementary RGB, depth, and infrared (IR) cues, but deployment remains challenging when modalities are unavailable or incomplete. Existing flexible-modality methods mainly use zero-filling or modality omission, potentially discarding cross-modal information and introducing modality-dependent bias. We propose the Flexible Modality Adaptation Network (FMA-Net), a unified framework that compensates for missing modalities through instruction-guided latent-space translation. The Face Modality Instruct Translator (FMIT) estimates target modality observations from RGB inputs, while context-aware category enhancement uses learnable text prompts as modality-invariant semantic anchors. A Facial Feature Adapter (F2A) integrates global facial structure and local spoof-relevant cues to enhance discriminative representations. Synthetic-to-Real Face Domain Alignment (SR-FDA) reduces feature discrepancies between translated and real modalities, with benefits depending on the missing-modality pattern and data domain. Experiments on WMCA and PADISI-Face validate the framework. On WMCA with a 70% modality missing ratio, FMA-Net achieves a mean ACER of 3.22% across four intra-domain missing-modality protocols, compared with 4.24% for the strongest baseline by the same criterion. When both depth and IR are entirely unavailable, it achieves 5.23% ACER, compared with 5.99% for the best competing result. Cross-domain experiments also reveal limitations of synthetic-to-real alignment under dataset shifts. These results support FMA-Net as a practical approach to fPAD with flexible and incomplete modalities.
papers.intro:
With the rapid advancement of face recognition technologies, face presentation attack detection (fPAD) has become a crucial component for secure identity verification. From smartphone unlocking to facial payment systems, face recognition is increasingly integrated into daily life. However, as a sensitive biometric trait, facial data is vulnerable to theft and misuse. Attackers can readily exploit publicly available facial images to launch presentation attacks by displaying photographs, replaying videos, or fabricating 3D masks. Consequently, fPAD aims to determine whether the presented face originates from a live subject rather than a spoofed medium, and has attracted extensive research attention, particularly in high-security applications.

Attackers can readily exploit publicly available facial images to launch presentation attacks by displaying photographs, replaying videos, or fabricating 3D masks. Consequently, fPAD aims to determine whether the presented face originates from a live subject rather than a spoofed medium, and has attracted extensive research attention, particularly in high-security applications.

Recent advances in fPAD highlight the effectiveness of multimodal approaches, which leverage complementary information from heterogeneous modalities such as RGB, depth, IR, and thermal. By combining diverse cues, these methods significantly enhance robustness against sophisticated attacks including high-quality replays and 3D masks. However, their reliance on specialized hardware and fixed modality configurations limits scalability and practical adoption. Prior work on flexible-modality fPAD [2] seeks unified models that handle arbitrary modality combinations. Yet, existing strategies for coping with missing modalities—such as zero-filling or direct omission [3]—inevitably discard valuable information and lead to suboptimal performance. This underscores a critical gap: how to effectively compensate for unavailable modalities while preserving the benefits of multimodal fusion. Motivated by this challenge, this work investigates modality translation as a flexible compensation strategy for incomplete-modality fPAD, aiming to exploit complementary modality cues without requiring all modalities to be physically available at inference.

papers.title: CRAFT-GBM: Selecting Best Features for Gradient-Boosted Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Feature subsampling is used to accelerate gradient-boosted trees, yet standard approaches fix the feature count in advance and largely ignore the split-gain evidence accumulated during training. We introduce CRAFT-GBM (Confidence-Ranked Adaptive Feature Tracking), a native LightGBM extension that uses this evidence to adapt which---and, by default, how many---features are searched each boosting round. CRAFT-GBM transforms root-split gains into bounded observations and constructs joint time-uniform bounds valid under adaptive, non-stationary training histories. In its default endogenous mode, after initialization, CRAFT-GBM retains exactly the features that cannot yet be ruled out as best, letting the selected feature-set size $K_t$ emerge from training history rather than a pre-specified fraction. With probability at least $1-\delta$, every feature with the largest expected gain is retained jointly across all rounds after initialization. When a feature fraction $f$ is specified instead, CRAFT-GBM ranks features by their interval point estimates and provides an approximate top-$K$ guarantee for feature budget $K_f$. We implement CRAFT-GBM within LightGBM while preserving its native feature-bundling representation, and evaluate it across 14 public and synthetic dataset families and four noise-augmented settings. In the fully endogenous setting, CRAFT-GBM reduces per-fit training time by 39.74\% with 1.04\% lower test loss in the geometric mean across all 18 RQ1 experiments. Under pre-specified feature fraction $f$, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM also yields aggregate training-time reductions up to 13.52 percentage points larger than random feature subsampling, with no increase in aggregate test loss relative to full-feature LightGBM. Accumulated training evidence can thus support adaptive feature search with statistical guarantees while retaining the practical advantages of native gradient boosting.

papers.intro:
Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) remain a strong choice for tabular learning (Grinsztajn et al., 2022; McElfresh et al., 2023), but high-dimensional training is expensive across hyperparameter search, cross-validation and retraining. Histogram-based boosting builds and scans every searched feature’s split statistics each round (Ke et al., 2017), although many features are weak, redundant, or rarely competitive for the best split. Random feature subsampling reduces this work, but fixes the fraction in advance and ignores earlier split-gain evidence. Related work addresses ensemble-wide sparsity (Ibrahim et al., 2024) and feature-rank uncertainty (Neuhof and Benjamini, 2024). We ask: can a boosting algorithm use its accumulated split-gain evidence to decide which features still need to be searched and, by default, how many?

Historical gain rankings alone are an obvious but insufficient solution. A valid screening rule must address four challenges: (C1) native split gains are unbounded and their scale drifts as the ensemble fits; (C2) a feature’s gain is observed only when it is searched, so missing observations are caused by earlier screening decisions; (C3) gains are non-stationary because they depend on the current learner; and (C4) screening decisions and the stopping round depend on the training history, so guarantees must hold at every round and for all features at once. Classical best-arm and subset identification handles adaptive sampling and stopping under fixed arm means (Even-Dar et al., 2006; Kalyanakrishnan et al., 2012). Racing handles adaptive sampling (Tiwari et al., 2022), while rising-bandit identification assumes nondecreasing, concave rewards (Mussi et al., 2024). Our target needs no such shape assumptions.

We introduce CRAFT-GBM (Confidence-Ranked Adaptive Feature Tracking), a native LightGBM extension that treats per-round feature screening as sequential inference. Its design is theory-driven: each component is the construction a formal guarantee requires under one of these challenges. For (C1), a feature gain transformation maps each searched feature’s best root-split gain to [0,1][0,1] using a scale fixed before the round, so observations are bounded and comparable across rounds. For (C2) and (C3), each feature’s accumulated expected gain averages its conditional expected transformed gains over the rounds in which it was actually searched, a target that follows the evolving learner without imputing gains for skipped rounds. For (C4), empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences (Howard et al., 2020; Howard et al., 2021) bound these targets jointly over all features and rounds under history-dependent selection and stopping, without independence or stationarity assumptions (Theorem 1). The empirical-Bernstein construction uses squared prediction errors to control deviations from conditional expected feature gains, with confidence interval widths adapting to both native LightGBM’s GOSS sampling variance and the accuracy of the historical predictor.

papers.title: Odd realisation numbers of rigid graphs
papers.abstract: Determining the number of realisations of a rigid graph for a specific choice of edge lengths is a fundamental problem in discrete geometry. Gortler, Healy and Thurston showed that the number of real realisations of a generic framework is always even or equal to one. Despite being rare, there do exist graphs whose number of complex realisations is odd and not equal to one. In this article, we exhibit two necessary conditions for a rigid graph to have an odd realisation number other than one. We also provide an infinite family of rigid graphs with an odd realisation number other than one.

papers.title: AMSchem: Automated Schematic Visualization of AMS Circuits via Verifiable Agentic Generation
papers.abstract: For decades, the netlist-to-schematic gap has remained a persistent challenge in design automation, especially for analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits. Netlists encode connectivity, not visual presentation, making their manual conversion into readable schematics time-consuming and dependent on expert conventions. The same gap leaves LLM-based design tools without structured visual feedback, forcing them to iterate on circuits they cannot see. We present AMSchem, a training-free, verifier-guided agentic framework that automatically generates human-readable schematics from AMS netlists. AMSchem separates circuit-aware visual planning (DrawingIntent) from executable schematic geometry (SchematicIR), and applies localized visual feedback with bounded, revalidated repair patches. Deterministic validators enforce device preservation, pin-net consistency, and geometric correctness throughout. For evaluation, we construct AMSchem-Bench comprising 64 circuits of 12 types. On the 40-circuit schematic subset, AMSchem with gpt-5.5 achieves 85.0\% validity (vs. 32.5\% direct generation). When integrated as a visual feedback module in LLM-based analog design, AMSchem resolves all 13 previously failed cases from AnalogCoder benchmark across five models, substantially improving the success rate. Our dataset and benchmark are available at https://www.amschem.com/benchmark

Unlike textual netlists, where a parser can validate syntax incrementally, schematic geometry admits no such intermediate verification. Although some methods use iterative visual refinement, preserving source-netlist connectivity remains challenging. A local error in symbol placement, terminal orientation, or wire routing can silently corrupt the entire schematic, while visual plausibility offers no guarantee of topological fidelity. Consequently, direct LLM generation remains brittle for producing schematics that are both readable and topologically correct.

papers.title: Analytic $GW$-Bethe--Salpeter Gradients with Quasiparticle Response in the Resolution of the Identity
papers.abstract: Analytic nuclear gradients for excited states from the Bethe$-$Salpeter equation (BSE) in the static screening approximation are presented within this work. The response of the screened interaction to nuclear displacements is treated within the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation, in close analogy to RI random phase approximation gradients, and is folded into the Lagrangian formalism of time-dependent density functional theory gradients. Quasiparticle gradients enter via the full analytic derivative of the corrections for RI contour-deformation $G_0W_0$ and ev$GW$, also taking into account that incomplete quasiparticle spectra are typically supplied. Comparisons to earlier approaches using a geometry-independent fixed quasiparticle correction are made. For the latter, the orbital-rotation terms are derived exactly, too. The implemented gradient scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$, and the three-index integrals are processed in batches with a memory demand of $\mathcal{O}(N_\mathrm{aux}^2 + N_\mathrm{occ}^2 N_\mathrm{aux})$. Excited-state geometries of a set of small molecules are compared to EOM-CCSD references and to TD-DFT. It is shown that the full quasiparticle gradient removes most of the systematic underestimation of the bond lengths in singlet excited states. A comparison along the C$-$C stretch of acetylene shows that the neglected derivative of the quasiparticle corrections is modest, but becomes erratic for $G_0W_0$ near poles of the self-energy, which ev$GW$ avoids.

papers.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
papers.abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.

papers.title: What Breaks Scribble-Supervised Segmentation? An Audit-Informed Benchmark for Scribble Annotation Robustness
papers.abstract: Scribble-supervised segmentation is typically evaluated with a fixed annotation set, leaving robustness to distinct semantic and geometric imperfections poorly understood. Motivated by an audit of 12,031 manual PASCAL Visual Object Classes (VOC) 2012 scribbles and prior work, we introduce six controlled perturbation operators. Class corruption, spatial offset, and directional perturbation directly operationalize audit signals. Stroke-length reduction is motivated by prior scribble studies, while random dropout and fragmentation serve as diagnostic controls. Each operator reports requested and achieved changes. We evaluate manual and automatic scribbles across two image domains, two principal backbone settings, and multiple training pipelines, with an additional MiT-B1 PFA anchor evaluation. In the five-seed Tree Energy Loss (TEL)-ResNet101 VOC study, mean intersection over union (mIoU) drops from 70.08 to 1.46 under class corruption, compared with 35.57 for spatial offset, 52.20 for directional perturbation, and 63.24 for stroke-length reduction at their strongest settings. At the evaluated endpoints, semantic-anchor corruption produces the largest degradation, while geometric and support responses depend on the pipeline and dataset. Our benchmark provides a reproducible protocol for diagnosing annotation robustness beyond clean-set accuracy. The operator code is available at https://github.com/Wmhiram99/scribble-operator-benchmark.

For weakly supervised segmentation, a scribble labels only a few pixels, yet those pixels may supervise an entire object. This makes scribbles an attractive alternative to costly dense masks (Papandreou et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2015; Bearman et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016). Modern pipelines propagate sparse labels through regularization (Tang et al., 2018b), affinities (Liang et al., 2022), pseudo-labels (Pan et al., 2021), feature distributions (Wu et al., 2023), or prototypes (Chan et al., 2024). These mechanisms extend sparse anchors beyond labeled pixels and can propagate the effect of an imperfect anchor.

We summarize scribble imperfections along three complementary properties: semantic identity, spatial geometry, and support/connectivity. An incorrect class changes what an anchor denotes; displacement changes where supervision enters; direction alters local geometry; and shortening, dropout, or fragmentation modify support and connectivity. We instantiate these properties through controlled perturbation operators, which transform clean scribbles into matched noisy training labels and together define the proposed robustness benchmark. Existing work largely optimizes a fixed scribble set or studies selected variations in class-aware cues (Zhang et al., 2024), generation (Schnell et al., 2024), and drawing style (Boettcher et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). General noisy-label pipelines focus mainly on class corruption, while segmentation robustness benchmarks typically perturb the input image rather than the training annotation (Patrini et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022; Kamann and Rother, 2020). Perturbing the training scribbles is necessary here because they define the sparse supervisory anchors whose semantic, geometric, and support errors are propagated during learning. A unified, audit-grounded benchmark for decomposing scribble imperfections is therefore still missing. To ground such a benchmark empirically, we first audit discrepancies between manual scribbles and dense references, then translate the observed modes into controlled perturbations with measurable achieved values.

papers.title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, Agentic-OPD improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing the latest frontier models GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search. Agentic-OPD recasts a finished RL run as a reusable pool of policies and establishes post-RL capability recovery as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm itself.

In agentic RL, an update can introduce a new behavior while erasing an earlier one. Across five agentic domains, we find that checkpoints from a single run collectively solve far more problems than any one checkpoint, revealing complementary capabilities along the training trajectory (Section 2).

Parameter-space merging produces one policy but can erase checkpoint-specific strengths, while separate inference increases deployment cost (Li et al., 2026b). Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) offers an alternative by consolidating these complementary capabilities into a single student policy (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). Prior work studies OPD with multiple teachers (Ma et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). Here, the teachers are temporal checkpoints from a single run, each of which may outperform the student on selected problems despite lower overall performance. This raises two challenges: teacher selection, choosing checkpoints that complement the student, and weak-to-strong distillation, transferring locally useful behaviors from globally weaker checkpoints to the student.

papers.title: The deuterium-rich atmosphere of a mature super-Jupiter
papers.abstract: The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio (D/H) has provided key insights into the origin and evolution of the Solar System. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, we detected deuterated methane at $48\sigma$ in a mature giant exoplanet, $\epsilon$ Ind Ab. We measure the planet's D/H ratio to be $(4.4 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-5}$, which is similar to those of Uranus and Neptune but about twice those of Jupiter, Saturn, and the protosolar nebula. $\epsilon$ Ind Ab's heavy elements (C, O, N, and S) are uniformly enriched to a level similar to Jupiter's. These measurements require $\epsilon$ Ind Ab to have accreted solids with $\mathrm{D/H} \gtrsim 1\%$, at least 30 times more deuterium-rich than typical Solar System comets. Such D/H values are found in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and in organic molecules in star-forming regions, indicating that $\epsilon$ Ind Ab accreted pristine solids formed in a very cold environment.

papers.title: Classical Cepheids in the 4MOST era I: Methodology for 4MOST variable stars and NLTE abundance gradients in the Milky Way
papers.abstract: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are key distance indicators and tracers of young stellar populations in the Milky Way. Their period-luminosity-metallicity (PLZ) relation also makes them calibrators of the Hubble constant $H_0$. Despite their importance, chemical composition, especially non-LTE (NLTE) effects, remains a significant source of systematics in PLZ applications. In preparation for the large CCs sample expected from the 4MIDABLE-HR (4MOST Consortium Survey 4: Milky Way Disc and Bulge High-Resolution) survey, we present a method for deriving Cepheid atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances in NLTE. Using the Payne artificial neural network (ANN) trained on NLTE spectra, we derive atmospheric parameters and abundances for 17 elements: O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Ba, Eu in NLTE and C and Cr in LTE. We apply the new method to archival spectra of Cepheids and derive radial chemical gradients in the Milky Way. We derive robust NLTE stellar parameters and abundances for Cepheids spanning metallicities from $\sim -0.87$ to $\sim +0.35$ dex. For stars with multi-epoch spectra, we find that NLTE abundances are consistent across the pulsation cycle, whereas LTE values show larger dispersions and biases. The resulting abundance distributions and gradients align well with Galactic disk expectations from chemical evolution models. We confirm that the gradients flatten in the outer disk beyond $R_{\rm GC} \sim 15\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and provide the first NLTE gradients for Co, Ni, Y, and Eu. We show that our NLTE astrophysical analysis yields robust solutions for atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances across spectra at the resolving power of 4MOST-HR. This enables large, homogeneous studies with upcoming surveys such as 4MOST 4MIDABLE-HR and provides a solid basis for tightening constraints on Galactic chemical evolution models and Cepheid distance-scale work.

papers.intro:
Classical Cepheids (CCs) are young, intermediate-mass (3-12 M⊙M_{\odot}) core He-burning stars (Turner 1996; Bono et al. 2000a; Bono et al. 2024) residing in the instability strip region of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Typical ages for CCs can span from 30 Myr to 600 Myr depending on the mass and chemical composition (Bono et al. 2005; Anderson et al. 2016b), and are therefore found in Galaxies with recent star formation. These stars exhibit radial pulsations with typical periods of a few days, although their periods can extend beyond 100 days (Catelan and Smith 2015). They have luminosities of ∼104−105​L⊙\sim 10^{4}-10^{5}L_{\odot} and radii of 20-200 R⊙R_{\odot} (Anderson et al. 2014). During their evolution, CC progenitors may cross the instability strip multiple times and experience dredge-up processes, shaping their observed pulsation properties and surface chemical abundances (Anderson et al. 2014; Anderson et al. 2016b).

During their evolution, CC progenitors may cross the instability strip multiple times and experience dredge-up processes, shaping their observed pulsation properties and surface chemical abundances (Anderson et al. 2014; Anderson et al. 2016b).

Owing to the tight relation between pulsation period and intrinsic luminosity, CCs are among the first and best-established standard candles (Leavitt 1907; Leavitt and Pickering 1912; Fernie 1969; Sandage et al. 2006; Riess et al. 2018; Ripepi et al. 2026). Due to their intrinsic brightness, CCs have canonically been used to calibrate the extragalactic distance scale (Madore and Freedman 1991; Udalski et al. 1999; Benedict et al. 2007; Riess et al. 2021) and thus to determine the Hubble constant (Freedman et al. 2012; Riess et al. 2016; Riess et al. 2019; Riess et al. 2022). Additionally, CCs are excellent tracers of structure and chemical evolution of young stellar populations in the Milky Way (Lemasle et al. 2017; Skowron et al. 2019) and other star-forming galaxies (Vilardell et al. 2007; Neeley et al. 2021; De Somma et al. 2025). In contrast to older stars affected by radial migration (Minchev et al. 2013; Lehmann et al. 2024; Kordopatis et al. 2025), CCs are more direct proxies of the composition of the present-day ISM (Lemasle et al. 2013), thereby providing constraints on models of Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) and parameters such as the efficiency of star formation (Palla et al. 2020; Matteucci 2021; Lian et al. 2023; Storm et al. 2026). Moreover, since CCs are spread across all four Galactic quadrants and are closely related with the spiral arms (Lemasle et al. 2022), they are of major use in the analyses of non-axisymmetric evolution (Spitoni et al. 2023), linked to the dynamics of the spiral arms and the bar (Fragkoudi et al. 2018; Hackshaw et al. 2024; Debattista et al. 2025).

However, the sign and magnitude of the metallicity effect remain highly debated. Some observational studies find that solar-metallicity Cepheids are brighter at fixed period than metal-poor counterparts (Breuval et al. 2022; Breuval et al. 2024; Trentin et al. 2024b), whereas other observations (Romaniello et al. 2008) and pulsation models (Bono et al. 1999a; Caputo et al. 2000; Marconi et al. 2005) suggest the opposite trend. Ripepi, see Bergemann et al. (2026)), to investigate the role of composition in the PLZ studies. The 4MIDABLE-HR survey (Bensby et al. 2019; Bergemann et al. 2026) will provide high-resolution (R∼20,000R\sim 20{,}000) optical spectra in three windows: 3926−43553926-4355 Å, 5160−57305160-5730 Å, and 6100−67906100-6790 Å (de Jong et al. 2019), of several million stars in the Milky Way disk and bulge. Its dedicated Cepheid sub-survey will collect high-quality spectra with the SNR of ≳100\gtrsim 100 per Å for 2 6432\,643 Cepheids with G≤16.5G\leq 16.5, covering the Galactic bulge and disk. Among these variable stars, 1423 are CCs, 90 are Anomalous Cepheids, 270 dwarf Cepheids, and 860 are type 2 Cepheids. This spectroscopic dataset will enable the determination of precise and homogeneous abundances of all key nucleosynthesis channels across the disk, including elements such as C, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Mn, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Ba, Eu. papers.title: The hierarchical structure of the Milky Way I. A model-agnostic clustering of 1 billion stars in 5D
papers.abstract: The Milky Way exhibits a hierarchical structure shaped by mergers, accretion, and internal dynamics. Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) enables a global view of this structure, but requires scalable, model-agnostic methods to extract multi-scale clustering patterns. We aim to characterise the hierarchical clustering structure of the Milky Way in a model-agnostic way and to assess how the resulting structures relate to existing catalogues. We apply the hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm AstroLink to a locally magnitude-complete subsample of over one billion Gaia DR3 stars with five-dimensional astrometric information. The data are corrected for selection effects and transformed using a distance contraction and feature scaling. We compare the resulting cluster hierarchy to catalogues of open clusters, globular clusters, dwarf galaxies, and stellar streams using custom availability-aware metrics and a bi-directional best-match framework. At a significance threshold of $S = 3.8\sigma$, AstroLink identifies 7410 statistically significant clusters spanning a wide range of morphologies. Compact systems are often recovered as reciprocal matches with many also exhibiting internal substructure, while extended structures are typically fragmented or partially recovered. A substantial fraction of clusters have no counterpart in the comparison catalogues, these may be new structures but additional physical checks are needed to verify this. A model-agnostic, hierarchical clustering approach can recover the multi-scale structure of the Milky Way at Gaia DR3 scale and provides a unified framework for comparing heterogeneous catalogues and identifying candidate structures.

papers.intro:
The Milky Way (MW) is a dynamically evolving, hierarchical system whose present-day structure encodes its formation history. Over cosmic time, it has grown through the accretion and disruption of smaller systems (White & Rees, 1978; Searle & Zinn, 1978; Kauffmann et al., 1993; Bullock & Johnston, 2005), while internal processes have shaped its disc, halo, and bulge (Sellwood & Binney, 2002; Kormendy & Kennicutt, 2004; Minchev et al., 2014; Obreja et al., 2019; Buck et al., 2018; Buck et al., 2019). The resulting stellar distribution exhibits structure across a wide range of spatial and kinematic scales, from compact bound systems such as open and globular clusters to extended tidal streams, dwarf galaxies, and diffuse components of the galactic disc and halo (Freeman & Bland-Hawthorn, 2002; Helmi, 2020). Characterising this hierarchy of structure is central to galactic archaeology, as it provides direct insight into past merger events, dynamical evolution, and the underlying cosmological model.

The Milky Way (MW) is a dynamically evolving, hierarchical system whose present-day structure encodes its formation history. The resulting stellar distribution exhibits structure across a wide range of spatial and kinematic scales, from compact bound systems such as open and globular clusters to extended tidal streams, dwarf galaxies, and diffuse components of the galactic disc and halo (Freeman & Bland-Hawthorn, 2002; Helmi, 2020). Characterising this hierarchy of structure is central to galactic archaeology, as it provides direct insight into past merger events, dynamical evolution, and the underlying cosmological model.

The advent of large-scale stellar surveys – most notably; SDSS (York et al., 2000; Kollmeier et al., 2026), DES (Dark Energy Survey Collaboration et al., 2016; Abbott et al., 2018), Gaia (Prusti et al., 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023), GALAH (De Silva et al., 2015; Buder et al., 2025), APOGEE (Majewski et al., 2017), and Pan-STARRS (Chambers et al., 2016) – has transformed our ability to study this structure (Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard, 2016; Helmi, 2020). These surveys have provided precise positions, proper motions, distances, and chemistries for many stars across the sky, enabling a global and homogeneous view of the MW. This wealth of data has led to the discovery and refinement of numerous stellar systems, as well as to the identification of previously unseen substructure in both the disc and halo (Price-Whelan & Bonaca, 2018; Shipp et al., 2018; Belokurov et al., 2018; Helmi et al., 2018). At the same time, the scale and complexity of these data sets present significant challenges, i.e. extracting meaningful structure from such a high-dimensional and heterogeneous data set requires methods that are both computationally efficient and robust to variations in density, morphology, and observational uncertainty.

A wide range of approaches have been developed to identify stellar structures in Gaia data. These typically make use of widely used centroid-based, model-based, or density-based clustering algorithms such as K-Means (MacQueen, 1967), EM (Dempster et al., 1977), DBSCAN (Ester et al., 1996), and HDBSCAN (Campello et al., 2015; McInnes et al., 2017). However there are also a growing number of fit-for-purpose clustering algorithms that use similar algorithmic concepts, e.g. Matched Filter (Rockosi et al., 2002; Balbinot et al., 2011), xGC3 (Johnston et al., 1996; Mateu et al., 2011; Mateu et al., 2017), StreamFinder (Malhan & Ibata, 2018), StarGo (Yuan et al., 2018), HSS (Pearson et al., 2022), Via Machinae (Shih et al., 2021; Shih et al., 2024), IOM (Lövdal et al., 2022), SigMA (Ratzenböck et al., 2023), SKYCURTAINS (Sengupta et al., 2025), StarStream (Chen et al., 2025), etc. These methods have been applied in the context of; open cluster searches (Cantat-Gaudin, T. et al., 2018; Hunt & Reffert, 2021; Hunt & Reffert, 2024), (chemo-)kinematic analyses of globular clusters and dwarf galaxies (Willman et al., 2005; Belokurov et al., 2006; Koposov et al., 2008; Minniti et al., 2017; Gran et al., 2019; Torrealba et al., 2019), and track-based or phase-space searches for stellar streams (Johnston et al., 1996; Mateu et al., 2011; Mateu et al., 2017; Ibata et al., 2019; Ibata et al., 2021; Malhan et al., 2022).
