papers.title: Demonstration of High fmax (> 80 GHz) in Recessed-Gate and Passivated $\mathrm{Al_{0.60}Ga_{0.40}N}$ Channel RF HEMTs
papers.abstract: In this work, ultra-wide bandgap (UWBG) $\mathrm{Al_{0.60}Ga_{0.40}N}$ channel high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) with an $\mathrm{Al_{0.81}Ga_{0.19}N}$ barrier and an $\mathrm{Al_{0.86}Ga_{0.14}N}$ back barrier were fabricated. The devices featured a recessed T-gate structure and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ passivation. Scaled devices achieved a cutoff frequency ($f_{\mathrm{T}}$) of 35 GHz, a maximum oscillation frequency ($f_{\mathrm{max}}$) of 82 GHz, and an average breakdown field $> 3 \mathrm{MV/cm}$, while maintaining a reasonable current collapse of $\sim 20\%$ under a 40 V drain bias in pinch-off condition. Devices with larger dimensions demonstrated a high off-state breakdown voltage of 883 V and an $f_{\mathrm{T}}$ of 24 GHz, yielding a high Johnson's figure of merit ($\mathrm{JFOM}$) of 21.19 $\mathrm{THz \cdot V}$. Across all device geometries, a high $I_{\mathrm{ON}}/I_{\mathrm{OFF}}$ ratio exceeding $10^6$ was observed with drain and gate leakage currents strictly below $10^{-6} \mathrm{A/mm}$. This work demonstrates an optimized design for $\mathrm{AlGaN}$ channel RF HEMTs and their excellent potential for X- to Ka-band applications.

authors.name: Guangying Wang
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: VLM as an Editing Pilot: VLM-Steered Velocity Control for Flow-Based Image Editing
papers.abstract: Text-guided image editing requires realizing the requested semantic change while preserving content unrelated to the instruction. FlowEdit provides an efficient inversion-free solution, but its source-anchored coupling can become overly restrictive, causing zero-edit, where the output remains close to the source and the requested change fails to emerge. We find that source coupling directly governs the preservation--editing trade-off, while a fixed coupling schedule cannot adapt to timestep-specific editing needs. Motivated by this observation, we propose V2C-Edit, a training-free VLM-steered velocity control framework. V2C-Edit constructs complementary coupling-controlled velocities and dynamically selects among them using Instruction-Level Similarity (ILS), which evaluates whether the predicted transformation follows the editing instruction. Adaptive spatial masking further preserves regions unrelated to the edit. Experiments on MagicBrush and PIE-Bench with FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 show that V2C-Edit consistently improves instruction alignment over FlowEdit while maintaining competitive structural preservation, and that ILS better reflects editing effectiveness than target-caption CLIP similarity. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kuanshen77/V2C-Edit.

papers.title: Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data
papers.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.

papers.title: Deintercalation Equilibria Control the Composition, Structure, and Electronic Quality in the Synthesis of 2$M$-WS$_2$
papers.abstract: Alkali-metal intercalation-deintercalation (AMID) enables access to metastable layered materials such as 2$M$-WS$_2$. Mechanistic studies of AMID have focused on intercalation; how deintercalation proceeds and influences crystal properties is comparatively poorly understood. Here, we assess 34 deintercalation treatments of 2$M$-K$_x$WS$_2$ and find that K$^+$ removal proceeds through coupled redox and ion-exchange equilibria, whose positions set the composition, structure, and electronic quality of the products. Across a series of neat solvents, K$^+$ deintercalation amount increased with solvent polarity and was driven to near-completion upon addition of nonoxidizing crown ether chelators, regardless of solvent polarity. Spontaneous reintercalation occurred when 2$M$-WS$_2$ was placed in dilute aqueous solutions of the strong base KOH but not the neutral salt KCl. These results suggest that the extent of deintercalation is governed by the stability of K$^+$ in solution, rather than oxidant strength alone, consistent with a reaction under thermodynamic control. Treatments that bias the deintercalation equilibrium most strongly toward the products while avoiding deleterious side reactions produce the highest quality 2$M$-WS$_2$. A six-hour treatment with acidified K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ gave the highest average residual resistivity ratio ($\overline{RRR}$). Residual K$^+$, quantified by ICP-MS, was found in all treated samples and appeared to impose an upper bound on $\overline{RRR}$. Treatments yielding crystals with $\overline{RRR}$ below this bound did not always afford 2$M$-WS$_2$; we observed two new structures in bleach-treated samples and signatures of alternative phases under other conditions. This work demonstrates that deintercalation is not merely a processing step in AMID but a mechanistically rich reaction that might be rationally tuned to improve and control metastable materials.

papers.title: Mean-level arithmetic computation via stochastic reaction networks
papers.abstract: Reaction networks provide a natural model for analog computation in which inputs and outputs are encoded by molecular abundances. Much of the work on analog computation with chemical reaction networks (CRNs) has focused on deterministic mass-action systems. In DNA- and protein-based circuits, however, low copy numbers can make intrinsic fluctuations significant, motivating the use of stochastic models. In this paper, we develop a framework for computation with stochastic CRNs at the level of stationary means. Specifically, we construct elementary arithmetic modules for identification, addition, and multiplication, and analyze their mean-level correctness and convergence rates. We focus on these three modules because they are simple enough to analyze explicitly while already exhibiting the new issues raised by stochastic mean-level computation. Unlike in deterministic systems, the computed value cannot be read from a single output measurement. Instead, readout requires Monte Carlo estimation, with error arising from transient bias as the system approaches stationarity and intrinsic sampling noise that persists even at stationarity. We therefore study the convergence rates of output means, variances, and autocovariances to their stationary values, as well as the stationary fluctuations governing sampling error. We also show that this readout cost can depend strongly, and sometimes unexpectedly, on the architecture of the computation. In particular, comparing linear-chain and binary-tree implementations reveals that binary trees can greatly reduce stationary variance for addition, but can instead produce exponentially larger variance for multiplication.

papers.title: Ultrawideband Polarization-Rotating Antenna for Enhanced Ground Penetrating Radar Detection
papers.abstract: Ground penetrating radar (GPR) represents a powerful and widely adopted tool for nondestructive subsurface detection and imaging. To overcome the impaired detection performance caused by polarization mismatch in conventional single-channel GPR systems, this paper presents an innovative ultrawideband polarization-rotating (UPR) antenna that achieves rotating linear polarizations (LPs) by varying the source frequency for enhanced detection. The developed UPR antenna achieves a continuous polarization rotation from $0^\circ$ to $170^\circ$ across 1.2 to 3.2 GHz, as verified by both full-wave simulations and experimental measurements. The antenna is subsequently integrated into a single-channel stepped-frequency GPR system and evaluated against targets of varying geometries in a sandy environment. Compared with a conventional fixed-LP GPR system, the UPR antenna-enabled GPR system delivers markedly more consistent detection performance across all target types, with particularly pronounced enhancements for polarization-sensitive targets. By enabling ultrawideband frequency-dependent polarization agility, the proposed GPR system enhances subsurface target detection while maintaining the simplicity and low cost of a single-channel measurement architecture.

papers.title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
papers.abstract: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1\% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $\mu \text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

papers.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
papers.abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.

authors.name: Mainul Hasan Mohsin
authors.institution: Shahjalal University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Mohammad Shahidur Rahman

papers.title: Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares
papers.abstract: Many scientific responses take values in Riemannian manifolds, with predictors that are scalar- and/or manifold-valued. A regression analysis in such settings must provide accurate prediction with hypothesis testing for individual coefficients. Yet no current manifold-regression framework accommodates both predictor types and enables per-coefficient hypothesis tests. We propose Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares (ROLS) as a tangent space conditional-mean model, which is the ordinary least squares (OLS) analogue for Riemannian manifolds. ROLS is well-defined under an explicit injectivity condition that keeps the logarithm maps single-valued, with cut-locus conditions for branch-sensitive cases outside it. Within the local geometric setting it admits a closed-form estimator, an $O(n^{-1})$ excess prediction-error bound with explicit curvature bias, and asymptotic $t$- and Wald tests for individual coefficients. With synthetic simulations and three real-data case studies, ROLS is shown to be competitive with the state-of-the-art baselines. In addition, the per-coefficient tests agree with effects reported in literature. We envision ROLS to be a standard tool for manifold-valued regression with coefficient-level inference to support scientific discovery, which can be interpreted in the same way as Euclidean OLS. The source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyuChenPub/ROLS.

papers.title: How Short Is Too Short? Length-Conditional Calibration and Abstention for Detecting AI-Generated Text
papers.abstract: Detectors of AI-generated text are usually tuned and tested on passages of several hundred tokens, yet many real cases are short. We study score-based detection as a function of passage length. We give a closed form for how the false-positive rate of a threshold set on long text changes as length falls, and a formula for the number of tokens a detector needs to reach a target true-positive rate. We calibrate thresholds within length bins with conformal p-values, and we add a bin-level rule that abstains when the detector cannot be informative at that length. On synthetic scores the formulas agree with simulation, and binned calibration holds the false-positive rate at its nominal value at every length. On three zero-shot detectors (log-likelihood, log-rank, Binoculars), three corpora and two open-weight generators, binned calibration gives a mean false-positive rate of 5.0% in every detector-length cell from 10 to 200 tokens, averaged over 300 random document-level resplits. A single threshold set at 200 tokens gives 29% for Binoculars at 10 tokens and about 1% for log-likelihood, as the closed form predicts. No detector reaches an 80% true-positive rate, and the best, Binoculars at 200 tokens, reaches 59%, so the rule abstains in every cell at that floor and releases only the 200-token bins at floors of 0.3 and 0.5.

papers.title: What Changed in Engineering Writing After Generative AI Chat Assistants: Evidence from 1.8 Million Articles
papers.abstract: This study asks what changed in engineering articles after conversational language models became publicly available on November 30, 2022, and develops methods for measuring such change in a field without a uniform abstract index. It assembled 1,839,962 articles published from 2015 to 2025 in 256 engineering journals, tracked twelve measures of wording, style, and article structure, and compared each with the projection of its own pre-2023 trend. Building the monthly series showed that records dated only by year fall on January 1 and create false January peaks unless removed. In abstracts, 31 words associated with language model output appeared 82% more often than projected (55.4 against 27.0 per 10,000 words in 2025), while four control words of the same formal register fell 16%. Words that soften a claim, such as may, fell 13%, words that strengthen one, such as clearly, rose 20%, and long words rose 11%. Author counts, reference lists, page counts, and publication volume stayed within 4% of trend. The change appears in all fourteen subject categories, and false release dates, dropping any one journal or word, and word lists chosen from the data support it. A random sample of 12,866 full texts from the same corpus, including subscription articles and weighted back to it, shows the same words rising 99% in article bodies. Statements disclosing AI writing assistance, measured apart from mentions of language models, went from none to 3.7% in 2025, four in five of them at one publisher. The design is descriptive, not causal.

papers.title: Developing a Street View Imagery Processing Pipeline for Building-Level Vacant House Assessment
papers.abstract: Street view imagery (SVI) is widely used to audit urban environments remotely. Automated assessments usually assume that each image shows the target building clearly. In practice, an image may lack task-relevant evidence or show a neighboring house. If this goes unchecked, a model's score cannot show whether it judged the correct building. We present a reproducible SVI processing pipeline that makes image suitability and target identity explicit and checkable. We apply it to vacant house assessment in South Korea, using 10,311 images of 1,609 detached-house parcels. Task-suitability filtering adapts its criteria to image composition and administrative area. This keeps coverage even across areas. While keeping as many images as a single uniform filter, our filtering left 101 more parcels with a usable image. Target-house alignment identifies the parcel's house from camera metadata and parcel boundaries. It needs no building footprints or additional training. Alignment matched human labels for 85.6% of images, compared with 79.8% for the best simple rule. In vacancy classification, filtering and alignment raised AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, but marking a different house in the same image still gave 0.709. Grad-CAM showed that the model often looked at areas outside the target house. Image suitability, target identification, and model evidence are therefore separate problems, and scores alone do not resolve them. Recording which images were used and which house was selected lets reviewers verify each assessment and can support human virtual audits.

authors.name: Sunjae Lee
authors.institution: Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology

papers.title: Stochastic Multilevel Sampling for Inverse Problems via Coarse-Space Identifiability
papers.abstract: Sampling only part of the data reduces the cost of each iteration in an inverse problem, but can make reconstruction updates unreliable. We study stochastic multilevel sampling, which computes updates on a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of correction spaces. The guiding idea is that a small sample may support a reliable coarse-grid update even when it provides insufficient information for a fine-grid update. For quadratic objectives, we identify conditions under which corrections computed from sampled data decrease the full-data objective. In small-batch experiments with computed tomography and periodic deblurring, the stochastic multilevel method improves reconstruction accuracy over matched single-level methods. In an increasingly ill-conditioned CT refinement with a fixed number of projection angles, the single-level error increases as the image dimension grows, whereas a deep hierarchy maintains or improves accuracy and outperforms full-data single-level optimization at the same number of forward and adjoint applications. The gains persist across the tested local solvers and strengthen with deeper hierarchies. A separate known-probe ptychography study provides complementary evidence for the benefit of hierarchical corrections for nonlinear inverse problems.

papers.title: Checking DER Commands Against Grid Context Catches Credentialed Attacks Static Checks Miss
papers.abstract: Authorization of distributed energy resource (DER) commands judges a command by who sent it and whether its value has been seen before. An attacker holding a legitimate credential who writes ordinary values passes both tests. We add a check that judges each DER write against the grid's operating context: the bus voltages around the target, the hour, the day- ahead price, system load, and irradiance, compared with what operators wrote under similar conditions in the feeder's own benign history. We evaluate it live on the IEEE 123-bus and 8500-node feeders, driven by a measured 2024 year of price, load, and irradiance, against nine attack scenarios. A lookup trained on the same history catches none of the writes of the four scenarios that send values already familiar on the targeted device; the context check refuses 91.7% of insider-abuse writes and 64.4% of DER-aggregation writes while denying 1.28% of benign writes. In an offline test that replays recorded moments with curtailment setpoints drawn from the benign range, issued at a positive price, it refuses 47.3% and 50.5% on the two feeders, against 18.5% and 16.0% for the same check without context; live, the few setpoints tested were mostly shallow and were mostly allowed. The context check complements the lookup.

papers.title: Frequency-consistent synthesis and selective transfer for medical image analysis
papers.abstract: Complementary imaging is not always available, and realistic synthesis does not necessarily improve downstream analysis. Here we introduce a training framework linking medical image synthesis to task learning through adaptive frequency consistency and selective feature transfer. Image-specific frequency constraints encourage consistency of structure and detail. Features are transferred only when a teacher using synthetic images achieves a lower task-error score than the student by a task-specific margin on a labelled training sample. Evaluations across five datasets show improved translation fidelity with three adversarial and diffusion-based translators trained without paired supervision, alongside gains in brain-tumour segmentation on tumour-containing slices and lesion centre-point detection. All 105 reported paired comparisons yielded point estimates favouring the proposed methods, including 36 external translation comparisons on post?treatment MRI without retraining. These findings support synthetic modalities as task-oriented complements to acquired scans when complementary imaging is unavailable.

papers.title: The Herzog--Sch\"onheim Conjecture for Solvable Groups
papers.abstract: The Herzog--Sch\"onheim conjecture states that if a group is partitioned into finitely many, and at least two, cosets of subgroups, then two of these subgroups have the same index. We prove the conjecture for all solvable groups, finite or infinite. Sun's bound on unions of cosets, applied in a quotient, is combined with divisibility restrictions on local indices relative to the subgroup generated by the $p$-elements, where $p$ is the largest prime divisor of the order of a minimal counterexample. These restrictions are obtained by counting fixed points in a primitive solvable quotient. This suffices except at the prime $7$, where the counting bound narrowly fails and an additional overlap argument is needed. The proof has been formalized in Lean~4 with mathlib.

papers.title: Sampling-based Model Predictive Control as Sequential Monte Carlo Inference
papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) is treated as a family of distinct algorithms: predictive sampling, MPPI, the cross-entropy method, and their biased, colored-noise, and annealed variants all sample control sequences and reweight them by cost. We show a single Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference algorithm implements them all, specified by three independent axes: the proposal, the update rule that reduces cost-weighted particles to a nominal plan, and the effective-sample-size threshold for resampling. We evaluate SMC-based planning on MuJoCo non-linear control, open-loop navigation through obstacle fields, 7-DoF motion planning, and non-prehensile push-T, in simulation and on a Franka FR3. Resampling combats particle degeneracy at long horizons. At a 28-knot horizon in our navigation domain it cut the collision rate by 30% over non-resampling baselines. Programmable proposals improve push-T success over perturbative baselines, improving from 1% to 100% in simulation and 10% to 90% on hardware.

papers.title: Optimal Polynomial-Query Approximation for Consistent Submodular Maximization with Short Lookahead
papers.abstract: Elements arrive one at a time, and after each arrival an algorithm holds a set of at most $k$ arrived elements. Its goal is a held set whose value under a monotone submodular function is close to the best value that $k$ arrived elements can achieve. The recourse of an update is the number of elements inserted into or removed from the held set, and we require it to be bounded independently of $k$ and of the number $n$ of arrivals. With evaluations only on sets of arrived elements and polynomially many of them, the best ratio a randomized algorithm can achieve is $2-\sqrt{2}\approx0.5858$. We show that seeing future arrivals raises the best ratio for polynomially many evaluations to $1-1/e\approx0.6321$, for deterministic and for randomized algorithms; no algorithm with polynomially many evaluations exceeds $1-1/e$, even when all elements are available at once. For every $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic algorithm that sees the next $\lceil\varepsilon k/3\rceil$ arrivals keeps a set of value at least $1-1/e-\varepsilon$ times the optimum at every time, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ elements per arrival and makes $(n+1)^{O(\varepsilon^{-2})}$ evaluations. With the whole arrival sequence known in advance, a deterministic algorithm attains the same ratio with $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ changes per arrival. A randomized algorithm with the same short lookahead makes $O(n^2k)$ evaluations, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ elements per arrival, and attains the same ratio in expectation at each fixed time. The main tool is a greedy algorithm with an explicit guarantee for each of its partial solutions combined with each initial segment of the known future arrivals. A second tool moves between two such solutions one element at a time while keeping the value high, and the deterministic algorithm times each move using upper bounds on the optimum from failed searches.

papers.title: Singular parabolic Anderson models - From flat space to geometric contexts
papers.abstract: These notes (which grew out of some lecture notes prepared for the first Aarhus Summer School in Analysis and Probability) are an introduction to the parabolic Anderson model (PAM), or otherwise stated the stochastic heat equation $\partial_{t} u \,=\, \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\, u \,+\, \beta\, u\,\dot{W}$. In this system, a multiplicative random potential $\dot{W}$ drives the solution away from the smooth spreading of the classical heat flow and toward intermittency. Namely one observes that mass concentrates, as time grows, on a few tall and widely separated peaks. Through the Feynman-Kac representation this analytic phenomenon has an equivalent probabilistic reading as the localization of a directed polymer in a random environment. We first develop this picture on the flat space $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, covering the construction of the driving noise, well-posedness of the equation, and two-sided bounds on the moment Lyapunov exponents that quantify intermittency. We then turn to the more original goal of the monograph: understanding how these phenomena, and the exponents attached to them, change when $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is replaced by a genuinely geometric background, such as a sub-Riemannian manifold or a fractal set. Throughout, the emphasis is on concepts, main results, and the intuition behind their proofs, rather than on exhaustive technical detail.

papers.title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/\epsilon)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/\epsilon^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $\epsilon^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/\epsilon^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC

papers.title: Agnostic Marginal-Nonuniform Learning
papers.abstract:
We study the problem of binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform learning framework in the agnostic setting. In this model, the constants in the learning rate may depend on the marginal distribution of the unlabeled data, but the guarantee must hold uniformly over all conditional distributions of the labels. We also study fine-grained rates.
  We consider two criteria.
  (1) The standard agnostic setting, where the learner competes with the best concept in the class. In this setting, an immediate consequence of standard agnostic PAC learning results gives us the optimal rate of $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for every class $\mathcal{H}$ with finite $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ and shows that arbitrarily slow rates are necessary otherwise. This also gives us the optimal fine-grained rate of $\sqrt{\tfrac{\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})}{n}}$. Therefore, the dependence on the marginal distribution does not help, which is in contrast to the realizable setting.
  (2) In the relaxed agnostic setting, where the learner competes with $(1+\lambda)$ times the error of the best concept for a fixed $\lambda \in (0,1]$, the picture from the realizable setting reappears. We obtain a trichotomy of the achievable optimal rates: exponential rates of the form $e^{-n}$ arise precisely when the class is finite; linear rates of the form $\tfrac{1}{n}$ arise when the class is infinite but $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is finite; and arbitrarily slow rates occur when $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})=\infty$. We also obtain the optimal fine-grained rate of $\tfrac{\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})}{\lambda n}$, where $\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})$ is a recently introduced combinatorial complexity dimension called the uncentered $\mathrm{VC}$-eluder dimension.

papers.title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.

authors.name: Zhaoying Pan
authors.institution: China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences

authors.name: Junyi Chai
authors.institution: College of Science & Technology Ningbo University

papers.title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
papers.abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.

authors.name: Zhaoying Pan
authors.institution: China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences

papers.title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift
papers.abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.

papers.title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
papers.abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.

authors.name: Amir Kimiyaie
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

papers.title: On Size-Biased Distributions and the Chainability of Positive Infinitely Divisible Distributions
papers.abstract: Bar-Lev and Letac (2025) introduced the concept of chainability of infinitely divisible distributions on $\mathbb R$. In this note, we show that a simpler notion of chainability can be used for infinitely divisible distributions on $[0,\infty)$. We derive some properties and give a probabilistic interpretation in terms of so-called size-biased distributions. As an application, we discuss simulation from size-biased distributions associated with an important class of tempered stable distributions.

authors.name: Michael Grabchak
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

papers.title: Harmonic and Monogenic Representations of White Noise and its weighted harmonic Bergman estimates
papers.abstract: Continuing Feichtinger's generalized stochastic process theory, we analyze harmonic and monogenic representations of white noise in Euclidean spaces. We define its convolution with square-integrable functions. Using the weighted Sobolev regularity of the white noise, we establish a high-dimensional Sokhotski-Plemelj formula for the white noise density. Furthermore, we embed these representations into new weighted Bergman spaces, proving that the weighted Bergman norms of the harmonic representations are bounded by the white noise's weighted Sobolev norms.

authors.name: Fang Yang
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

papers.title: One-Shot Federated Graph Learning via High-Fidelity Proxies and Transferability-Guided Collaboration
papers.abstract: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/Jumpy-Juice/FedHFT.

papers.title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.

papers.title: BP-based qLDPC Decoding under Long-range Correlated Noise: Trapping Configurations and Prior Mismatch
papers.abstract: We study the robustness of two state-of-the-art BP-based qLDPC decoders, Relay-BP and beam search, designed for independent noise when applied to spatially correlated noise with unchanged single-mechanism error probabilities. We generate correlated errors with a hidden Gaussian Markov random field, which lets us control the strength and range of the correlation while keeping every marginal error probability exact. This setting complements correlation-aware decoding: it asks how existing decoders perform when their assumed joint error model is mismatched. Across multiple tested circuits and code instances that we simulated, we observe that correlations can change logical error rates by orders of magnitude, reduce the finite-size distance advantage, and alter the relative ranking of Relay-BP, beam search, and BP-OSD. On one of the two tested circuits, Relay-BP and beam search become worse than BP-OSD, and increasing relay memory or beam width does not compensate for the degradation. Configuration analysis indicates that correlation primarily increases the probability of trapping configurations that are known to challenge these decoders; at matched error weight, correlated errors still cause decoding failures several times more often than i.i.d. errors. Finally, supplying the decoders with the marginals conditioned on the hidden field recovers most of the lost performance in the tested settings identifying prior mismatch as a major contributor to performance degradation under correlation.

papers.title: Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on similar data distributions tend to learn overlapping semantic structure, but their representations are distinct due to different model architecture, pretraining objectives and protocols. This prevents unified interpretability and cross-model feature reuse. Existing approaches extract interpretable concepts from individual models and align these concepts in a shared coordinate system using cross-reconstruction objectives, but the alignment only applies to latent coordinates while the concepts themselves remain model-specific and cannot be shared or reused. This paper introduces the Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoder (GB-SAE), which casts unified cross-model interpretability as a representation factorization problem and solves it by simultaneously learning a unified shared dictionary and multiple private model-specific dictionaries via a gated bottleneck sparse autoencoder framework. The shared dictionary encodes the cross-model common semantic structure in unified concepts that are reusable across all participating models (and beyond), while each private dictionary comprises residual concepts that capture model-specific biases. We evaluate GB-SAE with distinct foundation models including ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2, and ConvNeXt. GB-SAE demonstrates superior reconstruction capability, unified and faithful interpretability, strong reusability and generalization to unseen models and downstream tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/trustAIoT/GB-SAE_NeurIPS.

papers.title: A geometric K\"ahler--Ricci flow proof of the Calabi--Yau theorem
papers.abstract: We give a geometric proof that every K\"ahler class on a compact K\"ahler manifold with vanishing real first Chern class contains a unique Ricci-flat metric, and that the K\"ahler--Ricci flow converges smoothly to this metric. The fixed K\"ahler class and the bounded logarithmic volume density control the mean pairwise distance. Chow's scalar-curvature decay makes available, at a fixed spatial scale and all sufficiently late times, the relative-volume comparison of Jian--Song, derived from Bamler's pointed Nash entropy estimates. This comparison upgrades the mean-distance bound to a diameter bound without an absolute lower bound for entropy. A restarted heat-gradient estimate then gives exponential decay of the Ricci potential. A parabolic Schwarz estimate and the interior estimates of Sherman--Weinkove yield smooth exponential convergence. The proof does not invoke the Calabi--Yau existence theorem or global estimates for a scalar complex Monge--Amp\`ere equation.

papers.title: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
papers.abstract: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.

papers.title: Quantitative Homogenization and Global Lipschitz Estimates for Elasticity with Periodic Rigid Inclusions
papers.abstract: We consider the pure traction problem for linear elasticity in a bounded domain containing an $\varepsilon$-periodic array of perfectly rigid inclusions. For compatible $L^2$ boundary tractions on a Lipschitz domain, we prove an $O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$ error estimate in $H^1$ for a smoothed first-order two-scale expansion. If the exterior and inclusion boundaries are $C^{2,\beta}$, we also obtain a global Lipschitz estimate, uniform in $\varepsilon$, for compatible $C^{0,\sigma}$ tractions, where $0<\sigma<\beta$. The displacement is normalized modulo rigid motions, and the estimate controls the full gradient in the matrix and the inclusions. The boundary argument uses a local Neumann comparison estimate whose constant is independent of the choice of inclusions retained in cells cut by an artificial localization boundary. We prove this estimate by combining cellwise rigidification, divergence-free stress extensions, and duality, and then apply a boundary Campanato iteration and local estimates at the microscopic scale.

papers.title: Hilton's Conjecture on Uncomplemented Incomparable Families
papers.abstract:
A family ${\mathcal A}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ is \emph{uncomplemented} if it contains no set together with its complement. Families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t$ are \emph{strongly incomparable} if every set in one family is incomparable with every set in another family.
  In 1976, Hilton conjectured that if ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ are uncomplemented and strongly incomparable, then $$\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|\le 2^{n-1}.$$ We confirm this conjecture by a matrix rank argument that encodes incomparability and uncomplementedness in the same matrix, which is quite different from the earlier methods on this problem.
  We also study weak incomparability, in which the same set may occur in different families. Goldwasser, Hilton and Zheng conjectured an upper bound in this setting and claimed that their conjecture is equivalent to Hilton's conjecture. We give counterexamples to their conjecture for every $t\ge3$ and identify the error in the claimed equivalence. We then propose a replacement conjecture and confirm it when $t$ is large.
  The upper bound $2^{n-1}$ in Hilton's conjecture can be attained if some families are allowed to by empty. It is natural to consider the maximum size of $\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|$ for uncomplemented and strongly incomparable families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ when all families are required to be non-empty. Denote this maximum number by $M(n,t)$. We show that \[ 2^{n-1}-1\le M(n,t)\le 2^{n-1} \] for $n\ge3$ and $3\le t\le n$.

papers.title: Joint LSFC and Nakagami-m Estimation From Downlink SINR in GZF-Precoded CF-mMIMO
papers.abstract: Accurate characterization of the instantaneous signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) is important for reliability-sensitive cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems. This paper proposes a joint estimation method for link-specific large-scale fading coefficients (LSFCs) and a common Nakagami-$m$ shape parameter using power and downlink SINR measurements. A tractable SINR distribution is first derived under global zero-forcing (GZF) precoding, Nakagami-$m$ fading, and link-level fractional power control (FPC). Based on the derived probability density function (PDF), a model-driven neural network (NN) is developed to solve the resulting maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) problem. Simulations show that the reconstructed SINR distributions obtained with the estimated parameters closely match the empirical distributions. With $2 \times 10^{5}$ samples, the proposed method achieves an LSFC root-mean-square error (RMSE) of approximately 1.0 dB and an $m$ RMSE of approximately 0.085.

papers.title: Edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--\v{S}ir\'{a}\v{n} graphs $H_q$ for every prime power $q\geq 3$
papers.abstract: Motivated by Hamilton cycle problems and applications to collective communication, we study edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--\v{S}ir\'{a}\v{n} (MMS) graphs. The MMS graph $H_q$ (indexed by a prime power $q$) is a highly symmetric graph arising from finite fields. For every prime power $q\geq 3$, we prove that the MMS graph $H_q$ contains $\big\lceil\frac{q-1}{2}\big\rceil$ edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles. This resolves a problem of Li, Wang and Zheng, who established the result for prime $q$ and for $q=4$. Our construction uses graph lifts over finite fields and joins the components of lifted Hamilton cycles by adding edges within vertex fibres. The resulting cycles can be constructed using $O(|E(H_q)|)$ finite field operations, comparisons, and elementary list operations. As an application, these cycles provide edge-disjoint spanning rings for parallel ring-all-reduce algorithms on MMS networks.

papers.title: Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
papers.abstract: Topological phases, exceptional points, and bound states in the continuum (BICs) are three key concepts in condensed matter and classical wave physics. Their pairwise combinations have yielded a rich variety of intriguing singular modes, but the triple merger--exceptional topological BICs (ET-BICs)--has yet to be explored. In this Letter, we theoretically propose and experimentally demonstrate a universal approach for constructing such elusive exceptional structures. The system consists of four coupled topological chains: y-mirror stacking generates pairs of topological BICs, while z-stacking with biased loss yields a generalized mirror symmetry under which each pair--separated in different subspaces until their collapse--merges into an ET-BIC at a critical loss. Experimentally, using an acoustic platform with electrically tunable loss, we not only directly observe the coalescence of eigenenergies but also the coalescence of eigenstates, offering a complete verification of the ET-BIC formation. The triply synergistic ET-BICs may pave the way for wave devices that simultaneously demand robustness, sensitivity, and BIC confinement.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
papers.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

authors.name: He Zhu
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Decoupling Direction and Magnitude: Language-Steered Flow Matching for Super-Resolution in the Dark
papers.abstract: Image super-resolution in the dark is fundamentally challenged by extreme spatial heterogeneity: severely underexposed and noisy regions demand aggressive generative enhancement to reconstruct missing details, while relatively well-exposed areas require conservative updates to prevent hallucinated textures. Standard diffusion and flow-matching models, however, rely on globally uniform integration trajectories, making them sub-optimal for such spatially varying degradations. In this paper, we propose DeLang-SR (Degradation-Language steered Super-Resolution), a one-step flow-matching framework that explicitly decouples the restoration direction and magnitude. Rather than treating low-light corruption as arbitrary latent features, DeLang-SR translates measurable physical statistics into structured degradation language, harnessing the semantic prior of pretrained text-to-image models. The degradation-language intent, complemented by image-specific visual tokens, steers the velocity field (direction) toward restoration-relevant manifolds. Simultaneously, a continuous spatial update-strength field acts as a locally varying Euler step-size field (magnitude), applying stronger integration steps in heavily degraded shadows while enforcing conservative updates in reliable regions. Experiments on paired and real dark images, together with ablations and diagnostic analyses, show that DeLang-SR provides an effective and interpretable one-step route to super-resolution in the dark. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/moriyaya/DeLang-SR.

authors.name: Jiaxin Gao
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Liaoning

papers.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

papers.title: Distributionally Robust Rational Inattention
papers.abstract: We study a rational inattention model in which a decision maker chooses a stochastic choice rule while facing ambiguity about the prior distribution over states. Ambiguity is modeled through a distributionally robust formulation in which the prior belongs to an uncertainty set defined by a general phi-divergence. Our main result establishes an exact Lagrangian dual representation of the resulting max-min problem as a finite-dimensional concave optimization problem. This characterization yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the emergence of robust consideration sets and a tractable one-dimensional dual representation for the Cressie-Read family of divergences. We further connect the model to robust risk measures: Average Value-at-Risk arises from a particular non-smooth divergence, while Kullback-Leibler ambiguity is linked through Lagrangian duality to the entropic-risk multiplier representation. We then develop two extensions. The first allows the attention-cost technology and prior ambiguity to be governed by distinct phi-divergences, while the second introduces a deeper layer of ambiguity over the decision maker's baseline prior. Both extensions preserve the finite-dimensional structure of the model and encompass standard Kullback-Leibler robust rational inattention specifications as special or corresponding multiplier cases.

papers.title: DreamLander: A 6-DOF World Model based Reinforcement Learning Planetary Lander
papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.

papers.title: The sharp Fourier extension estimate for the sphere
papers.abstract: The full strong Fourier extension estimate for the unit sphere is established in every ambient dimension at least three. The finite Knapp boundary is obtained by combining a uniform diagonal estimate on rescaled spherical graphs with a transverse product bound. A Whitney decomposition and a dyadic dual pairing yield strong type at the exact scaling exponents. The critical local estimate and the strict mixed range come from the recent work on Euclidean local smoothing.

papers.title: TransArt3D: From Two States to Articulated 3D Reconstruction with Video Transition Priors
papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactable articulated assets from a few images is key to robotics and simulation, yet highly underconstrained. Existing optimization-based methods fit an articulated asset under a static 3D prior that scores each state independently, so per-state reconstruction errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D. To this end, we present TransArt3D, an optimization-based framework that reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from two endpoint images by translating this video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics. It first lifts frames generated between the endpoints with a transition-coupled 3D consensus that applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames, stabilizing unchanging regions and initializing the parts and joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement then lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field over the whole transition, while part assignment and a shared joint constrain the field throughout optimization, keeping per-state errors out of the articulation. Finally, a motion-aware canonical appearance fusion uses the recovered articulation to map both endpoint images onto one canonical surface, texturing regions that only one state reveals. On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D outperforms methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy, and surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.

authors.name: Chenhao Guan
authors.institution: Macau University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Tianshun Han
authors.institution: Macau University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Season by season causal analysis of the continuum and velocity-resolved H$\beta$ emission of NGC 5548
papers.abstract: We investigate possible causal influences in five historical seasons (1989-1993) of NGC 5548 using a version of the Synergistic-Unique-Redundant Decomposition (SURD) method adapted for this analysis, an information-theoretic causal discovery method for time series. Two four-variable sets contain the blue wing (B), core (C) and red wing (R) of H-beta together with either total H-beta (H) or the 5100 Angstrom continuum (F). We examine 7200 decompositions with common and unequal lags, two or three seasonal flux states, and base delays of 1-30 d. We rank the individual named components within each information family, reporting their amplitudes and simultaneous leakage. In 1989, unique continuum information about the core reaches 0.799 and 0.387 of target entropy for two and three states, with leakage 0.047 and 0.276. In 1992, the red-wing history supplies unique information about the future blue wing in both variable sets and both state counts, with peak target-entropy fractions 0.106-0.166. Distinct joint influences also emerge: for the 1991 core, the two-state S(F,B) and S(F,R) components contribute 0.187 and 0.125 at 20 d with leakage 0.087, although the unique continuum term vanishes. Strong core-wing redundancy identifies candidate inputs for simpler predictive models. Large late-lag leakage, reaching approximately 0.97 in the total set, identifies targets for additional driver measurements and richer temporal histories. The resulting seasonal map of individual, shared and joint influences complements the response delays and velocity structure measured by reverberation mapping, and provides specific causal hypotheses for the evolving broad-line region.

papers.title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers
papers.abstract: We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an 'approximate conditional-gradient step' for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.

papers.title: Flexible Edge Cover: A Disjunctive Programming driven Approximation
papers.abstract:
We introduce the flexible edge cover problem, denoted FLEX-EDGE-COVER: the input here is an undirected graph with non-negative edge costs along with a partition of the edges into safe and unsafe edges, non-negative integers $p$ and $q$, and the goal is to find a minimum cost subset of edges such that each vertex has either at least $p$ safe edges incident to it or at least $p+q$ total edges incident to it. We show that FLEX-EDGE-COVER is APX-hard in simple bipartite graphs. A greedy approach leads to a $2$-approximation in all graphs. We show that the $2$-factor can be improved in simple graphs via a novel disjunctive programming-based LP formulation. AI-tools were used in the analysis of our rounding algorithm.
  Our motivation for introducing and investigating FLEX-EDGE-COVER is its close connection to the Flexible Graph Connectivity problem (denoted $(p,q)$-FGC) which has garnered much recent attention. For $(p,q)$-FGC, we develop a tighter LP-formulation via the disjunctive programming approach. We hope that our disjunctive-programming based LP and rounding algorithms for FLEX-EDGE-COVER will serve as a starting point towards a constant factor approximation for $(p,q)$-FGC.

papers.title: Can open citation data detect citation stacking? An audit against Clarivate's journal suppressions
papers.abstract: Clarivate suppresses journals from the Journal Citation Reports when self-citations or concentrated citations from another journal ("citation stacking") distort their Journal Impact Factor. Its data are closed. Yearly journal citation networks were built from the OpenCitations snapshot of January 2024 (1.96 billion citations; 85,437 journals) and compared with Clarivate's suppression lists for data years 2015-2023, collected from primary sources. Where reference lists are present, open data reproduce Clarivate's published self-citation shares within ten points for 36 of 50 journals. The failures follow publishers that do not deposit references with Crossref, which also hides several stacking donors. Biodiversity data downloads registered with DataCite inflate naive impact-factor numerators of taxonomy journals. The leading open method, CIDRE, detects none of 15 named Clarivate pairs: it drops large donor journals, and lowering its donor threshold merges the pairs into large groups. A recipient-centric reading of CIDRE's own test flags stacking-listed journals 6 to 14 times more often than other journals, depending on consensus level, and 5 to 7 times more often than size-matched controls, sometimes years before the listing. At equal flag rate it finds more listed journals than a plain 43% donor-share rule (10 vs 3 of 28), and about as many as a rule with a citation floor. A prospective check on the 2024-2025 lists agrees in direction but is not significant (one of six). Flagged pairs show more citations per citing paper and weaker topical similarity than matched pairs. Open audits are feasible if coverage gaps are reported.

papers.title: Do links to retracted papers predict future retractions? An out-of-sample test on the open biomedical citation graph
papers.abstract: Tools that screen manuscripts for research-integrity problems flag papers that cite retracted work, and retrospective studies report that such papers are retracted more often. This study tests the signal prospectively on open data. Predictors were computed on the January 2024 OpenCitations graph using the retractions known at that date, frozen, and compared with retractions in the Retraction Watch database from February 2024 to October 2026. The design was pre-specified. Among 10.5 million biomedical papers published 2015-2023, 2.1% cited a paper already retracted, and 4,323 were retracted later (0.041%). Citing a retracted paper raised the later retraction rate from 0.035% to 0.27% with one such reference; excluding reviews (post hoc), it rose to 2.3% with five or more. Within journal and publication year the odds ratio was 2.99 (95% CI 2.73-3.27), and 3.03 when reference-list length was also held fixed (post hoc), so the signal is not explained by retraction waves in journals or by long reference lists. As a screen it is weak: 0.9% of the 1,000 highest-ranked papers were retracted later (2.2% with reviews set aside, post hoc), and 84% of later retractions cite no retracted paper. When the time point was moved into the late-2023 retraction wave, the journal's own retraction rate became the far better screen. NIH-funded papers cited already-retracted work as often as other papers in the same journal and year. Links to retracted papers are a useful flag but not a screen on their own.

papers.title: GEAR: A GPU-Accelerated Global Solver for Bounded Continuous Nonlinear Programs via Linear Bound Propagation
papers.abstract: We present a novel GPU-accelerated global solver for constrained nonlinear programming (NLP) inspired by the efficient linear bound propagation framework in neural network (NN) verification. Existing work on NN verification, a problem that can be cast as feasibility detection for a nonlinear objective, demonstrated orders-of-magnitude speedups with the linear bound propagation-based framework when compared to traditional solvers. Extending this paradigm to global nonlinear programming requires addressing many challenges: a global constrained NLP solver must effectively exploit all, possibly unstructured, nonlinear constraints to improve the objective, whereas NN verification typically handles simple input box constraints over a well-structured NN and does not directly optimize an objective function. We address these challenges by fully exploiting the linear bounds produced by bound propagation: these linear bounds can be viewed as relaxations of nonlinear constraints and used to provide lower bounds, check infeasibility, and guide the search for a primal solution. In addition, we propose tighter linear relaxations for bilinear, quotient, and other commonly used nonlinear functions in NLP problems, and a projected augmented Lagrangian method tightly coupled to our dual solving procedure to produce primal solutions. Our method solves 421 of 505 bounded and continuous NLP problems in the GAMS and MINLPLib benchmarks under a 180-second limit, more than each of the six global solvers we compare with, including Gurobi and BARON (commercial), and SCIP (open-source). Sixteen of these problems are certified by none of the six global solvers; all of them contain exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric terms, which are often challenging for traditional approaches. Project webpage is at https://verified-intelligence.github.io/GEAR.

papers.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
papers.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

authors.name: Tianqi Shao
authors.institution: Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology

papers.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
papers.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

papers.title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
papers.abstract: Occupancy-based controls regulate lighting and HVAC according to whether a space is in use. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors, the most common choice, respond to motion and can report an occupied room as vacant when its occupants remain still. Sound offers an alternative cue, since seated occupants type, turn pages and cough, but microphones raise privacy concerns. We therefore study a two-stage design: an on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, and a server-side temporal model turns the stream of embeddings into an occupancy state. To our knowledge, no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels, so we evaluate the two stages separately on public data. The encoder is trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech, and tested on unseen rooms, recordings and speakers for whether a second contains a sound made by a person. On 11 real office recordings (DCASE 2013) it reaches an AUC of 0.87, against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on the transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of the spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69 to 77% of the utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding, or sending only class probabilities lowers this to 38 to 55% without hurting detection.
