We study this failure mode with ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic for multilingual visual-linguistic role binding. Each item contains a two-person action image with visually marked participants, one red and one blue, and a sentence whose grammatical role structure either matches or conflicts with the image. The key design is diagnostic rather than benchmark-maximal: before interpreting a joint image–sentence error, we separately test whether the model can identify the visual agent from the image and whether it can identify the linguistic agent from the sentence alone. Only then do we ask whether the sentence correctly describes the image.

Our experiments reveal a structured pattern of errors. Some models fail before the integration test: Aya-Vision-8B [10], for instance, does not pass the image-only role gate on several actions. Other models pass visual gating, but fail to parse some patient-first sentences. Another failure is response compliance: LLaVA-OneVision-7B reaches chance on several joint cells because it almost always accepts the sentence, so those cells are reported separately rather than counted as clean integration failures. In selected cases, component questions are answered correctly while the direct joint image–sentence decision fails. Qwen3-VL-8B [4], for example, reaches 99.0% image-only accuracy on the full 192-image set, but drops to 63.3% on Japanese agent-first and 65.1% on Turkish patient-first joint matching despite perfect text-only scores in those settings. At the same time, larger models substantially reduce the effect: Qwen3-VL-32B [4] is nearly perfect across the same conditions, and InternVL3.5-38B [27] passes the full visual gate and remains at or above 90% in all patient-first joint settings. papers.title: Strong relaxed dynamics in stochastic control
papers.abstract:
We characterize relaxed dynamics for which any finite family of strong state solutions, together with their relaxed inputs, can be approximated by the prescribed controlled dynamics, ground-stably in law.
  Relaxed inputs include parametrizations of relaxed controls over the unit interval. Unlike relaxed controls, these parametrizations determine action couplings. The proposed relaxed dynamics is driven by a single cylindrical Brownian motion in a Hilbert space. For each relaxed input, its state is the unique strong solution of the corresponding equation. The collection of these states, over all relaxed inputs, satisfies the approximation requirement.
  Conversely, suppose one assigns to each relaxed input a continuous adapted state process on a fixed probability space. Pairwise approximation forces the assignment to be the strong solution map of the same dynamics, for a unique cylindrical Brownian driver. In fact, even for a state map indexed by (non-parametrized) relaxed controls, the relevant relaxed control class admits coherent parametrizations under separability and finite-family approximation assumptions, and the same type of dynamics is recovered again.

papers.title: SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.
papers.intro:
IoT devices in factories, buildings and hospitals create a steady stream of computing tasks, and each task can run on a small edge server near the device or on a large cloud server far away [1, 2]. This range of places is called the edge-cloud continuum, and choosing where each task runs is called task offloading [3, 4]. A service level agreement (SLA) sets a latency limit for each type of task, and a task that finishes late violates it. IoT tasks are not equally urgent: latency-critical applications may need an answer within tens of milliseconds, while latency-tolerant ones can wait more than 100 ms [3]. Both compete for the same edge servers, so when the edge is busy the offloading policy, the rule that picks a place for each task, must decide which tasks to protect.

IoT devices in factories, buildings and hospitals create a steady stream of computing tasks, and each task can run on a small edge server near the device or on a large cloud server far away [1, 2]. This range of places is called the edge-cloud continuum, and choosing where each task runs is called task offloading [3, 4]. A service level agreement (SLA) sets a latency limit for each type of task, and a task that finishes late violates it. IoT tasks are not equally urgent: latency-critical applications may need an answer within tens of milliseconds, while latency-tolerant ones can wait more than 100 ms [3]. Both compete for the same edge servers, so when the edge is busy the offloading policy, the rule that picks a place for each task, must decide which tasks to protect.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) [5] is a common way to learn this policy [6]: the agent looks at the system, places a task and gets a reward. Two gaps remain. First, some RL offloading methods give every missed task the same penalty, whatever its class [7], so the average can look good while critical tasks keep missing their limit. Some recent methods give each class its own penalty [8], but they also change the state, the action set and the network, and no ablation run changes only the class penalties, so the effect of the penalty alone is unknown. Second, few offloading studies compare their agent with an optimum. Some compare with the best decision for a single time frame [9] or a single task graph [10], found by exhaustive search, and exact Markov decision process solutions exist for some small queued offloading problems [3]. However, none of the deep RL offloading studies cited here compares its agent with the optimal policy of a system with queues. Most compare only with simple rules and other agents, so it is not known how much better the policy could be.

This paper builds offloading systems that are small enough to solve exactly but keep the hard parts of the problem: up to four edge nodes of different speeds, up to three task classes, random background traffic and a cloud that meets some limits only by chance. For such systems, dynamic programming (DP) [11] gives the optimal policy, the Pareto frontier of miss rates, and the exact expected score of any policy that is a table over the states, including a trained network. It also gives the policy that a perfect learner of a given reward would reach, called the DP policy of that reward, which separates what a reward asks for from how well an agent learns it. The agents are trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO), deep Q-network (DQN), advantage actor-critic (A2C) and a Lagrangian variant of PPO.

The paper is a benchmark and methodology study that proposes no new learner but measures exactly how far common reward designs and standard learners are from the optimum. It makes four contributions. First, it gives an exact model of a family of multi-class edge-cloud offloading systems, checked against the simulator. Second, it shows that a reward with a bonus for a met limit ranks misses by the penalty plus the bonus, an effect that is short to prove but not visible in published designs. It explains why, for a perfect learner, a class-blind penalty minimizes the overall miss rate instead of the SLA cost, and it gives a simple rule to correct the penalties. Third, it reports a study with equal tuning budgets and 10 seeds for PPO, DQN and A2C in the nominal system and for PPO in three larger systems, with one run ten times longer than the main budget. The agents are compared with rules tuned on the exact model, with rewards based on two published designs, with a constrained PPO-Lagrangian agent and with the optimum, and PPO is tested under five changes of the nominal system. Fourth, the code, the results, the policy tables and the trained PPO networks are released.

papers.title: Breaking Precision Walls in First-, Second-, and Zeroth-Order Optimizers: One Constant, Set in Advance
papers.abstract: Under power-law signal decay across directions, an optimizer can fit strong directions and miss weak ones while average loss hides it. A precision wall measures the steepest decay where the weakest direction recovers within 5% in a fixed budget. On low-rank matrix sensing and quadratics one constant sets the wall: once it dominates the denominator, Adam or grafted Shampoo is momentum descent at step $\eta/c$, setting the wall; in Shampoo, matching grafting's constant to damping restores the wall after three hypotheses failed. In zeroth-order Adam, $\varepsilon$ acts against $\varepsilon^\ast$ from a mean-square spectral model; below $\varepsilon^\ast$ error hits a noise floor. Set from true curvature or spectrum on new shapes, the rule raised the wall above the same-step default by a forecast amount: on two sensing shapes by $1.96, 1.15$ (Adam) and $1.59, 1.74$ (grafted Shampoo), and on two Hadamard-rotated quadratics by $1.12, 0.73$ (zeroth-order Adam, longer budget), rising on all seeds; fixed-step momentum at that step reaches those walls. A cosine-scheduled default (small constant giving weak modes large steps) is higher on one sensing shape, matched on new seeds of the other, and lower with the rule's constant. A default step retuned per budget catches up on rotated quadratics and population logistic regression, fails at 1 query/step on two diagonal quadratics (catching up at 16), and exceeds the rule on digits logistic regression (full-batch and minibatches, where gradient noise sets the $\eta = 0.01, 0.1$ default walls). On logistic regression the rule did not raise the first-order wall: same-step default Adam was higher (its wall on 4 new shapes at the forecast stability limit), while in zeroth order on the population loss setting $\varepsilon$ raised the wall by $0.98, 0.88$.

Optimizer benchmarks usually report an average: validation loss, or, as in AlgoPerf (Dahl et al., 2023; Kasimbeg et al., 2025), the time needed to reach a validation target. When the data follow a power law, as word frequencies do (Kunstner et al., 2024) and as many feature spectra do (Bordelon et al., 2024), that average is set by a few strong directions. It says little about whether the rare directions were learned at all.

papers.title: A 43-vertex 4-chromatic unit-distance graph in the plane with girth 5
papers.abstract: We exhibit a set of 43 points in the Euclidean plane whose unit-distance graph has 83 edges, girth 5 and chromatic number 4. The smallest previously known 4-chromatic unit-distance graph of girth 5, due to Hochberg and O'Donnell (1996), has 45 vertices. The new graph is 4-critical, has trivial automorphism group, and has exactly 2n-3 edges; it is a Laman graph and its unit-distance realisation is infinitesimally rigid. The coordinates are algebraic numbers, specified as the unique real solution of an explicit system of 82 quadratic equations inside an explicit rational box. Every claim is certified by exact computation: existence and uniqueness of the realisation by a rational contraction-mapping certificate (independently re-checked with interval Krawczyk arithmetic), and non-3-colourability both by exhaustive search and by a DRAT proof verified with drat-trim.
papers.intro:
A unit-distance graph is a graph whose vertices are points of the plane, two points being adjacent when their Euclidean distance is exactly 11. The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks for the chromatic number χ⁡(ℝ2)\chi(\mathbb{R}^{2}) of the graph on all points of the plane; it is known that 5≤χ⁡(ℝ2)≤75\leq\chi(\mathbb{R}^{2})\leq 7 [1, 11].

papers.title: Cascading Circle Loss: Order-Preserving Contrastive Learning for Graded Legal Retrieval
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Cascading Circle Loss (CasCL), a contrastive learning framework for legal retrieval tasks with graded relevance. CasCL combines an InfoNCE objective for positive-negative separation with a cascade of ranking boundaries that model ordered relevance levels between queries and legal clauses. The framework also includes a negative-aware self-paced optimization mechanism and a relevance gain weighting strategy to improve ranking quality. Experiments on legal passage retrieval benchmarks show that CasCL consistently outperforms existing methods, including InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE, across both binary retrieval and graded ranking metrics.
papers.intro:
Legal professionals rely on retrieval systems to surface the most relevant paragraphs and extracted legal information for a given query (Locke and Zuccon, 2022; Sansone and Sperlì, 2022). Unlike generic information retrieval, where a single best match is often sufficient, legal retrieval requires a ranked slate of outputs: paragraphs that explicitly contain target labels or directly relevant extracted entities must be ranked above paragraphs that are only loosely related through shared wording or contextual similarity, which in turn must precede minimally related passages. This graded notion of relevance is fundamental in legal applications (Saracevic, 2007; Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002), as incorrect ordering can lead to incorrect information extraction, poor downstream reasoning, and degraded decision-making quality (Kim and Lee, 2025; Reuter et al., 2025).

Unlike web search, where a single best result often suffices, legal queries are rarely answered by a single paragraph in isolation. A query such as what are the penalties for late delivery under this agreement ? sits inside a dense neighbourhood of related material (van Opijnen and Santos, 2017): the clause defining timely delivery, the liability cap bounding the penalty, the force majeure provision that may suspend it, and the governing law clause that determines interpretation. Each is topically related, yet only one directly answers the query; the rest occupy intermediate positions on a relevance spectrum.

Legal corpora exhibit three structural properties that make fine-grained ranking essential. First, high lexical overlap: statutes and contractual clauses use highly standardized language, so neighbouring paragraphs often share near identical phrasing while encoding distinct legal conditions (Mori et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), binary supervision cannot distinguish them. Second, hierarchical relevance: a legal topic (e.g liability, confidentiality) is rarely confined to a single paragraph but distributed across definitions, exceptions, and remedies, inducing a continuous relevance spectrum that discrete labels fail to capture (van Opijnen and Santos, 2017; Feng et al., 2024) . Third, sensitivity to misranking: when the top of the ranked slate mixes directly applicable clauses with merely related ones, ordering errors propagate to downstream tasks, extraction pipelines pull wrong spans, summarizers conflate distinct legal meanings, and reasoning systems inherit ranking errors as factual errors (Kim and Lee, 2025; Reuter et al., 2025).

A loss function suited to this setting therefore needs four properties simultaneously:

1. Robust positive–negative separation, so the retriever still excels at the binary task that existing systems are evaluated on; 2. Intra-positive ordering: among relevant passages, higher relevance must yield higher similarity, with gaps reflecting the relevance difference. 3. Top-of-ranking focus: not all ordering errors are equally costly (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002); swapping positions 1 and 2 matters far more than swapping 10 and 11. The loss should concentrate gradient on the top of the ranking. 4. Robustness to ambiguous relevance: in large batch training with graded labels, lower ranked items tend to carry more ambiguous relevance scores (Shao et al., 2023), a passage scored at r = 0.15 or r = 0.10 may reflect annotator (or LLM) noise (Zheng et al., 2023) rather than a genuine relevance difference. The loss should down weight ordering constraints where label uncertainty is highest.

No existing contrastive loss satisfies all four properties simultaneously. Binary losses such as InfoNCE (van den Oord et al., 2018) address property 1 but ignore intra-positive ordering entirely (Wullach et al., 2026; Esfandiarpoor et al., 2025). Self-paced losses like Circle Loss (Sun et al., 2020) lack inter-positive structure. Chain-based approaches such as Ladder Loss (Zhou et al., 2020) enforce ordering but with fixed margins and no self-pacing. Recent graded extensions, CLOC (Pitawela et al., 2025), Mine & Refine (Xi et al., 2026), and soft-target variants (Zhu et al., 2025; Denize et al., 2022), either require multi-stage pipelines, discretise the relevance spectrum, or provide no geometric ordering guarantee. We position CasCL against each of these methods in detail in §2.

We observe that positive–negative separation (property 1) and intra-positive ordering (property 2) are structurally independent: the first is a binary discrimination problem, the second a fine-grained relative comparison within the positive set. CasCL decouples them: InfoNCE sees only the best positive and all negatives, establishing the absolute scale; a cascade of self-paced circular boundaries orders the graded positives, with each item invisible to the other term. The design rationale is detailed in §3.1.

CasCL decouples them: InfoNCE sees only the best positive and all negatives, establishing the absolute scale; a cascade of self-paced circular boundaries orders the graded positives, with each item invisible to the other term. papers.title: DICOMPUTE: An Economic and Privacy-Aware Framework for Distributed Artificial Intelligence Inference
papers.abstract: The prevailing design of large-scale artificial intelligence inference concentrates accelerators, model weights, and request processing in centralized computing facilities. Centralization offers important benefits in accelerator utilization, high-bandwidth interconnects, operational control, and serving efficiency. Yet centralized infrastructure is not always the least-cost or most governance-compatible choice for every inference workload. This paper develops a research framework for DICOMPUTE, a heterogeneous distributed inference architecture in which policy-constrained scheduling can allocate suitable requests across privately controlled, regional, and independently operated computing resources. We derive a full-cost comparison that accounts for capital amortization, energy, network transfer, orchestration, utilization, failures, and trust-related expenses; characterize conditions under which distributed inference can outperform centralized alternatives; and specify a privacy model separating data residency, transport confidentiality, execution confidentiality, and verifiable accounting. We propose falsifiable hypotheses and a reproducible experimental design, without presenting simulated examples as measured performance. Our central conclusion is conditional: distributed inference is most promising for divisible, latency-tolerant or locality-sensitive workloads on underutilized compatible hardware, while centralized clusters retain structural advantages for tightly coupled, memory-intensive, high-throughput inference. The framework is intended to support rigorous evaluation rather than to assert universal superiority.
papers.intro:
Artificial intelligence infrastructure is often discussed as a choice between hyperscale data centers and small edge devices. In practice, inference demand spans a continuum: interactive language-model requests, document classification, radiology assistance, enterprise retrieval, batch embeddings, and autonomous software agents differ substantially in model size, memory footprint, privacy requirements, latency tolerance, and traffic patterns. An architecture optimized for one class need not be efficient for another.

Centralized inference can pool demand and exploit sophisticated serving engines, fast accelerator interconnects, continuous batching, and predictable operations. These advantages are substantial and must be treated as the benchmark rather than assumed away. At the same time, organizations own compatible compute that may be idle outside peak hours, while some data cannot leave an approved jurisdiction or institution. A heterogeneous inference fabric offers a way to allocate eligible workloads to available resources subject to explicit constraints.

It is deliberately not a software implementation audit, a token promotional document, or a claim that every conceptual privacy mechanism has been deployed. The research question is not whether distribution is intrinsically superior, but when, why, and at what full cost a policy-aware distributed system is preferable to a centralized one.

papers.title: Extending DBLog-Based Incremental Snapshots to Handle Orphan Rows in CDC Pipelines
papers.abstract:
Applications use heterogeneous datastores where a source feeds sinks such as search indexes or data warehouses via change data capture (CDC). As transaction logs have limited retention, CDC alone cannot bootstrap sinks, and traditional approaches either stall source writes or hold back log events. DBLog-based incremental snapshots, adopted by Debezium and Flink CDC, read tables in chunks interleaved with the log without blocking writes or long log stalls and resume where they stopped.
  After the initial bootstrap, a sink can drift when losing change events or receiving unintended writes. Even a repeated bootstrap can leave orphan rows that exist in the sink and not at the source. A common remedy is to populate a new empty sink, but repairing an existing sink avoids parallel pipelines, a switch and serving traffic from a drifted sink until the new sink is ready.
  In DBLog's original design, each chunk only emits the latest state of the rows the table still contains, so it does not handle orphan rows. We extend DBLog to delete them using what a chunk read already knows, namely the keys that the range select did not return, emitting a new kind of event that sinks apply as deletes. We also add a repair request that an external process calls with orphan candidates, which the connector checks with its own read, emitting these events for keys confirmed absent. This enables three modes. In the fully integrated mode, every chunk pass removes the orphans it finds during full or periodic repairs. In the second mode, an external drift process hands suspected orphans to the connector. The third mode combines both and is what we recommend.
  Together, they turn DBLog into a complete data synchronization engine whether a sink catches up on live changes or missing rows, holds wrong column values, or contains orphan rows. Their safety and convergence are formally verified in Isabelle/HOL and Lean 4.

papers.title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
papers.abstract: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

papers.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems face two costs that research comparisons rarely measure: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions carrying chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. On the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus we verify that, after deleting 10% of the documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare Lightfoot with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three datasets, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3-6x below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Against HippoRAG 2 it is significantly better on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10 on a held-out split) and on HotpotQA answers (+7.7 points exact match), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours; fast-graphrag has no deletion path. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG
papers.intro:
Retrieval-augmented generation [14] grounds a language model in documents retrieved at query time. Plain similarity search fails on multi-hop questions whose evidence is spread over passages that the question never names. GraphRAG systems address this by extracting entities and relations into a graph and traversing it at query time [4, 9, 10, 8]; surveys catalogue dozens of variants [11, 20].

GraphRAG systems address this by extracting entities and relations into a graph and traversing it at query time [4, 9, 10, 8]; surveys catalogue dozens of variants [11, 20].

Published comparisons focus on answer accuracy. Two properties that decide whether a system can be operated in an organisation receive little attention. The first is index cost: extraction dominates the bill, and frameworks differ by an order of magnitude because of second extraction passes, model-written entity summaries and community reports. The second is deletion. Retention policies, contract expiry and the right to erasure [6] require removing a document and everything derived from it. Summaries that blend information from many documents make this expensive or impossible. A merged entity description must be regenerated, and a community report cannot be attributed to its sources at all. Machine unlearning studies the analogous problem for model weights [1]. For retrieval indexes the problem is usually unmeasured.

papers.title: Advancements in Cloud-Native Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study of Reliability and Scalability across Cloud-Native, Edge-Native and AI-Enabled Systems
papers.abstract: Cloud-native systems now extend to the network edge and host artificial-intelligence (AI) workloads, including AI agents, but evidence on their reliability and scalability is scattered and uneven. We report a PRISMA 2020 systematic mapping study with an evidence-graded synthesis. Five logged OpenAlex searches on 11 October 2026 covered cloud-native systems, edge AI, agentic AI for operations, reliability of agentic applications and physical AI; 189 records from an earlier exploratory search were added separately. After 301 duplicate removals and an automated peer-review venue rule, 4,611 records were screened against written criteria and a five-level relevance scale. The review includes 1,794 primary studies from 2017-2026 and 95 secondary studies, with every decision released in Dataset S1. Each primary study was assigned to a 13-category taxonomy and graded as simulation, prototype or testbed, production data, production deployment, or not determinable from the abstract. Of 1,003 studies with a determinable level, 66.2% used prototypes or testbeds, 18.0% simulations and 15.8% production data or deployments. A 93-study synthesis core, appraised from indexed abstracts, shows production deployments of cascading-failure prevention, trace- and graph-based root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling, and production-trace evaluations of cold-start mitigation. Edge reliability and physical AI rely mainly on simulations and testbeds. AI-agent reliability uses tool-grounded diagnosis, explicit safety properties, trace-driven repair and workload-aware scheduling, while empirical studies show that agent frameworks remain fragile. Conclusions are limited to the documented corpus. The principal gaps are production evidence for edge-native systems, shared resilience benchmarks and dependable agentic operations.

papers.title: Two barriers for minimal time firing squads, with applications to four and five states
papers.abstract: A minimal-time solution of the firing squad synchronization problem synchronizes every line of n cells at time 2n minus 2. Six states suffice; whether five do has been open since 1987. Every line agrees with the half line until its right ends echo returns. For minimal time solutions with any number of states, we prove that cells at distance j behind the half lines front become time-periodic only after time (1.5 minus epsilon)j, for every epsilon greater than 0 and infinitely many j, and that the half line is never periodic in time and space on a wedge at its left border, hence not eventually regular in our sense. With certified satisfiability checks, we exclude four states using the lines of lengths 2 to 5 and parts of the next five, and show that every five state minimal time solution uses at least 15 non quiescent neighbourhoods on its half lines first 78 anti-diagonals. We give five state rules synchronizing exactly the lengths 2 to 14.

papers.intro:
The firing squad synchronization problem, posed by Myhill in 1957 and made popular by Moore [1], asks for a finite automaton with the following property. Copies of the automaton are placed in the cells of a line of arbitrary length nn. At time 00 the leftmost cell, the general, is in a special state and all other cells are quiescent. At each step every cell updates its state from its own state and the states of its two neighbours. All cells must then enter a firing state at the same time, and none of them earlier. The difficulty is that the cells are identical, that each sees only its two neighbours, and that a cell with kk states cannot count up to nn: the same finite rule has to synchronize lines of every length.

No line can be synchronized before time 2​n−22n-2: the order of the general needs n−1n-1 steps to reach the far end of the line, and the news that the far end exists needs n−1n-1 more steps to come back. Goto [2] and Waksman [3] showed that time 2​n−22n-2 can be achieved, and a solution that synchronizes every line of length n≥2n\geq 2 at time 2​n−22n-2 is called a minimal-time solution. Since then, the least number of states of a minimal-time solution has been a benchmark question of cellular automata theory [4, 5, 6]. Waksman’s solution has 1616 states, Balzer’s 88 [7], Gerken’s 77 [8] and Mazoyer’s 66 [9]. In the other direction, Balzer [7] reported a computer search showing that no four-state minimal-time solution exists; Sanders [11] confirmed this with a search of his own, and Yunès [10] repeated the search and observed that the lines of lengths 2,…,92,\dots,9 suffice. Many six-state minimal-time solutions are known today [12, 13]; solutions with at most five states are known for restricted families of lengths, such as the powers of two, some of them in non-minimal time [14, 15], and four-state protocols synchronize the rings whose lengths are powers of two [16]. Whether a five-state minimal-time solution exists has been open since Mazoyer’s construction [5, 6].

A rule can be refuted by a single line that it fails to synchronize, but a minimal-time solution has to synchronize every line, so a proof that five states do not suffice must exclude all rules. The difficulty is to find conditions that are strong enough and cheap enough to check. This paper proves such conditions for every number of states and measures how far they reach for four and five states.

papers.title: Triangle-overlap cores and density bounds for Tuza's conjecture
papers.abstract:
For a finite simple graph $G$, let $
u(G)$ be the maximum number of edge-disjoint triangles and let $	au(G)$ be the minimum number of edges meeting every triangle. We prove $	au(G)\le2
u(G)$ when each edge belongs to at most four triangles, the edges belonging to four triangles form components with at most two edges, and the maximum average degree is at most $25/2$. No upper bound on maximum vertex degree is imposed. We also localize the density condition. Let $K$ be the Hifumi core, defined as the vertex set of the 4-core of the spanning subgraph formed by edges belonging to at least three triangles. It suffices to impose the density condition on $G[K]$, including all original edges between vertices of $K$. More generally, when the four-triangle edges have maximum degree at most two, reductions produce a subgraph $R\subseteq G[K]$ with $	au(G)-2
u(G)\le	au(R)-2
u(R)$. Consequently an empty core gives a density-free sufficient condition. For the first graph class, a quantitative surplus argument strengthens both the global and localized density conditions to the strict bound $25/2+2/56775$. The proof combines edge reductions, discharging, finite certificates and a weak K"onig--Egerv'ary lemma for links of arbitrary order. The general conjecture and the removal of the density condition from the first graph class remain unresolved here.

papers.title: Samyama-SDG: A Declarative GraphQL @count and Regex/Ontology Synthetic Data Compiler with $O(1)$-Memory Referential Integrity and Causal Ground Truth
papers.abstract:
Synthetic data generators face a divide between declarative relational mockets and domain causal simulators. Declarative generators specify entities, regexes, and foreign keys via schemas, but buffer parent primary-key pools in RAM ($O(N)$ memory) and lack ontology bindings or causal ground truth. Conversely, domain simulators emit realistic streams and ground-truth labels, but require thousands of lines of procedural code per domain.
  We present Samyama-SDG (sdg-rs), a Rust synthetic data compiler unifying declarative schema compilation with ontology-bound causal simulation. At Layer 1, Samyama-SDG compiles Cardinality-Extended GraphQL schemas (@count, @pk, @ontology, @regex, @dist, @fk, @after) and an Attribute Data Dictionary into a topologically sorted DAG. Combining stateless counter-based seekable PRNGs (SplitMix64 over $(\text{seed}, \text{entity}, \text{row}, \text{field})$) with index-bijective primary keys $f_{\text{PK}}(s, E, i)$ lets child tables resolve uniform or Zipfian foreign keys and multi-hop @after constraints in $O(1)$ memory without buffering parent tables. At Layer 2, causal processes layer fault propagation and machine-scorable ground truth (ground_truth.jsonl) over the same seekable PRNG and samyama-ontologies binder. Across three schemas, Samyama-SDG generates $1{,}000{,}000$ records in $128.79\text{ ms}$--$172.43\text{ ms}$ ($5.80\text{M}$--$7.76\text{M}$ rows/s) and $5{,}000{,}000$ records in $676.12\text{ ms}$--$808.56\text{ ms}$ at flat $31.4\text{ MiB}$--$35.1\text{ MiB}$ memory, with $0$ conformance errors across $1{,}150{,}000$ foreign keys and $900{,}000$ temporal constraints.

Benchmarking relational databases, property graph engines, and machine-learning pipelines requires synthetic datasets that simultaneously satisfy structural integrity, statistical realism, vocabulary compliance, and reproducibility. Benchmarking relational databases, property graph engines, and machine-learning pipelines requires synthetic datasets that simultaneously satisfy structural integrity, statistical realism, vocabulary compliance, and reproducibility. Over the past three decades, synthetic data generation has evolved along three largely separate tracks:

1. Declarative schema and constraint generators. Systems following Gray et al. [1], Bruno and Chaudhuri’s Data Generation Language (DGL) [2], Houkjær et al. [3], and modern developer tools allow users to declare table schemas, attribute regular expressions, and foreign-key relationships. Consequently, memory consumption grows linearly (O⁡(N)O(N)) with dataset scale, and sequential stateful random number generators couple column values: adding one attribute to a schema shifts the random stream for every subsequent attribute and table. 2. papers.title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
papers.abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.
papers.intro:
Agents built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [1] and similar function-calling interfaces act on behalf of a user through tools: mail, calendars, file stores, banking and messaging APIs. Whatever the agent reads can carry instructions. In indirect prompt injection [2], an attacker plants text in a document, web page, or tool description that the agent later reads, and the agent then issues calls such as “send these files to this address” that no one authorized. Defenses that inspect text or reasoning may be bypassed by a sufficiently persuasive payload, so a complementary line of work constrains what the agent can do rather than what it reads [3, 4, 5, 6].

Our system belongs to that line. Its premise is that the user’s objective already determines most of what a legitimate run needs: the tools involved, some argument values (the named recipient, file, channel, hotel, dates), and sometimes an order. We ask an LLM once per task, before any tool output is read, to write this down as an executable intent graph, and then audit every call against it with plain code. Because the graph is produced from the trusted objective and the static tool catalog only, an injected instruction cannot enlarge it. The price of least privilege is false positives: a plan misses tools that a legitimate run needs. We reduce them in two ways. First, calls that only read the user’s own state bypass the audit: an injected read does no harm unless the agent then writes or sends something, and those steps stay audited. Second, a reasoning guardian re-examines the calls that are still flagged and can verify claims with executed code, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models [7].

In an AgentDojo task, the user asks, “Who else is invited at the ‘Networking event’ on May 26th? Please give me their email addresses and a summary of the event.” The extracted plan lists calendar and contact lookups only. The agent reads the event, whose description contains an injected instruction to send an email to an attacker-controlled address, and issues send_email. The undefended agent was compromised in the logged run. send_email is not in the plan, so the audit blocks it, in each of three independent graph extractions, while the two legitimate calls pass.

(1) We describe an intent-graph audit with a leak-free LLM extraction step and a deterministic runtime loop, including a hardened scope-expression language (Section 4). (2) We show that classifying tools as local reads, external reads and writes removes a large share of false positives at no cost in harmful-step attack success, while bypassing an external read such as a URL fetch does cost security (Section 6). (3) We add a START-style reasoning guardian for flagged calls and show that it preserves security while reducing benign flags (Section 8). (4) We give an evaluation protocol on AgentDojo that avoids three shortcuts that arise easily when policies are generated or calibrated from session data: label-informed policy calibration, a session-derived tool list given to the extractor, and overlap between calibration and evaluation data (Section 5). (5) We quantify the security/utility trade-off with ablations that approximate tool-allowlist, per-call argument-policy, and planned-dependency-graph defenses (Section 6). (6) We test, and reject, the hypothesis that feeding the audit’s alignment score into an identity-drift detector improves detection (Section 9).

papers.title: Gamma classes, central connection matrices, and tt* geometry
papers.abstract: We review the gamma class of complex projective space, but from the point of view of topological-antitopological fusion. We deconstruct the central connection matrix which appears in the work of Dubrovin, Galkin-Golyshev-Iritani, and Cotti-Dubrovin-Guzzetti.
papers.intro:
This article is a contribution to the task of understanding better the gamma class, the Dubrovin Conjecture (which relates quantum cohomology, Stokes data, and exceptional sequences), and some of the underlying physics. We shall focus on the well known but remarkable example of complex projective space ℂ​Pn\mathbb{C}P^{n}, a gamma function calculation that was pioneered by Hosono and Iritani, and the role of the tt* equations.

papers.title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
papers.abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.
papers.intro:
Many deployed agents are small open models whose weights stay fixed. What can still change is the harness: the prompt, notes, tools and control logic around the model. A growing literature lets the agent, or a larger teacher, rewrite this harness from the agent’s own traces (records of its interactions) [1, 2, 3, 4]. We ask whether giving a teacher model access to a frozen Qwen3.5-9B agent’s interaction traces helps it write notes that improve the agent’s performance. We compare notes written with and without failure traces on generated retail decisions. We then compare the trace-written libraries with the standard harness in official retail conversations. Separately, we screen individual lessons; on BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard) multi-turn, the lessons the screen admits are also tested on held-out tasks. Every primary analysis was pre-registered.

Every primary analysis was pre-registered.

Comparing a learned harness with its starting point mixes several sources of gain. The first is search: a writer that proposes texts and keeps the best ones on a development set can improve the agent without reading any failure. The second is evidence: the writer read the agent’s failures and encoded something about them. Our comparison tests the added value of access to the episode contents within this procedure. Our control only partly separates these sources of improvement. It used the same budget limits and retained development feedback, but the actual search could differ. Its gains could therefore come from search, candidate selection, restating supplied rules, or adding text.

The question matters because recent work is sceptical. Under matched budgets, harness evolution did not beat parallel sampling [5]. Failure-derived experience repairs the source tasks of self-evolving agents but rarely transfers to unseen ones, on backbones that include ours [6, 7, 8]. Some frontier agents do improve from their own artefacts [9]. On the same retail domain, ALTK-Evolve reports pass^4 rising from 57.5 to 67.5 on 40 held-out tasks from GPT-4.1’s own traces, without a matched no-evidence control (a since-closed issue reported that its retail adapter mined test-split tasks by default) [10, 11]. On SkillsBench, skills an agent wrote for itself scored 42.9%, against 45.5% with no skills [12]. Several late-2026 studies report regressions, without significance tests: all sixteen evolved agents in one study lost tasks they had previously solved [13]; a coding harness evolved across successive task types forgot earlier ones [14]; previously solved instances regressed in 8 of 18 method–task pairs [15]; and memories of benign sessions led agents to skip confirmation on later high-stakes tasks [16]. Gains are also reported around frozen models from evolving prompts, tools and memory [17], and exposing the scorer’s success criteria to the learner can yield gains that reflect the verifier rather than the task [18]. Model developers instead mostly turn agent failures into training environments for the weights [19], or rewrite the agent’s verified runs into training data [20]. What is still missing is a way to tell, when a loop does show a gain, whether the agent’s traces produced it.

(2) That search alone reached about 60% of the gain over the standard harness. (3) The same lesson libraries showed no demonstrated improvement in official τ2\tau^{2} retail conversations. papers.title: Sections of the Kottwitz homomorphism and affine pinnings
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a connected reductive group split over $\mathbb{Z}$. The Kottwitz homomorphism identifies the group of connected components of the loop group of $G$ with the group $\Omega$ of length zero elements of the extended affine Weyl group. We show that this homomorphism always has a homomorphic section, and that the section can be chosen inside the normalizer of $T$ in $G(\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}])$. We then ask whether the section can be chosen to preserve an affine pinning. This is possible if no simple factor of $G$ is of type $B_{2m}$ or $C_{2m}$. It is impossible for $(SL_2\times Sp_{2n})/\mu_2$ and $(SL_2\times Spin_{2n+1})/\mu_2$ when $n$ is even. We show that the obstructions for $G$ and for its Langlands dual group are dual to each other, and we compute them by a lattice computation with a Coxeter element. As an application, we show that the component group of the centralizer of any semisimple element lifts to the centralizer. Under the same condition on the simple factors, the lift can be chosen to preserve a pinning of the neutral component.

papers.title: Global Classification of the Flat Singular Escobar-Yamabe Equation
papers.abstract: In every dimension $n\geq3$, we classify positive solutions of the flat Escobar--Yamabe equation on the Euclidean half-space with a possible isolated boundary singularity at the origin. Solutions with a removable singularity are boundary bubbles. Up to dilation, the nonremovable solutions are the cylindrical solution and a family of periodic Delaunay solutions uniquely parametrized by the necksize $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, the minimum of the normalized boundary trace. In each fundamental period $T_\epsilon$, the trace has exactly two critical points, a nondegenerate minimum and a nondegenerate maximum. The period and the solution centered at the trace minimum and rescaled to period one depend smoothly on $\epsilon$. As $\epsilon \to 0$, $T_\epsilon = \frac{4}{n-2}\log(1/\epsilon)+O(1)$. As $\epsilon \to 1$, the solutions converge to the cylindrical solution and their periods tend to that of its linearized oscillation. We use uniqueness in the odd and even classes for linear Robin equations to obtain reflection symmetry and continuation in the necksize.

papers.title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: My Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
papers.abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $\pi_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
papers.intro:
RoboEval [1] asks for policies that are “not just successful but well-behaved”. The challenge has eight bimanual tasks with two Franka arms (lifting a pot or a tray, stacking blocks, shelving or picking a book, a cube handover, packing a box, and rotating valves), each evaluated on 50 seeds with randomised positions and orientations; I train a single policy for all eight. The RoboEval Diagnostic Score (RDS) combines, per task, the outcome O=0.7​success+0.3​stage progressO=0.7\,\text{success}+0.3\,\text{stage progress} with behavioral metrics (safety, efficiency and coordination) scored against the median human demonstration: RDS=0.4​O+O⁡(0.3​S+0.2​E+0.1​C)\text{RDS}=0.4\,O+O\,(0.3\,S+0.2\,E+0.1\,C). A perfect score needs every stage of every task, every time, done at least as cleanly as a human does it.

I treated it as two problems. The generic one is “make a pretrained VLA better at an arbitrary score”, which my LeHome solution [2] already does: it optimises any target that can be computed, and its exploration acts exactly where this score is decided — speed, smoothness, and how action chunks connect. The competition-specific one is everything this recipe cannot reach: behavior that no demonstration shows and that is too far from the policy to be found by local exploration.

papers.title: A note on exact external information complexity
papers.abstract: We study the prior-free zero-error private-coin external information complexity $B(f)$ of finite two-party functions, with correctness on every input. An elementary rectangle/entropy argument gives $B(\mathsf{AND})=\log_2 3$. A complete classification of Boolean $3\times3$ matrices leaves, up to input permutations and output complementation, only the two-overlapping-rectangles function $F$ without an exact value. An entropy potential and a finite rational protocol give $2.1212661667060486842\ldots\le B(F)<2.130998318$. We also determine its deterministic external information and zero-error communication costs. A separate product-prior certificate and internal-information additivity yield $R_0^{\mathrm{pub}}(F^{\times t})\ge2.021991187178562\ldots\,t$, strictly exceeding the fractional-cover rate $2t$.

papers.title: Random Configurations and Fourier Decoupling
papers.abstract: We use tools from high dimensional probability to analyze random configurations of balls in the context of Fourier decoupling and we answer a question on the structure of superlevel sets in the setting of decoupling due to Guth.

papers.intro:
In this article we will study random configurations in the context of Fourier decoupling theory and will answer a question of Guth [15]. Heuristics coming from probability theory often play an important guiding role in Fourier analysis. The notions of square root cancellation, pseudo-randomness and probabilistic models for various Fourier-analytic and number theoretic objects can often tell us how these objects should behave. These heuristics can help us formulate conjectures and could also help us determine the types of inquiry that may yield progress on important problems. With this in mind, it can be fruitful to study random configurations in the context of Fourier analysis. For example, the work of Bourgain and Talagrand on Λ⁡(p)\Lambda(p) sets [2] [19], and the work of Mockenhaupt and Schlag [17] on the Hardy-Littlewood majorant problem have helped govern heuristics for the study of exponential sums and have also found applications in compressed sensing and signal processing (see [16], [5], [21] for illustrative examples). We investigate ideas along these lines in the context of Fourier decoupling. A central question in this context is: what is the typical behavior of natural Fourier analytic objects? In [18] the author investigated random configurations in the context of the Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture, and showed that the Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture is true most11 1 To be precise, it was shown that a generic random weight satisfies a sharp inequality of Mizohata-Takeuchi type. See [18], [3], [4] for context and discussion on this problem. of the time. We use some of the tools developed in [18] and refine them to answer questions about the typical behavior of configurations that naturally arise in the context of Fourier decoupling.

papers.title: Derived invariance of the space of holomorphic two-forms
papers.abstract:
Let $\Phi:D^b(X)\to D^b(Y)$ be a derived equivalence between smooth projective complex varieties, and let $h=c_1(L)$ for an ample line bundle $L$ on $X$. For $z\in\mathbb{C}$, transporting the cup-product action and evaluating at $e^{zh}$ gives a homomorphism of graded algebras $\Theta^\bullet_{F,z}:H^\bullet(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\to H^\bullet(X,\mathcal O_X)$, where $F$ is the cohomological transform of $\Phi$. We prove that $\Theta^\bullet_{F,i}$ is an isomorphism in degrees one and two. In particular, $X$ and $Y$ have the same number of holomorphic two-forms. The proof in degree two uses the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations on $X$ and on $X\times X$.
  We also prove derived invariance of all Hodge numbers when $K_X$ is trivial and the conjugate of a holomorphic volume form belongs to the subalgebra of $H^\bullet(X,\mathcal O_X)$ generated in degrees one and two. In even dimension, the evaluation isomorphism allows us to compare the ranks of cup product by powers of symplectic two-forms on the Hochschild diagonals. These ranks determine the Hodge numbers individually.

papers.title: The Alt-Phillips Multiple Membrane Free Boundary Problem
papers.abstract: Motivated by diffusion--reaction processes in porous catalysts, we study an Alt--Phillips model for ordered membranes with weighted gap interactions. The model connects adhesive harmonic junctions \cite{DSS24} and forced multiple membranes \cite{SY19} through the exponent $0<\gamma<1$. For arbitrary positive weights, we prove optimal $C^{1,\beta-1}$ regularity, where $\beta=2/(2-\gamma)$, and obtain nontrivial $\beta$-homogeneous blowup limits through Weiss almost monotonicity. Under strict discrete concavity of the weights, we establish a gluing principle, minimality of flat single-gap cones, and $C^{1,\alpha}$ free boundary regularity at points admitting such blowups. We also classify all one-dimensional vertically critical cones. For three membranes, we identify cone families that are non-minimizing for small $\gamma$ and minimizing near $\gamma=1$.

papers.title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
papers.abstract: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes and evicts 26 bystander pods, because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single io.MultiWriter. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.
papers.intro:
Serving a large model on Kubernetes, on a managed cloud service or a self-run cluster alike, begins with a delivery problem: hundreds of gigabytes of weights must reach the node before the first prediction. Eager image pulling pays that cost up front and scales linearly with size; lazy pulling—eStargz/stargz-snapshotter [3] and AWS SOCI [4]—mounts the image immediately and fetches content on demand, making cold time-to-first-prediction essentially independent of model size [2]. For autoscaled and scale-to-zero serving fleets, where every replica added under load pays the delivery cost before serving a single request, this is the difference between seconds and tens of minutes [1].

The price of that deferral is paid by a component most operators never configure and the platform does not account for: the snapshotter’s node-level cache, shared by every lazily mounted image on the node, into which every fetched chunk is written. In prior work we characterized what happens when its volume fills under purely legitimate load [2]: pods that are already Ready and serving begin failing reads of their model files—67–94% of files at high residual occupancy—while the pod’s readiness, health endpoint, and prediction endpoint remain green (for at least 196 s in our instrumented timeline). The failure is invisible to every management-plane signal Kubernetes exposes—readiness, liveness, prediction endpoints, node conditions, events—and observable only in snapshotter-specific telemetry that serving stacks do not collect by default. It is a fault with no symptom at the layer that owns remediation.

Why not just monitor better, or let the platform react? These are the two remediation routes a cluster operator actually has, monitoring and platform-driven eviction, and we close both empirically before building. First, detection-side mitigation is structurally limited: we built the natural mitigation—a readiness probe that reads sentinel files through the mount—and it reported green while 272 of 280 files were unreadable, because damage concentrates in file regions the probe’s sample does not cover. A sampling probe converts silent corruption into a dice roll, not a guarantee. Second, platform-side remediation acts on the wrong accounting: with the cache partition exported to kubelet’s image filesystem accounting and production eviction thresholds enabled, kubelet correctly raised NodeHasDiskPressure—and then freed 0 bytes, because containerd reports 741 KB of reclaimable image storage while 91.1 GiB of cache sits on disk, and fell through to evicting 26 pods that had never touched the partition. The platform is sighted but powerless: the gap is not signal; it is an actuator keyed to accounting that does not know the cache exists. Elimination must therefore happen inside the component that owns the bytes.

This paper makes four contributions: • Two measured impossibility results. Monitoring-side and platform-side remediation, the two routes available to an operator, are each shown by experiment to be unable to contain this failure class: a sentinel probe stays green while 272/280 files are unreadable, and kubelet with full pressure visibility frees nothing and evicts bystanders. These generalize to any node-local cache outside the platform’s reclamation accounting (Sections II, VI). • A bounded cache that survives its own accounting. Byte-budget eviction driven by a durable chunk index, with the pressure signal keyed to filesystem truth precisely because the index is lossy by contract: the filesystem decides how much, the index decides which. The budget held against ∼\sim301,000 dropped accounting updates where a naïve rule died at ∼\sim127,000 (Sections III, V). • An honest data path, with its root cause. Pass-through semantics—a chunk that cannot be cached is served to its caller and simply not kept—sever the failure structurally; the coupling they sever is traced to a single io.MultiWriter on the fetch path, with a regression test that fails on the parent commit and passes on our fix (Sections III, IV). • Evaluation on AWS against the failure suite of our companion study, through tenancy and fleet scale. The before/after is run on identical rigs: upstream fails 273/280 files at 90% pre-fill (three independent reproductions); our system serves 280/280 across the full 150.3 GB read at +18.5% completion cost, with the budget never exceeded while 224.6 GB is evicted under the read. papers.title: Calibrated Alarm Thresholds for Compact Fire and Smoke Detectors
papers.abstract: Compact object detectors such as YOLOv8n are a common choice for camera-based fire and smoke detection on low-power devices. These detectors are usually evaluated with box-level metrics such as mean average precision, and their outputs are turned into decisions with a fixed confidence threshold such as 0.25 or 0.5. A fire monitoring system, however, makes one decision per image: raise an alarm or not. In this paper we evaluate two publicly available compact detectors on the D-Fire test set at the image level. We compare three simple rules for turning box detections into one alarm score per image, and we use a split conformal procedure to choose the alarm threshold from held-out images so that the expected fraction of missed fire and smoke images stays below a chosen target. We find that the same fixed threshold leads to very different miss rates for the two detectors, 17.3 and 8.4 percent at a threshold of 0.5, while the calibrated threshold meets miss-rate targets of 10, 5 and 1 percent for both detectors and all three rules. At a 5 percent target, the false alarm rate on images without fire or smoke stays between 1.2 and 3.0 percent. We also find that smoke-only images stay below the target even when the overall target is met, and we describe the main failure cases.
papers.intro:
Early detection of fire and smoke can limit damage and save lives. Camera-based detection is attractive because cameras are cheap and already installed in many places. Early vision methods used hand-crafted color rules for flame pixels [1]. Later work moved to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [2], and today most systems use object detectors from the YOLO family [3]. Small variants of these detectors, such as YOLOv5n or YOLOv8n, are popular because they can run on low-power devices [4, 5].

Early detection of fire and smoke can limit damage and save lives. Camera-based detection is attractive because cameras are cheap and already installed in many places. Early vision methods used hand-crafted color rules for flame pixels [1]. Later work moved to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [2], and today most systems use object detectors from the YOLO family [3]. Small variants of these detectors, such as YOLOv5n or YOLOv8n, are popular because they can run on low-power devices [4, 5].

Most papers in this area report box-level metrics such as precision, recall and mean average precision (mAP) on benchmarks like D-Fire [4]. A deployed system, however, has to answer a simpler question for every frame: is there fire or smoke in this image or not? Two choices sit between the detector output and this answer. The first is how to turn a set of boxes into one decision. The second is which confidence threshold to use. In practice the threshold is usually fixed, for example at 0.25 [6], and evaluations of detector calibration often fix it at 0.3 or 0.5 [7]. Detector confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities [8], so the same threshold can mean different things for different models. For a fire alarm, the most important quantity is the fraction of fire and smoke images that are missed, and a fixed threshold gives no control over it.

papers.title: A Cheeger-M\"uller Theorem For Flat Superconnections
papers.abstract: For a flat superconnection ${\mathbb{A}}$ on a ${\mathbb{Z}}_2$-graded vector bundle $E$ over a closed oriented odd-dimensional manifold $M$, we prove a Cheeger-M\"uller type theorem as proposed by Arias Abad and Sch\"atz. Namely, that the topological Reidemeister norm of ${\mathbb{A}}$ as defined by them equals the Ray-Singer metric defined by Mathai and Wu. The main step proves an analytic reduction result identified by Arias Abad and Sch\"atz and formulated as a conjecture by the author, that the Ray-Singer metric coincides with that of the fibrewise cohomology $H(E,\partial)$ with its Gauss-Manin connection, where $\partial$ is the component of ${\mathbb{A}}$ of form degree zero, under the Knudsen-Mumford isomorphism associated to the form-degree spectral sequence. As an application, we consider Goette's Morse flat superconnection of a fibrewise Morse function on a fibre bundle with even-dimensional fibres over an oriented odd-dimensional base.

papers.title: BMO Vorticity Strong Ill-Posedness for the 2d Incompressible Euler Equation
papers.abstract: For the two dimensional incompressible Euler equation, Yudovich, and independently Serfati, extended the classical existence and uniqueness class to include vorticity with mild singularity. This class is sometimes called the generalized Yudovich class. Then, Vishik extended the uniqueness class to include vorticity in BMO, allowing for stronger singularities than the generalized Yudovich class. In this work, we prove strong ill-posedness of vorticity in BMO.
papers.intro: The two dimensional incompressible Euler equation in vorticity form is: ∂tω+u⋅∇ω=0,u=∇⟂Δ−1​ω,\begin{split}\partial_{t}\omega&+u\cdot\nabla\omega=0,\\ u&=\nabla^{\perp}\Delta^{-1}\omega,\end{split} (1.1) where uu is the velocity field, and ω\omega is the vorticity. The classical work of Yudovich [49] proved global existence and uniqueness of integral and bounded vorticity ω0∈L∞∩L1\omega_{0}\in L^{\infty}\cap L^{1}. Yudovich [50], and independently Serfati [43], extended the global existence and uniqueness class to include mildly unbounded vorticity which is sometimes called the generalized Yudovich class. This generalized Yudovich class includes vorticities with a log⁡(|log⁡(⋅)|)\log(|\log(\cdot)|) type singularity. Then, Vishik [47] extended the uniqueness class of the 2d Euler equation to include vorticities in the Bounded Mean Oscillation (B​M​OBMO) space, thus enlarging the uniqueness class for 2d Euler since functions in B​M​OBMO can have a |log⁡(⋅)||\log(\cdot)| type singularity. The point to emphasize here is Vishik’s result [47] gave only uniqueness in B​M​OBMO, so the goal of this work is to prove strong ill-posedness of vorticity in B​M​OBMO. papers.title: $\mathrm{RO}(G)$-graded norms for de Rham-Witt forms
papers.abstract: We make two case studies of $\mathrm{RO}(G)$-graded homotopy in connection with $p$-adic cohomology. First, we identify the $\mathrm{RO}(\mathbf T)$-graded $\mathrm{TC}^-$ and $\mathrm{TP}$ of quasiregular semiperfectoid rings as multi-Rees algebras for the Nygaard and $\phi^\bullet(I)$-adic filtrations. We additionally compute $E^{h\mathbf T}_\bigstar$ and $E^{t\mathbf T}_\bigstar$ when $E$ is a general even $\mathbf E_\infty$-ring with $\mathbf T$-action, and compute $(\mathrm{TR}^n)^{h\mathbf T/C_{p^n}}_\bigstar$ in terms of iterated Nygaard filtrations. Next, we compute the $\mathrm{RO}(\mathbf Z_p)^\land$-graded $\mathrm{TR}$ of smooth algebras over a perfectoid base, providing a pushout of the works of Hesselholt and Angeltveit-Gerhardt along the base case $\mathbf F_p$. Using this, we extend Angeltveit's Norm map of Witt vectors to the de Rham-Witt complex, which participates in a "Witt coordinates" decomposition of the $p$-primary Adams operations.

papers.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Industrial-Level Chip Floorplanning: A Framework and Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Floorplanning is an early step in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip: it positions large circuit modules and constrains the space available for subsequent logic placement and wiring. These decisions affect congestion and timing, but their physical consequences emerge through downstream implementation. For AI agents, the task requires translating engineering constraints into spatial decisions whose quality cannot be judged by successful tool execution alone. We present an evaluation framework that connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality, and reports resource use. On one industrial design whose 99 macros occupy approximately 71\% of a fixed L-shaped layout region, we compare our specialized system Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and agents restricted to file access, obtaining complete physical measurements for 39 layout outputs. Under our 0--100 composite quality score, Nova-SI achieves a mean of 57.97 without online feedback from the prescribed power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The difference is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks. Layout-level analysis further shows that similar global utilization can conceal substantially different local congestion. Together, the protocol and case study assess agents through the physical consequences of their delivered layouts and provide evidence about system performance on this industrial instance.
papers.intro:
Tool-using AI agents are being evaluated on increasingly substantial engineering tasks, including machine-learning experiments and command-line workflows (Chan et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026). Chip design presents a further question: can an agent turn its actions into a physically useful engineering artifact? A successful script or plausible explanation is not sufficient. The delivered design must preserve the intended circuit and constraints, and its quality may become apparent only after downstream tools have implemented decisions made earlier.

The delivered design must preserve the intended circuit and constraints, and its quality may become apparent only after downstream tools have implemented decisions made earlier.

We study floorplanning, an early stage in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip. The circuit specifies components and their connections; floorplanning assigns positions and orientations to large, fixed-shape modules called hard macros. Electronic design automation (EDA) tools then place the smaller logic elements, called standard cells (std), and construct their connections. Macro choices determine the space and passages available to those later stages. Even when every macro fits, concentrated connection demand can exceed local routing capacity, causing congestion, while long or slow paths can miss timing requirements. Early placement decisions thus constrain later implementation. Geometric packing and wirelength proxies alone do not capture this quality (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b).

Our industrial instance makes these requirements concrete: over 230,000 instances must be implemented within a prescribed L-shaped region, with hard macros of varying sizes alone occupying approximately seven-tenths of its area. The missing corner excludes apparently available space within the bounding rectangle; the remaining area must accommodate logic and connections. Layout decisions therefore jointly organize large modules, smaller modules, and local passages rather than merely minimize a bounding box. Evaluating this instance asks not only whether an agent can produce legal coordinates, but also what physical conditions those coordinates leave for downstream implementation.

In particular, it distinguishes changes made by normal downstream std optimization from changes to the submitted macro layout; it also keeps invalid geometry separate from poor quality and missing measurements. papers.title: Translating KV Caches Between Hybrid-Attention Language Models: MLA Latents, Linear-Attention States and Sparse-Attention Indexers
papers.abstract: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.
papers.intro:
When a conversation moves from one language model to another, for example from a small model to a larger one or between two generations of a model family, the second model normally re-reads (prefills) the whole history. KV-cache translation avoids this. A small learned map converts the source model’s key–value cache into the target model’s cache format, and the target continues from the translated cache as if it had read the prompt itself. KV-Lingo (Castin et al., 2026) showed that, for two grouped-query attention (GQA) models with the same tokenizer, per-layer linear maps fitted in closed form and refined by self-distillation give the target its native quality at a fraction of the prefill cost, and that translating each conversation segment once keeps multi-turn quality at the re-prefill level.

Model switches are routine: routers send each turn to a cheaper or a stronger model (Ong et al., 2024), agent pipelines hand one conversation between models, and serving fleets move users to a new model generation. Today the receiving model either re-reads the full history, whose cost grows with the prompt length and the model’s size, or it receives a text summary of it, which is shorter to read but drops content the summary did not keep and still has to be prefilled. Latent agent-to-agent communication (Fu et al., 2026; Rossi et al., 2026) passes richer information but keeps both models in the loop and does not replace the target’s prefill. A translated cache gives the target the complete history in its own format, at a cost that grows with the prompt length but not with the target’s size, and with no text in between: in the two directions we timed at 64K tokens the target starts answering 18.7 and 46.8 times sooner than after a re-read, with task quality within the paired confidence interval of its native level.
