Table 1 lists the cache objects of recent releases of the seven open-weights families with the most-downloaded models on Hugging Face. Within one year every family except Meta’s has moved its newest model away from a plain per-token K/V cache, and the newest models of DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Qwen combine two or three different objects in one stack. Multi-head latent attention (MLA) (DeepSeek-AI, 2024) caches one 512-d latent plus a 64-d rotary key per token and layer instead of per-head keys and values. Sparse-attention indexers such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) add a small indexer key per token, and each query attends only to the top-kk tokens the indexer selects. Linear-attention or state-space layers such as Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team, 2025), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025) and Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) keep no per-token cache at all, only a fixed-size recurrent state. Each of these objects breaks an assumption of the GQA recipe: a token-wise map cannot produce a recurrent state, an MLA latent is normalised and partly rotated before it is cached, and an indexer key decides which tokens attention reads at all. Which translation mechanism works for each object, and where in the layer it should read and write (its capture point, §2, Figures 2–6), is open.

Sparse-attention indexers such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) add a small indexer key per token, and each query attends only to the top-kk tokens the indexer selects. Linear-attention or state-space layers such as Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team, 2025), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025) and Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) keep no per-token cache at all, only a fixed-size recurrent state. Each of these objects breaks an assumption of the GQA recipe: a token-wise map cannot produce a recurrent state, an MLA latent is normalised and partly rotated before it is cached, and an indexer key decides which tokens attention reads at all. Which translation mechanism works for each object, and where in the layer it should read and write (its capture point, §2, Figures 2–6), is open.

We report quality, switch speed and multi-turn behaviour in both directions for Pairs A and B, an explicit account of where each object is captured and injected, and the indexer rehearsal on Pair C. papers.title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
papers.abstract: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

papers.title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $\rho$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $\rho$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $\rho$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
papers.intro:
Mechanistic interpretability is grounded in the meaning behind transformer head activations. Some approaches are activation patching (Conmy et al., 2023), probing classifiers, or behavioral diagnostics on crafted inputs (Olsson et al., 2022). Recent work connecting RoPE to heads relies heavily on data (Barbero et al., 2024). In this paper we ask: how much can we learn from the weights alone? Analogously to physics, where theories often have fewer observables than parameters, the attention mechanism admits basis-invariant quantities. These, in turn, characterize heads independently of the choice of basis.

papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
papers.intro:
Serving large language models (LLMs) in production is paid for in GPU memory and GPU hours. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models change the balance between the two. A model with 30B parameters, of which about 3B are active for each token, computes like a small dense model but must hold all of its experts in memory: 61.1 GB for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and 65.8 GB for Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B in BF16. The weights compete with the key–value cache for memory (Kwon et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026), and decoding is bound by memory bandwidth (Yu et al., 2025). For high-volume workloads, the memory a model needs therefore decides how many GPUs it takes.

Expert compression attacks this cost directly. It removes whole routed experts from every MoE layer and leaves a smaller checkpoint of the same architecture, which serving stacks such as vLLM load unchanged; the one-shot methods need only a calibration pass. Two families compete, pruning and merging, and we compare the current state-of-the-art method of each. REAP (Lasby et al., 2026) is the state of the art in expert pruning: it outperforms earlier pruning and merging methods, argues that merging introduces an irreducible error in fine-grained MoEs, and shows pruning ahead on generative benchmarks. REAM (Jha et al., 2026) is the state of the art in expert merging: it builds on REAP’s own saliency and, with the best of ten calibration mixtures, reports slightly higher generative scores than REAP at 25% compression of the same Qwen3 model that we study.

papers.title: Inequality-Aware Regulation
papers.abstract: I study regulation of a screening monopolist when the regulator cares about the distribution of surplus across heterogeneous consumers and the firm. Consumers privately know their willingness to pay for quality, and the firm privately knows its production costs. Regulatory contracts specify quality-price options that the firm must offer. I show that when the regulator gives greater weight to consumers with lower willingness to pay, baseline regulation is optimal: the regulator requires affordable basic options but leaves the firm free to design and price premium options. Under strong consumer-side redistributive concerns, a single required basic option suffices. The regulator uses the firm's incentive to extract surplus from premium buyers to support low regulated prices for basic options.

papers.intro:
Market power and distributional concerns are central motivations for regulatory intervention in private markets. These two rationales for intervention often interact: a firm exercising market power designs its offering strategically, affecting the distribution of surplus both among consumers and across market sides. For example, concentration in the private health care industry—a major policy concern in many countries—has implications for the quality of care available to the poor and the mark-ups paid by the rich.

These two rationales for intervention often interact: a firm exercising market power designs its offering strategically, affecting the distribution of surplus both among consumers and across market sides. For example, concentration in the private health care industry—a major policy concern in many countries—has implications for the quality of care available to the poor and the mark-ups paid by the rich.

The theory of regulation has developed a rich understanding of how to control market power when firms know their operating environment better than the regulator. However, the standard approach evaluates consumer welfare through aggregate surplus, largely abstracting from how that surplus is distributed among consumers. I develop a theory of optimal regulation that places consumer heterogeneity and redistributive concerns at the center of the analysis. This brings together two interacting design problems: the regulator screens a privately informed firm with a regulatory mechanism that shapes how the firm screens consumers and distributes surplus among them.

The theory of regulation has developed a rich understanding of how to control market power when firms know their operating environment better than the regulator. However, the standard approach evaluates consumer welfare through aggregate surplus, largely abstracting from how that surplus is distributed among consumers. I develop a theory of optimal regulation that places consumer heterogeneity and redistributive concerns at the center of the analysis. This brings together two interacting design problems: the regulator screens a privately informed firm with a regulatory mechanism that shapes how the firm screens consumers and distributes surplus among them.

I consider the following model. As in a standard model of second-degree price discrimination, a profit-maximizing firm offers a menu of qualities and prices, and consumers choose from the menu according to their privately known willingness to pay (WTP) for quality. A regulatory contract specifies which quality–price options the firm must make available to consumers; the firm may also offer additional options not required by regulation. As in a standard model of regulation, the firm’s production costs are privately known, and the regulator may offer a choice of contracts to screen the firm. The regulator maximizes a weighted utilitarian objective, placing greater weight on consumers on average than on the firm and weakly higher weights on consumers with lower WTP. This captures applications in which low WTP tends to reflect limited economic resources.

This captures applications in which low WTP tends to reflect limited economic resources.

My main result shows that optimal regulatory contracts take the form of baseline regulation. The regulator requires the firm to offer affordable basic-quality options consumed by low-WTP consumers, while leaving the firm free to design and price its premium options. When consumer-side redistributive concerns are strong, it suffices to require a single basic option, chosen by a range of low-WTP consumers. The regulator may screen the firm through the choice of such contracts.

Baseline regulation uses the firm’s pricing incentives to support redistribution. The surplus the firm extracts from premium buyers enables the regulator to require affordable basic options for consumers whose utility it values more. These options provide utility guarantees that also shape the firm’s additional offers. Even consumers choosing premium options benefit relative to laissez-faire: their ability to choose a basic option limits what the firm can charge them.

Baseline regulation uses the firm’s pricing incentives to support redistribution. The surplus the firm extracts from premium buyers enables the regulator to require affordable basic options for consumers whose utility it values more. These options provide utility guarantees that also shape the firm’s additional offers. Even consumers choosing premium options benefit relative to laissez-faire: their ability to choose a basic option limits what the firm can charge them.

Basic qualities lie between the unregulated monopoly and surplus-maximizing levels. Two redistributive considerations favor limiting basic quality. First, lower basic quality makes these options less attractive to high-WTP consumers, who value quality more. This permits higher premium prices that support lower regulated prices for basic options. Second, since production costs are privately known, requiring higher basic quality entails either leaving more information rents to low-cost firms—shifting surplus from consumers to the firm—or accepting a greater probability of shutdown.

Strong consumer-side redistributive concerns can make optimal regulation especially simple: a single basic option suffices. Such concerns make it optimal to pool a range of low-WTP consumers on a common basic option, as separating them would create rents that the regulator values relatively little. For higher-WTP consumers, strong redistributive concern makes the regulator focus on the revenue they generate to support this basic option, so that it can rely on the firm’s pricing incentives to supply the premium menu.

Policies resembling baseline regulation are used in a range of markets. In broadband, for example, New York’s Affordable Broadband Act requires providers to offer an affordable basic-speed product but allow pricing flexibility for higher-speed services. Providers can choose between a lower-speed basic service under a lower price cap and a faster basic service under a higher cap. This paper shows how such a choice among basic quality–price requirements can optimally screen firms with private information.

papers.title: MNN-Pocket-0.3B Technical Report
papers.abstract: This technical report presents MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a compact 300M-parameter dense language model designed for efficient on-device deployment and supporting context lengths of up to 32K tokens. With an INT4 deployment footprint of only 173 MB and decoding throughput of up to 466 tokens/s on iPad Pro M5 (Metal), it can be seamlessly integrated into applications on edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is developed through the co-design of its architecture, data, training pipeline, and inference system. Hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning balance model capability with on-device memory and compute constraints. A four-stage pre-training pipeline covering approximately 4.1 trillion high-quality Chinese and English tokens equips the model with broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. This is followed by a three-stage post-training pipeline comprising instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and quantization-aware training. Finally, hardware-specific optimizations in the MNN inference engine enable fast, memory-efficient inference and long-context processing. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MNN-Pocket-0.3B achieves frontier-level performance among models of comparable size, with particularly strong results in Chinese and English knowledge and reasoning, mathematics, coding, and instruction following. It consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models and even surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks. We release MNN-Pocket-0.3B with open weights and ready-to-use MNN deployment packages. We hope it will provide a practical foundation for capable, responsive, and memory-efficient edge applications while advancing research and development in on-device language models.
papers.intro:
On-device intelligence has already created substantial value in applications such as search and recommendation, short-form video, live streaming, and extended reality. In the era of large language models, a unified on-device model has the potential to consolidate multiple task-specific models while delivering low-latency responses, reducing cloud inference costs, protecting user privacy, supporting offline operation, and simplifying model maintenance and iteration.

Recent work has explored compact LLMs ranging from sub-billion to a few billion parameters. SmolLM [20], LFM [31, 1], and MiniCPM [35] focus specifically on small language models, while major open model families—including Gemma [14], Qwen [38], Hunyuan [21], and ERNIE [3]—offer variants as small as 0.3–0.6B parameters. Despite this progress, deployment in large-scale consumer applications remains challenging. Such applications must support diverse mobile hardware under stringent resource budgets, often requiring 200–300 MB of resident memory and less than 300 MB of peak memory, while targeting generation speeds approaching 200 tokens/s. Existing models rarely balance memory footprint, inference speed, and task performance simultaneously. Addressing this gap requires an edge-first approach in which the model and inference system are jointly optimized across architecture, data, training, quantization, and runtime execution.

MNN-Pocket-0.3B is built around four key innovations: • Edge-first architecture–tokenizer co-design. Guided by on-device measurements with MNN [23, 43], we select a 300M-parameter dense decoder-only architecture and refine its depth–width allocation to balance model quality, memory footprint, and decoding throughput. We complement this design with a compact 64K bilingual tokenizer derived through dependency-aware vocabulary pruning, balancing sequence compression against embedding memory and output-projection cost. • Data-centric, stage-aware pre-training. We curate and synthesize Chinese, English, math and code data, grouping samples by domain, quality, knowledge density, difficulty, and style. Proxy runs and model-update interpolation screen candidate recipes, which are refined through direct training on data mixtures. The four-stage pipeline coordinates data mixtures and learning-rate schedules across approximately 4.1 trillion tokens to build knowledge and reasoning capabilities within a compact model. • Capability-centric, deployment-aware post-training. A three-stage pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning with the SFT Loop Engine, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), and quantization-aware training (QAT). MOPD routes student-generated trajectories to domain-specialized teachers, consolidating knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and coding capabilities into a single compact model. Finally, Self-OPD with QAT aligns the quantization-aware student with its frozen BF16 counterpart to mitigate quantization-induced degradation for W4A16 deployment. • Model–runtime optimization for efficient edge deployment. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is deployed with MNN through standardized model assets and a unified inference interface with hardware-specific backends. Phase-aware low-bit kernels, fused Transformer operators, and backend-specific attention and KV-cache implementations enable efficient INT4 inference, achieving 8,721 tokens/s in prefill and 466 tokens/s in autoregressive decoding on an iPad Pro M5 with Metal. Optional speculative decoding further accelerates generation, with gains depending on the device, backend, and workload.

papers.title: VNA-Only Calibration of Waveguide Thermistor Mounts with Self-Consistent Determination of the Thermistor-Port Impedance
papers.abstract: A method is presented for determining the calibration factor and the effective efficiency of waveguide thermistor mounts from vector-network-analyzer reflection data alone, without a microcalorimeter, extending the three reflection-coefficient method of the coaxial case. In waveguide the thermistor is coupled to the line through a matching structure and the reference impedance of the thermistor port, $Z_0$, is not known a priori; it is inferred through a power-consistency relation between pairs of states, under the convention that it is real. The method reproduces the factory certificates (U = 2 %) of four K486A mounts within 1.0 % rms and the PTB-traceable values (U = 0.85 to 0.98 %) of a fifth within 0.34 % rms; its expanded measurement uncertainty is 0.5 to 1.16 % (k = 2) for the best specimen and below 2 % for the five. A mount with its waveguide-to-coaxial adapter is calibrated directly, without characterizing the adapter, from the model factor of the mount and the geometric factor measured through the adapter. The scattering matrix implied by the solution is not passive; a minimum-norm correction of the thermistor impedances along the two directions invisible to the calibration factor - the ratios of the efficiencies of the three states - brings it to the floor of passivity, where the efficiency depends on the load only through its mismatch factor, leaves the result unchanged, and gives the sensitivity of the efficiency to the bias resistance in closed form: below $4\times10^{-5}$ $\Omega^{-1}$ in band mean, proportional to the mismatch of the operating state and to the loss of the mount.
papers.intro:
Waveguide bolometric sensors are a working standard in metrology laboratories worldwide and serve as highly stable transfer references. The microcalorimetric method is the primary route for their calibration and provides a direct link to the physical quantities involved; however, such services are increasingly scarce and costly, and are available only at a limited number of frequencies. Moreover, since these mounts are no longer manufactured, each unit becomes more valuable within a laboratory, and the possibility of an in situ calibration – at lower cost and with uncertainties adequate for use as a transfer standard – is attractive. National laboratories quote effective-efficiency uncertainties of the order of 1%1\% or somewhat below (k=2k=2) for these sensors when calibrated in WR-42 waveguide; the NIST service reports an absolute expanded uncertainty of 1.1×10−21.1\times 10^{-2} over 18–26.5 GHz [2], and comparable figures are declared by other national metrology institutes [3].

papers.title: Fiscal Commitment and the Additionality of Philanthropy: Heterogeneous Donor Purposes in a Shared Public Budget
papers.abstract: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio. Policy frameworks frequently seek to ensure that private finance supplements rather than displaces public funding. We distinguish baseline additionality, which preserves pre-gift public funding, from portfolio preservation, which preserves a service's provision after all gifts are pooled under discretionary budgeting. A larger gift to one service raises the discretionary provision of every service and reduces the protection slack available to the others. This cross-donor fiscal externality yields an exact feasibility result: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation. Conversely, a reform that expands at least one donor-backed service while preserving all others exists exactly when every maximum floor reaches the reference. The paper characterizes the complete preservation set and its welfare-maximizing element. Under logarithmic preferences, donation shares determine protectability, while heterogeneous donor valuations determine welfare incidence. Baseline additionality may therefore hold while a service loses fiscal benefits generated by other gifts.
papers.intro:
Public authorities increasingly interact with philanthropists who direct resources toward particular public services. Donors often value these services differently from the budget authority and from one another, so private finance introduces heterogeneous purposes into a common fiscal system. Policy practice frequently seeks to preserve the additional character of such finance. The United Kingdom’s 2026 place-based philanthropy strategy, for example, states that philanthropy should complement public money rather than substitute for state funding (Department for Culture, Media and Sport, 2026). Similar principles appear in maintenance-of-effort and supplement-not-supplant requirements for public grants; current U.S. law, for example, requires specified federal education funds to supplement rather than supplant non-federal resources (U.S. General Accounting Office, 1980; U.S. Code, 2026). These rules share a basic objective: external finance should expand supported activity instead of releasing an equal amount of public funding. The terminology in this paper is model-specific. Policy documents also use “additionality” for other principles governing the relationship between government and philanthropy, including donor independence (Department for Culture, Media and Sport, 2026).

We distinguish these two references throughout the paper. Baseline additionality means that the public appropriation in a donor-backed service is preserved when its own gift arrives. Portfolio preservation is stronger: the service retains the provision it would receive after all gifts are pooled and the authority allocates the enlarged budget freely. A full protection rate guarantees baseline additionality in the model. Portfolio preservation may nevertheless fail because the service may lose fiscal benefits created by gifts to other purposes. We use portfolio preservation as a diagnostic policy benchmark rather than as a distributive entitlement. It asks whether an additionality rule is able to preserve a service level already generated by the full portfolio of philanthropic finance; the welfare analysis later treats preservation as an explicit institutional constraint.

The service receiving the larger gift also raises its own maximum contractual floor one-for-one, whereas the contractual ceilings of the other services remain unchanged. Consequently, a larger own gift expands a service’s protection slack, while larger gifts to other purposes reduce it. This cross-donor fiscal externality links heterogeneous philanthropic purposes even before any protection rule binds.

Fiscal fungibility, preference heterogeneity, voluntary provision, and regulatory burden shifting have established foundations. Our object of analysis is the protection slack created by the difference between a service’s contractual ceiling and its pooled post-gift reference. Taxes, pre-gift appropriations, enforceability, and the budget authority’s objective remain predetermined. Public matching above the original appropriation expands the instrument set and leads to a different policy problem.

papers.title: Phrase-Level Speculative Decoding on a Frozen Target
papers.abstract:
Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant. It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary.
  We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width. The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking.

With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.

papers.title: Semisimple Deformations of Contraction Algebras for Smooth Threefold Flops
papers.abstract: Building on Bryan--Katz--Leung, Hua--Toda and Kawamata, we study deformations of contraction algebras and the local geometry of the scheme of associative algebra laws. Let $A$ be the basic contraction algebra of a completed projective flopping contraction of a smooth complex threefold. We construct a finite free polynomial family that is constant and semisimple away from the origin, with the original curve projectors fixed. For each restricted positive root $\beta=(\beta_i)$, with coordinates indexed by the retained vertices, the split generic fibre has $n_\beta$ matrix blocks of size $\sum_i\beta_i$, and the labelled projector $e_i$ has rank $\beta_i$ on each block. Here $n_\beta$ is the corresponding genus-zero Gopakumar--Vafa invariant. If the geometric generic fibre of a finite free associative formal deformation of $A$ is semisimple, it has the same matrix factors, and any lifts of the original projectors have the same ranks on those factors. The scheme of associative algebra laws is smooth at $A$. The closure of the corresponding semisimple orbit is its unique irreducible component through $A$. The proof uses the curve divisors of Katz--Morrison and Nabijou--Wemyss, presentations of the universal contraction quotient and its cocenter, and the orbit method of Jelisiejew--Smoktunowicz. These presentations prove the geometric Hua--Toda flatness assertions. In the geometric families considered here, the relative contraction algebra, its centre and its cocenter are finite free over arbitrary complete Noetherian local complex bases. On a smooth open neighbourhood of $A$ in the scheme of algebra laws, the centres and cocenters form dual vector bundles compatible with arbitrary base change. For the type $D$ algebras $D_{n,2}$ with $n\ge2$, the centre morphism gives counterexamples to the smoothness assertion in Conjecture 1.4(2) of Jelisiejew--Smoktunowicz.

papers.title: Holonomy, Spectral Topology, and Detailed Balance in Classical and Open Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: Band topology and non-Hermitian spectral theory are now applied to mechanical metamaterials, chiral active fluids, stochastic networks, and open quantum systems. We give a tutorial synthesis organized by holonomy and by one question: what can the spectral data of a linear generator reveal about detailed balance? Three holonomies recur: the Berry phase of a band, the Burgers vector of a dislocation (the integrated torsion of the defect geometry), and the cycle affinity of a Markov network (the holonomy of the connection $\ln(W_{ij}/W_{ji})$). We rederive the Chern numbers $C_m=m(\mathrm{sgn}\,\Omega+\mathrm{sgn}\,\nu_o)$ of a compressible odd-viscous fluid and restate the dislocation zero-mode count of Paulose, Chen, and Vitelli as a pairing of integrated torsion with topological polarization. Our central message is that spectral topology can obstruct detailed balance but does not determine the magnitude of dissipation. Detailed balance is self-adjointness in the inner product fixed by the stationary state, so a non-real eigenvalue, an exceptional point (EP), or a nonzero point-gap winding number of a Markov generator rules it out and forces entropy production $\sigma>0$, with $\sigma\ge k_B j^2/D$ for any current, whereas a real, diagonalizable spectrum does not in general certify it. In the Hatano-Nelson ring, which is normal yet has complex spectrum, $\sigma$ sweeps $(0,\infty)$ at fixed winding number. EPs need a separate assessment of the dynamics: with generalized detailed balance including time-reversal parity, an EP is compatible with equilibrium only through time-reversal-odd dynamics, as at critical damping of a Langevin oscillator, whereas an EP of a system with only even variables, such as an odd elastic medium, certifies a nonequilibrium steady state; in both cases $\sigma$ is analytic across the EP. We propose benchtop tests for each statement.
papers.intro:
The recognition that band structures can carry integer invariants [1, 2, 3, 4] has, over the past fifteen years, been exported far beyond electrons. Topological phonons were identified in microtubules [5] and isostatic lattices [6], then built in gyroscopic and pendulum metamaterials [7, 8, 9, 10]. Chiral active fluids, in which odd viscosity [11, 12, 13] breaks time-reversal symmetry without dissipation, support topologically protected sound [14, 15, 16, 17]. Stochastic networks driven out of equilibrium carry chiral edge currents in configuration space [18, 19, 20]. In parallel, the spectral theory of non-Hermitian operators, with its exceptional points (EPs) [21, 22, 23], its point-gap invariants, and its skin effect [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29], has become a field in its own right [30, 31, 32].

In parallel, the spectral theory of non-Hermitian operators, with its exceptional points (EPs) [21, 22, 23], its point-gap invariants, and its skin effect [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29], has become a field in its own right [30, 31, 32].

These literatures share words (topological, chiral, non-Hermitian, torsion) whose meanings overlap only partially. That overlap invites two opposite errors: treating a shared formalism as evidence of shared physics, and missing a genuinely common structure because each community phrases it differently. This article is a perspective and tutorial aimed at both. Its organizing device is holonomy, and its central message concerns detailed balance.

Holonomy. In each system an observable is the result of transporting something around a closed loop: a Bloch state around a cycle of the Brillouin zone (the Berry phase) [2, 3], a lattice frame around a dislocation core (the Burgers vector) [33, 34, 35], or a probability flux around a cycle of a Markov network (the cycle affinity) [36]. In each case the holonomy is gauge invariant, can be written as the flux of a curvature or torsion through a surface bounded by the loop, and is tied by an index theorem or a conservation law to something observable at a boundary, a defect, or in a current.

In each case the holonomy is gauge invariant, can be written as the flux of a curvature or torsion through a surface bounded by the loop, and is tied by an index theorem or a conservation law to something observable at a boundary, a defect, or in a current.

Detailed balance as self-adjointness in a physical inner product. Each system has a linear generator ℒ\mathcal{L} of its dynamics: a dynamical matrix, a linearized hydrodynamic operator, a rate matrix, a Langevin drift matrix, or a Lindbladian. The physics singles out an inner product, set by the energy for conservative dynamics and by the stationary state for stochastic dynamics. For stochastic dynamics whose variables are all even under time reversal, detailed balance is precisely self-adjointness of ℒ\mathcal{L} in the stationary inner product. Spectral data (non-real eigenvalues, EPs, spectral winding) can show that ℒ\mathcal{L} is self-adjoint in no inner product at all, and therefore obstruct detailed balance. In general they cannot certify it, because self-adjointness in some inner product, which is all a real, diagonalizable spectrum provides in general, is weaker than self-adjointness in the stationary one; special spectra are an exception (Sec. IV). Nor is normality, the commutation of ℒ\mathcal{L} with its adjoint, the relevant property: a normal generator can be far from equilibrium. When some variables are odd under time reversal, as momenta are, equilibrium permits an anti-self-adjoint part of ℒ\mathcal{L}, and EPs become compatible with detailed balance.

papers.title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
papers.abstract:
Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer.
  I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured.
  This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.
papers.intro:
A team of LLM agents has an organization whether or not anyone chose it. A chain of specialists, a hub that collects proposals, a round of debate among peers and a fully connected chat each decide who sees what and when. The choice is usually buried in the architecture of the orchestration framework [24, 17, 35, 43], or delegated to an optimizer that searches over communication graphs against a benchmark signal [47, 46, 18]. Both approaches answer the organizational question before the work starts and give the user little to inspect or adjust once it has.

Human-team research has a long, unfinished argument about the same question. One tradition treats the team as the context in which individual attributes add up: the input–process–output (IPO) framework [28, 14] and the compositional reading of team-level constructs [22]. A second tradition moves to the system level while keeping psychological constructs—emergent states such as shared mental models, trust and psychological safety that develop over repeated episodes [26, 20, 9]. A third treats team cognition as something a team does in interaction rather than something it has [6, 11], and reads variability in coordination as a source of adaptability rather than noise. Gorman and colleagues [11] summarize the divide as non-system versus system explanations: whether a team phenomenon is located in the members or in the interaction process.

The present paper takes these distinctions seriously as design questions for LLM-agent teams, while refusing the shortcut of assuming that human findings carry over. If the organization of an agent team changes what it produces, a user should be able to choose the organization explicitly, observe the work through more than one explanatory lens, and intervene in ways whose scope is recorded. teamknitt is a concrete attempt to make that possible. It is a follow-up to Labtune [32], which treated laboratory organization and information sharing as controlled variables for LLM-agent research, and to the author’s thesis work on the dynamics of distributed software teams’ creative processes [31]. Where Labtune offered six editable laboratory designs for research missions, teamknitt generalizes the mission to tasks, brainstorming and goals, replaces lab designs with fourteen routing topologies over 1–16 members, binds the team’s problem-solving structure explicitly, and adds research-informed views and human-led intervention. It ships its own runtime and makes no automated organizational improvement.

The paper has five commitments: • Configuration before execution. Purpose, members, routing, sharing, bindings, models, tools and finite budgets are explicit and user-selected. Topology filters exposure; it grants no decision authority and creates no capacity (Section 4). • Two explanatory lenses on one record. Non-system and system views project the same configuration and trace. Switching views never changes the team (Section 5). • Three distinctions kept apart. Explanatory locus (non-system/system), form of emergence (compositional/compilational) and process/state/outcome are related but separate axes, and the implementation does not collapse them (Section 2). • Explicit, bounded intervention. Reviewed reconfiguration, planned disturbances and boundary-applied feedback, pause, resume and stop, with queued, applied, assembled, understood and improved recorded as distinct claims (Section 6). • Declared non-measurement. Trust, cohesion, psychological safety, efficacy, potency, shared understanding, emergence, synchrony and attractors are not inferred from software traces. What is recorded is operational; what is not measured is named.

papers.title: Perception-Limited UAV Positioning: On the Reliability of Line-of-Sight Constraints in Sensing-Driven Aerial Networks
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles carrying access points or base stations are widely positioned so as to hold line-of-sight links with every ground user at once. The algorithms that do so are evaluated against obstacle information treated as exact, whether that information comes from a surveyed map or, more recently, from onboard vision. This paper analyses what becomes of that requirement when the obstacle information is estimated rather than given, and derives the detection accuracy it implicitly demands. Three results follow. The probability of satisfying the requirement decays geometrically with the number of users, so that a detector accurate enough for one user is not accurate enough for a network. Spatially correlated detection error raises that probability but concentrates failures into systematic blind spots. Relaxing the requirement from all users to ninety per cent of them widens the tolerable detection error by more than an order of magnitude, far beyond what any plausible improvement of the detector could deliver. papers.title: Functorial Homological Mirror Symmetry for Acyclic Cluster Varieties
papers.abstract: We introduce the formalism of cluster models, a class of log Calabi-Yau varieties obtained from smooth quasi-affine toric varieties by iterated affine blowups along non-toric codimension 2 centers determined by a really full rank quiver. Cluster models include the truncated cluster varieties of Gross, Hacking, and Keel with respect to really full rank quivers, all really full rank acyclic cluster varieties, and all open toric subvarieties of $\mathbb{C}^n\times(\mathbb{C}^*)^m$. We then construct mirrors to cluster models via iterated Weinstein handle attachments to toric mirrors, so that the corresponding skeleta acquire compact pieces, and we prove homological mirror symmetry for all cluster models, compatibly with freezing, deleting, and contracting vertices of the quiver. This extends toric mirror symmetry and its naturalities beyond the cotangent bundle. In particular, we obtain homological mirror symmetry for all really full rank acyclic cluster varieties. We develop this package with a view towards conjectures of Marsh, Rietsch, and Williams about mirror symmetry for Grassmannians and closed positroid varieties. Motivated by these, we also conjecture that open positroid varieties are self-mirror. Assuming a natural ansatz, we prove this for a class of positroid varieties that includes nontrivial cells in every Grassmannian and all cells in finite-type Grassmannians. Towards this end we introduce a new combinatorial input, the notion of weak $k$-booleanness for permutations and braids.

papers.title: Delaunay Asymptotics for the Singular Escobar-Yamabe Equation
papers.abstract: In dimensions $n\geq3$, we prove that near an isolated boundary singularity a positive solution of the Escobar--Yamabe equation for a smooth metric approaches a fixed periodic Delaunay solution or the cylindrical solution if its trace lies between positive multiples of $|\overline x|^{-(n-2)/2}$, where $\overline x$ is the tangential Fermi coordinate. The relative error decays at a positive power rate, with weighted estimates through two derivatives in Fermi coordinates. The necksize is unique, and the translation parameter is unique modulo the least positive period in the periodic case. The Hamiltonian smoothly parametrizes the periodic family modulo translation. We classify Jacobi fields of polynomial growth at both ends without assuming symmetry. Translation and energy differentiation generate these fields along periodic solutions, and two oscillatory fields generate them along the cylindrical solution. We also exhibit a first-order obstruction to improving these asymptotics by boundary-preserving conformal deformations of the flat models.

papers.title: A complete symmetric rank-two modularity classification, obtained through a sharp uniform degree bound
papers.abstract:
We classify modular Nahm sums with a rational symmetric positive-definite two-by-two matrix and rational shifts. Up to coordinate exchange, every modular datum belongs to three explicit rational-point families, is a product of two modular rank-one sums, or is one of thirty-four exceptional triples on twelve matrices. The list consists of Zagier's rank-two examples, the Vlasenko--Zwegers additions and split products; no further data occur. The proof first bounds the joint degree of the distinguished Nahm point by four, using an initial degree bound of twenty-four and exact local exclusions at the prime 7. Explicit height and exponent bounds then give exhaustive arithmetic classifications in degrees one through four. Exact polynomial elimination determines all rational shifts, and published identities of q-series establish modularity of the survivors. The degree bound is sharp. The finite steps are accompanied by exact certificates, verification programs and independently implemented checks.
